Duncan (2011, 2013, 2018) Susceptible animal groups: All ectothermic vertebrates including amphibians, reptiles, and fish. Ranavirus infections have been documented in at least 262 species from 67 families including 177 amphibian species in 25 families, 51 fish species in 25 families and 37 reptile species in 17 families. Some ranaviruses can infect hosts from all three classes (e.g. frog virus 3, common midwife toad virus), while others may be more host specific (e.g. ambystoma tigrinum virus). Overall, susceptibility to clinical disease and death varies by virus as well as taxonomically and by age class. In amphibians, larvae and metamorphs are more likely to experience morbidity and mortality than adults. Some species may have covert infections and be able to shed and transmit virus to other susceptible animals without ever exhibiting clinical signs (e.g. American bullfrogs [Lithobates catesbeianus]).

Some species may have covert infections and be able to shed and transmit virus to other susceptible animals without ever exhibiting clinical signs (e.g. American bullfrogs [Lithobates catesbeianus]). Clinical disease and death are reported more frequently in chelonians compared to other reptilian taxa, though infections have also been documented sporadically in squamates and prospective surveillance efforts are lacking. Causative organism: Ranaviruses are members of the Iridoviridae, a group of double stranded DNA viruses that can exist in enveloped and non-enveloped forms. There are currently seven recognized species in the genus Ranavirus: - Ranavirus rana1 (frog virus 3, FV3): most widespread ranavirus globally with reports in North & South America, Europe, Asia, Oceania, and Africa. Infects amphibians, fish, and reptiles - Ranavirus ambystoma1 (ambystoma tigrinum virus, ATV): found in North America. Infects amphibians - Ranavirus alytes1 (common midwife toad virus, CMTV): found in Asia, Europe, North America. Distribution appears to be spreading.

Infects amphibians, fish, and reptiles - Ranavirus perca1 (epizootic hematopoietic necrosis virus, EHNV): found in Europe and Oceania. Notifiable disease in fish according to WOAH and the EU. Infects fish and reptiles - Ranavirus gadus1 (European North Atlantic ranavirus, ENARV): found in Europe and the North Atlantic. Infects fish - Ranavirus epinephelus1 (Singa pore grouper iridovirus, SGIV): found in Asia. Infects fish.

Distribution: Worldwide although some ranavirus species have an apparent geographic predilection that may or may not be be an artifact of surveillance effort. Ranaviruses are considered to be globally emerging infections. - Africa: FV3 - Asia: FV3, CMTV, SCRV, SGIV - Europe: FV3, CMTV, EHNV, ENARV - North America: FV3, ATV, CMTV, SCRV - Oceania: FV3, EHNV - South America: FV3 Incubation period: Variable: Less than 5 days to several weeks. Incubation is affected by ambient temperatures, dose of virus exposure, immunosuppression, developmental stage, and species differences in susceptibility to different ranavirus species and strains.

- ∞ Amphibians: Subtle to severe hemorrhages in the ventral skin, especially at the base of the hind limbs and around the vent opening, cutaneous erythema ("red leg" syndrome), fluid accumulation under the skin or within the coelom, and skin ulceration and/or epithelial proliferation may be seen. Lethargy, inappetence, and ataxia are common. Infection does not always cause clinical disease, particularly in adults and certain tolerant species, such as American Bullfrogs {Lithobates catesbeianus). - ∞ Chelonians: Significant oral cavity lesions (ulceration and oral/pharyngeal plaques), conjunctivitis, blepharoedema, oculonasal discharge, and cervical/limb edema are commonly reported. Depression, lethargy, and anorexia are also common. Cutaneous lesions (ulceration, abscessation, sloughing), hemorrhage, and respiratory distress can also be present. - ∞ Fish: Cutaneous hemorrhages, gill erythema and edema, and coelomic distension are common. - ∞ Long-term nonclinical ranavirus carriers have been identified in multiple species. Under the right conditions, these animals can shed live virus while displaying mild or no clinical signs.

- ∞ Long-term nonclinical ranavirus carriers have been identified in multiple species. Under the right conditions, these animals can shed live virus while displaying mild or no clinical signs. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: In amphibians, necrosis and/or hemorrhage is present in multiple tissues, especially skin, liver, kidney, spleen/ hematopoietic tissue and gastrointestinal tract. In chelonians, necrotizing and fibrinous stomatitis/esophagitis, splenitis and vasculitis are seen. Thrombosis and secondary sepsis are common. Histologically intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies may be seen; however, they are difficult to identify, are not always due to the virus, and may be absent or inconspicuous in many cases. Diagnosis: A number of conventional and quantitative PCRs have been described for the detection of ranaviruses. Contacting the diagnostic laboratory prior to submitting samples is recommended to ensure selection of the most sensitive and specific tests for the particular diagnostic needs of the situation.

Contacting the diagnostic laboratory prior to submitting samples is recommended to ensure selection of the most sensitive and specific tests for the particular diagnostic needs of the situation. Virus isolation, immunohistochemistry, in situ hybridization, transmission electron microscopy, and serology (not widely available or validated for most species) have also been used to identify infected animals, but cost, availability, turn-around time, interpretation challenges, and the frequent need for molecular confirmation typically limit the use of these tests in clinical practice. Histopathology is helpful in deceased animals and/or during mortality events, but lesions can be nonspecific and confirmatory testing is usually required.

- ∞ Antemortem: Studies comparing the relative diagnostic sensitivity of different antemortem ranavirus samples to a gold-standard are lacking. For all samples false negatives are possible due to the timing of sample collection, low viral load, or lack of active shedding in chronic carriers while false positives are possible due to environmental/water contamination. Generally, test sensitivity for antemortem PCR increases with time post-exposure and development of clinical signs of illness. - o Swabs: The least invasive option, but may have limited sensitivity compared to tissue - § Reptiles: oral or combined oral/cloacal (preferred) - § Amphibians: skin or combined skin/oral/cloacal (preferred) - o Whole blood: Viral detection in blood and swab samples can occur asynchronously. Testing of both swabs and blood may increase diagnostic sensitivity for detecting infection - o Tissue: tail and/or toe clips may be more sensitive than swabs, but are also more invasive - ∞ Postmortem: Any tissues with lesions should be collected and frozen for testing, especially liver, kidney, and spleen.

toe clips may be more sensitive than swabs, but are also more invasive - ∞ Postmortem: Any tissues with lesions should be collected and frozen for testing, especially liver, kidney, and spleen. Frozen tissues are required for virus isolation and are generally best for molecular analysis; however, freezing is not acceptable for histology. For histology, tissues should be submitted fresh or fixed in 70% ethanol or 10% neutral buffered formalin. Ethanolpreserved tissues may be used for some molecular testing. Formalin-fixed tissues may also be used for some molecular testing if the length of time in formalin is minimal at days to weeks but it is possible to perform PCR on paraffin embedded tissues (false negative results may occur). Contact individual laboratories for more information regarding available testing approaches and sample requirements.

- ∞ Quarantine new arrivals. The health history of animals being brought into a population needs to be reviewed - if there have been deaths or illness due to confirmed or suspected ranavirus infections in the source population the risk of disease transmission with introduction is considered higher. Perform thorough physical examinations at arrival and egress from quarantine and test for ranaviruses of concern using an appropriate antemortem sample and test. Animals dying during quarantine should be screened using PCR and histopathology, at minimum. Strict biosecurity measures must be followed to avoid transmission of infection to other susceptible animals. This includes the use of PPE, regular disinfection of enclosures and equipment including footwear, and treatment of wastewater to inactivate ranaviruses. - ∞ Outside of quarantine, avoid movement of animals, water, equipment, or other materials between enclosures. Disinfect all enclosures and instruments after and between uses. In the case of outdoor exhibits, consider methods to deter or exclude native herpetofauna, or consider temporary or permanent movement to indoor housing options with good biosecurity.

Survivors of ranavirus infection may become long-term carriers and should be handled and housed accordingly or considered for humane euthanasia to safeguard other members of the collection. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Ranaviruses can remain viable for days to months depending on environmental conditions, making appropriate cleaning and disinfection one of the most useful ways to prevent infection and control spread. First, remove organic debris from surfaces using an appropriate surfactant agent and water. 1% Potassium peroxymonosulfate (Virkon®), 3% sodium hypochlorite and 1% chlorhexidine are all effective at inactivating ranaviruses after 1 min. contact duration. Amphibians are particularly sensitive to disinfectant residues - thorough rinsing is required after use. Biosecurity measures must include treatment of waste and effluent from ranavirus infected animals.

- ∞ Ranavirus infections of amphibians and EHNV infections of fish are notifiable under the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH 2024 - Aquatic Animal Health Code). - ∞ In the USA, amphibian ranavirus infections are classified as monitored (not notifiable) diseases under the USDA National Animal Health Reporting System. Clinicians practicing in the United States should consult specific state guidelines for non-federal notifiable status for this disease agent. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: Currently none. The OIE states that importation of live aquatic animals intended for use in zoos from a country not declared free from ranaviruses should be followed by lifelong holding of the animals in biosecure facilities for continuous isolation from the local environment and treatment of all effluent and waste materials in a manner that inactivates ranaviruses. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Animals should not be introduced to those showing clinical signs of disease, with exposure to known infected animals, or that have survived previous infection.

Some species including the red-backed salamander (Plethodon cinereus), four-toed salamanders (Hemidactylium scutatum), and mountain yellow-legged frogs (Rana muscosa) carry the bacteria Janthinobacterium lividum on their skin that produces the fungal metabolite, violacin, that provides resistance to Bd and likely also Bsal. Causative organism: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) and Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans (Bsal), non-hyphal zoosporic fungi. The infective stage is an individual motile flagellated zoospore. Zoonotic potential: No. Distribution: World-wide wherever amphibian populations are present for Bd, with chytridiomycosis implicated as the cause of massive amphibian population declines. Bsal has currently only been identified in Asia and Europe. Incubation period: 14-70 days. Clinical signs: Erythematous or discolored skin, abnormal posture, neurologic signs, excessive skin shedding, behavior changes are most common with Bd.

Asia and Europe. Incubation period: 14-70 days. Clinical signs: Erythematous or discolored skin, abnormal posture, neurologic signs, excessive skin shedding, behavior changes are most common with Bd. Salamanders with Bd may also have tail autotomization and dark, melanized spots that clear with skin shedding. Ulcerative skin and anorexia are most common with Bsal. Clinical signs may not be apparent prior to acute death. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Gross lesions are often not present but may include increased sloughing of the skin, discolored skin, erosions. Skin ulceration is also common with Bsal. Histologic lesions involve focal hyperkeratosis and epidermal hyperplasia with sloughing of the keratin layer. While hyperkeratosis is common in anurans, it is less common in salamanders with Bd. Fungal zoosporangia are found within the keratin layers. The fungal lesions are not evenly distributed on the skin surface. Predilection is noted for the digits, ventral aspect of the hind limbs, inguinal and pelvic regions, and in tadpoles, mouth parts. Diagnosis: PCR (skin swab best), cytology, histopathology.

PCR is best for detecting subclinical infection, whereas histopathology and cytology are most useful for clinically significant infection. Cytology and histopathology require experience. Material required for laboratory analysis: Shed skin, skin scraping, skin swab or skin sample (preferably from the ventral pelvic patch and bottoms of feet) from adults. In deceased animals, GI contents may contain shed skin. Mouthpart swabs from live tadpoles, mouthparts from deceased tadpoles. Using fine-tipped swabs (not wooden-handled), gently swab skin 20-30 times. Break swab 23 cm from tip and place in screw-top tube, avoiding contact with outside of tube. Allow to air-dry for 5 minutes. Samples can be kept at room temperature or 4 degrees C for 1- 2 weeks or frozen for longer-term storage. Avoid exposure to high temperatures and direct sunlight.

Lewbart (2013, 2018) Susceptible animal groups: Carp and koi (Cyprinus carpio) and common carp hybrids; there is evidence that goldfish (Carassius auratus) and other cyprinids, sturgeon, and other freshwater species can be non-clinical carriers of the virus. All age groups susceptible, particularly young fish <1 year old. Survivors may be persistently infected, sub-clinical carriers with periodic reactivation from latency.

Causative organism: Cyprinid herpesvirus-3 (CyHV-3) is also known as Koi Herpesvirus (KHV), and is the causative agent of lethal koi herpesvirus disease (KHVD). It is within the genus Cyprinivirus of the family Alloherpesviridae, which infect fishes.

Distribution: Global, especially in temperate geographical areas, except for Australia. The disease was first identified in England in 1996. Incubation period: Incubation period varies depending on water temperature; most cases are detected at 22-25.5 o C. Latent infections can likely persist for months or even years. Arthropods such as the fish louse (Argulus sp.) are likely vectors. Clinical signs: Clinical signs include, but are not limited to, lethargy, enophthalmia, tachypnea, depigmented areas and blisters of the body surface, branchitis characterized by pale, swollen, mottled gills, branchial hemorrhage, branchial necrosis, inappetence, erratic swimming, and high mortality. Post-mortem, gross, or histologic findings: At necropsy, affected fish may have generalized - possibly sanguineous - edema, organ hemorrhage, intestinal inflammation, massive branchial epithelial hyperplasia with degenerative and necrotic changes, branchial hemorrhage, mottled organs with parenchymal necrosis, and excessive coelomic adhesions. Intranuclear inclusion bodies may be seen in affected tissues. Diagnosis: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is the gold standard for identification.

Non-lethal direct methods utilizing PCR can be performed on blood, gill tissue biopsies, and feces. More recently a quick recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) test has been developed. Non-lethal indirect methods include enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), virus neutralization (VN) on blood, and serum neutralization (SN). Positive indirect method samples only indicate that a fish has produced antibodies to the virus and may not, or ever have been, infected with CYHV-3, although this can vary by testing specificity. Virus isolation from spleen or caudal kidney on a susceptible cell line such as Koi Fin (KF) usually requires sacrificial euthanasia and is not reliable. The OIE Manual of Diagnostic Tests for Aquatic Animals gives specific guidance on KHV diagnosis. Material required for laboratory analysis: Live, moribund fish or freshly collected organ samples (gill, kidney, spleen) are the best specimens for an accurate diagnosis.

The current optimal antemortem tissue for PCR is fresh gill tissue (filaments) placed in 80-100% ethanol.

Generally considered resistant are lake trout (Salvelinus namaycush) andarctic char (Salvelinus alpinus). Causative organism: Family Rhabdoviridae, genus Novirhabdovirus, IHNV. Several clades of virus exist with certain clades or strains originating within certain geographic regions. Zoonotic potential: None. Distribution: Enzootic to Pacific coast of North America (Alaska to California). Epizootics reported from other regions of the United States. Now commonly identified in Asia and Europe.

None. Distribution: Enzootic to Pacific coast of North America (Alaska to California). Epizootics reported from other regions of the United States. Now commonly identified in Asia and Europe. There are clear differences in virulence depending on viral strain and host species; strains isolated from historical phylogeographic host species tend to be more virulent. Incubation period: Temperature dependent, ~5-45 days. Clinical signs: The clinical presentation is more common in fry and fingerlings. Mature fish can be infected with little to no clinical signs. Acute mortality may occur without apparent cause. Lethargy with sporadic hyperactivity and abnormal swimming patterns including whirling, spiraling, and flashing are seen. Coelomic distension presents due to ascites. Pale fecal casts are observed trailing from vent. Skin darkening, petechiation, erythema, bilateral exophthalmia, opaque fecal casts, and pale gills due to anemia are observed. Rapidly escalating mortalities occur which may reach >90%. Scoliosis and lordosis are common in 5-60% of fry and fingerling survivors.

fecal casts, and pale gills due to anemia are observed. Rapidly escalating mortalities occur which may reach >90%. Scoliosis and lordosis are common in 5-60% of fry and fingerling survivors. On hematology, leukopenia, neutropenia, and anemia with increased numbers of bi-lobed erythrocytes may be observed. Post-mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Petechiation, erythema, and pallor may be observed grossly. Necrosis of renal hematopoietic tissue and spleen; possible focal necrosis in liver, adrenal cortex, and gastrointestinal tract can be seen. Degeneration and necrosis of granular cells in the lamina propria, stratum compactum, and stratum granulosum of the gastrointestinal tract is sometimes considered pathognomonic for IHN. Pleiomorphic intracytoplasmic and intranuclear inclusions in the pancreas can be observed. Older fish show fewer histological lesions. Diagnosis: Early detection is crucial to control and prevent spread. Presumptive diagnosis is based on species, clinical signs, age, water temperature, and geographic location. Definitive diagnosis for OIE requires viral isolation in tissue culture followed by molecular or immunologic identification.

Other tests are available, e.g., virus neutralization, ELISA, indirect fluorescent antibody testing, RT-PCR, and staphylococcal co-agglutination. Virus can be detected for months to over a year post-exposure. Material required for laboratory analysis: Post-mortem aseptic collection of kidney, pyloric ceca, spleen, heart, and/or encephalon, or whole fish, kept cool but not frozen. Ovarian fluids may also be used for diagnostic purposes. Pool tissues from up to 10 fish (>0.5 g) with viral transport media and antibiotics (e.g., 4 ml 10% fetal calf serum and 200 IU penicillin, 200 μg streptomycin, and 200 μg kanamycin per ml). Transport at 4˚°C ASAP. Virological examination must begin no later than 48-72 h after sample collection.

Relevant diagnostic laboratories: Veterinary diagnostic laboratories; state, federal, or tribal natural resource management fish health laboratories; university laboratories specializing in fish virology, e.g., UC Davis Fish Health Laboratory; WADDL at Washington State University. Treatment: None. Consider culling and disinfecting grounds. Management of positive populations in endemic areas requires treatment of secondary infections. Recovered fish may be carriers. Prevention and control: Biosecurity and disinfection are the most important prevention measures. - Disinfect all eggs upon receipt of shipment or at spawning. For stocking, only acquire disinfected eggs (commonly iodophor disinfection) or eggs from IHNV-free stock. Use virus- - free water, or disinfect with ozone or UV. Resistance breeding or using less susceptible species can help reduce INHV's impact on aquaculture. - Several vaccines have been developed; however, few have been regularly implemented.

Resistance breeding or using less susceptible species can help reduce INHV's impact on aquaculture. - Several vaccines have been developed; however, few have been regularly implemented. - In the face of an outbreak, cull and disinfect affected animals. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Virus is inactivated by formalin, sodium hypochlorite, iodophors, gamma and UV irradiation, pH <4 or >10, or temperatures >60°C for 15 minutes. Notification: Reportable disease, must notify the USDA APHIS via the AVIC, and WOAH. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to an infected animal: Not recommended; do not introduce susceptible fish to affected animals. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: When the disease is first detected, an infected zone and a buffer zone is established peripheral to the problem. All infected animals are either culled or removed from the infected zone to reduce the risk of disease transmission and the area is disinfected. Biosecurity measures are reviewed and modified as needed within the infected zone.

Surveillance is established until no virus is detected for at least two years. Freedom from infection may be declared based on lack of IHNV isolation in cell culture, targeting the most susceptible stages of the most susceptible species for examination, and including reproductive fluids/tissues from adult fish at spawning.

-  Fish: 140+ susceptible marine and freshwater species. -  The virus has also been detected in amphipods, leeches, and turtles. It is not known what role these non-fish species play in the ecology of the virus. Causative organism: Viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus (previously known as Egtved virus), in the Family Rhabdoviridae.

Distribution: Viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus has a broad distribution in the northern hemisphere. Four primary strains of VHSV are known to exist, distributed in Europe (VHSV-Ia-e, II, III), East Asia (VHSV-I, III, IV), and North America (VHSV-IV). VHSV-IV is further divided into marine (VHSV-IVa) and freshwater (VHSV-IVb). In North America, VHSV-IV has been detected off the Northern Pacific and Atlantic coasts as well as in the Great Lakes region. Incubation period: An inverse correlation has been recorded between virus stability and water temperatures ranging from 1°C to 20°C. Transmission occurs at cooler temperatures (1-12°C) with an incubation time of 1-2 weeks at high temperatures and 3-4 weeks at low temperatures.

-  Acute: Results in rapid destruction of endothelial cells and extravasation of the blood supply, which may ultimately result in diffuse or petechial hemorrhage, ascites, exophthalmia, organ failure, anemia (pale gills), and high mortality. -  Chronic: Results in prolonged disease with neurologic-type behavior characterized by anorexia, erratic swimming, or lethargy. -  Clinical presentation is dependent on a variety of factors including host, pathogen, or environmental variables. Some species exhibit no clinical lesions while infected with high levels of VHSV, while others develop severe lesions with low levels of VHSV. Presumptive diagnosis can be difficult and secondary testing is recommended. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: VHSV has a predilection for endothelial cells and will often induce hemorrhagic lesions throughout the body visible by gross and histologic examination. The virus will also cause necrosis and degeneration of hematopoietic tissues, macrophage proliferation within renal tissue, and degeneration and vacuolization of hepatic tissue. Diagnosis: The gold standard for VHSV detection is virus isolation by cell culture.

tissues, macrophage proliferation within renal tissue, and degeneration and vacuolization of hepatic tissue. Diagnosis: The gold standard for VHSV detection is virus isolation by cell culture. Suitable cell lines include Epithelioma Papulosum Cyprini (EPC), Rainbow Trout Gonad (RTG-2), Bluegill fry (BF-2), Chinook salmon embryo (CHSE-214), and the Fathead minnow (FHM) cell lines incubated at 15°C. Cytopathic effects are typically observed within 4-6 days, but may take up to four weeks and two passages to appear. Secondary testing by RT-PCR or IFA are recommended. Real-time RT-PCR is becoming widely used for preliminary diagnosis and surveillance testing and can be performed on non-lethal samples (i.e., fin or gill biopsy). Material required for laboratory analysis: Contact the diagnostic lab where tissues will be sent to determine the types of tissues they will accept for non-regulatory testing and their recommended method of preservation. -  Virology: Fresh tissue homogenate of the kidney and spleen should be placed in plastic tubes or whirlpack bags with 1g tissue to 10mL dilution with virus transport media (i.e. Hank's Balanced Salt Solution).

Fresh tissue homogenate of the kidney and spleen should be placed in plastic tubes or whirlpack bags with 1g tissue to 10mL dilution with virus transport media (i.e. Hank's Balanced Salt Solution). Ship samples overnight on frozen gel packs. -  RT-PCR: Tissue should be placed in tubes with RNAlater or immediately frozen. Tissue storage in 70% ethanol is an option, but freezing is necessary for long term storage.

-  Given the lack of available therapeutics, preventing the introduction of VHSV is the primary method of control. In addition, early detection of the virus by proactive surveillance programs provides value in determining areas or activities of risk. Strict biosecurity protocols should be implemented in areas of risk. -  Prevention can be achieved by eliminating the transfer of the virus via contaminated fomites, eggs, fish, and water. Typical anti-viral disinfectants, such as chlorine, sodium hypochlorite, and UV irradiation are effective. Iodophor treatment of eggs is not always effective at removing the virus from the eggs' surface. However, at this time, no evidence for true vertical transmission of VHSV has been recorded; viral adherence to the egg surface and presence in ovarian fluid has been documented. -  The virus has also been shown to survive freeze-thaw cycles, so this is an ineffective prevention strategy.

-  If captive fish test positive, the population should be isolated or euthanized. Surviving fish may become lifelong carriers and continue to spread disease via contaminated water. -  Housing facilities should be cleaned and disinfected with standard products such as chlorine and sodium hypochlorite. Facility effluent should also be disinfected with similar chemicals. For recirculating facilities, in-line UV sterilization should be incorporated to prevent the transmission of the virus via contaminated water. Notification: VHSV is a reportable pathogen to the OIE and USDA. Upon suspicion or preliminary diagnosis, the area veterinarian in charge should be notified. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: The National Aquatic Animal Health Plan provides some guidelines for surveillance of aquatic animals. There is no coordinated surveillance plan for this disease in wild populations; however, regulatory and research surveys do occur. Any suspect case in a new species or geographic region needs to be reported to AVIC USDA APHIS.

Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Susceptible species of naïve fish should not be introduced to a previously infected population. It may be possible to co-habitat nonsusceptible species with a previously infected population; however, this approach is risky because the host range is broad and rapidly expanding. Arthropods such as the fish louse (Argulus sp.) are likely vectors. Clinical signs: Infected fish may present with a variety of clinical signs including, but not limited to, lethargy, isolation, coelomic distention, exophthalmia, lethargy, pale gills, darkening of the body surface, fecal casts, skin and branchial hemorrhage, and distention or protrusion of the vent.

Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: On necropsy, affected fish may have generalized edema which may be sanguineous, organ hemorrhage, intestinal inflammation, and the gastrointestinal tract may contain mucus and no ingesta. Histopathologic examination may reveal multifocal necrosis in liver and pancreas, pericarditis, and renal tubular degeneration. Diagnosis: WOAH acceptable confirmatory diagnosis is usually made with cell culture (viral isolation from spleen and/or caudal kidney), conventional PCR, and amplicon sequencing. In addition, immunohistochemistry, Ag-ELISA, and IFAT provide a presumptive diagnosis in clinically affected animals. It is important to note that SVCv infected fish also may present with opportunistic Gramnegative bacterial infections. Gastrointestinal IgM plays an important role in the immune response of common carp (Cyprinus carpio).

- ∞ A minimum of 10 moribund fish or 10 fish exhibiting clinical signs of SVCv must be collected. Fish should be sent live to the laboratory or sacrificed and packed separately in sealed aseptic refrigerated containers or on ice. Depending on the size of fish, whole fish (body length ≤4 cm) or the entire viscera including kidney and encephalon (>4 body length ≤6 cm) should be collected. If the fish is larger, liver, kidney, spleen and encephalon should be collected aseptically. Samples should be combined to form pools of a maximum of five fish per pool that should not exceed 1.5g. Tissues should be placed in sterile vials and stored at 4°C until virus extraction is performed at the laboratory, which is recommended to begin within 24 hours of sample collection. - ∞ For detecting asymptomatic carriers, tissue samples of kidney, spleen, gill and encephalon should be collected. Depending on the population size, fish collection must encompass a statistically significant number of specimens. The sampling should be designed to enable detection, at a 95% confidence level, of infected animals.

- Low host specificity. - Various teleost species, usually those found in warm water. - Common in American, European, and Japanese eels, channel catfish, mullet, chinook salmon, carp, bass, Japanese flounder, tilapia species, Betta splendens, zebrafish, and many tropical marine teleosts. - It is an important pathogen of aquacultured species. - It can also cause disease in some aquatic invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles, and mammals. Causative organism: Gram-negative, rod-shaped, facultative anaerobic bacteria which are mostly motile but have been reported to lose their flagella. Enterobacteriaceae: Edwardsiella anguillarum, E. hoshinae, E. ictaluri, E. piscicida, and E. tarda. E. piscicida was previously identified as E. tarda. Zoonotic potential: Yes for Edwardsiella tarda. Usually necrotic skin wounds or gastroenteritis but it can spread systemically, leading to meningitis and liver abscesses. Distribution: Worldwide. Incubation period: 5-7 days.

- Acute or chronic presentation may include lethargy, inappetance, full-thickness skin ulcers that may be accompanied by significant tissue necrosis, bacteremia, hyperemia, petechiation, erythema, pale gills, organ swelling, coelomic distension and ascites, rectal hernia, positive buoyancy, loss of balance, bursts of abnormal activity, and ocular lesions (such as keratitis, uveitis, and exophthalmia). - Mortalities may be acute but often chronic depending on the degree of stressful environmental conditions; mortalities range but can be substantial, over 50%. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Congestion and/or focal necrosis of spleen, liver, kidney, and heart are observed. Malodorous abscesses in the viscera or skeletal muscle may be seen. Small (1 mm x 2-3 mm), straight, Gram-negative rods which may be motile can be present. Inflammation, often suppurative but may be granulomatous, can be observed in infected organs, such as kidneys. Diagnosis: Bacterial culture from lesions, blood, or organs on nutrient rich media, such as TSA or HBI agar at 28°C incubation.

Lewbart (2011, 2013) Susceptible animal groups: Fishes (particularly Cichlidae, Syngnathidae, and Cyprinidae), aquatic invertebrates (reported in molluscs, crustaceans, cnidarians, echinoderms, and sponges); more common in adult and geriatric organisms. Cases have been reported in mammals (including humans), reptiles, and amphibians. Causative organism: Atypical (non-tuberculous) Mycobacterium spp., with >120 species recognized in the genus Mycobacterium. Common isolates include M. marinum, M. chelonae, M. neoaurum, M. fortuitum, and M. haemophilum. The organisms are Gram-positive and acid-fast staining. Zoonotic potential: Yes; about 1/3 of non-tuberculous Mycobacteria species are zoonotic. Exposure is a moderate risk, particularly through wound contamination, and can result in mild to moderate clinical signs in humans (usually restricted to extremities). A localized skin nodule or granuloma may ulcerate and start to exude a serosanguinous or purulent discharge.

Depending on immunological status of infected individual, nodular cutaneous lesions can progress to tenosynovitis, arthritis, and osteomyelitis. Distribution: Global and most commonly associated with aquatic environments. The optimal temperature range for growth is 24-28C (76-82F). The bacteria can survive for up to 2 years in the environment. Incubation period: Varied, weeks to months in fishes; 2 days to 6 weeks in humans. Clinical signs: Chronic progressive infection is most typically reported and may include skin hemorrhage, ulcerations, and granulomas with possible exudate, and/or white nodules on viscera; hyperemia of fins; exophthalmos, corneal ulcer, granulomatous endophthalmitis; lethargy, anorexia, poor growth, weight loss, coelomic edema/ascites, cutaneous edema, reduced pigmentation, loss of scales, spinal deformities, low fecundity.

Clinical signs in invertebrates may also include dark-pigmented, raised lesions on the internal organs, and/or orange-colored nodules in the muscle. Acute mortalities may occur with more virulent strains and animals may lack substantial gross changes such as granulomas. Animals may be subclinically infected without evidence of disease. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Gross changes presented in clinical signs and often include organomegaly, granulomas, congestion, and necrosis. Microscopically, acid-fast organisms are frequently detected in both granulomatous and non-granulomatous tissues, but not all acid-fast organisms are Mycobacterial species (differential diagnoses: Nocardia spp., Cryptosporidium spp., myxozoans). Staining intensity can vary.

Occasionally isolated from invertebrates, insects and molluscs. Causative organism: Aeromonas hydrophila, A. salmonicida, A. shigelloides, A. formicans, A. sobria, A. caviae, A. veronii, and other pathogenic Aeromonas sp. It is a Gram negative, oxidative positive, facultative anaerobic, polar flagellated bacterial rod. They are non-spore forming, ubiquitous in environment, and may comprise part of the normal intestinal flora. Opportunistic infections are common. Zoonotic potential: Yes, but also direct environmental exposure. Opportunistic zoonotic pathogen especially in immunocompromised or debilitated individuals. Distribution: Worldwide distribution. Common in fresh, brackish and salt water environments, particularly with increased detritus or sewage and carried by some invertebrate and vertebrate species.

-  Fish: Acute mortality, septicemia, erythema, exophthalmia, hemorrhages in skin, fins, muscle and oral cavity, with skin boils and ulceration. Fecal casts or bloody discharge from vents. -  Amphibians: Acute mortality, septicemia, anorexia, ventral erythema with cutaneous hemorrhage especially ventral thighs, edema in subcutis, anasarca, hemorrhagic ulcerations of digit tips and jaw. May feature digital amputation due to vasoconstriction, secondary to septicemia. -  Reptiles: Acute mortality, septicemia, pneumonia, ulcerative stomatitis particularly in snakes, dermal ecchymoses, epidermal ulceration, anorexia, listless, labored respirations, harsh respiratory sounds, mouth gaping, steady decline in status, rule out predisposing or underlying environmental or host factors. -  Waterfowl: Upper respiratory tract infections, salpingitis, enteritis, septicemia, localized abscessation, and arthritis. -  Marine mammals: Septicemia, pneumonia. -  Humans: Gastroenteritis, watery diarrhea which can be chronic in nature, septicemia, pustular dermatitis, cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis, pneumonia, peritonitis, cholecystitis, bacteremia and hepatitis.

Diagnosis: Isolation on routine media (e.g. heart infusion agar, blood agar, MacConkey agar, Tryptone soy agar, Tryptone soy broth) with subsequent identification, commercial systems, molecular identification (16s RNA gene PCR with gyrB amplification, amplified fragment length polymorphism (AFLP) analysis). -  Antibiotic selection is dependent on susceptibility testing. In general, these bacteria are susceptible to aminoglycosides, carbapenems, extended spectrum cephalosporins, azithromycin, monobactams, nitrofurans, extended spectrum penicillins (piperacillin, piperacillin-tazobactam), phenicols, fluoroquinolones, and tetracyclines, with variable susceptibility to potentiated antifolates (trimethoprim-sulfas). -  Aeromonas spp. produce strong B-lactamases, so they resistant to narrow spectrum penicillins (e.g. amoxicillin, ampicillin, ampicillin-sulbactam, ticarcillin, oxacillin, penicillin) and cephalosporins (e.g. cefoxitin), sulfamethoxazole, erythromycin, and clarithromycin. Prevention and control: In species other than fish, infections are often opportunistic or secondary to debilitation, immunosuppression or penetrating wounds. Maintain good environmental hygiene, water quality and optimal husbandry conditions; ultraviolet irradiation or ozonation of water sources; proper food storage and handling recommendations; follow all wound care procedures recommended by veterinarian/physician; practice good hygiene and disinfect fomites often.

BFDV is highly prone to mutations, and therefore is genetically diverse (can be considered a viral quasispecies). Circovirus infections have also been documented in Anseriformes (duck CV, swan CV, goose CV), Columbiformes (pigeon CV), Passeriformes (canary CV, finch CV, raven CV, starling CV), Galliformes (chicken CV) and Charadriiformes (gull CV). Zoonotic potential: No known human transmission has occurred.

Distribution: Likely evolved in Australia and has been disseminated globally through transcontinental movement of infected birds. BFDV could be found on any continent with a sufficient population of free-ranging or captive psittacine birds to support virus survival and transmission. BFDV will continue to spread in untested or, until available, unvaccinated psittacine birds. Incubation period: The minimum incubation period is 21-25 days with a maximum period of up to several years.

-  Acute Form: most commonly occurs in nestlings/fledglings, and may begin with signs unrelated to the beak or feathers. It causes acute fatal infections in nestling cockatoos and less frequently in other species. Depression, anorexia, regurgitation, diarrhea, biliverdinuria and acute death are reported. - o The peracute form of the disease is particularly common in African grey parrots and is characterized by severe leukopenia and anemia, hepatic coagulation-necrosis, and an absence of feather abnormalities. - o Feather abnormalities in already developed feathers (from causes other than BFDV) should be distinguished from abnormalities associated with the developing feather (from the pulp cap to the feather base). Visible developmental feather abnormalities include: retention of the feather sheath, hemorrhage of the pulp cavity, shortened deformed feathers and circumferential constrictions at the feather base. Stress lines are common in affected feathers. Affected feathers are often loose, break easily, may bleed, and elicit a pain response with minimal manipulation.

Some chicks die within days to weeks of the first signs of feather abnormalities and others survive with progression to chronic disease. -  Chronic Form: Newly developing powder down and contour feathers are the first to show clinical changes in birds that exhibit feather abnormalities after their remiges and rectrices are developed. The visible changes in these feathers are similar to those described above. - o In psittacines other than lovebirds, feather lesions associated with PCV-1 become progressively worse with each successive molt and if the bird survives for years it may become mostly or completely featherless as feather follicle damage prevents replacement. Progressive disease is associated with organopathies that are likely associated with immune suppression and birds usually die from secondary bacterial, fungal, parasitic, or other viral infections. -  Birds with PBFD shed substantial quantities of extremely environmentally stable virus in their feather dander and should not be maintained in environments (aviaries or hospitals) or by care takers that have direct or indirect contact with other birds. Comparatively, PCV-2 appears clinically less virulent and lories and lorikeets with moderate feather abnormalities have been shown to recover as indicated by a return to normal feather plumage and no detectable viral DNA in their blood. The follicular epithelium also may be necrotic, but this lesion is reported less commonly. Feather sheath hyperkeratosis prevents the feather from ex-sheathing resulting in retention of the feather sheath. Feather pulp lesions are characterized by suppurative inflammation, including perivascular accumulations of heterophils, plasma cells, macrophages and rarely lymphocytes. The characteristic basophilic intracytoplasmic - and less commonly intranuclear - inclusions are usually, but not always present in diseased feathers. Hyperkeratosis and separation of the cornified outer layer from the underlying tissues and bone may also be evident, and are often accompanied by secondary necrosis and osteitis of associated tissues -  In peracute cases, histologic lesions may be limited to severe bursal or thymic necrosis with the presence of viral inclusion bodies. Feather pathology in these cases may not occur or may be limited to edema in the follicular epithelium (if present). -  In birds with beak disease, necrosis and inflammation of the epithelial lining of the tongue, beak cavity, and crop have also been reported. Secondary Gram-negative bacteria and fungi are commonly isolated from beak lesions and may be associated with acute or chronic inflammatory reactions.

-  Bloodwork changes: Leukopenia in the acute form. Hypoproteinemia in the chronic form. -  PBFD should be considered in any bird presenting abnormal feather loss or developmental abnormalities. PBFD can only be diagnosed by detection of the virus using in situ hybridization, immunohistochemistry or electron microscopy to document the virus or viral components in diseased tissues. For antemortem diagnosis, a biopsy of 3-4 diseased feathers and their associated follicle is recommended. It is critical for the clinician to biopsy diseased feathers. Both diseased and normal feathers can be present directly next to each other and failure to obtain a biopsy of diseased feathers can result in an inaccurate diagnosis. Birds with the peracute and early acute forms of the disease may die before the development of feather abnormalities and disease is documented by histopathologic evaluation of internal organs including the bursa, thymus and liver. -  PCR-based testing can be used to detect target segments of viral DNA in the blood of suspect birds before feather abnormalities develop but this condition does not confirm the presence of disease.

Most birds infected with PCV develop a transient infection that can be detected by - finding viral DNA in whole blood. Most infected birds subsequently respond with an appropriate immune response and clear the virus with no recognizable clinical changes. A bird that is PCR positive for PCV-1 and does not have dystrophic feathers must be retested in 90 days to determine if the bird has cleared the virus. It is important that birds be maintained in a virus free environment during this 90-day period. -  Biopsy of dystrophic feathers and their associated follicle in formalin for histologic diagnosis. Whole blood collected by venipuncture. Blood samples collected by toe nail clipping should be considered environmental samples and not a bird specific sample. Feathers submitted for PCR-based testing should also be considered environmental samples and are not bird specific. Viral DNA can be detected by PCR-based testing in environmental swabs. These can be used to document the extent of environmental contamination (air filters, fan motors, nest boxes, etc.) and for evaluating cleaning efforts following an outbreak. -  Post-mortem samples include bursa, thymus, liver, spleen, kidney, and dystrophic feathers (if present) in formalin. Swabs of tissues collected from the cut surface of the bursa, thymus or liver can be used for rapid detection of viral DNA. Only disposable scalpel blades should be used for collecting post-mortem samples or swab may be positive because of transfer to the cut surface of the organ from viral contaminated instruments. -  Prior to shipping, blood samples should be stored refrigerated (4 o C/39.2 o F). Samples must be shipped in a padded envelope or box.

-  Transmission of the virus is primarily through inhalation or ingestion of air or food containing viral contaminated feather or fecal dust. Contaminated clothing, hair and body surfaces of care takers can also serve to disseminate the virus as can contaminated bird carriers, feeding utensils, nest boxes and nesting materials. Two of the most severe modern (post PCR-based testing) outbreaks the author investigated were associated with use of a contaminated grinder for nail grooming and the sale of a contaminated egg incubator. Maternal transmission has been documented. The virus is extremely environmentally stable and for the safety of birds any contaminated environment should always be considered a source of - infectious virus. Any diseased birds should be maintained in strict isolation and the care takers of these birds should always be considered contaminated with the virus. Maintain strict quarantine and testing protocols for new birds prior to entering the collection. Protect flocks from contact with wild birds in countries where free-flying PBFD-infected birds may exist. -  PCR-based testing should be used during entry quarantine to detect viral DNA in the blood.

Because of the difficulty in decontaminating a typical clinic, it is not recommended that known diseased birds be evaluated or maintained in the hospital. PCR-based testing of environmental swabs can be used to document the severity of viral contamination in the environment. -  A PCV vaccine has been developed by the Emerging Diseases Research Group at the University of Georgia and the vaccine awaits a USDA approved manufacturer to take the necessary steps to register the vaccine for commercial use. While specific data on the susceptibility of PCV to disinfectants is unknown, it is known that other circovirus are among the most environmentally stable and disinfectant resistant of all viruses. -  The goal in a contaminated facility is to wash the virus out of the environment, expose contaminated surfaces to prolong drying and direct sunlight and then seal any remaining virus to a substrate with paint (or equivalent). Any contaminated surface that is porous (not made of metal or plastic) should be discarded. All metal, concrete and plastic surfaces should be washed with a sodium hypochlorite (e.g. Clorox)- containing detergent, rinsed and allowed to dry in direct sunlight. The procedure should be repeated 3-4 times. -  Air handling systems should be professionally cleaned by a company experienced with decontaminating hospital air systems. Once repeated cleaning has been accomplished, a pressure painter should be used to coat all remaining surfaces (floor, walls and ceiling). If a diseased bird has been maintained in an incubator, one should make certain that the fan and motor housing are decontaminated and PCR negative for viral DNA before the fan is returned to service.

Distribution: Presumably worldwide due to bird trade, but it is most prevalent in densely populated captive psittacine collections. Case reports have documented confirmed disease in North America, Europe, Africa, Australia/New Zealand, the Middle East and Asia. A study suggested a 7% prevalence of PsHV-1 infection in the general US population of parrots. It is suspected that these viruses have evolved with Central and South American parrots. Incubation period: Experimentally, 5-10 days to establish infection. Papillomas develop within a year.

-  Pacheco's disease (acute): Sudden death, depression, anorexia, diarrhea, biliverdinuria. Leukopenia and marked AST elevation can be seen. -  Mucosal papillomatosis (chronic): Tenesmus and presence of fresh blood in the droppings can be seen with cloacal papillomas. Oral papillomas are most often found at the base of the tongue or on choanal margins. When bile duct and pancreatic duct carcinomas develop, signs of chronic liver disease (overgrown beak, poor feather quality, wasting) can occur.

texto: -  Pacheco's disease: Due to rapid death, acutely affected birds may show no gross lesions. However, when abnormalities are present, they may be in the liver, spleen, kidneys and intestines. Histopathological findings include multi-organ (e.g., spleen, intestines, pancreas, trachea, air sacs) necrotizing lesions, hemorrhage and congestion of the liver, spleen, and kidneys and hepatomegaly or splenomegaly may be seen. Intranuclear inclusion bodies (Cowdry Type A) are most common in the liver, but have been demonstrated in the kidneys, spleen, pancreas and small intestines. -  Mucosal papillomatosis: In the chronic form of the disease, mucosal papillomas can be seen, most commonly in the oral and cloacal mucosa or upper gastrointestinal tract. These lesions are found in the disease complex termed internal papillomatosis of parrots (IPP). A high prevalence of carcinomas in the bile duct and pancreatic duct has been observed in aviaries where IPP had been noted in birds infected with PsHV-1 genotype 3. These tumors can be detected with coelomic ultrasound and are sometimes associated with a rise in serum GGT. Many ventricular and cloacal carcinomas appear to be caused by PsHVs.

Birds that are serologically positive are likely latently infected. -  Post-mortem specimens: Characteristic histologic findings, electron microscopy, cell culture, immunofluorescent antibody staining and PCR. -  Screening and isolation of infected individuals is critical. PCR positive birds should be housed separately from other parrots. Macaws, conures and Amazon parrots should be carefully examined prior to acquisition. That being said, not all PsHV-1 genotypes are serologically cross reactive, meaning that infection with one variant of the virus does not protect from infection from another. -  Control methods in the midst of an outbreak are debated. While some veterinarians support catching and moving individual birds, others advocate minimal disturbances until the outbreak is over. Immediate treatment of exposed birds with acyclovir at 1mg/ml drinking water and 400mg/kg of soft mash) is indicated. Gavage feeding at 80-100mg/kg TID has also been suggested. -  Commercial monovalent vaccine (killed virus) for PsHV-1 is derived from a single, unreported serotype. Clinical signs: The signs vary with virulence of the virus, susceptibility of the host, distribution and type of lesions in an infected bird, and other complicating factors. Manifestations are cutaneous ("dry"), diphtheritic ("wet"), systemic, or some combination of the three. Cutaneous lesions are characterized by the appearance of nodular lesions on feather-free regions of the body. In nongallinaceous species, these lesions often occur as single nodules which may resemble a proliferative neoplasm. Diphtheritic lesions are moist, necrotic lesions on the mucous membranes of the mouth and upper respiratory tract. Septicemic form is associated with acute depression, anorexia, dyspnea and death, and is most frequently reported in certain passerine species (e.g., canary). Infected birds can have peracute infections (death) or may become latent carriers.

Also note that when stressed (e.g., during transfer intra- and inter-zoo, other illness), it has been suggested that birds may recrudesce and develop new lesions which may first appear as red-swollen areas. Any bird with these developing lesions should be immediately isolated while avian pox is or is not confirmed. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Gross lesions are proliferations of epithelial cells. Diphtheritic form may appear as white, opaque, slightly elevated nodules to coalescing yellowish, caseous, necrotic material with the appearance of a pseudomembrane. Diagnosis: Gross lesions in cutaneous infections are often highly suggestive of pox infection but are not definitively avian pox. Diphtheritic infections are often harder to diagnosis on gross observations due to differential diagnoses (e.g., trichomonosis). Histologic evaluation for Bollinger bodies (eosinophilic intracytoplasmic epidermal inclusions) on light microscopy is acceptable for diagnosis.

-  Birds - Will depend on the virulence of the Chlamydia strain and the immune status of the host. Clinical signs may include any or all the following: lethargy, ruffled feathers, anorexia, oculonasal discharge, conjunctivitis, diarrhea, signs of liver disease such as excretion of green to yellow-green urates, weight loss. Some birds may manifest respiratory signs ranging from sneezing to respiratory distress. Neurologic signs such as tremors, torticollis, or leg paresis may be found in subacute to chronic cases. Infected carriers may not have overt clinical signs. -  Humans - fever, chills, myalgia, malaise, nonproductive cough sometimes with chest tightness and/or breathing difficulty; sometimes a nonspecific rash and enlarged spleen are also present. -  Other mammals - linked to abortions in horses, cattle, and sheep; variety of clinical disease presentations in dogs including respiratory and reproductive signs. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: The organism is susceptible to many detergents and disinfectants as well as heat. However, it is resistant to acid and alkali. Effective disinfectants include 1% Lysol, a 1:1,000 dilution of quaternary ammonium compounds (e.g., Roccal, Zephiran), accelerated hydrogen peroxide products, or freshly prepared 1:32 dilution of household bleach (½ cup/gallon). Do not use a vacuum cleaner or pressure washer. Notification: Reportable disease under USDA-APHIS-VS National Animal Health Reporting System. Psittacosis in humans is a Nationally Notifiable Disease - and most states require physicians to report to appropriate local or state health authorities. for introducing animals to infected animal: Infected birds should be isolated and treated. Posttreatment birds should be tested using a PCR-based method 2 weeks following completion of treatment. Other birds should not be introduced until treatment is completed and the infected bird's facility is thoroughly cleaned and disinfected. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Infected pet birds or other valuable birds and their contacts may be isolated and treated. Treated birds may become reinfected. New birds entering a facility can be tested for the disease but cannot truly be declared "disease-free." Fungi use a nomenclature inconsistent with the rest of biology as separate names for asexual anamorph stages and sexual teleomorph stages of the same organism exist, resulting in multiple species names and paraphyletic taxa. The anamorph genus Aspergillus is the same fungus as several teleomorph genera, including Neosartorya, Eurotium, and Emericella. Zoonotic potential: Aspergillosis is reported in people, but the infections usually are acquired from environmental exposure in immunocompromised individuals. Theoretically, any lesions where sporeforming conidia are present (e.g., some air sac granulomas in birds) may release spores into the environment which could be inhaled, and thus pose some zoonotic potential. In immunocompetent humans, the most common clinical presentation is wheezing, sneezing and coughing due to allergic bronchopulmonary disease or fungal sinusitis. Distribution: Worldwide; ubiquitous in the environment.

humans, the most common clinical presentation is wheezing, sneezing and coughing due to allergic bronchopulmonary disease or fungal sinusitis. Distribution: Worldwide; ubiquitous in the environment. The fungus proliferates in soil, decaying vegetation, and moist environments with poor ventilation. Pre-formed spores can also be easily aerosolized in dry, dusty environments. Contaminated ventilation systems and active construction around hospitals have been a risk factor for disease. Incubation period: Highly variable. May cause acute disease or prolonged chronic infections. Clinical progression depends primarily on immune response and degree of environmental exposure. Clinical signs: Clinical manifestation depends on the infectious dose, pathogen distribution and the individual's immune response and presence of comorbidities. A. fumigatus primarily affects the respiratory system and may cause dyspnea, stridor, cyanosis, coughing, vocalization changes, altered buoyancy in water birds, and sneezing in mammals.

A. fumigatus primarily affects the respiratory system and may cause dyspnea, stridor, cyanosis, coughing, vocalization changes, altered buoyancy in water birds, and sneezing in mammals. The organism frequently infects cavities, such as sinuses, air sacs, guttural pouches, and similar locations forming aspergillomas but can affect other organs such as eyes and skin. Signs of disseminated disease depend on the organs affected. Fungal plaques on large blood vessels may cause rupture and fatal hemorrhage. Nonspecific signs of disease such as lethargy, weakness, and weight loss are common. In birds, aspergillosis can result in marked leukocytosis. In humans, phospholipase, protease, elastase and gliotoxin all play a role in pathogenesis.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: - Gross: Rhinitis, sinusitis, tracheitis, air sacculitis, pneumonia, disseminated granulomatous lesions in any organ. Lesions are yellow to pale pyogranulomatous or granulomatous nodules or plaques. In some air sac lesions, white or green, cottony spore-forming conidiospores can be observed. - Histologic: Granulomatous inflammation with intralesional fungal hyphae measuring 3-6 µm with parallel walls, evenly distributed septa, and progressive dichotomous branching at acute angles. Angioinvasion with thrombosis. Diagnosis: Difficult due to nonspecific clinical presentation. - Fungal culture combined with cytology or histopathology of affected tissues is the gold standard for a definitive diagnosis. Aspergillus spp. can be cultured from normal tissues without pathologic lesions, so it is important to combine culture with microscopic evaluation. Fungi can be enhanced with special stains (e.g. periodic acid-Schiff [PAS], Grocott's methenamine silver [GMS]) or immunohistochemical labels to aid in microscopic evaluation. PCR of tissue samples may also be useful.

Causative organism: Single stranded RNA viruses belonging to the genus Pestivirus and Family Flaviviridae. Two strains, BVDV-1 (11 sub-genotypes) and BVDV-2 (2 sub-genotypes), have different profiles. Within the strains, two 2 biotypes of BVDV classification are based on their effects on cell culture (cytopathic [CP] or non-cytopathic [NCP]). Infections with NCP strains are the most common and are the strains that result in PI animals. Because BVDV is an RNA virus it readily mutates resulting in genetic, antigenic, and pathogenic variation.

with NCP strains are the most common and are the strains that result in PI animals. Because BVDV is an RNA virus it readily mutates resulting in genetic, antigenic, and pathogenic variation. Zoonotic potential: No, but in vitro infection of human cell lines is possible. Distribution: Worldwide distribution. The principal reservoirs of BVDV are persistently infected (PI) domestic cattle. Numerous wildlife species, both captive and free ranging have been shown to be serologically positive for BVDV. Persistently infected individuals have been identified in captive and free- ranging wildlife, primarily cervid species. Incubation period: Experimental infection in mule deer, white-tail deer & cattle indicates that virus may be isolated from white blood cells, serum, plasma or nasal secretions 2 days post infection. Incubation tends to be 6-12 days in cattle with infection lasting generally 1-3 days.

-  Infections can be transient with no apparent clinical signs or severe with pronounced morbidity and mortality. Both BVDV-1 and BVDV-2 can cause the full spectrum of clinical presentations. BVDV is lymphotrophic and immunosuppressive, so diseased animals have an increased susceptibility to other infectious diseases. Hematology may show mild to severe lymphopenia and neutropenia depending on the virulence of the strain to the host. -  "Acute", "Transient" or "Primary" disease syndromes are described from horizontal transmission which include: - o Respiratory - Oculonasal discharge. Due to BVDV immunosuppressive effects clinical signs may be indicative of disease caused by other respiratory pathogens. - o Gastrointestinal - Diarrhea and clinical signs resulting from lesions which are primarily ulcerous or erosive and which may involve any region of the GIT. Mixed infections with other common gastrointestinal organisms are not uncommon. - o Hemorrhagic/thrombocytopenic - Thrombocytopenia, bloody diarrhea, prolonged bleeding times, petechiae & ecchymoses, epistaxis, death. - o Mucosal disease - Seen only in PI animals that become super infected with a CP strain of BVDV.

bloody diarrhea, prolonged bleeding times, petechiae & ecchymoses, epistaxis, death. - o Mucosal disease - Seen only in PI animals that become super infected with a CP strain of BVDV. Clinical signs are secondary to severe ulcerative and erosive lesions throughout the gastrointestinal tract and potentially including lameness secondary to lesions associated with inter-digital ulcerations. -  From vertical transmission, disease syndromes include: - o Reproductive and fetal - Early fetal losses, mummified fetuses, abortions, stillbirths and congenital defects, poor doer during neonatal period. - o Persistently infected animals - Persistently infected animals result if the dam becomes infected during the first trimester of gestation. In cattle, infection must occur before 125 days of gestation with a NCP strain of BVDV. In white-tail deer, infection occurring between days 45-52 of gestation resulted in a PI fawn. The fetus becomes infected and is immunotolerant to the infecting strain of BVDV and will shed high amounts of virus from all bodily fluids throughout its life. The PI animal may mount an immune response to heterologous strains of BVDV.

to the infecting strain of BVDV and will shed high amounts of virus from all bodily fluids throughout its life. The PI animal may mount an immune response to heterologous strains of BVDV. Persistently infected individuals may exhibit, runtiness, immunosuppression and secondary infections, but clinically normal animals have been documented. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: There are no pathognomonic lesions for BVDV. Pathological diagnosis may be made based on virus isolation or demonstration of the virus within tissues. Transiently infected animals will have gross and histopathological lesions consistent with their clinical syndrome. Persistently infected, but healthy animals may have few postmortem and histopathological lesions. Lymphoid depletion has been reported in both PI cattle and experimentally infected fawns.

-  The primary goal is to identify PI animals. Virus isolation is the gold standard. However, antigen capture ELISA, immunohistochemistry and RT-PCR are commonly utilized tests as they are rapid, sensitive, affordable, and repeatable amongst diagnostic laboratories. Many tests do not differentiate between BVDV1 and 2 and other pestiviruses such as classical swine fever virus, border disease virus (endemic worldwide), pronghorn virus, HoBi-like [isolated in South America and Southeast Asia, Bungowannah (isolated in Australia) and giraffe (isolated in Africa)]. -  Most tests cannot differentiate between an acute and a persistent infection. The standard for diagnosis of PI infection is two positive tests on samples collected at least two weeks apart.

-  Antemortem: Haired skin sample (ear notch or caudal tail fold), or whole blood (buffy coat) collected in EDTA are preferred samples. -  Postmortem: Haired skin and lymphoid tissue (mesenteric lymph nodes, thymus, tonsils) spleen, and brain. These tissues should be collected for culture or immunohistochemistry (fresh and formalin fixed). Archived formalin fixed tissue blocks can be tested for BVD via PCR; however, detection rates drop after 3 months-1 year. Relevant Diagnostic lab: Check with your local veterinary diagnostic lab to see what tests they perform and the limitations of these tests for the species you are testing. Treatment: Supportive care of transiently infected animals. Cull persistently infected individuals. Prevention and control: Identification and removal of PI individuals. All incoming artiodactyls (particularly domestic cattle, sheep, and goats) should be quarantined and tested for the presence of BVDV virus. -  Animals that can only be handled once and with risk of exposure to BVDV.

They should be quarantined until the offspring is born, then test that offspring for persistent infection via whole blood - (buffy coat) RT-PCR in combination with ELISA or immunohistochemistry on a haired skin sample.

This will differentiate presence of virus in the face of maternal antibodies if the offspring is sampled post nursing. -  Animals with viremia should not be introduced to other artiodactyls that may be in the first trimester of gestation. -  Individuals utilizing reproductive manipulation techniques should be alerted that BVDV has been isolated from commercial fetal calf serum. -  Vaccination has not been well studied in wildlife. - o Alpacas are reported to be protected with no negative effects when vaccinated with a MLV. - o Vaccination in cattle is primarily focused on the prevention of fetal infections. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: BVDV is an enveloped virus and susceptible to the following classes of disinfectants when used per recommended protocols - hypochlorite, chlorhexidine, alcohol, iodine and iodophors, quaternary ammonium compounds, phenolic disinfectants, and aldehydes. Environmental survival can be dependent on temperature and moisture level.

chlorhexidine, alcohol, iodine and iodophors, quaternary ammonium compounds, phenolic disinfectants, and aldehydes. Environmental survival can be dependent on temperature and moisture level. Notification: None required. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Pregnant animals should not be exposed to animals that are viremic. PI animals should be identified and removed from the herd. In cattle, once BVDV is present, all calves born over the next 12 months should be screened for PI. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Identify and remove PI individuals. Any off spring born to dams that were pregnant during the outbreak should be tested to insure that they are not PI and all new additions that may be at risk for infection with BVDV should undergo testing and quarantine prior to introduction to any artiodactyl species.

Young animals at weaning age and those in crowded conditions are especially susceptible; however, the disease does occur in adult animals, especially non-vaccinated pregnant ruminants. Positive serologic responses have been noted in free-ranging lowland tapirs in Brazil. Causative organism: Bovine alpha-Herpesvirus type 1 (BoHV-1) with subtypes 1.1 (Respiratory) - Infectious Bovine Rhinotracheitis (IBR), 1.2a (Genital) - Infectious Pustular Balanoposthitis (IPB) and Infectious Pustular Vulvovaginitis (IPV), and 1.3 (Encephalitic) (reclassified as BHV-5). Zoonotic potential: None.

Distribution: Worldwide distribution. Eradication is present in several countries with control measures in place in others. Incubation period: 2 to 6 days. Outbreaks reach a maximum intensity by the 2nd to 3rd week with most recovered by the 4th to 6th week. Uncomplicated BoHV-1 (IBR) can resolve in 4 to 5 days and BoHV-1 (IPB & IPV) in 10 to 14 days, if no secondary infections are present. Clinical signs: Early signs are a decrease in milk production and a decreased appetite. Respiratory signs can be seen at 2 to 3 days to include: pyrexia, dullness, salivation, discharge from the eyes, "Red Nose" i.e. ulceration of the mouth and nose, serous to mucopurulent nasal discharge; halitosis, coughing, and respiratory distress. These signs can last up to 10 days. Secondary infections are possible and can lead to bronchopneumonia. Ophthalmic signs include conjunctivitis with an ocular discharge and corneal opacity, or panophthalmitis. Reproductive signs include erosions, ulcers, pustules, and vesicles on the vaginal mucosa, penis, and prepuce.

Mid- to late-term abortions via viral transport in the WBCs to the placenta which can occur up to 100 days post exposure with infection of the dam and genital tract. Infertility and birth defects have also been seen. Neonates may present with a generalized infection with clinical signs of pyrexia, ocular and nasal discharges, respiratory distress, diarrhea, incoordination, convulsions, and possibly death over a short time period. IBR has been associated with a high mortality rate in calves (< 1 month of age) with no preceding signs. However, this virus mainly affects those greater than 6 months of age. IPB lesions are seen on the penis and prepuce. Initial sign of IPV is vaginal discomfort, i.e. frequent urination with a raised tail. Numerous round, white, raised lesions of the vestibular mucosa that can progress to pustules, erosions, and ulcers leading to mucopurulent discharge. Clinical signs can be observed within 1 to 3 days of mating. Subclinical infections can occur.

The virus can become latent in the trigeminal ganglion, possibly in the tonsils, and peripheral blood leukocytes. Severe cases presenting with purulent rhinotracheitis and pneumonia can result in death. Uncomplicated respiratory cases can recover in 4 to 5 days after clinical signs are seen and after 10 to 14 days for genital cases. Postmortem, gross, or histologic findings: Upper respiratory tract and trachea: petechial to ecchymotic hemorrhages are observed in the mucous membranes of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses. Focal areas of necrosis are present in the nose, pharynx, larynx, and trachea which may join to form plaques. The sinuses can be filled with a serous to a serofibrinous exudate that may extend into the pharynx with blood tinged fluid later seen in the trachea. The pharyngeal and pulmonary lymph nodes may become swollen and hemorrhagic. If the tracheitis extends into the bronchi and bronchioles, the epithelium can be sloughed into the airways.

Nasal lesions consist of clusters of gray necrotic foci on the mucous membranes of the septal mucosa and/or with pseudo-diphtheritic yellow plaques. Neonates may have erosions and ulcers with debris in the nose, esophagus, and forestomachs with white foci in the liver, kidneys, spleen, and lymph nodes. Aborted fetuses may have multifocal, pale, necrotic, foci throughout the kidneys, spleen, lymph nodes, and especially the liver. Necrotizing vasculitis can be present in the placenta. Necrosis of the vaginal and vestibular epithelium with intranuclear inclusion bodies and a necrotizing endometritis and cervicitis can be seen with IPV. Immunologic staining of the kidneys, lung, placenta, adrenal glands, and especially the liver for diagnosis. Diagnosis: For acute cases, PCR may be performed and is the most reliable. RT-PCR can be used for aborted and infected fetuses.

A virus neutralization test can be used with paired serum antibody titers at least 2 weeks apart, except in abortion cases as the titer is already at its highest level. ELISA for an antibody titer with a concurrent rise is available with the indirect ELISA more commonly used over the competitive ELISA. Indirect hemagglutination and complement fixation serology can also be performed. Virus isolation via swabs of nasal fluids or vaginal secretions at the early onset of disease is possible. Cell Culture. Immunoperoxidase, virus isolation, and fluorescent antibody staining on fetal tissues can be performed in abortion cases. Swabs from individuals with corneal lesions can be used to detect IBR. Gross lesions at necropsy and histopathology. Material required for laboratory analysis: Nasal fluids, serum, plasma, milk, placenta, and/or tissues, for example the liver. Relevant diagnostic laboratories: Any state laboratory can perform the testing.

Treatment: While no treatment for the virus itself exists, secondary bacterial infections can be treated with antibiotics and supportive care. Most respiratory cases recover in 4 to 5 days if secondary infections are not present, while genital cases can take 10 to 14 days to recover.

- ∞ Vaccination with a modified live vaccine (MLV) given IM or IN is possible. MLV given IM during pregnancy may cause abortions, especially in the third to eighth month of gestation, therefore a MLV is best administered twice before breeding with the second administration occurring 30 days prior to pre-breeding and the next vaccination within 12 months afterwards. The MLV is not safe for nursing calves unless the dam has been vaccinated within the last year and at pre-breeding with the same vaccine. Vaccinating with an inactivated multivalent vaccine given IM will protect against abortions if given prior to breeding. The use of the IN vaccine may be helpful for: a local rapid immune response; in those that are already pregnant; and may prevent new cases in an outbreak as long as the individuals vaccinated are not showing any clinical symptoms at the time of IN vaccination. - ∞ Inactivated and attenuated-live vaccines may not prevent infection, but they can reduce clinical signs and can significantly reduce shedding of the virus.

Inactivated vaccines in exotic hoofstock may be preferred, because of abortions and initiation of disease, however, this has not been appropriately studied. - ∞ A killed vaccine can also be used. - ∞ For control it is important to vaccinate at 6 to 8 months of age, 2 to 3 weeks before introduction into the herd, prior to breeding, and annually thereafter. Quarantine all new individuals for 4 weeks after arriving, with testing for IBR before arrival and before entrance into the herd. It is important to remember that the spread of the virus is affected by the host, the surrounding environment, and management of clinical cases. Eradication can be attempted by serologic surveillance, removing any seropositive reactors, biosecurity, and vaccination. The best way to differentiate between the natural virus versus a vaccine titer is to use ELISA to test for Glycoprotein E (gE).

The best way to differentiate between the natural virus versus a vaccine titer is to use ELISA to test for Glycoprotein E (gE). gE is present in natural infections, however, newer "marker" (deletion mutant) vaccines have deleted gE from their make-up. Caution must be used as conventional vaccines still contain gE and can cause a false seropositive result. Currently, BoHV-1 is eradicated in Austria, Denmark, Finland, Sweden, Switzerland, and Norway. Operations to control the virus are present in Australia, Belgium, India, Poland, Turkey, Canada, and the United States. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: As an enveloped virus, it can be managed by lipid solvents, bleach, hydrogen peroxides, formalin, quaternary ammonium compounds, and phenol derivatives. This virus is also inactivated by UV light and heat.

Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: A period of 2-3 weeks after the illness starts should be waited before introducing any new individuals into the herd. Viral particles can still be seen in nasal secretions throughout this time. All new arrivals into the herd must be vaccinated prior to entry and then revaccinated in 3 months and again at 6 months. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Serologic testing to detect any seropositive individuals. Removal of these individuals and/or creating 2 separate herds. The animals that fully recover from this disease will have long-term immunity to future outbreaks. Experts who may be consulted: Any state veterinarian.
