Susceptible animal groups: Ungulates (cattle, bison, buffalo, elk, goats, sheep, reindeer, camel, etc.), swine, carnivores, rodents, pinnipeds, cetaceans, horses, and humans. Causative organism: Brucella species generally have a preferred natural host but will frequently infect other hosts. Brucella abortus (cattle and humans) is the primary causative agent. However, there are other Brucellae that include: B. melitensis (small ruminants and cattle) although it is not present in US, this organism has been seen in humans in the US from imported non-pasteurized dairy products. B. ovis (small ruminants), B. suis (swine, reindeer - biovarian 4, cattle), B. canis (dogs), B. neotomae (rodents), B. microti (boars, voles, and foxes), B. vulpis (red foxes), B. papionis (baboons), B. ceti (cetaceans), B. pinnipedialis (pinnipeds), B. inopinata (humans, frogs), and B. amazoniensis (humans). Brucellae are gram negative non-enteric facultative intracellular coccobacilli. Zoonotic potential: Relatively high. Distribution: World-wide, although regionally it is limited in North America (Greater Yellowstone Area - B. abortus in bison and elk).

intracellular coccobacilli. Zoonotic potential: Relatively high. Distribution: World-wide, although regionally it is limited in North America (Greater Yellowstone Area - B. abortus in bison and elk). Brucella suis transmitted from feral swine is increasingly occurring in cattle housed in the southeast US. Increasingly B. melitensis is occurring in cattle in central Asia and the Middle East. Incubation period: Quite variable, 2 weeks to 1 year or longer.

- ∞ Abortion, weak calves, neonatal death, placentitis, endometritis, epididymitis, seminal vesiculitis, orchitis, testicular abscess, and spondylitis may occur. Often, no other outward clinical signs. Chronically infected animals may be "poor doers". In horses, infection may produce "fistulous withers". - ∞ In humans, severe "flu-like" signs, fatigue, headache, fever, chills, night sweats, joint pain, backache, weight and appetite decreases, spontaneous improvement but recrudesces ("undulant fever"). More severe signs in humans can include endocarditis, meningitis, and osteomyelitis. In cattle, B.suis does not appear to cause abortions in cattle but does colonize the mammary gland with subsequent high CFU within milk.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: - ∞ Aborted fetus: autolysis (common intra-uterine death), subcutaneous edema, serosanguineous fluid in body cavities (peritoneum, pericardium and pleura), possible splenoand hepatomegaly, pneumonia. Placentitis (inflamed or necrotic cotyledons), "leathery" intercotyledonary zones. - ∞ Adults: granulomatous to purulent inflammation of reproductive tract, hygromas, draining tracts, retained placenta.

- ∞ Serology (agglutination - screening; FPA, BAPA, BMAT, and CF - confirmatory; ELISA - available), Milk ring Test (BRT), perhaps bacterial isolation, newer PCR tests are available. There are ELISA tests available for both milk and serum. The card test may be used as an official test to classify reactors in certain circumstances. - ∞ Culture, PCR, and experimental dot blot assay have been used to differentiate infection caused by RB51 vaccine vs. wild-type B. abortus in cattle. - ∞ Presumptive tests: Buffered acidified plate antigen (BAPA), Rapid automated presumptive (BAP), fluorescent polarization assay (FPA). - ∞ Confirmatory tests: Culture of the organism is the "Gold Standard" for diagnosis. Confirmatory tests include standard tube agglutination test, Rivanol test, complement fixation test (CF), particle concentration fluorescence immunoassay (PCFIA), semen plasma test, and standard plate test. 9 CFR Ch. Culture of fetal membranes, fetal stomach contents, many fetal organs, vaginal secretions, milk, semen, arthritis or hygroma fluids (not often successful). Relevant Diagnostic lab: Samples are to be tested for brucellosis only in cooperative State-Federal brucellosis laboratories or by persons who are authorized by Program officials to conduct the tests. See "Brucellosis Eradication: Uniform Methods and Rules" by the USDA APHIS. Treatment: None in ruminants. Causative organism: The etiological agent is a misfolded prion protein (PrP TSE ), which acts as a template to induce normal prion protein molecules to cascade into the same misfolded configuration. Infectivity is associated with an aggregate (or polymer) of 14-28 misfolded protein molecules, and an as yet unidentified host molecule (?chaperone, ganglioside, non-coding RNA) is probably necessary as a cofactor in replication. The degree of similarity in the primary structure of the protein in different species influences the ease with which the protein can induce inter-species disease. In the classical form, disease is transmitted through the feeding of prion-infected tissue from a diseased to a healthy host. This has also resulted in zoonotic transmission of BSE when humans consumed BSEcontaminated meat products, resulting in human variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Until 2004, it appeared that a single "strain" caused all cases of BSE. It is now known that there are at least two additional strains called L-Type and H-Type atypical BSE. Much less is known about atypical BSE. In atypical BSE, the development of disease is rare, unassociated with the consumption of infected tissues, and appears to occur spontaneously in older cattle. Almost all cases have been in older cattle (usually > 8 years of age) that have shown little resemblance to the clinic-pathological picture seen in classical disease. It has been suggested that the disease may be caused by a genetic mutation or environmental factors, but this is still currently under study.

Secondary human to human vCJD transmission has been observed through blood and blood products, and there is potential risk via organs and tissues, or contaminated surgical instruments and medical devices.

Distribution: The first cases of BSE were recognized in the United Kingdom in 1986 and because of recycling of offal into animal feed, the disease rapidly became epidemic in the UK and spread to most other European countries via the trade of contaminated meat and bone meal and infected animals that entered slaughter channels. Worldwide, the number of cases at the end of 2012 was approximately 190,000, all but 6,000 of which were within the UK. In addition to the officially reported and confirmed cases, it is estimated that as many as 3.5 million animals were infected and may have entered the food and feed chains in the UK without being detected. BSE has also been detected in Brazil (atypical), Canada, Falkland Islands (import), Israel, Japan, Oman (import) and the US (import and atypical). Incubation period: The incubation period for BSE is measured in years and in cattle can range from 28 years. Clinical signs: Affected animals develop a progressive degeneration of the nervous system. They may display changes in temperament, abnormalities of posture and movement, and changes in sensation, including signs of apprehension, nervousness or aggression, incoordination, especially hind-limb ataxia, tremor and difficulty in rising, and hyperesthesia to sound and touch. In addition, many animals have decreased milk production and loss of body condition despite continued appetite. Only a small proportion of affected cattle exhibit what would be considered typical "mad cow" signs. BSE can be mistaken for other conditions or go unnoticed due to subtlety of the signs. The TSE cases in exotic ruminants had a younger onset age and a shorter clinical duration compared to that in cattle with BSE. Clinical signs in the exotic ungulates are similar to those seen in cattle and include ataxia and wasting. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: No gross pathological lesions are found in animals affected with BSE and histological changes appear to be confined to the CNS. The primary lesions found are non-inflammatory vacuolation of neuronal perikarya and grey-matter neuropil and are usually bilaterally symmetric. Astrocytosis may also be observed. Infected animals may not manifest these lesions until end stage disease. Histological changes that are seen in cattle are similar to those seen in the other animal species affected by Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies (TSEs) caused by abnormally misfolded prions. -  Given that the primary, if not sole, route of BSE transmission is through the feeding of contaminated meat-and bone-meal (MBM) to cattle, countries with any risk factors need to implement feed controls. The level of restriction is usually dependent upon the amount of contamination thought to be in the system. Three main factors can increase the stability of a national feed production system: -  Feed bans - these regulations can range from the basic prohibition of feeding ruminant MBM back to ruminants; to prohibiting most animal proteins from being fed to all animals used for food production, including fish. -  Specified Risk Materials (SRMs) ban - this ban requires that high infectivity tissues such as bovine brain and spinal cord be removed from both the food and feed chain and be destroyed. The intent of this control is to remove the primary source of infectivity from the entire system to prevent the possibility of cross-contamination. -  Regulation of rendering - although no rendering process can completely remove all detectable infectivity, some are more effective than others. The best procedure identified to date requires 133°C at 3 bars of pressure for 20 minutes.

No complacency can be tolerated. -  Bovine products and byproducts are widely used for both food and pharmaceuticals, and hence require the highest level of safety. Because of the hardy nature of the BSE agent and its high potential for cross-contamination, the most effective approach to protect bovine products and bovine-derived materials for human use from contamination by BSE is to ensure that infected animals or carcasses never enter processing plants.

Because there are presently no diagnostic tools sensitive enough for detection of the disease during its long preclinical incubation, governments must rely on measures to prevent exposure through feed (see above) or prohibit high risk tissues (SRMs) from being used for food or pharmaceuticals. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: BSE is not known to spread horizontally between cattle or other animals or from environmental reservoirs; hence it is not necessary to disinfect a premise where infected cattle have been. Regarding BSE, the need for disinfection may arise in diagnostic laboratories, food processing and pharmaceutical manufacturing plants. Like other prions, the BSE prion demonstrates the property of unusual resistance to destruction. Many of the standard disinfection methods are ineffective, including irradiation or exposure to various chemical disinfectants.

Even harsher conditions that are capable of inactivating all other known pathogens (including bacterial spores), such as heating under pressure at 121°C, exposure to dry heat at 600°C, or immersion in 0.1 N NaOH or 0.5% bleach cannot assure complete inactivation. Currently, the only procedures known to completely eliminate detectable infectivity are exposure to dry heat at 1000°C, immersion in either 1 N NaOH or fresh undiluted bleach, and steam heating under pressure at 134°C. The preferred method is a sequential exposure to both NaOH and steam autoclaving inactivation treatments. Notification: BSE is a reportable disease in the US. Cytoplasmic inclusion bodies in the gastric mucosa and bile ducts and diffuse interstitial giant cell pneumonia often followed by suppurative bronchopneumonia. Often lymphoid depletion, diffuse interstitial pneumonia, and perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltration in areas of demyelination and neuronal degeneration of the CNS. Causative organism: enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses of the Family Poxviridae, Genus Capripoxvirus. While it is recognized that sheep pox virus and goat pox virus are different, but related viruses, both agents can infect either sheep or goats causing a disease that is clinically and pathologically identical. These viruses are closely related to lumpy skin disease virus, a capripoxvirus that infects cattle; all three are serologically indistinguishable.

Distribution: Endemic in Middle East, Indian subcontinent, Africa (north and central), and Asia including parts of China, Russia, and Mongolia. This disease is one of the most actively spreading diseases affecting small ruminants during the last 5-10 years. Incubation period: 4-21 days but usually 1-2 weeks. Clinical signs: Infection can range from mild or asymptomatic cases to severely ill animals with numerous internal and external lesions. -  Pyrexia usually precedes skin lesions. -  Skin lesions start as erythematous macules and progress to hard papules. The center of the papules become depressed and turns a whitish grey color. The area then becomes necrotic and is surrounded by an area of hyperemia. Necrotic skin lesions culminate in scabs that leave a scar after scab loss. Lesions are usually easier to find in areas of the body that have sparse hair (i.e., muzzle, ears, axillary or inguinal areas and under the tail). Mucous membranes can develop similar lesions that may become necrotic. Lymphadenopathy, dyspnea, nasal discharge and conjunctivitis also can occur. -  In endemic areas, the disease can be mild or the infection subclinical.

-  Humans: Generally, an occupational disease in veterinarians, farmers, and slaughterhouse workers. Animal exposure in petting zoos is another source of human infection. Humans can also become exposed to the virus by exposure to sheep and goat vaccines containing live Orf virus. Viral transmission may be facilitated by biting insects. Human to human transmission is rare. Orf virus causes scabs and wart-like lesions on the hands and arms and less often in the face and genitalia of people handling infected animals. Lesions progress quickly from erythema, papule, vesicle, pustule until they become crusty lesions. People whose immune systems are compromised due to infection with HIV, lupus, or cancer therapy can develop serious symptoms following Orf virus infection. In uncomplicated cases, the lesions will heal in 2-6 weeks without scarring. -  Animals: Skin lesions consist of erythema, papules, vesicles, pustules, crusts, scabs and papillomatous wart-like growths. Occasionally, lesions can develop in the oral cavity, esophagus and forestomachs. Histologically, Orf lesions are characterized by papillomatous, hyperplastic dermatitis with acanthosis, parakeratotic hyperkeratosis, ballooning degeneration, and subcorneal vesicles and pustules. Eosinophilic intracytoplasmic viral inclusions may be found in the stratum spinosum in some cases.

The affected epidermis may be eroded with replacement by a thick serocellular crust, foreign debris, and large numbers of mixed bacteria. Within the dermis, there is capillary proliferation, edema, and infiltration of neutrophils, macrophages and lymphocytes.

-  Skin biopsies of lesions or scab material should be submitted for diagnosis at room temperature or refrigerated in sealed, leak-proof, sterile, plastic bags or containers for transmission electron microscopic (TEM) examination or for testing by real time PCR (rtPCR). Skin biopsies for histopathology need to be submitted in 10% neutral buffered formalin. Members of the Parapoxvirus genus are morphologically distinguished by TEM from other poxviruses (sheeppox virus, goatpox virus) by their ovoid shape and their relatively small size (about 260 nm in length). Other parapoxviruses including bovine papular stomatitis virus, pseudocowpox virus, parapox virus of red deer and squirrel parapoxvirus, are indistinguishable by TEM. Currently, real time PCR (rtPCR) is the most common diagnostic test. rtPCR and sequencing of viral DNA is required to differentiate Orf virus from other parapoxviruses. -  Numerous molecular diagnostic methods including loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), multiplex PCR, duplex fluorescent microsphere immunoassay (FMIA) and other molecular tests have not been validated for routine Orf virus diagnosis but may play a role in the future.

Orf virus isolation using different tissue culture systems and embryonated chicken eggs are potential options; however, the growth rate of ORFV can be slow and variable. -  Differential diagnoses include other vesicular or proliferative disorders including capripox and sheep poxviruses, papilloma viruses, bluetongue virus, foot and mouth disease, dermatophilosis and pearmouth (dermatitis of lips and muzzle causes by ingestion of prickly pear cactus). Material required for laboratory analysis: Scabs and biopsies of lesions, fresh or refrigerated for TEM or rtPCR, or skin biopsies fixed in 10% buffered formalin for histopathology. Relevant Diagnostic lab: Laboratories capable of performing transmission electron microscopy of skin biopsies and scabs can identify to the level of parapoxvirus.

Treatment: Lesions are generally self-limiting, but in some severe cases supportive care and antibacterial therapy for secondary infections is indicated. The antiviral drug cidofovir has been used with some success in the treatment of some poxvirus infections. However, little if any benefit was subjectively noted during a course of intravenous treatment of cidofovir in two muskox calves as compared to an untreated herd mate. An experimental trial using topical spray of cidofovir, sucralfate and sodium dihydrogen phosphate has shown benefit in sheep and cidofovir cream has been useful to treat lesions in people. In severe, unresponsive cases (malignant Orf) prognosis is poor and without extensive supportive care, the severity of progressive lesions often necessitates humane euthanasia. Prevention and control: Vaccination should not be used in areas where the disease has not occurred.

In endemic areas, sheep and goats may be vaccinated with live virus vaccine which can be obtained from Colorado Serum Company, Denver, CO, USA; 303-295-7527. The vaccine is an attenuated live virus product which can cause disease in naïve animals and in susceptible species and people. Experimental viral vector vaccines and recombinant DNA and subunit vaccines have been developed and are considered promising candidates, but it is unlikely that they will be licensed for animal use soon. Neither natural infection nor vaccination confers long-term immunity, but subsequent infections are generally less severe. Vaccines are more protective when developed from virus obtained from the same species infected. Infected animals should be isolated if scab material is present. Orf virus is environmentally resistant and has been recovered for up to 12 years in wool and contaminated material in cool dry climates.

Survival may be shorter in wet conditions Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Removal and incineration or burial of organic material. Sunlight, heat, and humidity lead to more rapid inactivation of Orf virus, but the virus may persist for months to years if frozen or present in cool, dry locations. Sodium hypochlorite and two quaternary ammonium-based commercial disinfectants are effective against Orf virus with proper concentration and contact time. Ethanol is ineffective. Organic debris will decrease disinfectant efficacy. Steam sterilization and dry heat at 59°C for 30 minutes may also be utilized for decontamination. Notification: Public health officials may need to be notified if zoonotic transmission occurs, depending on the state. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: Currently none Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Maintain infected animals in a quarantine situation until lesions have healed and scabs have been lost.

Orf virus can be carried by clinically normal sheep; it is reported to remain viable on the wool and hides for approximately one month after the lesions have healed. If feasible may want to bathe infected animals to remove all virus from fur. Do not introduce infected animals to an animal with a compromised immune system. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Wait for all scabs to be lost from infected animals. Remove bedding and biological material to the extent possible and disinfect with sodium hypochlorite and two quaternary ammonium-based commercial disinfectants.

Distribution: Worldwide -  US, Canada, Europe - up to 81% seroprevalence (especially in long-established dairy herds) -  Southern Africa - "relatively free" of CAE. Incubation period: Seroconversion occurs in 2-8 weeks, but disease may be clinically latent for years. Once an animal is infected, it remains infected for life. Clinical signs: Seen in 10-20% of seropositive animals in their lifetime -  Arthritis - Chronic, progressive; goats > 6 mo of age; progressive lameness. Swelling of carpal joints most common and preferentially may affect hocks, stifles, hips, and atlantooccipital joints. Radiographs show soft tissue swelling and periarticular calcification. -  Interstitial pneumonia - chronic, more common in adults -  Mastitis - indurative ("hard udder"), hypogalactia or agalactia around parturition in young does -  Chronic wasting - poor body condition, rough hair coat -  Leukomyeloencephalitis - Typically kids 2-4 mo of age but may be seen in adults; ataxia progressing to tetraparesis; blindness, head tilt, facial paralysis, hypertonia/reflexia, opisthotonos may occur. Clinical course 1-2 weeks. Very poor prognosis for recovery.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: - Arthritis - thickened joint capsule, periarticular mineralization; chronic lymphoproliferative synovitis with subsynovial mononuclear infiltrates. - Interstitial pneumonia - firm, nodular lymphoid aggregates; proliferation of smooth muscle; massive infiltration of the alveolar walls by lymphoid cells; hypertrophy of bronchial lymph nodes - Mastitis - Inflammatory cell foci within interstitium. Extensive nodular lymphoid proliferation can be observed around the alveolar ducts. In chronic cases, mononuclear infiltration and connective tissue replace the normal parenchyma. - Leukomyeloencephalitis - increased protein concentration in CSF with mononuclear pleocytosis. Asymmetrical foci of discoloration in the brain and/or spinal cord. Widespread perivascular infiltration by mononuclear cells. Coagulative necrosis & demyelination.

However, negative test results do not reliably rule out CAE virus infection, because the time for post-infection seroconversion is variable and occasional goats have a very low titer that may not be detectable (rare). Low antibody titers are common in late pregnancy. -  ELISA -  PCR. - Synovial fluid analysis - red/brown color with low viscosity; increased cell count, with the majority mononuclear cells (lymphocytes); synovial biopsy for histopathology. -  Quarantine or cull affected and seropositive animals. Serologic testing of herd recommended every 6 mo, beginning with kids at 6 mo of age. Test co-housed sheep for OPP and separate positives from goats. -  Remove kids from affected dams immediately after parturition, and keep them isolated from older animals. Feed newborns heat-treated (56-59oC for 1 hour-DO NOT exceed 60oC) colostrum immediately, then raise kids on pasteurized goat or cow milk, milk from CAEVnegative goats, or milk replacer. Caesarean section may help prevent vertical transmission. Milk CAEV does last in dairy herds. Chemical disinfection of equipment. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Phenolic and quaternary ammonium compounds Notification: Reportable for disease monitoring to the World Organization for Animal Health (OIE), USDA APHIS, and many state veterinarians. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Not recommended Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: No seropositive animals remaining in herd after two successive testing periods. Causative organism: Chlamydia abortus (previously known as Chlamydia psittaci serotype 1, or Chlamydophila abortus) is a Gram-negative intracellular replicating bacterium which belongs to the Chlamydia genus of the Chlamydiacea family. When this organism causes abortion, it is commonly referred to as enzootic abortion in sheep and goats. This infectious organism is known as one of the most common abortion causing bacteria for sheep and goats in the United States. Zoonotic potential: Yes, Chlamydia abortus infections have the potential to cause serious infections in pregnant women and may lead to miscarriage. Pregnant women are discouraged from having contact with the flock/herd during lambing/kidding season. In non-pregnant humans, infection can produce flu-like symptoms.

and may lead to miscarriage. Pregnant women are discouraged from having contact with the flock/herd during lambing/kidding season. In non-pregnant humans, infection can produce flu-like symptoms. It is recommended that when people work with sheep and goats during parturition, to wear personal protective equipment (PPE) to reduce their exposure of the infectious organism found in uterine fluid, the placenta, and fetal tissues. Distribution: World-wide distribution. Incubation period: Infection occurs through oronasal ingestion and/or inhalation of the organism from aborted tissues, vaginal discharge, and or contaminated neonates/enviroments. The Chlamydia abortus organism naturally colonizes and multiplies in the intestinal tract but can also be found to multiple in the genital tract or conjunctiva as well as cells of the reticulo-endothelial system. This organism can invade the bloodstream and subsequently infect the placenta and developing fetus causing inflammation and necrosis of these tissues, leading to abortion of the fetus. Incubation can be as short as 2 weeks, although typically proliferation of the organism occurs at about day 90 of gestation.

Infection may be latent in lambs and non-pregnant ewes and may become activated at conception. Be mindful that Chlamydia pecorum may also can also colonize the gastrointestinal and reproductive tracts but more commonly cause polyarthritis, encephalomyelitis, pneumonia, and diarrhea. Abortions are less commonly caused by C. pecorum. Clinical signs: Non-specific malaise and transient fever of the dam may be seen. Dams may develop pneumonia or hepatitis at the time of abortion, due to this pathogen, will display clinical signs of anorexia, be febrile, and have abnormal vaginal discharge. Abortion within the last two months of pregnancy, stillbirth, or birth of weak offspring does occur with Chlamydia abortus infections. Abortions in all ages and all parities can occur when a flock/herd is first exposed to the organism, but it is usually the primiparous females that are affected in endemic scenarios (1-15% abortion rate).

in all ages and all parities can occur when a flock/herd is first exposed to the organism, but it is usually the primiparous females that are affected in endemic scenarios (1-15% abortion rate). An abortion rate of up to 60% can occur when a naïve flock/herd is exposed to this pathogen. Final trimester abortions may occur in ewes infected at 5-6 weeks of gestation. Abortion in a subsequent pregnancy may happen if there is insufficient time for placental damage to occur (~40 days) during the current pregnancy following infection (otherwise known as a latent infection). Abortion can occur at any time during gestation for goats but is usually observed in the last two months (particularly seen in the last two weeks) of pregnancy. In both species, fetuses typically appear to be fresh and retained placenta can rarely occur. Normal fertility in dams typically returns following an abortion if there are no complications but there are thoughts that dam immunity may wane and future abortions may occur. Rams may become infected with Chlamydia and isolation of the organism has been found in the semen and genital organs. The infection in rams may also cause orchitis.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: -  Gross: Placental tissues are of immense diagnostic importance in Chlamydia abortus abortions. These infected placental tissues contain multifocal to coalescing areas of red discoloration and are edematous. The tissues can have a thick, leathery appearance as well. Changes are typically diffuse but more significant changes may be noted in the cotyledonary rather than the intercotyledonary areas. The aborted fetus is often well preserved although can be autolyzed; it may have multifocal areas of hemorrhage in muscle, lymphoid tissues, and the subcutis as well as pinpoint yellow areas of discoloration on the surface of the liver, which may also be enlarged. -  Histology: Placental changes histologically are characterized by fibrinoid vascular necrosis, thrombosis, and severe neutrophilic, lymphocytic and macrophagic infiltration (placentitis) particularly at the hilar region. Superficial necrosis and the presence of elementary bodies in the epithelium of the chorion tissues are seen.

texto: lymphocytic and macrophagic infiltration (placentitis) particularly at the hilar region. Superficial necrosis and the presence of elementary bodies in the epithelium of the chorion tissues are seen. Trophoblasts often contain numerous intracytoplasmic organisms that distend the cells, which are difficult to see with routine hematoxylin/eosin staining and are positive with special staining using a modified ZiehlNeelsen, Gimenez, or Giemsa stain. Vasculitis is significant and may help distinguish this infection from a Coxiella infection. Changes in the aborted fetus are few and characterized by foci of coagulative necrosis in the liver and spleen that may be associated with peripheral mononuclear cell inflammation. Mild subacute inflammation can be seen in the lungs and mild meningoencephalitis has also been reported.

-  History of abortion or previous Chlamydia abortus infections within a flock or herd provides suspicion for perform testing for Chlamydia abortus. -  Serology: Several commercial ELISA tests are available for chlamydia diagnosis in sheep and goats. When choosing an appropriate ELISA for a specific diagnostic issue, it's essential to consider variations in specificity and sensitivity. ELISAs based on LPS or EB antigens cannot distinguish between C. pecorum and C. abortus infections. For specific detection of anti-C. abortus antibodies, ELISAs using synthetic peptides of MOMP, recombinant MOMP, or POMP90 have been developed. An indirect ELISA based on POMP90 has been commercialized, demonstrating high sensitivity and specificity for C. abortus, especially in differentiating animals infected with C. pecorum. Complement Fixation (CF) has been used in the past but is less commonly utilized due to more false-positives tests due to cross reactions with C. pecorum. -  Tissue sections: Used for histology and electron microscopy.

(CF) has been used in the past but is less commonly utilized due to more false-positives tests due to cross reactions with C. pecorum. -  Tissue sections: Used for histology and electron microscopy. -  Special staining: Positive staining of organisms with modified Ziehl-Neelsen, Gimenez, or Giemsa in cytologic preparations or placenta; alternatively, can try to identify the organism on cytology of a vaginal swab. To improve diagnostic results, vaginal swabs should be taken within 3 days of an abortion event. -  Definitive diagnosis: Species-specific real-time PCR, PCR microarray hybridization, indirect inclusion fluorescent antibody test, immunohistochemical staining, tissue culture or egg inoculation. C. abortus specific PCR assays provide a definitive diagnosis from fresh placenta (best sample type), fetal stomach content, and fetal tissue sample types. PCR provides high sensitivity and specificity on vaginal swab sample types as well.

-  Placental tissue are preferred and/or fetal tissues: Fresh tissue for cytologic preps; 10% neutral buffered formalin fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) tissue for histology or immunohistochemical staining; fresh (or FFPE) for PCR, or cell culture. Contact the referral laboratory for tissue storage/fixation for fluorescent antibody testing. -  Vaginal swab, within 3-7 days post-abortion, for PCR, cell culture, and/or cytology. -  Sera from aborted animals: For ELISA testing as described above.

-  Chlamydia abortus is sensitive to tetracyclines although sensitivity testing on cultured organism may aid treatment strategy. In face of outbreak, recommendations include treating all pregnant females during final 4-6 weeks of gestation. -  For disease prevention in large flocks or herds, a two-week treatment with oral oxytetracycline or chlortetracycline in feed (400 to 500 mg/head/day) is suitable as a flock/herd approach remembering that this course of therapy will need a Veterinary Feed Directive (VFD) in place. This approach is not ideal for milking flocks/herds used for human consumption as milk will have to be discarded and not used for human consumption due to the milk withdrawal period. Administration of injectable of long-acting oxytetracycline (20 mg/kg IM or SC) every 10-14 days until parturition or a twice a week treatment in the last 4-6 weeks gestation in dairy herds has been reported in outbreak senarios. Another antibiotic that has been used in outbreak situations is Tylosin. Alternately, animals may be treated with one injection of long-acting oxytetracycline 6 to 8 weeks prior to parturition and 3 weeks post parturition.

Chlamydia abortus has been shown to be susceptible to both chloramphenicol and rifampin, antibiotics used in other countries, but their use is restricted in the United States.

-  Environmental hygiene is critical in reducing the spread to susceptible animals (ie. Newborns, Uninfected pregnant dams) -  As high numbers of organisms are shed in aborted or stillborn fetuses and in infected placental tissues or uterine discharge; and organisms remain viable for several days or longer in cold or freezing temperatures, isolate aborting dams (for several weeks) and separate first lambing/kidding dams from rest of flock. Animals that abort develop natural immunity of ~3year duration. -  Infected or contaminated materials, such as fetuses, placentas, bedding material, farm equipment, etc. should be removed, destroyed (burned or buried), or cleaned and sanitized. Feed sources should be kept free of fecal material and animals should not be fed from the ground. Pest control should be practiced as transmission can occur via rodents and birds which can also serve as a reservoir for this organism. -  Vaccination: Live (available in Europe) and inactivated (killed) vaccines are available for use (with some sporadic availabilities) in areas where vaccination is permitted. Vaccination reportedly can prevent abortion and reduce excretion.

Vaccination can assist in control but will not eradicate/eliminate the infection from a flock/herd. Vaccinations should NOT be considered 100% effective. -  Vaccination of all animals including breeding males may occur prior to breeding season to reduce incidence of abortions. -  Most vaccinations are labeled for sheep. Administering these vaccines to goats would be considered off label. Adverse side effects have been described in goats as experiencing marked soreness and stiffness -  Especially in endemic flocks/herds annual revaccination is recommended as well as vaccination of the doelings and yearling ewes. -  Culling individuals that have had previous abortions due to C. abortus may be a (aggressive) means of controlling this infection within a flock/herd.

secao: Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak:
texto: -  The following are requirements of the OIE Terrestrial Code: 1. Sheep flock or goat herd is under official veterinary surveillance; 2. No sheep or goats have shown clinical evidence of infection for past 2 years; 3. A statistically appropriate number of sheep/goats > 6 months of age were test negative for EAE within past 6 months; 4. All sheep, goats are permanently identified; 5. No sheep or goat has been added to the flock in the last 30 days prior to the flock/herd testing referred to in point 3 above unless: - either the additions were isolated from other members of the flock/herd in the establishment of origin for a minimum period of 30 days and then were subjected to a diagnostic test for EAE with negative results, before entry into the new flock/herd; or - they originated from an establishment of equal health status.

Variable, mild to fatal. Severity is typically worse in young animals and may vary between species Zoonotic? No Current update by Julie Ter Beest (2026) Reviewed by Richard R. Sim (2026)

- ∞ Definitive or natural host: White-tailed deer (WTD; Odocoileus virginianus) serve as the natural host and are rarely affected clinically; they can shed numerous 1 st stage larvae in their feces. Up to 80-90% of WTD are infected in endemic regions. - ∞ Aberrant or dead-end hosts: Other cervid species (moose, caribou, mule deer, black-tailed deer, elk, sika deer); camelids (camels, llamas, alpacas); pronghorn; some bovids (many antelope species, bighorn sheep, Angora goats, bison, rarely domestic cattle); rarely equids (reported in domestic horses); rarely guinea pigs. Overall, these species rarely shed larvae in their feces. Disease significance: Mortalities in captive species; failed reintroduction of cervid species such as elk and caribou; suppression of elk and moose populations; suspected cause of moose population declines in central and eastern North America. Causative organism: Parelaphostrongylus tenuis, an extrapulmonary lungworm nematode. Also known as meningeal worm or brain worm. - ∞ The natural host (WTD) acquires the infection through accidental ingestion of terrestrial gastropods infected with 3 rd stage larvae.

nematode. Also known as meningeal worm or brain worm. - ∞ The natural host (WTD) acquires the infection through accidental ingestion of terrestrial gastropods infected with 3 rd stage larvae. The larvae migrate from the GI tract along spinal nerves, into the spinal cord, and develop into reproducing adult worms, then move to the

- meninges & cranial venous sinuses where they lay eggs. The eggs pass into the venous - circulation, develop into 1 st stage larvae in lung capillaries, and migrate into the lung tissue. These larvae are expectorated, swallowed, and passed in the feces. Terrestrial gastropods (snails and slugs) acquire larval infection with fecal contact, and the parasite develops into - the infective 3 rd stage larvae within this intermediate host. - ∞ In the aberrant host, infection is acquired by the same route. However, migration of the larvae in the spinal cord tends to be non-directional and larvae often die before reaching the brain. The aimless migration and larval death result in more local tissue damage as compared to the natural host. Larvae infrequently develop into reproductive adults in the aberrant host.

Distribution: Occurs throughout forested regions of eastern and central North America, concurrent with WTD populations. It is unclear why WTD of western North America and the southeastern coastal plains are not infected, though this is likely to relate to climatologic and ecological factors limiting transmission.

- ∞ Natural host: 82-137 days, inversely proportional to infection dose. - ∞ Aberrant host: 30-60 days; as short as 5 days reported in experimental infections. Clinical signs: Neurologic signs result from inflammatory lesions in the brain or spinal cord caused by larval migration, and may range from single-limb lameness or hindlimb paresis to head tilt, ataxia, circling, blindness, progressive loss of motor function, and death. Ocular signs associated with larval migration into the uvea have been reported. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Lesions in aberrant hosts consist primarily of inflammatory and degenerative changes within the brain and spinal cord. Histologic findings may include meningitis and encephalitis; perivascular cuffing with infiltrations of eosinophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells; migration tracks; focal traumatic malacia caused by developing nematodes; calcified larval remnants; gliosis; disruption of the ependyma; and neuronal and myelin degeneration. Eggs and larvae may occasionally be found in the leptomeninges, brain parenchyma, cranial nerve roots, or ocular tissues.

- Natural host: Modified Baermann technique for retrieving 1 st stage larvae from feces. PCR is necessary to differentiate P. tenuis from related species (P. andersoni; muscle worm). - Aberrant hosts: - o A serologic assay (ELISA) is available (University of Tennessee) that detects antibodies against 3 rd stage larvae in elk and moose; preliminary studies suggest it also works well in caribou; a modified test is under development to detect antibodies in domestic camelids. - o Ante-mortem CSF eosinophil percentage and concentration are sensitive and specific methods for diagnosing P. tenuis in camelids residing in endemic regions. - o Post-mortem diagnostics include PCR on tissues collected at necropsy, post-mortem recovery of adult worms, or identification of larvae in neurologic tissue.

- ∞ Captive species: Administration of anthelmintics every 4 -6 weeks to target 3 rd stage larvae before they migrate to neural tissue; minimize exposure of captive animals to gastropods by establishing gravel roads or other vegetation breaks to act as snail and slug barriers; use molluscicides with caution due to potential for environmental toxicity; allow non-susceptible species to initiate grazing on new or overgrown pastures; reduce WTD population and/or exclude with fencing. - ∞ Free-ranging species: Control of WTD population to reduce exposure. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Molluscicides (e.g., iron phosphate, sodium ferric EDTA, copper barriers) may be used with caution to target the intermediate host; older products (e.g., metaldehyde, methiocarb) are no longer recommended, as they are animal and environmental toxins. Notification: None. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None.

-  Natural infection: mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus), white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus), Rocky mountain elk/wapiti (Cervus canadensis nelsoni), red deer (Cervus elaphus elaphus), moose (Alces alces), sika deer (Cervus nippon), and reindeer (Rangifer tarandus tarandus). -  Experimental infection (intracerebral inoculation): muntjac (Muntiacus sp.), domestic cattle (Bos taurus), sheep (Ovis aries), fallow deer (Dama dama), domestic ferrets (Mustela putorius furo), mink (Mustela vison), hamsters, mice, squirrel monkeys (Saimiri sciureus), and voles of the genera Mictotus and Myodes. - o Lack of transmission to Cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis) was recently reported. Causative organism: A transmissible spongiform encephalopathy caused by a prion (infectious protein). Two prevalent strains with divergent biochemical characteristics have been identified and strain variation may occur. Direct animal-animal contact and contact via ingestion and inhalation of contaminated material from the environment is the primary route of transmission. Agent shed in feces, saliva, urine; other mechanisms (e.g., nasal secretions, milk) also are possible.

Contaminated environments, especially in places where cervids are in high densities (soil, mineral licks, feces, offal, carcass), can contribute to infections for years (i.e., scrapie 16+). Zoonotic potential: To date, no evidence of CWD transmission to humans has been reported. Some epidemiologic studies have focused on identifying human prion disease in hunter population presumed at increased risk for exposure to potentially CWD-infected deer or elk meat. In the last 60 or so years in regions where CWD is present and such exposure is known, no evidence of an increase in any neurodegenerative disease condition of humans has been identified. CWD prions have been found in muscle (meat), as well as other tissues of cervids, and could enter the food supply. While evidence presented to date is suggestive that CWD is not infecting humans, the possibility has not been ruled out.

Distribution: Maps of the current distribution of CWD in USA suggest gradual spread from original identification in Colorado, USA. As of this update, infection has been identified in free-ranging & captive cervids in 29 US states, 4 Canadian provinces, South Korea and Sweden, Finland, and Norway. Incubation period: Infected deer and elk can appear normal in the early stages of CWD and may take two or more years before they show clinical signs. -  Minimum incubation time in experimental infection: 15 months, but can exceed 25 and 60 months in deer & elk, respectively.

-  Early clinical signs are subtle and nonspecific: behavior changes (excitability, interaction with conspecifics, somnolence, periods of repetitive behavior, vacant facial expression). -  A few weeks to several months prior to death: emaciation, abnormal behavior, progressive weight loss, ataxia, tremors, blank facial expressions, excessive salivation, loss of appetite, excessive thirst and urination, listlessness, teeth grinding, abnormal head posture, and drooping ears are observed. -  End-stage: esophageal dilation, difficulty in swallowing results in aspiration pneumonia, disease is progressive and always fatal. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Changes on post-mortem due to CWD on late stage animals are emaciation and pneumonia. Histological changes have been shown to vary based on species, disease progression and genotype. Typically cellular changes start in the dorsal vagal nuclei in the obex region of the brain, and characteristically, degeneration and loss of neurons will be reported.

- Ante-mortem: IHC has historically been done on tonsil tissue biopsies, but is rarely done now and can be dangerous for the animal. Rectal-anal mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue biopsies can be another site for IHC. Additional testing methods such as real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC), protein misfolding cyclic amplification (PMCA) and additional samples/tissues types are in the process of being tested/validated. Diagnostic sensitivity and specificity can vary using ante-mortem samples, and should be accounted for when evaluating results. - Post-mortem: IHC or ELISA is used on obex (specifically parasympathetic vagal nucleus in the dorsal portion of the medulla oblongata at the obex), and the medial retropharyngeal lymph nodes. While Western Blot, RT-QuIC, and PMCA assays are available, IHC and ELISA are the only assays currently accepted officially by USDA. Material required for laboratory analysis: Cervid post-mortem sites of interest: brain (obex) and lymph tissues (medial retropharyngeal lymph nodes) Some laboratories will allow tonsil.

-  Free Ranging: Surveillance/monitoring programs testing hunter harvested, targeted, androad killed cervids; some studies suggest local population reduction in infected areas; bans on feeding (congregating) wild cervids; restrictions on transporting hunter-killed carcasses from enzootic regions; and transportation restrictions and monitoring of captive cervid operations will reduce transmission. Cooking or heat does not inactivate prions. Educational efforts is critical as management once disease has entered area has been very ineffective so prevention is paramount. -  Captive: Routine surveillance and testing of cervids (all species) held in zoo collections. Early detection and removal of infected individuals Depopulation of infected captive herds is recommended unless regular antemortem testing of remaining animals is possible and strict biocontainment is followed; however, ante-mortem testing has lower sensitivity than postmortem testing. Regulation of international and interstate movements of cervids and restricted importation of captive cervids. Consider antemortem testing of animals prior to movements. No effective vaccine at present. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Environmental contamination is a major concern in eradication and prevention in new cases. Prions are extremely resistant and resilient to heat, pH, ultraviolet, and disinfectants. The following have been reported to be effective: -  Sodium hypochlorite (household bleach, greater than 2% free chlorine) at 280 ml in 720 ml of water at room temperature, for one hour. -  Sodium hypochlorite (40%), 5 min soak; effective on stainless steel wire coated items. -  Sodium hydroxide (caustic soda, soda lye) at 38g in one liter of water at room temperature for one hour. - ∞ Microchiropteran bats and primarily hibernating species. In North America, little brown bats (Myotis lucifugus), tri-colored bats (Perimyotis subflavus), and northern long-eared bats (Myotis septentrionalis) are the most susceptible, with population decreases of 90% since the introduction of the pathogen. Other known susceptible species include big brown bat (Eptesicus fuscus), eastern small-footed bat (Myotis leibii), western long-eared bat (Myotis evotis), Indiana bat (Myotis sodalis), gray bat (Myotis grisescens), Yuma bat (Myotis yumanensis), fringed bat (Myotis thysanodes), long-legged bat (Myotis volans), and cave bat (Myotis velifer).

and pallid bat (Antrozous pallidus). - ∞ In Europe and Asia, 30 species of bats have been confirmed with WNS, and an additional 12 species have been detected with Pd but no diagnostic signs of WNS. It has been proposed that some Palearctic species, including Myotis myotis, co-evolved with the fungus and are thus better able to tolerate or clear infection. - ∞ For updates on affected species, see www.whitenosesyndrome.org. Causative organism: Pseudogymnoascus (formerly Geomyces) destructans is a psychrophilic (coldloving) fungus that forms asymmetrically curved conidia, and does not grow at temperatures above 20°C. The fungus is native to Europe and Asia and the isolate that was introduced to North America is of European origin (Ukraine). Two distinct fungal clades (Pd-1, Pd-2) occur in Europe and share the same geographic range while, to date, only a single clade (Pd-1) has been identified in North America. Zoonotic potential: Not likely; psychrophilic character of fungus makes warm hosts unsuitable, although related Geomyces species have been known to rarely induce superficial infection of the skin and nails in humans.

Not likely; psychrophilic character of fungus makes warm hosts unsuitable, although related Geomyces species have been known to rarely induce superficial infection of the skin and nails in humans. Distribution: Since its first diagnosis in a New York cave in early 2007, WNS has continued its spread across eastern North America with newly affected sites identified annually. At this sheet completion, WNS has been confirmed in hibernating bats in 42 U.S states and 10 Canadian provinces. Additionally, Pseudogymnoascus destructans has been found in 5 U.S states and 1 Canadian province without confirmation of disease to-date. The fungus remains viable in suitable underground environments year-round even in the absence of bats. WNS Occurrence Maps for North America are updated at least annually. The Pd fungus has also been found on bats or in caves across Europe and in Russia, Mongolia, and China, but without mass morbidity or mortality. Incubation period: In the wild, WNS occurs seasonally with the earliest confirmed case in late September and the latest confirmed cases detected through late June in northern latitudes.

Peak infections and mortality occur about 120 days after bats enter hibernation. Experimentally-induced infections result in epidermal pathology as early as 49 days and mortality as early as 88 days postinfection. Clinical signs: White-nose syndrome was named for the characteristic white fungal growth on the muzzles, pinnae, and wings of hibernating bats. However, this sign is not always apparent in bats with WNS, nor is it specific for the disease as other non-pathologic dermatophytes may have a similar appearance. Epidermal erosions and destruction of wing tissue by Pd cause disruptions in homeostasis resulting in dehydration, electrolyte imbalances and acid-base disturbances. Abnormal behaviors associated with WNS include increased frequency of arousal from torpor, movement to roosting areas near cave entrances or other exposed sites, and increased day flights from hibernacula during mid-winter.

with WNS include increased frequency of arousal from torpor, movement to roosting areas near cave entrances or other exposed sites, and increased day flights from hibernacula during mid-winter. This increased activity likely contributes to premature depletion of fat reserves seen in infected individuals. Bats with WNS may present with obvious damage to wing membranes (increased fragility, decreased elasticity, irregular pigmentation, and tears or holes in the patagium) as they emerge from hibernation and become euthermic. Wing damage may increase over the first few weeks post-emergence due to an excessive inflammatory response, but these lesions can heal completely by mid-summer (approximately 4-6 weeks). Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Visible white fungal material on the muzzle and wings often disappears when a bat is removed from the hibernaculum. Infected wings typically look normal during hibernation, but areas of 'contraction' or tears can be present and wing membrane may stick together when the wing is extended.

Bats that die from WNS during hibernation often have reduced subcutaneous fat and when touched with a gloved finger during necropsy, exposed pectoral muscle may be tacky suggesting ante-mortem dehydration. Microscopic findings are characterized by dense aggregations of Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive hyphae eroding through epidermis forming distinctive 'cups' filled with fungus. Invasion may extend into the deeper connective tissue. Hyphae are often seen replacing adnexal structures, filling skin glands and follicles. Curved conidia may be present on the surface of infected skin. Cellular inflammation is usually not present during hibernation but can become intense following emergence from hibernation as the bat becomes active and euthermic.

Diagnosis: Although gross lesions can be suggestive of WNS, confirmation of WNS requires histopathologic visualization of lesions (cupping erosion of dermis) with PAS stain and confirmation of presence of Pd by real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis of wing tissue or a swab sample from the wing. Molecular detection of Pd has also been demonstrated in guano collected from bats. PCR primers targeting the multi-copy intergenic spacer (IGS) region of Pd rRNA gene complex rather than the internal transcribed spacer (ITS) region or alpha-L-rhamnosidase (ALR) gene of Pd are both highly sensitive and specific for Pd and considered the gold standard for molecular detection of Pd from samples obtained from bats or the environment. Alternatively, Pd may be cultured from samples using fungal media (Sabouraud dextrose agar or dextrose-peptone-yeast extract agar) and incubated at cold temperatures (approximately 5 - 10 °C) for six weeks before calling the culture negative.

Curved conidia produced by Pd are morphologically distinct from other fungi generally found on bats, but molecular identification of the isolate by PCR is necessary for definitive confirmation. Biopsies of wing tissue can be taken as non-lethal samples (vide infra) for histological examination, but should be guided by visible signs to increase sensitivity. Ultraviolet light can be used as a screening tool to assist with targeted specimen selection in the field; the cupping dermal erosions have been associated with orange fluorescence under long-wave (368-385 nm) UVA light. The unknown specificity of UV fluorescence precludes this technique from being diagnostic. Material required for laboratory analysis: Non-lethal swab samples of the muzzle and wing skin surface can be collected to test for the presence of Pd. However, confirmation of WNS requires histopathological examination of skin.

Skin tissue from the wing and/or muzzle can be submitted for PCR analysis, fungal culture, and histopathology (PAS stain). Areas submitted should preferably demonstrate white fungal growth or abnormal appearance. The use of long-wave UVA light can aid in identifying areas likely to be affected, particularly when non-lethal sampling is desired. A 3-5 mm biopsy of wing tissue may be submitted for histopathology if analysis of a whole carcass is not available or otherwise not an option. Although tape impressions of fungal growth on bats can be mounted on glass slides to search for conidia characteristic of Pd, suggestive samples should be confirmed by PCR and histopathology. Pd detection via real-time PCR is also possible using swabs collected from environmental substrates in direct contact where bats roosts or sediment or guano samples accumulating underneath bat roosts.

Environmental samples obtained at underground hibernacula may be sampled year-round due to the stable environmental conditions at subterranean sites while the timing of environmental sampling at above-ground roosts likely mirrors that of Pd detection on bats. Pd detection probabilities differ among the different sample types with skin swabs or guano collected during winter from bat species with known susceptibility to WNS providing the highest likelihood of Pd detection while environmental substrate swabs collected in the spring at summer roosts have much lower likelihood of Pd detection and necessitates more intensive sampling efforts. Following spring emergence, Pd detection on bats becomes more reliable by sampling guano pellets from the individual bat than relying solely on a skin swab due to grooming behaviors. Relevant Diagnostic lab: Samples known or suspected to harbor viable Pd should, at minimum, be handled in a biosafety cabinet in a Biosafety Level-2 laboratory.

For investigations of wild bat mortalities in the US, see submission guidelines of the USGS National Wildlife Health Center. In Canada, report sick and dead bats to the Canadian Wildlife Health Cooperative. Treatment: Currently, the only effective treatment for WNS is supportive care of homeothermic bats. Natural recovery of free-ranging bats that survive infection during hibernation and subsequently clear all signs of disease has been documented. However, in wild free-flying bats, wing damage may prevent successful foraging, causing additional mortality. Disease management options are still in the investigation phase, including use of vaccination, antifungal compounds, ultraviolet light and biologic control. Although there have been some demonstrations of effectiveness against Pd in the laboratory, safety, efficacy, and transferability of this research to wild bats, as well as potential ecological impacts of these management actions, are currently being studied.

At this time, improving survival of bats outside of hibernation is a management action directed at population recovery in the face of WNS. The North American Bat Monitoring Program focuses on monitoring bat populations, to detect the impacts of WNS and inform bat population management decisions. Prevention and control: Current prevention and control strategies focus on biosecurity and restricting access to hibernacula (primarily caves and mines) to limit movement of people and contaminated equipment between hibernacula and other sites used by bats. To support this effort, a national cave access advisory and standardized decontamination protocols have been developed. Other studies assessing the utility of artificial hibernacula, chemical and biocontrol agents, and vaccination are currently in progress.

Suggested disinfectants for housing facilities: To minimize the spread of Pd, decontamination protocols should be followed whenever moving bats or equipment that may have been exposed to Pd or contaminated environments. Biosecurity and decontamination procedures should also be implemented for rehabilitation facilities to limit spread of Pd between individuals and geographic areas following release of bats back into the wild. While multiple treatments are being investigated, to date, there are no disinfection methods that are known to be safe and effective for natural or manmade hibernacula. Notification: Currently, notification of WNS or detection of the Pd fungus is voluntary. Reports of WNS observations can be sent to the state wildlife resources agency, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the USGS National Wildlife Health Center, or the Canadian Wildlife Health Cooperative. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None.

Clinical signs: Changes in hemogram (leukopenia, monocytopenia, thrombocytopenia) often occur before clinical signs of illness are detectable. Initial signs may be mild or vague: lethargy, decreased food or water intake, mild colic, diarrhea, lameness or stiffness, oral mucosal lesions, ocular lesions, and alterations in sleep patterns may occur. More severe signs include edema of the head, neck, trunk, and thoracic limbs, lingual cyanosis, and DIC appear as the disease progresses. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Gross necropsy findings may include pericardial effusion with diffuse petechial hemorrhages throughout the heart, tongue, and visceral surfaces. Lingual cyanosis and hepatomegaly may also be seen. Ulcerations of the oral cavity, larynx, and large intestine have been seen. Histologic findings may include extensive microhemorrhages and edema in the heart and tongue, with lymphocytic, monocytic, and neutrophilic infiltration of the myocardium.

texto: - ∞ Gross: Variable sized yellow/cream colored firm masses with mineralization and/or caseonecrotic centers (chronic granulomas), primarily in lung and associated thoracic lymph nodes. Occasionally granulomas found in other organs and lymph nodes in advanced cases. - ∞ Histology: Tubercles are granulomatous lesions with a caseo-necrotic and/or mineralized center bordered by epithelioid cells, some of which may form multinucleated giant cells. - ∞ Ante-mortem: Laboratory examinations of trunk wash lavage using acid-fast staining and culture/PCR of the fluid. Ancillary tests include Elephant TB DPP® for antibody detection. Veterinarians should consult current elephant TB testing guidelines. Additionally, mycobacterial organisms rarely have been isolated from other body fluids such as vaginal secretions. Increased frequency of trunk wash culture/PCR and serological testing have been shown to increase the likelihood of diagnosis in elephants with a history of contact with infected elephants (or humans), based on intermittent shedding of tubercle bacillus. Intradermal tuberculin testing is not recommended for elephants due to the non-specific reactions. - ∞ Post-mortem: Post-mortem culture/PCR and histopathological examination should be performed on any suspect lesions. Blood may be collected for Elephant TB DPP and other in vitro supplemental tests. Consult the current elephant TB testing guidelines (i.e., AAZV website).

-  EHV1 abortion: Inactivated vaccines have been used to prevent abortion, with dosing at 5, 7, and 9 months of pregnancy. Literature does not currently indicate a protective effect of vaccination, but vaccines are successful at producing a high antibody response and limit nasal shedding. A modified EHV-1 vaccine may provide partial protection. In cases of outbreaks, prophylactic vaccination of all horses is controversial. Isolation of pregnant mares and maintenance of closed groups is recommended to prevent further outbreaks in cases of infection. Any horse with respiratory signs also should be isolated. Horses will become infected life-long, with possible recrudescence during times of stress. -  EHV1 myeloencephalopathy: quarantine exposed horses. Incubation period: 3-14 days depending on form of infection: acute respiratory form 3-5 days, cardiac form 1-2 weeks, fever form 4-14 days. Clinical signs: The respiratory form can be acute or peracute causing fever (40-42 °C), respiratory distress (RR>50), paroxysmal coughing, nasal discharge, congested conjunctiva, and abnormal stance. Mortality rate may reach 95%. The cardiac form causes fever (39-41 °C), swelling of the supraorbital fossa extending to head and neck causing dyspnea and colic. Mortality rate may be 50% or higher. The most common form is the mixed form. A combination of respiratory signs with head and neck swelling is seen with a mortality rate of 70% or higher. The fever form is characterized by mild pyrexia (40-40.5 °C) with occasional congestion of conjunctiva, depression and inappetence but minimal mortality. In endemic areas, this disease can be confused with equine pirpoplasmosis, equine encephalosis or equine viral arteritis.

Glanders is basically a disease of animals which can be transmitted from animal to animal, and to a lesser extent, from animal to human. Human-tohuman transmission is not usually common. In addition, anthroponosis or transmission from humanto-animal has not previously occurred in nature. It is considered a Tier 1 Select Agent and Class B biothreat agent by the USDA and CDC Federal Select Agent Program. Distribution: Re-emerging trans-boundary disease endemic with increasing outbreaks in parts of the Middle East, Asia, as well as Central and South America (also seen in Africa). Four lions and one tiger died from the disease, and an imported tiger from Russia was the probable carrier. The disease has been eliminated from North America, Australia, Japan and European Union countries through surveillance and destruction of affected animals, and strict import restrictions. Clinical signs: The organism is zoonotic with four basic forms in both horses and humans: cutaneous "farcy", upper respiratory, pulmonary, and septicemic, and they may occur simultaneously. In equids, the acute cutaneous form is more common in mules and donkeys, with death typically occurring in 47 days to 3- 4 weeks after onset of illness. The chronic cutaneous form of the disease (farcy) is more common in horses and causes regional lymphadenopathy and skin nodules that ulcerate and drain, with induration, enlargement, and nodularity of regional lymphatics on the extremities and in other areas.

Nodules with 1-2.5 cm diameter appear on the line of lymphatic vessels and will probably further ulcerate, discharging yellowish pus called 'farcy oil' similar to dark honey in terms of color and viscosity. The septic form of glanders results in coughing, a high fever and release of an infectious nasal discharge, often followed by fulminant septicemia and death within days. Multi-organ abscesses develop predominantly in the lungs, liver and spleen and often lead to septic shock. Other lesions that can be seen are osteomyelitis, meningitis, orchitis and brain abscesses. Further clinical manifestations are exercise intolerance, dyspnea due to chronic respiratory insufficiency, arthritis, hind-limb joint swelling, lameness and hematuria. Death may occur within 1-2 weeks or several months. Apparent survivors act as carriers and maintain the spread of the disease. Zoo and wild felids consuming infected meat will develop localized nodules on nasal mucosa and conjunctiva with bloody nasal discharge within 8-14 days after consuming contaminated meat. Final differentiation of cultures of B. mallei from B. pseudomallei (melioidosis) can be done with rapid low risk DNA testing at a designated laboratory (with 16S rRNA sequencing and the use of a variety of molecular typing methods: fliC PCR, flip RT-PCR, etc.). A Western Blot test has been developed and an ELISA test using another immunoreactive protein is in development. ELISA is recommended as companion test and its specificity reported at 99.8% versus 97% for CFT. Other diagnostic tests for glanders are PCR-RFLP, Rose Bengal Test (RBT), Agar Gel Immunodiffusion (AGID), Indirect Fluorescent Antibody Test (IFAT), Indirect Hemagglutination Assay (IHA) and Counter Immunoelectrophoresis (CIE).

Differential diagnosis: Symptoms and manifestations of glanders could be mistaken with other diseases that affect mucous membranes of the upper respiratory tract and sinuses and produce mucopurulent discharge or result in skin lesions. These diseases may include Strangles (Streptococcus equi), Ulcerative Lymphangitis (Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis), Pseudotuberculosis (Yersinia pseudotuberculosis), Epizootic Lymphangitis (Histoplasma capsulatum var. farciminosum), Tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis), Botryomycosis (Staphylococcus aureus) and Sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii).

Causative organism: Eastern equine encephalitis virus (EEEv; Family Togaviridiae, genus Alphavirus). There are four lineages of EEEv. -  Group I is endemic in North America and the Caribbean and causes most of the human cases. -  The other three groups (IIA, IIB, III, and IV) cause primarily equine illness in South or Central America and are now classified as the Madariaga virus.

-  Culiseta melanura is the important vector in the maintenance of the enzootic cycle in birds, as it rarely feeds on mammals or humans. The majority of human cases occur from mosquito bites from bridge vector mosquito species which more commonly feed on mammals (e.g., some Aedes, Coquillettidia, and Culex species). -  Transmission to humans can also occur during necropsy of EEEv infected animals; either via contamination with infected material or aerosolized material (especially brain and spinal cord material).

-  North American variant is found in eastern Canada, eastern and northern United States, and the Caribbean islands. Larger scale epizootics have historically occurred most often in Michigan, Massachusetts, Florida, Georgia, Connecticut, New Jersey, New York, and North Carolina. Onset is from late spring to early fall in northern states & could be any time of year in southern states. -  The South American variant is confined to central and South America. Incubation period: 4 to 10 days, and rarely up to 3 weeks.

-  Equids: altered mentation, impaired vision, aimless wandering, head pressing, circling, anorexia, grinding of teeth, esophageal paralysis, irregular or ataxic gait, paresis, paralysis, seizures, coma and death. Many horses progress to recumbency within 12-18 hours of onset of neurological abnormalities. Most deaths occur within 2-3 days after onset of signs. Mortality of equids with clinical signs is 50-90%. -  White-tailed deer (free-ranging): circling, ataxia, paralysis, dyspnea, pytalism, blindness, head tilt, loss of fear of humans, death. Serologic evidence of exposure varies across areas. Clinical disease and fatalities do occur, especially during regional epizootics. -  Canids: pyrexia, depression, nystagmus, ataxia, lateral recumbency, & acute death. Cases are rare and occur in animals that are <6 months old. -  Birds: Acute death without premonitory signs is common. If clinical signs are observed, susceptible birds (e.g., cassowaries, pheasants, whooping cranes, passerine, psittacines) may present with lethargy & ataxia. In contrast to the pathogenesis in most other avian species, EEEV has visceral tropism in emus and rheas leading to GI signs.

Two types, systemic or encephalitic, can develop. Systemic: abrupt onset of malaise, fever, chills, arthralgia and myalgia lasting one to two weeks. Recovery is complete if there is no CNS involvement. Encephalitic: fever, headache, irritability, restlessness, drowsiness, anorexia, vomiting, diarrhea, cyanosis, altered reflexes, convulsions, and coma. ~30% case mortality rate within 2 to 10 days. Survivors have irreversible neurological damage. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Gross lesions are rare but congestion may be present in the meninges of acutely affected animals. Histologic findings are typically present in the cerebral cortex, thalamus, and hypothalamus and include lymphocytic/neutrophilic meningoencephalitis with neuronal necrosis and neuronophagia, severe gliosis, and perivascular cuffing. Immunohistochemistry should be performed on the brain to confirm suspected lesions.

Diagnosis: Clinical presentation in an enzootic area or during an outbreak, EEEV-specific IgM ELISA or plaque reduction neutralization test of acute and convalescent phase serum specimens and PCR on cerebrospinal fluid samples (CSF). Material required for laboratory analysis: Serum samples are collected from live animals to detect virus-specific IgM and neutralizing antibodies. PCR can be performed on CSF samples. Postmortem samples, including brain, spinal cord, and other tissues, may be collected for histopathology, as well as immunohistochemistry, PCR, and virus isolation. Relevant Diagnostic lab: EEEv is covered under the Federal Select Agent Program, which limits diagnostic testing. Only a few state laboratories (MSU VDL, etc) or other specialized laboratories (NVSL) are capable of doing the testing. Treatment: Supportive and symptomatic care. Animals and humans that recover may have long-term neurologic dysfunction. Prevention and control: There is no vaccine for humans.

Prevention depends on reducing exposure to mosquitoes, mosquito control, and vaccination in equids and other high-risk species. Vaccination of captive, at risk bird species birds in areas with high virus activity is often practiced. No cross-immunity obtained when vaccinated for other alphaviruses (e.g., western equine encephalitis virus) or flaviviruses (e.g., West Nile virus) or bunyaviruses (e.g., La Crosse virus). Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Clean infected environment with an approved EPA disinfectant. Notification: Suspected cases are reported according to individual State procedure, typically by notification of the State Arboviral Coordinator or State Animal Health Official. Reports of positive equine cases of arboviral disease are reported to ArboNET, an internet-based arbovirus surveillance and reporting system managed by state health departments and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

ArboNET captures laboratory-confirmed positive cases in humans, horses, other mammals, birds, and mosquitoes across the U.S. Equine cases vary by state, but those reported to ArboNET are confirmed by State Veterinarians prior to reporting. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: In most states, reporting is mandatory, as EEEv is covered under the Federal Select Agent Program. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Maintain infected animal in a quarantine situation. Mammals are typically dead end hosts. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Mosquito control strategies are the best way to mitigate disease. Experts who may be consulted: None identified for this document. Humans have succumbed to infection following aerosol exposure during laboratory work. Distribution: North and South America - Argentina through Canada. In the US, WEE has generally occurred west of the Mississippi River. Numerous outbreaks of the disease affected horses and humans on both continents during the early through mid-twentieth century. Both human and animal WEE cases declined markedly during the later 1900s. Various genetic and ecological factors may have been involved in submergence of the disease agent at that time. Currently WEE is a rare disease of humans and horses in the US. However, in South America, WEE virus recently re-emerged as a formidable pathogen after years of relative quiescence. Substantial outbreaks, which included fatalities among horses and humans, have occurred since 2023, particularly in Argentina and Uruguay.

Changes in seasonal temperatures, rainfall, and genetic factors related to the virus may have been involved in the South American resurgence of the disease. The true incidence and distribution of the disease may be challenging to precisely determine given geographic and temporal variations in surveillance intensity plus the passive nature of reporting systems.

- ∞ Mammals: Equids infected with WEE have shown fever, anorexia, lethargy, impaired vision, difficulty swallowing, tremors, ataxia, incoordination, circling, head pressing, paresis, paralysis, seizures, and recumbency. The disease can be fatal. Clinical signs may be similar to other neurologic disease including rabies, necessitating cautious examination and appropriate protective equipment. The virus may cycle in other mammalian vertebrates without causing illness as various wildlife species have tested seropositive for WEE. - ∞ Humans: Fever, headache, stiff neck, disorientation, altered consciousness, coma, convulsions, and paralysis can be present, and death may occur. Infection is of particular concern for infants and the elderly. Humans can also have asymptomatic infections. - ∞ Primates: Theoretic concern for nonhuman primates as fatal human illness has occurred. - ∞ Birds: Infected emus have demonstrated watery diarrhea, weight loss, neurologic signs, and fatalities. A drop in egg production may occur in poultry. The potential for WEE to cause disease in other avian species, particularly nonnative birds, exists.

-  Gastrointestinal: weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, and hematochezia. Laboratory abnormalities include eosinophilia, anemia, hyperglobulinemia, hypoalbuminemia, and rarely hypercalcemia. Abdominal radiography and sonography usually reveal severe segmental thickening of the gastrointestinal tract, an abdominal mass, and/or mesenteric lymphadenopathy. -  Cutaneous: Non-healing wounds and invasive masses that contain ulcerated nodules and draining tracts. In horses, the formation of hard masses ("kunkers") within the lesions may occur. Nasopharyngeal lesions, invasive subcutaneous masses, draining nodular lesion, and ulcerated plaque-like lesions are found in cats. -  Pythium insidiosum has been also reported affecting bones, lungs, lymph nodes, eyes and blood vessels. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Histologically pythiosis is characterized by eosinophilic pyogranulomatous inflammation associated with broad (4-7 micron), poorly septate hyphae. Affected tissues contain multiple foci of necrosis surrounded and infiltrated by neutrophils, eosinophils, and macrophages.

inflammation associated with broad (4-7 micron), poorly septate hyphae. Affected tissues contain multiple foci of necrosis surrounded and infiltrated by neutrophils, eosinophils, and macrophages. In addition, there are discrete granulomas composed of epithelioid macrophages, plasma cells, multinucleate giant cells. Hyphae stain well with GMS but less well with PAS. Histologically pythiosis, other oomycoses, and zygomycosis have a similar appearance. Diagnosis: Veterinarians and physicians with expertise in this disease could suspect pythiosis because the clinical features of the disease. However, a clinical specimen (biopsy, kunkers) is always recommended to support the findings. Confirmation is usually histopathology followed by PCR confirmation of pythiosis in paraffin-embedded tissues. Serology has been performed successfully in canids, exotic felids, and several species of ursids, but this frequently requires species-specific antibodies. Cytologic evaluation of exudates from draining tracts or fine-needle aspirates of enlarged lymph nodes may be suggestive of fungal infection.
