Distribution: World-wide distribution is in all members of Felidae. Disease is most common in multicat environments (e.g., shelters, breeding facilities) and in feral cats. The latter has been implicated in spreading this virus to a zoological institution in North America. Reports of this infection have been made in other zoological institutions. There is some evidence that FCV can be spread by hematophagous arthropods or blood transfusion in addition to fomites, aerosols, and cat to cat transmission. Acutely infected cats predominantly shed FCV via oral and nasal secretions, but the pathogen is also detected in the blood, urine, and feces of infected cats. -  Prevention: Vaccination using Fel-O-Vax PCT + CaliciVax® vaccine to minimize severity of infection, particularly of virulent systemic strains; only killed vaccines should be used in exotic felids. There have been several cases of suspected vaccine-induced calicivirus in tigers and lions in the USA. Antibody testing not recommended to determine when to vaccinate. It is not known what antibody titer is considered protective. The level of mucosal IgA is a stronger correlate of protection than blood antibody levels, but levels of mucosal antibodies cannot be measured easily. -  Control: limit access to feral cats that can carry and spread FCV and recovered animals can shed infectious virus for months to years. Proper cleaning as FCV can survive up to 14 days on inanimate objects. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: 1:32 dilution of commercial bleach; potassium peroxymonosulfate; chlorine dioxide; substituted phenolic compounds; quaternary compounds formulated at appropriate concentration and pH. Sodium bicarbonate at 5% concentration can be used. Virucidal disinfectants may be effective but not all are. Easily destroyed by detergents. Notification: None required.

FCoV-2 may be linked more to disease outbreaks, such as that in 2023 with the novel FCoV-23. FCoVs have been assigned to two biotypes, which can be referred to as feline enteric coronavirus (FECV), which mainly replicates in the enteric epithelial cells, and feline infectious peritonitis virus (FIPV), which results in a mostly lethal infection with efficient systemic replication in

monocytes or macrophages. Both FCoV-1 and -2 can exist as pathotypes FECV or FIPV. Only a portion (<10%)of cats infected with FECV develop FIP disease, and is dependent on viral mutation, genetic predisposition, and environmental and other stressors. When cats are exposed to FECV the virus enters enterocytes and typically causes self-limiting gastroenteritis or may spread systemically without causing FIP. In some cats a mutation may occur, leading to FIPV with tropism for macrophages and monocytes. This virus is no longer transmissible through the fecal-oral route. In some cats, a strong cell-mediated immune response clears the virus; however, if a humoral immune response predominates, wet FIP, characterized by vasculitis and effusion, develops. If there is a partial cell-mediated immune response, dry FIP develops which is characterized by granuloma formation.

-  Early signs of the disease may be non-specific: lethargy/malaise, fluctuating fever, loss of appetite, weight loss, and may cause failure to thrive in young cats. -  The disease is categorized as two forms: - o Effusive/wet form with vasculitis and polyserositis - ascites, thoracic and/or pericardial effusion. The effusive form is the more common form of the disease. - o Non-effusive/dry form with granulomatous lesions in kidneys, intestinal tract (leading to chronic diarrhea), lymph node enlargement. -  Ocular and neurologic signs occur in <9% of cats with the wet form but are relatively frequent in cats with the dry form. Ocular signs may include chorioretinitis and retinal perivascular cuffing, keratic precipitates in the anterior eye, and uveitis. Neurologic signs may include nystagmus, cranial nerve defects, seizures, ataxia, hyperesthesia, and behavioral changes.

texto: -  Effusive (wet) form of FIP: gross findings: viscous thoracic or abdominal fluid; pyogranulomas that tend to follow the course of the cranial mesenteric artery - leading to thickened omentum containing pyogranulomas, and pyogranulomas covering the serosal surface of the abdominal viscera. The pyogranulomas appear as small, coalescing, fibrinous plaques. -  Dry form: gross findings: pyogranuolomas that appear as raised, gray-white nodules (>0.5 - 2 cm) in the kidneys, liver, intestines, and visceral lymph nodes. CNS lesions and ocular lesions are more common in the dry form. Eye lesions may include iridocyclitis or chorioretinitis, and anterior uveitis, retinitis with hemorrhage and/or retinal detachment, and optic neuritis. Pyogranulomas may be found in the brain and spinal cord, or CNS lesions may manifest as diffuse meningitis.

-  The disease can be difficult to diagnose. Currently, there is no test specific for FIP. Clinicians must consider signalment, history, clinical signs, clinicopathologic findings, serology, and histology, and immunohistochemistry. -  Antibody testing: serology may be useful to screen a population for FCoV but is not typically beneficial on the individual level as it cannot distinguish FECV exposure from FIPV. -  Antigen testing: immunohistochemistry on effusions or lesions containing infected macrophages is the gold standard for FIP diagnosis. Cytology of enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes collected via ultrasound guided aspiration may also be used for diagnosis. -  The Rivalta test is an inexpensive, in-clinic test of effusions with a high negative predictive value for FIP. Readers are referred to other references for details (Kornya or Tasker). -  PCR testing is a useful tool for direct detection of viral RNA. FCoV PCR-positive samples (tissue or effusion) is consistent with FIP but not definitive, as healthy animals that are non-FIP could test PCR-positive for FCoV; however, FIP is unlikely if FCoV PCR-negative.

It is challenging to effectively test cats prior to introduction to a group; however, attempts to detect FECV shedders may be possible with a series of at least three RTqPCR tests at intervals of one week to one month. Strict hygiene (especially for litter boxes) and keeping cats in small groups can help reduce viral contamination. -  Although a licensed FIP vaccine is available, it is not generally recommended by the American Association of Feline Practitioners Feline Vaccine Advisory Panel. This vaccine is labeled for >16 weeks of age in kittens, but most become infected before this age. It also contains a serotype strain of FIP virus that is not the one that predominately circulates and does cause cross- reactive humoral immunity.

PCR and viral isolation performed on oronasal swabs can indicate presence of the infectious organism, but do not confirm FHV-1 as the causative agent of disease. PCR performed on facial dermatitis lesions and some ocular lesions (including corneal sequestra) is highly correlated with FHV-1 as the causative agent of disease. -  Inactive and modified live vaccines, either injectable or intranasal formulations, usually in combination with other felid viruses are available. Vaccination does not prevent infection or shedding but can reduce severity of signs and decrease the amount of shedding. Generally, only inactivated vaccines are used in non-domestic felids. Primary vaccination consists of 1 ml of vaccine (Fel-O-Vax, Boehringer Ingelheim) given every 2 - 3 weeks from 6 weeks through 18 weeks of age or a minimum of 3 vaccines in an unvaccinated adult cat. Response to vaccination should be documented with serum neutralization (SN) titer 2 - 3 weeks after the last vaccine. A SN titer of > or equal to 1:16 is considered protective. Antibody titers frequently decline rapidly in exotics and may not accurately reflect susceptibility. Cellular and mucosal immunity are important in moderating or preventing disease. Triennial booster vaccinations are recommended, but more frequent vaccination may be required if there is high exposure risk, due to the rapid antibody decline is some species.

The first confirmed case of FeLV-associated lymphoma in a nondomestic felid occurred in a cheetah. The critically endangered Iberian lynx (Lynx pardinus) may be particularly susceptible to FeLV. The virus is otherwise not considered endemic in exotic felids, although antigen-positive animals have been documented, as well as seropositive, asymptomatic animals. FeLV has been isolated in leopard cat, European wildcat, and cougar. Causative organism: A retrovirus, of the genus Gammaretrovirus of the family Retroviridae. Zoonotic potential: Not a zoonosis Distribution: Rare but documented antigen-positive exotic cats have been found worldwide. In a study of more than 18,000 domestic cats, 2.3% of cats were FeLV antigen positive on ELISA testing. Prevalence was higher (3.6%) among cats allowed outdoors. Prevalence was highest among sick feral cats; 15.2% of tested ill feral cats were FeLV positive. Incubation period: Infected cats may experience a prolonged period of clinical latency.

Clinical signs: In domestic cats, anemia, chronic inflammatory conditions, lymphoma, susceptibility to secondary and opportunistic infections, cutaneous abscesses, oral inflammation, and reproductive problems. Most cats remain infected for life following exposure but may revert to an aviremic state (regressive infection). In the case of a regressive infection, no antigen or culturable virus is present in the blood, but FeLV proviral DNA can be detected in the blood by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). -  Three outcomes of FeLV exposure can be considered: - o Abortive infection: infection is cleared - o Progressive infection: domestic cats typically succumb to FeLV-associated diseases within a few years. However these retrovirus positive cats may live without related illness for several years. A decision about euthanasia should not be made based on a positive test alone.

A decision about euthanasia should not be made based on a positive test alone. - o Regressive infection: cats have an effective immune response, virus replication is contained, and there is no viral shedding. These cats have little risk of developing FeLV associated disease. Exotic cats typically belong to this group. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Cats infected with FeLV that develop progressive infection may develop FeLV-related diseases including lymphoid malignancies, non-regenerative anemia, and myeloproliferative disorders. Findings may also include diseases secondary to immunosuppression, such as severe bacterial infections and toxoplasmosis.

-  See the most recent research and guidelines such as AAFP Guidelines for testing for cats in various scenarios. -  Antigen testing: ELISA: This screens for the core viral antigen p27. This antigen is produced in large quantities in most infected domestic cats and most will test positive within 30 days of exposure. However, when results of antigen testing are negative but recent infection cannot be ruled out, repeat a minimum of 30 days after the last potential exposure. -  Antigen testing: IFA: Antigen testing using immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) testing also detects p27 antigen within infected blood cells via bone marrow or blood smears. However, false negatives may occur in the following scenarios with domestic cats: leukopenic cats, cats with regressive infection, or cats that resist bone marrow infection. False positives may occur with sample preparation error, when background fluorescence is high, or when results are interpreted by inexperienced lab personnel. -  Confirmatory testing: Cats that test positive on screening tests should be further tested with confirmatory tests.

A second soluble antigen test should be performed, preferably using a test from a different manufacturer. (Virus culture is the gold standard, but not readily available in North America.) Practitioners should be aware that cats developing regressive infection may be only transiently antigenemic and may revert to negative status on soluble antigen tests. Confirmatory testing with PCR: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) can detect FeLV RNA or DNA within one week of viral exposure in domestic cats; even when FeLV p27 antigen is not yet detectable. PCR testing detects either viral RNA or cell-associated DNA (provirus) in blood, bone marrow, and tissues. Material required for laboratory analysis: Whole blood for antigen testing; blood, bone marrow or tissues for PCR testing. Relevant Diagnostic lab: Most commercial & state veterinary diagnostic labs. Treatment: Immune modulators and interferon inducers are used in retrovirus-infected domestic cats, including FeLV-infected cats.

Although reports of uncontrolled studies frequently suggest dramatic clinical improvement, these effects generally have not been reproduced in controlled trials. Preliminary laboratory studies have identified four drugs with anti-FeLV activity that may warrant further study into their mechanisms of action and feasibility for veterinary use.

-  In domestic cats, identification and segregation of infected cats is considered the single most effective method for preventing new infections with FeLV. Feral cats should be excluded from contact with exotic cats in zoos. While retroviruses are generally unstable outside their host, they can remain viable in dried biological deposits for more than a week. -  As with domestic cats, zoos should determine the FeLV status of all exotic cats. Cats should be tested for FeLV infection at quarantine and routine exams. If exotics cats are to be vaccinated, testing before initial vaccination is also recommended. However, since routine screening tests detect antigen, not antibody, vaccination does not typically interfere with FeLV testing. -  Injectable inactivated vaccines are commercially available in the United States. The vaccine is not currently recommended as a core vaccine for exotic cats in zoos, but may be used in situations of high-risk, such as extensive exposure to infected feral cats.

Diagnosis: Western blot and ELISA assays are the most commonly used method of diagnosing FIV. Western blot is available for domestic cats, cougars, and African lions and may be more sensitive than domestic cat FIV based ELISA. PCR is available, but is not as reliable because strain genetic variation is high. Material required for laboratory analysis: Serum, plasma or whole blood can be used for diagnosis. Relevant Diagnostic lab: Any laboratory capable of running the FIV ELISA is able to diagnose FIV; however, this assay may be less sensitive than strain specific Western Blot. Treatment: Most non-domestic felids do not need any treatment. Treatment is for any specific clinical signs that arise and is supportive. Prevention and control: Felids should be tested by ELISA prior to introduction into a new facility with other felids. Special care should be taken to prevent interaction with feral cats. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: FIV is labile outside the host animals.

It is easily inactivated by detergents and routine disinfectants. Routine cleaning procedures will prevent transmission. Dental and surgical instruments, anesthesia circuits, endotracheal tubes, and other items potentially contaminated with body fluids should be thoroughly cleaned and sterilized between uses. Fluid lines, multi-dose medication containers, and food can become contaminated with body fluids (especially blood or saliva) and should not be shared. Notification: Receiving institutions should be notified of an infected animal. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: No specific measures need to be taken. Whether or not to introduce infected and non- infected animals should be based on a population management decision, knowing that non-infected animals may become infected. Knowledge of the strain and likely clinical disease can assist with these decisions.

-  Felids: - o Cytauxzoon felis has been reported from domestic cats, bobcats (Lynx rufus), puma (Puma concolor), and captive exotic felids (e.g., tigers [Panthera tigris]) in the USA. Bobcats, and other wild felids (e.g. puma), serve as natural reservoirs but chronically infected domestic cats can also serve as a source of infection for ticks. - o C. manul infects the Pallas cat. - o Cytauxzoon spp., some genetically similar to C. felis, have been reported from domestic cats and numerous free-ranging and/or captive exotic felids in South America, Africa and Europe. An increasing number of reports are being seen in European non-domestic felids. -  Non-felid reports: related Cytauxzoon spp. in meerkats (Suricata suricatta) from South Africa and Formosan pangolins (Manis pentadactyla pentadactyla) from Taiwan. Causative organism: Cytauxzoon spp. are Apicomplexan parasites in the Order Piroplasmida which are related to important human and veterinary pathogens in the genera Babesia and Theileria. Zoonotic potential: No.

-  USA: due to range expansion of the lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum), C. felis is thought to be endemic in most of the southeastern, south-central, and mid-Atlantic states. -  South America, Africa, Europe and Asia: related Cytauxzoon spp.; they likely represent novel species or have been described as separate species (e.g., C. manul), but genetic data indicates that Cytauxzoon from Brazil is closely related to C. felis from the USA. Incubation period: C. felis can typically be detected in erythrocytes of infected cats approximately 1-3 weeks after an infected tick bite. Clinical signs typically occur 5-16 days after infected tick bite.

-  Domestic cats: most develop severe clinical disease. The most common sign is fever, though hypothermia can occur late in disease; the clinical course is Usually rapid. Presenting signs can also include tachypnea or rare neurologic signs. Most common laboratory findings include thrombocytopenia, anemia, or pancytopenia, and hyperbilirubinemia or electrolyte derangements; there can be evidence of DIC. Some never develop clinical signs, but instead remain chronic carriers. -  Captive wild/exotic felids: development of clinical signs is highly variable and may depend on felid species, strain of parasite, or some other factor. Fatal cases have been reported in tigers housed in the USA and lions in Brazil; however, asymptomatic infections have been detected in tigers, ocelots (Leopardus pardalis), oncilla (Leopardus tigrinus), jaguar (Panthera onca), puma. -  Wild felids (natural reservoirs): wild reservoir species rarely develop clinical signs but very rare acute mortality has been reported among young bobcats.

In addition, three infected cougars in the USA developed a transient anemia and increased serum bilirubin concentrations and increased alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase activities soon after infection; however, all recovered rapidly without treatment. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Gross lesions are typically severe as death occurs due to severe occlusions of vessels by developing parasites. Felids may have pale or icteric mucosal membranes, petechiae and ecchymoses in the lung, heart, lymph nodes and on mucosal membranes, splenomegaly, lymphadenomegaly, and hydropericardium. Numerous large schizonts will be noted in the cytoplasm of infected macrophages that often occlude the lumens of numerous vessels of many tissues, especially the lungs; rarely these shizont-laden macrophages can be seen on peripheral blood smear. Visualization of these cells is diagnostic for disease since schizonts are not present in chronically infected carriers.

-  Parasitemias of C. felis on blood smears are generally absent or low (<5%) early in disease, but piroplasms can be seen in up to half of erythrocytes as disease progresses; however, subclinical chronic carriers generally have very low parasitemias. Although feline babesiosis has not been reported in domestic cats in the USA, C. felis trophozoites are morphologically similar to other small piroplasms so PCR testing is necessary to definitively identify C. felis. -  Leukopenia or pancytopenia may be present as well as thrombocytopenia and normocytic, normochromic anemia. -  A fine needle aspiration of a peripheral lymph node, spleen, or liver should be performed to identify schizonts in macrophages, if not seen on peripheral blood smear. These intracellular schizonts are not found in babesiosis cases so can be used to definitively identify Cytauxzoon infections. Splenic aspirates were reported to have higher sensitivity for the detection of schizonts, when compared to blood or lymph node aspirates, using novice observers. -  Several PCR protocols have been developed for the detection of C. felis. The greatest success has been obtained using atovaquone (15 mg/kg, PO, q8h for 10 days) and azithromycin (10 mg/kg, PO, q24h for 10 days) with supportive care (fluid therapy and heparin). This has a reported success rate of up to 60% in domestic cats, if initiated in a timely manner. Limited success has been obtained using imidocarb and diminazene diaceturate while even less success has been obtained using parvaquone, buparvaquone, trimethoprim/sulfadiazine, and sodium thiacetarsamide. No treatment protocol has been shown to clear infection of persistently infected felids. Prevention and control: Because Cytauxzoon is tick-borne, limiting exposure of felids to ticks is necessary to prevent transmission. For domestic cats, the best prevention is to keep cats indoors and use year-round effective oral, topical, or collar tick preventatives.

For exotic or wild felids or domestic cats that are allowed outdoors, an effective acaracide or acaricide-treated collar should be used to prevent or limit tick infestation. Distribution: Disease has been reported in > 40 countries and is endemic in Australia, New Zealand, Cuba, parts of Asia and Africa, and most of Europe, will likely be endemic in British Columbia, Washington and New Mexico as of 2020. Sporadic reports in several countries including Mexico (now eradicated), Canada (2011), Uruguay (2004), and the United States (Iowa 2000, Utah 2001, Illinois 2001, New York 2001, Indiana 2005, Minnesota 2010, RHDV2 Ohio 2018, RHDV2 San Juan Islands (WA) 2019, RHDV2 in wild rabbits New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, Colorado 2020), although was thought to have been eradicated in the US in 2019. It also has been reported in China, Republic of Korea, India and the Middle East. It is more likely to be detected in large congregations than in single (e.g. individual pet) rabbits; disease spread exacerbated in crowded conditions. Incubation period: Incubation 1-3 days; death often occurs within 12-36 hours of fever onset.

-  Classical RHDV/RHDVa: Often subclinical, especially in young rabbits (less than 4-8 weeks of age). In older animals, peracute and acute disease are common presentations. Peracute clinical signs may include fever and sudden death within 12-36 hours of fever onset. Sometimes, terminal squeals are the only clinical sign followed by subsequent collapse and death. Acute clinical signs may include depression, dullness, anorexia, congested conjunctiva, prostration, reluctance to move, congested genitalia, neurologic signs (incoordination, inappropriate excitement, opisthotonos and paddling), and respiratory signs (dyspnea, cyanosis, and in final stages, hemorrhagic, frothy discharge from mouth or nostrils may be seen). In animals that survive, infection, jaundice, weight loss, and lethargy may be seen. -  RHDV2: Affects both old and young animals, experimentally infected animals generally survive longer with fewer peracute/acute presentations of disease. Clinical signs are otherwise similar to classical RHDV.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: -  Gross findings: The primary lesion identified in animals infected with RHDV, RHDVa, and RHDV2 is hepatic necrosis. Most commonly identified lesions include friable liver, splenomegaly (congested), dark brown kidneys, evidence of DIC (hemorrhage and/or infarcts in various organs, especially thymus) and pulmonary congestion, edema and/or petechiae; multifocal petechiae in other organs or serosanguineous tracheal fluid may be present (trachea often hyperemic). -  Histologic findings: More common lesions: mild to (more often) severe hepatic necrosis, disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC), splenic congestion, multifocal lymphocytolysis. Less frequently, multifocal acute pulmonary edema, congestion or hemorrhage and multifocal hemorrhage in other sites may be present.

-  Serologic tests: hemagglutination inhibition (HI), indirect ELISA (I-ELISA), competitive ELISA (CELISA). -  Pathogen identification: hemagglutination test (HA), electron microscopy (negative staining EM, immuno-EM, immunogold EM), virus detection ELISA, RT-PCR, RT-LAMP, Western blot, histology, immunostaining, inoculation study (RHDV never grown in cell cultures); in situ hybridization; liver contains highest viral titers and has been proposed as most diagnostic organ to submit for virus identification.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: - Rabbits - Pneumonitis, hepatitis, and splenitis with granulomatous lesions primarily found in the brain, kidney and eye. - o CNS - Encephalitis with multifocal to disseminated mononuclear or granulomatous inflammatory infiltrates. Perivascular cuffing inflammatory infiltrates are common findings with granulomas being more rare. The cerebrum is most commonly affected followed by the leptomeninges. Vesticular cores, cerebellum and spinal cord are rarely affected. Intracellular organisms are commonly seen in the vascular endothelium of the brain. Early disease can show neuronal degeneration and partial myelin loss with reactive, diffuse gliosis against the spores. Spinal nerve root inflammation can also occur. - o Renal - Glomerulonephritis. Intracellular organisms seen in the glomeruli and renal tubular epithelium. - o Ocular - phacoclastic uveitis, cataracts (unilateral or bilateral). - o Cardiovascular - Myocarditis, vasculitis - o Histopathological lesions may not correlate with the severity of clinical signs. - Canine (juvenile) - encephalitis and nephritis. - Domestic felines - meningoencephalitis, interstitial nephritis, anterior uveitis and cataracts.

- Microscopic identification of Gram positive organisms in histologic sections and/or spores in body secretions (urine sediment or CSF) using modified trichrome stain (Ziehl-Neelsen is preferred) or chitin-binding Calcofluor or Fungi-Fluor stain. - Anti-mortem PCR testing of liquified lens material aspirated during phacoemulsification is possible for animals with phacoclastic uveitis. PCR of feces is performed in humans. - Serology via MFIA, IFA, ELISA, or CIA. Negative IgG rules out E.-cuniculi as the cause of current neurological signs. Elevated IgM helps to indicate early infection (IgM levels decline to zero 35 days after infection). IgG antibodies can be found in urine of rabbits with strong seroreactivity. - Plasma or serum electrophoresis and C-reactive protein testing can be helpful, non-specific, adjunctive tests. CSF analysis is another supportive, but non confirmatory test.

Smith (2011, 2013) Susceptible animal groups: This disease generally affects macropods and potoroids. MaHV-1 was first described in parma wallabies (Macropus parma) and has been experimentally induced in brush-tailed possums (Trichosurus vulpecula). MaHV-2 was first described in grey dorcopsis wallabies (Dorcopsis muelleri luctuosa) and quokkas (Setonix brachyurus). MaHV-3 was first described in eastern grey kangaroos (M.

vulpecula). MaHV-2 was first described in grey dorcopsis wallabies (Dorcopsis muelleri luctuosa) and quokkas (Setonix brachyurus). MaHV-3 was first described in eastern grey kangaroos (M. giganteus), both captive and free-living. Non-specified herpesvirus infections have also been reported in tammar wallabies (M. eugenii), western grey kangaroos (M. fuliginosus), brushtailed rat kangaroos (Bettongia penicillata) and rufous rat kangaroos (Aepyprymnus rufescens). Recently, MaHV-4 was detected in a free-living eastern grey kangaroo and a captive-bred Lumholtz's tree -kangaroo (Dendrolagus lumholtzi). Causative organism: Macropod herpesviruses fall within both the subfamilies Alphaherpesvirinae and Gammaherpesvirinae of the family Herpesviridae. There are four herpesvirus species isolated from macropods: three alphaherpesviruses termed Macropodid Herpesvirus 1 (MaHV1), Macropodid Herpesvirus 2 (MaHV2), and Macropodid Herpesvirus 4 (MaHV4) and one gammaherpesvirus named Macropodid Herpesvirus 3 (MaHV3).

Distribution: Initially clinical disease was only reported in captive animals, but MaHV-3 has been detected in free-living eastern grey kangaroos exhibiting respiratory disease and possibly neurologic disease and MaHV-4 has been newly described in a free-living eastern grey kangaroo with respiratory disease. One study reported seropositive rates of 23% of wild marsupials and 41% of captive marsupials in Australia, although specificity of the serologic testing is unknown. The largest study to assess disease status via PCR showed a prevalence of 25% in eastern grey kangaroos and an overall prevalence of 25%. The results of this study were consistent with the epidemiology of herpesvirus in other species: herpesviruses that were identified are host species-specific, and multiple different herpesviruses were detected within a single host species. MaHV-1, MaHV-2 and MaHV-4 have only been reported in animals in Australia. MaHV-3 has been reported in captive eastern grey kangaroos in the US as well as in wild eastern grey kangaroos.

-  MaHV-1: Fatal systemic infections resulting in severe clinical signs including pyrexia, respiratory signs, conjunctivitis, and anogenital vesicles. -  MaHV-2: Fatal systemic disease characterized by conjunctivitis and lesions on the oral and anogenital mucous membranes. -  MaHV-3: Typically a subclinical systemic disease. Mild to moderate ulcerative cloacitis found in immunocompromised individuals may be associated with this virus. -  MaHV-4: Respiratory and possibly neurological disease. May be fatal.

texto: -  MaHV-1: - o Gross: Vesicles and ulcers of skin, lips, eyelids, and anogenital mucosa; rhinitis; mild to severe keratitis. - o Histologic: Necrotic epithelium and inflammatory debris; numerous large basophilic or eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions. -  MaHV-2: - o Gross: Purulent conjunctivitis; red edematous lung lesions; pinpoint (1mm) yellow foci in the liver; erythematous mucosal lesions in the gastrointestinal tract; mesenteric lymphadenopathy; erythematous mucous membranes; yellow plaques on reproductive tract. - o Histologic: Disseminated focal necrosis; intranuclear acidophilic or basophilic inclusions. -  MaHV-3: - o Gross: Ulcerative cloacitis was found in MaHV-3 positive individuals. A definitive association with the virus has not been proven. - o Histologic: No inclusions were identified in PCR-positive tissues. The opaleye fish (Girella nigricans) is believed to be the primary host of the virus that may be passed to marine mammals and swine. Causative organism: VESV and SMSV are in the genus Vesivirus within the family Caliciviridae. SMSV is morphologically indistinguishable from VESV. Many immunologically unique serotypes have been demonstrated including 13 serotypes in swine, 16 serotypes in marine mammals, and other serotypes in bovine, primate, cetacean, walrus, skunk, mink, rabbit and reptiles. All of these viruses except for SMSV-8, SMSV-12 and mink calicivirus form a single virus species, VESV. Zoonotic potential: VESV has occasionally been isolated from humans with blisters; however, the virus is not considered to be a serious public health threat. Distribution: VESV has been found only in the United States and was eradicated in 1956. SMSV is found on the Pacific coast of North America. Incubation period: 1-5 days. Clinical signs: VESV infection in swine is clinically indistinguishable from foot and mouth disease, vesicular stomatitis, Seneca virus A, and swine vesicular disease. Pyrexia may occur transiently.

secao: Vesicular exanthema of swine virus (VESV) & San Miguel sealion virus (SMSV)
texto: Clinical signs: VESV infection in swine is clinically indistinguishable from foot and mouth disease, vesicular stomatitis, Seneca virus A, and swine vesicular disease. Pyrexia may occur transiently. Vesicles progressing to erosions develop on the feet (coronary bands, soles), around the mouth (snout, lips, oral cavity), and on the teats. Lesions tend to be deeper than the lesions of other vesicular diseases, with granulation tissue formation on the feet. Lesions on the feet may cause lameness. Lesions around the mouth may cause anorexia and salivation. VESV has also been associated with reproductive failure and mild encephalitis in swine. Pinnipeds infected with SMSV develop vesicles that progress to erosions on the flippers and rarely exhibit gastrointestinal signs (abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, vomiting, regurgitation). Pregnant pinnipeds may abort. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Vesicles on coronary bands, snout, lips, oral cavity, and teats. Hydropic degeneration and edema of stratum spinosum of the affected epidermis, followed by ballooning degeneration of keratinocytes that then float into the vesicular fluid. Stratum basale may be disrupted.

Brucella species typically have different host preferences, virulence, and zoonotic potential despite 97-99% similarity at genome level. Marine mammal Brucella spp. are currently identified as B. ceti (cetacean-origin strains) and B. pinnipedialis (pinniped-origin strains). Molecular characterization of Brucella ceti suggests two major clades, one group primarily associated with porpoise isolates and another primarily associated with dolphin isolates. Brucella strains have been placed into various sequence types (STs) that are often grouped into clusters, but strains do not always appear to be family or order specific. For example, B. ceti ST27 has been identified in cetaceans, California sea lions, and naturally acquired cases in humans. Currently, data indicates differences in pathogenesis among the various B. ceti STs in cetaceans and infection with multiple STs appears possible. Zoonotic potential: Yes. Outside of laboratory-associated infection, the route of exposure is not known, but food-borne exposure (i.e. raw seafood) is suspected.

Distribution & Seasonality: Globally distributed in wild species of cetaceans (including Phocoenidae, Delphinidae, Monodontidae, Balaenidae, and Balaenopteridae) and pinnipeds (including Phocidae, Otariidae, and Odobenidae). Seroprevalance fluctuates in wild populations over time, suggesting cyclicity in epidemiology of infection. Increased prevalence of infections in the spring, associated with calving season, has been noted in wild cetacean populations off the coast of South Carolina. Incubation period: Not known. Clinical signs: Variable, depending on affected organ system and strain of bacteria. Although strains are host-associated, cross-species infections occur frequently and may affect expression of disease. -  Cetaceans: stranding, inanition, infertility, abortion, neurologic signs, cutaneous and pulmonary abscessation and musculoskeletal disorders.

-  Cetaceans: lesions are primarily seen in reproductive tract (orchitis/epididymitis, necrotizing placentitis/endometritis), reticuloendothelial/hemolymphatic systems (lymphadenitis, splenic necrosis), central nervous system (meningoencephalitis), musculoskeletal system (discospondylitis, osteomyelitis, and arthritis), and lung (interstitial pneumonia, pulmonary abscesses and granulomas, and lungworm associated pneumonia). Additional findings have included blubber abscesses, visceral necrosis, steatitis, mastitis, hepatomegaly, and vegetative endocarditis. -  Pinnipeds: Evidence for Brucella-related pathology is scant. A single Northern fur seal placenta sample demonstrated severe placentitis in association with positive PCR testing and immunostaining for Brucella. Cholangitis was observed in three grey seals in which Brucella was isolated from the livers and Brucella DNA was detected in the liver flukes (Pseudamphistomum truncatum). Focal areas of pneumonia have been described in harbor seals with Brucella-infected lungworms. Of note, the pathology observed in the aforementioned grey and harbor seal cases may have been associated with the parasites and/or the Brucella.

Diagnosis: Diagnosis is achieved via direct identification and with indirect screening methods. -  Bacterial isolation in culture from infected tissues (most commonly CSF, brain, lymph node, and lung) remains the gold standard; however, this method is difficult at best. Farrell's media or Brucella-agar with 5% horse blood may be used and incubated with 5-10% CO2 for up to 14 days. -  Molecular characterization by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) methods include outer membrane protein polymorphisms, infrequent restriction site-derivative PCR, insertion sequence IS711 profiling, multilocus sequence typing (MLST), and multiple loci variable number tandem repeat analysis (MLVA). Detection of Brucella from a blowhole swab utilizing real-time PCR appears to correlate well with detection of Brucella in internal lung tissue.

Blowhole, blood, and/or fecal PCR may identify animals actively shedding bacteria, which require isolation. General biosecurity and quarantine protocols are recommended for marine mammal rehabilitation and aquarium facilities. Distribution: Infection has been confirmed in free-ranging pinnipeds in the northern and southern Atlantic and Pacific Oceans and Antarctica. Also identified in captive pinnipeds and human caretakers at rehabilitation centers in North America and Europe. Incubation period: In captive animals, 2-5 week incubation period. -  Pinnipeds: Highly contagious with low mortality and very high morbidity. Juveniles, stressed, and newly-housed animals are the most likely to have active disease, but can be seen in otherwise healthy adults. Presents with firm skin nodules (1-3 cm) on the head, neck, and thorax. Nodules may also be found on the abdomen, flippers, and mucosa or oral cavity. Nodules can progress to inflamed, ulcerated and necrotic and are usually self-limiting after 46 weeks (though can persist for months) and result in a raised, gray, alopecic scar. Nodules near lips and eyes can cause hyporexia. -  Humans: Handlers of affected animals can contract the disease through cuts or breaks in the skin. Typically, presents as a single, painful nodule (3mm-1cm) and may be accompanied with flu-like symptoms. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Gross findings: Firm cutaneous nodules 1-3 cm diameter. Lesions can be inflamed and ulcerated, and solitary, in clusters, or generalized along the body. Histologic findings: marked epidermal and follicular hyperplasia with ballooning degeneration in the stratum spinosum.

and ulcerated, and solitary, in clusters, or generalized along the body. Histologic findings: marked epidermal and follicular hyperplasia with ballooning degeneration in the stratum spinosum. Moderately sized, round to chunky eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions bodies can be are noted within epidermal and follicular keratinocytes. The dermis and epidermis may have mixed inflammatory infiltrate and necrosis. Diagnosis: Often presumptive diagnosis through clinical suspicion. -  Skin biopsy and histopathology can be performed. Poxvirus particles in negatively stained, unfixed lesion material can be seen. Molecular assays for viral DNA detection include PCR, RFLPs, and sequencing. -  An indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for detection of antibodies has been developed for California sea lions. - ∞ The common house mouse (Mus musculus) is the natural host and primary reservoir of LCMV. Mice typically show no clinical signs of infection, although some may display some reproductive decline. Hamsters are non-natural reservoirs but can become infected through contact with LCMV-infected mice, and can cause a chronic, fatal, wasting disease in young individuals. - ∞ The host range of LCMV includes nonhuman primates, dogs, rabbits, and other rodents. Pigs have been experimentally infected as well. Several genera of new-world nonhuman primates of the families Callitrichidae (Callithrix sp., Saguinus sp.), and Callimiconidae (Callimico goeldii), are considered especially susceptible. In golden lion tamarins (Leontopithecus rosalia) and pygmy marmosets (Cebuella pygmaea) under human care, the virus accounted for 43% and 71% of deaths, respectively. - ∞ Infections in humans from pet rodents have been reported. Infected mice and hamsters have been shown to shed the virus in large quantities through their saliva, feces, urine, and nasal secretions.

Antibodies to LCMV have also been found in rats (Rattus norvegicus) in Spain, wood mice (Apodemus sylvaticus) from Austria and Spain, yellow-necked field mice (Apodemus flavicollis) and voles from Italy.

- ∞ Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is a lipid-enveloped single-stranded RNA virus (family Arenaviridae, genera Mammarenavirus). It is within the Old World Arenavirus group, and is considered the prototypic arenavirus. Nowadays, five (I-V) lineages of LCMV are recognized, with lineages I and II being the most common sequences worldwide. Lineage III has only been found in one patient from Georgia, USA, while lineage IV was identified through the sequence of RNA segments from wood mice (Apodemus sylvaticus) from Southern Spain. A novel lineage, V, was identified in wood mice in Germany. - ∞ Rodents, particularly the house mouse (Mus musculus), are the principal reservoirs, carry persistent, inapparent infections, and remain viremic. Recently, researchers have proposed that LCMV lineages I & II might be host-specific; thus, lineage I is harbored by Mus musculus domesticus, while lineage II is harbored by M. m. musculus. - ∞ LCMV exhibits high mutation rates and important strain variations. Rodent reservoirs pass the virus to their offspring and shed the virus in urine and oral secretions and allowing the virus to remain in circulation.

mutation rates and important strain variations. Rodent reservoirs pass the virus to their offspring and shed the virus in urine and oral secretions and allowing the virus to remain in circulation. In zoo settings, transmission has occurred via feeding live or frozen domestic mice to nonhuman primates. Animals not eating mice neither became ill nor seroconverted to LCMV even after close contact with sick primates. Thus, direct primateprimate transmission of LCMV has not been observed yet, although such a mode of transmission remains a possibility. Vertical transmission of LCMV to an aborted tamarin fetus, however, was demonstrated in a US zoo.

- ∞ LCMV was the first arenavirus isolated from cerebrospinal fluid of people with aseptic meningitis and is now considered a globally recognized zoonotic pathogen. Serological studies indicate that approximately 5% of adult humans in the USA show antibodies to this virus. In humans, LCMV causes influenza-like clinical signs, including photophobia, headache, fever, stiff neck, and nausea. Rarely, the virus can manifest as neurologic complications, such as aseptic meningitis or encephalitis. Infection may be asymptomatic in up to one-third of patients. Less severe cases of adult human infection are likely underreported and often misdiagnosed. It is noteworthy that infection with LCMV has historically been underreported, making it difficult to determine incidence rates or prevalence. - ∞ Infections with LCMV can result in severe fetal anomalies and has also been associated with sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) in humans. Several reports of LCMV acquired during pregnancy have demonstrated severe disruption of brain development, especially during the third trimester, and can lead to effects such as mental retardation, hydrocephalus, and chorioretinitis.

In 2009, the Center for Disease Control and Prevention confirmed a case of LCMV-associated congenital hydrocephalus and chorioretinitis in a child from New York. The mother´s history referred to exposure to mice during pregnancy. Given its potential to cause severe birth defects, some experts advocate including LCMV in the TORCHS screening group for congenital infections. - ∞ LCMF poses a risk to animal handlers, laboratory workers, and people exposed to infected rodents. . In Maryland and Alabama, seroprevalence in people over age 30 reached 5.4%, - compared to 0.3% in younger individuals. In Baltimore, human seroprevalence was 4.7%, with rodent prevalence between 3.9-13.4%. A survey in New Whales, Australia, identified 30-52% of feral mice seropositivity to LCMV, while countries such as Slovakia and Bratislava have shown foci of murine LCMV. In Germany alone, a total of 48 human cases of LCMV were reported between 1968-1973 many originated from pet golden hamsters (Mesocricetus auratus).

In April 2012, the CDC was notified about a patient diagnosed with aseptic meningitis who was an employee at a rodent breeding facility in Indiana and whose testing revealed LCMV. Further testing showed evidence of prevailing or past LCMV infection in 13 out of 52 employees at the same facility. - ∞ While human-to-human transmission is extremely rare and LCMV is seldom fatal, it remains an underrecognized public health concern due to its neuroinvasive potential and risk to pregnant women. Less severe or asymptomatic infections are likely underreported and may be misdiagnosed. Increased awareness among clinicians is critical for early diagnosis and prevention.

- ∞ LCMV is found worldwide and has been reported in Europe, Australia, the Americas, and Japan. Despite its broad distribution, Central Europe is of particular interest for studying LCMV ecology and host specificity. This region contains a hybrid zone between two house mouse subspecies (Mus musculus musculus and M. m. domesticus), yet exhibits a surprisingly low prevalence of LCMV, suggesting complex host-virus dynamics. Wild red foxes (Vulpes vulpes) in Spain were likely to become infected with LCMV by feeding on infected rodents, which can provide information on affected areas, thus, this could be another route for humans coming in contact with this arenavirus. - ∞ Although LCMV antibodies have been detected in a range of rodent species, serological crossreactivity among arenaviruses complicates interpretation. Notably, outbreaks in callitrichid primate colonies have occurred in zoological institutions in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Germany, emphasizing the virus's potential to cause disease in captive nonhuman primates.

Incubation period: In non-human primates, the incubation period is from one to three weeks, but deaths can reach 100% in an outbreak and may occur over a period of weeks to months.

- ∞ In infected callitrichid primates (marmosets, tamarins, and Goeldi´s monkeys), clinical findings are often acute and severe and can include lethargy, anorexia, anemia, weakness, fever, dyspnea, mucus-covered feces, jaundice, seizures, petechiation and hemorrhage. Abortion and dystocia in captive tamarins and marmosets are also reported. Grand mal seizures or sudden death without prior clinical signs has also been reported. - ∞ Clinical laboratory findings include elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and bilirubin most commonly. Aminotransferases and bilirubin in plasma can be elevated several times above normal reference ranges in LCMV infections in zoo-kept marmosets and tamarins. Serologic evidence of LCMV in marmosets without clinical signs has been documented. - ∞ In experimentally infected rhesus macaques, LCVM-WE strain has led to fatal liver disease which was formerly described as Lassa fever (LF) hepatitis.

Postmortem, gross, or histologic findings: Gross necropsy findings in nonhuman primates includes histopathologic findings in the brain, liver, and lymphoid tissues, and can include lesions such as hepatitis, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, pleural and pericardial effusions, lymphadenopathy, jaundice, and subcutaneous or intramuscular hemorrhages. Classic histologic findings include multifocal hepatocyte necrosis and degeneration with infiltration by lymphocytes and neutrophils, portal vein vasculitis, necrosis of spleen, lymph nodes, adrenal cortex, and intestinal tract. Acidophilic bodies (Councilman bodies), which represent apoptotic hepatocytes, have been observed in sinusoids and Kupffer cells of affected liver tissues. Brain tissues may show encephalitis, minimal meningitis, and vasculitis.

- ∞ In nonhuman primates, diagnosis of LCMV should be considered with consistent clinical signs and history of exposure to rodents through the environment or diet. Reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) on brain tissue has been utilized to aid in the diagnosis of a golden lion tamarin in Germany, with confirmation of the sequence in a wild house mice (M.m. domesticus). - ∞ Histopathology, virus isolation, electron microscopy, nucleic acid hybridization analysis, immunofluorescence, and immunoblot can be used for virus detection. Suggested tissue samples that can be used include liver, spleen, lung, adrenal glands, lymph nodes, intestine, kidneys, urinary bladder, heart and brain. Confirmatory diagnosis is by viral isolation (VI) or PCR. - ∞ In humans, confirmatory diagnosis is usually by virus isolation or PCR in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which is best isolated early in the course of the disease. Semi-Quantitative Indirect Fluorescent Antibody in CSF is also utilized.

secao: Susceptible animal groups (affected by different viral genera):
texto: -  Psittacines: Infection by Psittaciform 1 and 2 orthobornaviruses has been reported in more than 80 species of captive psittacine birds in at least 33 different genera. Certain species, such as African grey parrots, blue and gold macaws, cockatoos, and Amazon parrots, seem most - frequently affected. Others: budgerigars, lovebirds and quaker parrots appear relatively resistant to infection or clinical signs of infection. -  Passerines: Passeriform 1 and 2 orthobornaviruses have been described from captive canaries (Serinus canaria), a Bengalese/Society finch (Lonchura striata domestica) and 3 estrildid finches. -  Anseriformes, Laridae: Waterbird 1 orthobornavirus infection was initially recognized in North America in free-ranging mute (Cygnus olor) and trumpeter swans (Cygnus buccinator), and in Canada geese (Branta canadensis). This and related viruses have since been identified in a range of wild goose and duck species, as well as in several species of gulls. Investigations in Europe have identified Waterbird 1 orthobornavirus infections in three additional species of geese in Denmark and a Eurasian oystercatcher (Haematopus ostralegus) in Germany.

Thus, molecular sequencing of bornaviruses obtained from avian host groups or species not listed above is highly recommended. In other words, the complete host range for these viruses likely remains unknown; the discovery of additional bornaviral genotypes soon is also likely. Causative organism: The first avian-associated bornavirus (ABV) was identified in 2008 as the cause of PDD in psittacine birds. Bornaviruses are enveloped, unsegmented, negative single-stranded, RNA viruses in the family Bornaviridae. Currently, five species of bornaviruses are known to affect birds: Passeriform 1 orthobornavirus (canary bornaviruses 1-3; munia bornavirus 1), Passeriform 2 orthobornavirus (estrildid finch bornavirus 1), Psittaciform 1 orthobornavirus (parrot bornaviruses 1-4, 7), Psittaciform 2 orthobornavirus (parrot bornavirus 5), and Waterbird 1 orthobornavirus (aquatic bird bornaviruses 1-2).

Parrot bornaviruses 2 and 4 are the most commonly identified viruses in psittacine birds and have been linked to PDD. Additional viruses await formal classification. Zoonotic potential: None reported.

-  Parrot bornaviruses: the clinical syndrome of ABV infection in psittacine birds (then called PDD), was first identified in the late 1970's in the United States. Today, ABV infection and associated diseases have been described in captive psittacines around the world. Worldwide dissemination is assumed to have resulted from the trade in captive birds. Despite some evidence for the presence of exposure of wild parrots to ABV in South America, a reservoir in wild psittacine birds lacks confirmation. Viral RNA for genotypes PaBV-2 and PaBV-4 have been detected in samples from non-psittacine wild birds in Japan. -  Canary bornaviruses: These viruses appear prevalent in captive European canaries. Canany bornavirus 1 (CnBV-1) has also been reported in a small number of captive and wild birds in Brazil. -  Aquatic bird bornaviruses: Infection, initially recognized as widespread in North America, has also been reported from free-ranging wild birds in Denmark, Germany and Poland. A lack of reports from other parts of the world likely reflects a lack of dedicated investigation.

-  Recent ABV inoculation time-based studies in cockatiels reveal that after intramuscular inoculation of parrot bornavirus 2 (PaBV-2) in the pectoral muscle the virus was first detected in macrophages and lymphocytes in the inoculation site and adjacent nerves at day 5 post innoculation. Virus then reached the brachial plexus, centripetally spread to the thoracic - segment of the spinal cord, and subsequently invaded the other spinal segments and brain at 25 days post infection. After reaching the central nervous system (CNS), PaBV-2 centrifugally spread out the CNS to the ganglia in the gastrointestinal (GI) system, adrenal gland, heart, and kidneys at day 80 post inoculation. At late points of infection, PaBV-2 was not only detected in nerves and ganglia but widespread in the smooth muscle and/or scattered epithelial cells of tissues such as crop, intestines, proventriculus, kidneys, skin, and vessels at 100 days post infection. -  Anecdotal reports suggest an acute form in which birds may die within days or weeks after the acute onset of symptoms and in the persistent form birds may able to live for years without clinical impairment.

reports suggest an acute form in which birds may die within days or weeks after the acute onset of symptoms and in the persistent form birds may able to live for years without clinical impairment. In one author's experience (JJH) many acute presentations are likely in birds that have tolerated PaBV infection for years, but changes in the immune system associated with age result in advanced signs of ABV infection (neurologic malfunction) and an acute presentation. Clinical signs: Descriptions of PDD in psittacine birds predate the discovery of ABV. Birds infected with ABV may or may not develop clinical disease. Clinical signs result from pathology in the autonomic, central, and/or peripheral nervous systems, and vary in nature, severity, and duration. Non-specific signs include depression, lethargy, weight loss, muscle atrophy, abdominal enlargement, polyuria, and polydipsia, as well as sudden death. Classic gastrointestinal signs associated with myenteric plexus dysfunction include dysphagia, crop stasis, regurgitation, impaction, maldigestion (passage of undigested seeds), and progressive loss of body condition.

Central and peripheral nervous system signs include changes in behavior, awareness, and demeanor, tremors, seizures, erratic head movements, torticollis, head-pressing, opisthotonos, abnormal gait and posture, inability to perch, proprioceptive and motor deficits, ataxia, paralysis, status epilepticus, and ophthalmologic abnormalities (dilated pupils, anisocoria, chorioretinitis, retinal degeneration, and blindness). The factors that govern the development of clinical disease in ABV-positive birds are not known but are likely related to features of the host's immune status and the infecting virus (genotype, strain). Affected birds can develop secondary opportunistic infections that increase mortality. Because PaBV can cause skin inflammation histologically, clinical signs of feather abnormalities, feather picking, and self-mutilation, should be cause to include PaBV on the rule-out list for affected parrots.

Post-mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Consistency among clinical signs and gross and histologic findings is not always present. Gross lesions include mild to severe emaciation, crop, proventricular, ventricular, and or intestinal distension. Proventricular rupture and resulting peritonitis are rare. It is not uncommon that no gross lesions are observed. Microscopic lesions consist of non-suppurative inflammation in peripheral, central, and autonomic nervous tissues. Similar infiltrates may also be present in adrenal glands and myocardium. Cerebellar Purkinje cell necrosis, neuronophagia, myelin degeneration, gliosis, and axonal swelling can accompany the inflammatory lesions. Diagnosis: Because PaBV infection does not reliably equate to proventricular dilation (PDD) we prefer the term Avian Inflammatory Neurologic Syndrome, to the misnomer of PDD.

Histological lesions in biopsy or post-mortem samples remain the gold standard for diagnosis of AINS, which is from infection with PaBV. Detection of virus/viral RNA/viral antigen or antibodies against ABV provides evidence of infection or exposure, but does not differentiate among patients with clinical PDD, asymptomatic shedders and previously exposed birds. There is no standardized screening protocol for PDD and/or ABV infection in psittacine flocks. Still, screening programs involving separation of birds based on a combination of repeated RT-PCR assessment of choanal and/or cloacal swabs (feather sampling has also been recommended) and serology have been used to derive flocks without evidence of ABV infection. -  Clinical signs and pathologic lesions: ABV infection should be considered as a differential diagnosis for clinical signs referable to the neurologic and/or digestive systems.

Prior to the identification of the avian bornaviruses, techniques for the antemortem diagnosis of PDD included plain and contrast radiography, contrast fluoroscopy, and crop biopsy. Crop biopsy has a variable and often low sensitivity. -  Detection of virus, RNA or antigen: - o Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR): Both gel-based and realtime RT-PCR have been developed using primers for various segments of the ABV genome, particularly the N and M genes. Not all primers will detect all bornaviruses that affect avian species. - o Immunohistochemistry (IHC): IHC can be used to identify ABV antigen in formalinfixed biopsy or necropsy specimens. Moderately intense, diffuse, intracytoplasmic staining accompanied by intranuclear staining in neurons and certain epithelial cells is considered positive for viral antigen presence. - o Virus culture: Various genotypes of ABV have been successfully grown in a range of avian cell lines.

Cytopathic effects do not occur, the virus must be demonstrated by Western blot, immunohistochemistry, indirect immunofluorescence, or RT-PCR. - o Sequence analysis: The recognition of an increasing number of bornaviral species and genotypes makes genome sequencing a critical component in the diagnosis of ABV infection and of PDD. -  Detection of antibodies: Indirect immunofluorescence (using infected cell cultures that present multiple antigens), Western blot, and indirect ELISA assays using various sources of monoclonal primary antigen have been used in psittacine birds and waterfowl. Several private laboratories offer serologic testing, which is also used as a research tool. Test specificity and sensitivity are difficult to determine and compare due to the absence of a gold standard for diagnosis, and the relatively poor correlation between the presence of antibodies, fecal shedding of ABV, and the presence of pathologic lesions and/or clinical disease.

-  Ante-mortem: Crop tissue (histology +/- IHC +/- RT-PCR); choanal and cloacal swabs, feces (less sensitive than cloacal swabs), and possibly calami of plucked chest contour feathers (RTPCR); plasma or serum (serology). Pooling multiple cloacal swabs or droppings from a single bird over several days or samples from multiple birds in an aviary increases test sensitivity as shedding of virus is frequently intermittent. -  Post-mortem: Brain, proventriculus, ventriculus, adrenals, and vitreous of the eye (most consistently infected tissues) (RT-PCR +/- sequencing); brain, proventriculus, ventriculus (histology +/- IHC). As lesions vary in location and severity, submission of a full suite of tissues is highly recommended. RT-PCR can also be performed on formalin-fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) tissues in some laboratories.

Atkinson (2013) Susceptible animal groups: Sheep, cattle, goats, camels, African buffalo, water buffalo, Asian monkeys, humans, some rodents, neonate cats and dogs can be infected. Sheep and goats appear more susceptible than cattle or camelids. Susceptibility of cervids is not known. Death in wild African ruminants is rare but there are recent reports of abortion and/or deaths with virus isolation in African buffalo, wildebeest, waterbuck, giraffe, sable, springbok and impala. African monkeys, baboons, equids, pigs and domestic carnivores are considered resistant, experiencing only asymptomatic viremia. Gray squirrels, mice, hamsters and newborn dogs and cats can be experimentally infected but don't usually play a role in the transmission. Causative organism: RVF virus is an RNA Phlebovirus of the family Bunyaviridae. Only one serotype is recognized but strains of variable virulence exist. Virus circulates in endemic areas among wild ruminants and major hosts appear to be members of genera Aedes, Culex, Anopheles. Certain Aedes species act as reservoirs during inter-epizootic periods and increased precipitation in dry areas leads to an explosive hatching of eggs.

Certain Aedes species act as reservoirs during inter-epizootic periods and increased precipitation in dry areas leads to an explosive hatching of eggs. Precipitation cycles of 5-25 years produce RVF-immuno naïve animal populations, and introduction of virus can lead to explosive outbreaks. Virus can be transmitted by many species of mosquitoes and other biting insects during viremic phase in mammalian hosts. Zoonotic potential: Humans are infected via direct or indirect contact with blood, body fluids (except in urine or feces), or tissues of infected animals. Transmission can be via inoculation (including by mosquito or fly vectors) or inhalation. There is some evidence that humans may be infected by ingesting unpasteurized or uncooked milk of infected animals. Most human cases are mild, but severe forms (ocular, meninencephalitits, and hemorrhagic fever) are noted. It is possible that humans can act as amplifying hosts. No human-human transmission has been documented. Distribution: Serologic or virologic evidence over most of Africa.

texto: - Abortion storms occur in domestic livestock at any stage of pregnancy. Biphasic fever up to 106° F (up to 104° F in humans, to 107° F in sheep.) - Lambs/kids: High fever, listlessness, inactivity, anorexia, abdominal pain, increased respiration rate, GI hemorrhage. Mortality rate of 90%. - Adult sheep/goats: Peracute disease more common; fever, weakness, anorexia, diarrhea, bloody nasal discharge, jaundice, increased respiratory rate, leukopenia, elevated liver enzymes. Mortality rate of 30-50%. Frequent abortion (up to 100%) - Calves: Jaundice, fever, weakness, anorexia, hematochezia. Mortality rate 20%. - Adult cattle: Peracute disease more common. Weakness, anorexia, hematochezia, blood nasal discharge, hypersalivation. Mortality rate 5-10%. Up to 85% abortion rates. - Camelids: Abortion, sudden death or acute syndrome with fever, neurological signs, expiratory wheeze, dyspnea, icterus, hemorrhagic nasal discharge, conjunctivitis, blindness. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Focal or generalized hepatic and splenic necrosis; enlarged, discolored, soft, friable liver with irregular congestion and white necrotic foci (~1 mm diameter).

Lesions are most severe in aborted fetus and young animals. Widespread cutaneous hemorrhages, petechiae and ecchymoses on serosal membranes. Gall bladder wall edematous with possible hemorrhage. Spleen and lymph nodes are edematous, enlarged and may show petechiae. Hemorrhagic enteritis, intestinal contents dark chocolate-brown. Diagnosis: It is suspected in endemic areas when presented with abortions and relevant signs combined with febrile disease in humans after heavy rains and/or flooding. Histopathology of liver is relevant. Most tissues will contain virus and can be used for detection (virus isolation, RT-PCR, ELISA antigen detection) and numerous serologic tests exist: VN, ELISA, IgG and IgM. Material required for laboratory analysis: Blood, liver (major site of replication), spleen, brain, kidney, lymph nodes, and aborted fetuses are tissues of choice.

contact with diseased carcasses or via animal products (meat, bone meal, leather, wool, bristles) Current update by Tess Rooney (2023) Reviewed by Ed Ramsay (2023) Originally compiled by Thomas W. deMaar (2011), updated by Vikki Milne (2013) Susceptible animal groups: Domestic and wild ruminants are most commonly affected. However, humans, equids (horses, zebras), and other mammals - such as elephants, wild pigs, and carnivores are susceptible. Suids and carnivores may develop subacute to chronic gastrointestinal type disease after eating infected carcasses (African wild dogs in Kruger National Park experience outbreaks, but often survive despite infection). Anthrax has also been reported in ostriches and rheas. Resistant animal groups: Scavenging birds and mammals, primarily carrion feeders, have particularly acidic stomachs, which are able to kill vegetative cells; thus, these species are able to pass spores through their digestive systems without becoming infected. Causative organism: Bacillus anthracis (spore-forming, non-motile, Gram-positive rod).

cells; thus, these species are able to pass spores through their digestive systems without becoming infected. Causative organism: Bacillus anthracis (spore-forming, non-motile, Gram-positive rod). Zoonotic potential: Humans affected via contact with diseased carcasses or via animal products (meat, bone meal, leather, wool, bristles, drum skins) from contaminated carcasses. Cutaneous, gastrointestinal, and inhalation forms of disease occur. It is considered a potential bioterrorism agent. Distribution: World-wide, especially in areas with neutral or alkaline calcareous soils. Outbreaks can occur after soil disturbance following drought or flood conditions. In the US, it occurs sporadically with limited distribution and is more common in western and midwestern US, and is enzootic in west Texas, North and South Dakota, and northwest Minnesota. Incubation period: Typically, 3-7 days (range 1-14 days) (OIE standards: up to 20 days). Spores maybe inactive in lungs for several weeks before causing disease.

-  Peracute (ruminants): sudden death. -  Acute (ruminants and horses): Abrupt fever and excitement followed by depression, respiratory/cardiac distress, staggering, convulsions, severe colic, and anterior edema; cutaneous signs can be seen in cattle and horses with biting fly infections. Process can lead to death. -  Chronic (pigs and carnivores): Oropharyngeal and gastrointestinal signs of disease, usually followed by recovery but death occurs if systemic. Death is not uncommon in free-ranging African lions. Post-mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Carcass presented with absence of rigor mortis and rapid decomposition. Dark blood may ooze from the mouth, nostrils, eyes, ears, vulva and anus. Edema may be apparent. Carcasses will show lack of blood clotting and hemorrhages of serosal surfaces. Organs, particularly the spleen, will be congested and enlarged (splenic swelling and exuding dark, tarry blood on cut section). Oropharyngitis, pharyngeal edema, diptheric membranes or ulcers of tonsils are seen in suids and carnivores. Gastrointestinal inflammation and mesenteric lymphadenitis may be seen in suids and carnivores.

-  Cytology: the bacteria are visible as large bacilli with square ends and a clear/pale halo - this is considered the most efficient diagnostic method. Central or subterminal endospores that do not cause the bacterial cell to swell may be visible. -  PCR, culture, IFA, ELISA and Western Blot tests are also available. Material required for laboratory analysis: If anthrax is suspected, necropsy should be aborted (carcass should NOT be opened and should be protected from scavengers). -  The carcass should not be moved until test results are available. -  Samples to collect using PPE: - o Blood (nick the ear or coronary band that are closest to ground) - o Aspirate from the thoracic cavity - o Tissue (submaxillary lymph node, spleen) -  Sample processing: air dry, fix in methanol, stain with polychrome methylene blue or Giemsa stain.

-  Rapid detection and prevention of disease spread via quarantine and removal of affected animals. Do not open carcasses in suspected cases. If the carcass tests positive, incineration or burial (at least 2m deep) should be performed to prevent sporulation and destroy bacteria. Where burial is not possible, in a tropical environment, B. anthracis bacteria will be destroyed in 4 days if not opened; guards can be posted for this duration to protect the carcass from scavengers. -  Post exposure antibiotics are recommended after exposure to aerosolized spores. -  Vaccination of susceptible animals in enzootic areas. -  Do not use meat or animal products from uninspected or unknown sources, cases of sudden death, or emergency slaughters. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Cremation or deep burial of carcasses and contaminated materials. Disinfect using formaldehyde, oxidizing agents such as peroxides, 5% lye, quicklime (anhydrous calcium oxide), and bleach; however prolonged contact is required. A commercial product Mold Control 500® has been approved. Several protocols for large scale premise decontamination have been utilized.

Formaldehyde (5%) can be used on soil if contamination is minimal otherwise soil removal is advised. Notification: Reportable to USDA National Animal Health Reporting System, who report to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH/OIE) if confirmed. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Wait at least 21 days after outbreak is completed and quarantine varies although the recommended time is 21 days before movement is allowed. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Where the disease is known to be endemic, disease-free status will only be granted after an extended period, ~10 years, without cases and with surveillance. For normal sporadic cases, there should be at least 5 years without cases but with vaccination.

secao: Clinical signs: Three general disease manifestations:
texto: -  Enteric coronaviruses (e.g., BCoV, CCV, ECoV, FCoV, FECV, PDCoV, PEDV, TGEV) with tropism for GI epithelial cells cause malabsorptive diarrhea with dehydration, metabolic acidosis, and possibly death; generally seen in young animals, especially BCV, TGE and PED. In BCV and TGE, the diarrhea is often mucoid and yellow in color with possible "milk clots". In FECV, the diarrhea begins as green and mucoid progressing to a rice-water, granular stool. -  Respiratory coronaviruses (e.g., PRCoV, MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2) enter and reproduce in the upper respiratory mucosa causing fever, nasal discharge, cough, pneumonia, and possibly death. Of note: BCoV has been implicated as a part of bovine respiratory disease complex, although whether this is due to the same or different virus remains unclear. -  Systemic coronaviruses infect and persist in macrophages, causing lethargy, weight loss, anorexia, anemia, peritonitis, vasculitis, bicavitary effusions, and death.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: -  Enteric coronaviruses: gross lesions include thin-walled, flaccid small intestine, often with yellowish contents; fluid in the colon and/or cecum; microscopically, villous atrophy and blunting, with club-shaped, stumpy villi, often fused; hyperplastic crypt epithelium. -  Respiratory coronaviruses, specifically SARS and MERS: gross lesions include pulmonary edema and consolidation; microscopically, diffuse alveolar damage with acute exudates with edema, hyaline membranes, and fibrosis with mixed cellular infiltration. -  Systemic coronaviruses, specifically FSCV: gross lesions include whitish nodules through peritoneal viscera ± peritoneal effusion; microscopically, pyogranulomatous inflammation of visceral peritoneum, mesenteric adipose tissue, liver, lungs, kidneys, lymph nodes, spleen, pancreas, and other peritoneal viscera. Diagnosis: Molecular detection using PCR is the standard test for most coronaviruses for antemortem sampling. For the US, coordination with local, state, and federal agencies is required for SARS-CoV-2 testing: https://www.aphis.usda.gov/animal\_health/one\_health/downloads/sars-cov2-testingstrategies.pdf

Medical Diagnostic Laboratory: Porcine, BCoV, CRCoV (PCR); BCoV, FeCV (IFA); also has EM. -  Currently SARS-CoV2 testing requires pre-approval for sample submission often with NVSL confirmation. https://www.aphis.usda.gov/animal\_health/one\_health/downloads/faq-publicon-companion-animal-testing.pdf Treatment: Treatment is usually supportive. SARS-CoV-2 treatment can include monoclonal antibodies, dexamethasone, convalescent plasma; oxygen support may be needed. Respiratory coronaviruses are often self-limiting. In the case of enteric coronaviruses, treatment of the dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities should be accompanied by antibiotics to guard against secondary bacterial infections. Treatment of systemic coronaviruses is generally focused on controlling clinical signs. Prevention and control: Enteric coronaviruses are best prevented by reducing fecal contamination of environment through routine cleaning and removal of feces, disinfection of enclosures, bowls, and other material with bleach once weekly. Isolation of sick individuals and quarantine of new animals is important to reduce exposure of naïve animals to shed virus.

However, the virus may cause clinical concerns for other mammals, including nonhuman primates, as well as for birds. Interactions of the SLE virus with reptiles and amphibians are largely unknown due to sparse research. Wild birds are known to act as asymptomatic reservoirs and amplifiers of the virus. Several zoo animal taxa (mammals and birds) were found to have positive serologic tests for SLE virus during arbovirus surveillance studies.

Several zoo animal taxa (mammals and birds) were found to have positive serologic tests for SLE virus during arbovirus surveillance studies. The relationship of positive SLE virus serology to clinical disease in these species was not completely understood and asymptomatic animals were included in sampling. Evidence for the propensity of SLE virus to cause severe illness in animals includes SLE virus isolation from a domestic horse with fatal neurologic disease and an orca at a zoological park that died following brief illness. Causative organism: A single stranded RNA virus in the genus Flavivirus, family Flaviviridae; it is closely related to West Nile virus. Zoonotic potential: Yes - Primarily via mosquito vector, usually Culex spp. Distribution: Human SLE viral infections are known from Canada to Argentina. Human illness occurs throughout the US, including eastern, central, and western states. Serologic evidence for SLE viral infection in animals has been reported from wildlife and domestic animals in North America, Central and South America.

Serologic evidence for SLE viral infection in animals has been reported from wildlife and domestic animals in North America, Central and South America. Biotic and abiotic factors, plus anthropogenic changes such as land use alterations, may alter SLE virus ecology, influence geographic spread of different viral strains, and affect incidence of disease outbreaks in both humans and animals. The disease is likely underreported in both humans and animals due to passive diagnostic and reporting systems and a clinical presentation similar to that of West Nile virus, as well as geographically uneven implementation of sentinel flocks and serosurveillance studies. Incubation period: 5-15 days in people. Clinical signs: Wild birds serving as viral reservoirs and amplifying hosts generally do not show signs of illness. Signs of SLE illness in animal species are incompletely understood and may be similar to the array of signs known in people. In humans who develop symptoms, fever, fatigue, and headache commonly occur.

Horgan (2026) Reviewed by Heather Schwartz (2026) Susceptible animal groups: West Nile Virus is primarily maintained in a mosquito-bird-mosquito transmission cycle, as birds are the primary amplifying hosts for the virus. Species that have been implicated in the spread of the virus include thrushes, blackbirds, American robins, and house sparrows. Mammals are unlikely to serve as amplifying hosts for West Nile virus (WNV), as viremia titers are relatively low in these species as compared to birds, and the duration of infectious viremia is short (often approximately 1 day). Very young and old animals are most likely to experience morbidity and mortality as a consequence of infection. - ∞ Birds: WNV has been reported in over 300 avian species. All bird species are likely susceptible to WNV infection, although most infections in most species are subclinical. North American birds that are of particularly high susceptibility to WNV-associated morbidity and mortality include corvids and raptors.

Species of special concern due to apparently high rates of susceptibility and conservation status include California condors, Florida scrub jays, greater sage grouse, ruffed grouse, loggerhead shrike, and native Hawaiian birds. High rates of death were observed in free-ranging, juvenile American white pelicans in nesting colonies, captive - lesser scaup ducklings, experimentally-infected and free-ranging greater sage grouse and experimentally-infected ruffed grouse. Other birds have been documented with WNV infection, including flamingos, penguins, emus, wild turkeys, cormorants, bronze-winged ducks, sandhill cranes, common coots, red-legged partridges, and others. A variety of psittacine species housed in outdoor aviaries, many of which were of Australian origin, had clinical WNV disease. Reports of WNV disease and death in New World psittacines are relatively rare. Antibodies to WNV have been detected in a vast array of avian species, sometimes at high prevalences.
