It has rarely been reported in alpacas, sheep, reindeer, harbor seals, Indian rhinoceroses, a polar bear, a wolf and several domestic canids, a Barbary macaque, white-tailed deer, and a killer whale. Antibodies to WNV have been detected in a variety of mammals including cattle, dogs, cats, goats, rabbits, raccoons, Virginia opossums, coyotes, striped skunks, bats, black bears, suids, elephants, red foxes, two-toes sloths, primates and killer whales, indicating prior infection. - ∞ Reptile and amphibian: Alligators and crocodiles are susceptible to infection, and can serve as viral amplifiers due to viremia lasting for up to 2 weeks. Other reptiles and amphibians are susceptible to experimental infection, including the green iguana, crocodile monitor, garter snake, various chelonians, western fence-lizards, lake frog and North American bullfrog.

Causative organism: West Nile virus is a single-stranded, enveloped, RNA virus of the Japanese encephalitis antigenic group, genus Flavivirus and Family Flaviviridae. It is an arthropod-borne virus ("arbovirus") transmitted by mosquitoes. There are nine lineages of the virus, with strains in lineages 1 and 2 considered the most virulent. Culex spp. and Aedes spp. are primary vector species. Culex pipiens, in particular, is an important bridge vector from avian hosts to humans. Zoonotic potential: Yes. Transmission to humans is predominantly via mosquito bite but risk is also present during handling tissues and fluids, as transmission can occur via aerosols, mucous membrane contact, open cuts and puncture wounds from a needle stick or contaminated equipment. Masks with face shields and gloves should be worn when handling suspect animals, animal tissues, and bedding. Distribution: Worldwide with the exception of Antarctica.

Climate change has contributed to its spread by expanding the distribution of vectors, altering avian migration patterns, and because high environmental temperatures accelerate viral replication, enhance transmission efficacy, and shorten the incubation period in vectors. Incubation period: Approximately 3-15 days in horses, 2-14 days in humans, and 4-14 days in birds. Some birds become detectably viremic by 1-day post-inoculation.

Infection may be asymptomatic, cause symptoms (primarily fever) without neurologic manifestations, or cause neuro-invasive symptoms. - ∞ People: The majority of infected people are asymptomatic, although some have mild, nonspecific symptoms ("West Nile fever," involving fever, headache, fatigue and/or myalgia/arthralgia; skin rash is also possible), and rarely (<1% of those diagnosed with WNV) experience severe, neurological symptoms, involving encephalitis, meningitis, and/or paralysis. The fatality rate for patients with neuroinvasive disease is approximately 10%, and is higher for geriatric patients. Complications, such as cognitive dysfunction, can develop many years later related to the initial WNV infection. - ∞ Birds: Clinical signs vary and can include depression, ruffled feathers, anorexia, dehydration, rapid weight loss, decreased activity to lethargy, torticollis, opisthotonos, nystagmus, ataxia, diarrhea, nasal discharge, drooping wings, labored breathing, and sudden death. Ocular lesions can also be seen and include anterior uveitis, chorioretinitis, and vision impairment.

Most affected birds deteriorate rapidly following the onset of clinical signs; however, there are several reports of captive birds exhibiting clinical signs for weeks or months. In some cases, WNV-infected raptors have had feather abnormalities, including stunted growth and pinched-off feathers with a constricted calamus tip. - ∞ Equids: An estimated 10-39% of infected horses show clinical signs. The neuroinvasive rate is 8-10%. Signs may include anorexia, colic, depression, ataxia, paresis, paralysis, teeth grinding, aimless wandering, convulsions, circling, tremors of facial and neck muscles, cranial nerve deficits, dysphagia, hyperesthesia, hyperexcitability, facial edema, coma, impaired vision, conjunctivitis, urinary dysfunction, fever, and head pressing. Injuries and secondary pneumonia due to prolonged recumbency can also occur. The mortality rate of animals with neuroinvasive disease ranges from 22-36%. Survivors usually show improvement within 7 days of onset of signs.

Treatment: Supportive care (i.e., fluids, nutrition, heat or cold) can be provided with the goal of reducing CNS inflammation, preventing injuries, minimizing the effects of prolonged recumbency, and nursing the animal through clinical signs. Morbid birds and horses can have neurologic deficits that range from ataxia to paralysis and seizures, and therefore, padded caging may be necessary to prevent further injury. Long-term (i.e., up to several years) neurologic defects have been observed in some raptors following WNV infection. Immunoglobulin therapy has been used in horses (serum based, Novartis Animal Health and a plasma-based product, Lake Immunogenics, Inc.). A recent publication reported survival of 5 WNV-infected American crows, a species with previously reported 100% mortality, that were treated with supportive care, NSAIDs, and prophylactic antifungals and antibiotics. Mild cases may resolve without treatment.

- ∞ Mosquito control measures should be implemented: screened housing, fans, repellants (10% DEET), avoiding stagnant water, larvicides, and stocking mosquito fish in ponds. Isolation of infected individuals and quarantine of new animals is recommended. Avoid feeding potentially contaminated meat/carcasses. - ∞ Four vaccines are currently licensed for use in horses by the USDA: two are killed viruses, one is a recombinant vaccine in a canarypox vector, and one is an inactivated flavivirus chimera. Many zoological facilities vaccinate non-domestic equids, sensitive avian species and crocodilians with available vaccines. - ∞ Extra-label use of vaccines or use of vaccines that have not been adequately assessed in the target animal (i.e., controlled challenge studies) should be used with caution and not assumed to be protective. Numerous vaccines have been tested to various degrees in birds (some without challenge) with varied responses. Flamingoes failed to seroconvert after a single vaccination with the killed product.

Numerous vaccines have been tested to various degrees in birds (some without challenge) with varied responses. Flamingoes failed to seroconvert after a single vaccination with the killed product. This vaccine provided some level of protection at a small dose in ruffed grouse; vaccinated grouse had no clinical disease, lower viremia titers and milder microscopic lesions than non-vaccinated grouse. A modified live vaccine was tested in domestic geese in Israel with 75-94% protection. The killed equine vaccine, DNA plasmid vaccine, and recombinant equine vaccine provided partial protection in island scrub jays. Some red-tailed hawks vaccinated with a DNA-plasmid vaccine had partial protection while American robins and California condors vaccinated with the same vaccine seroconverted. Results were variable among adult and juvenile thick-billed parrots vaccinated with the killed equine vaccine. Seroconversion occurred in some penguins following administration of DNA plasmid and killed vaccines. A DNA plasmid vaccine failed to protect greater sage grouse from mortality. Oral vaccines in fish crows were ineffective. The Recombitek vaccine was immunogenic in rhinos.

A chimeric vaccine was effective at preventing WNV viremia and skin lesions in farmed saltwater crocodiles. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: As an enveloped virus, WNV does not persist for long periods in the environment and can be destroyed by many disinfectants, including ethanol, bleach, hydrogen peroxide, and exposure to UV light. 70% ethanol and bleach are sufficient for general cleaning. Notification: West Nile Virus is a multi-species notifiable disease under the USDA APHIS National Animal Health Reporting System, and a listed disease under the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH).

secao: Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan:
texto: - ∞ Confirmed cases should be reported to state animal health officials. - ∞ Laboratory-confirmed positive cases in humans, horses, other mammals, birds and mosquitoes from across the United States are collected by ArboNET (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; https://www.cdc.gov/west-nile-virus/data-maps/index.html). Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Direct horizontal spread of WNV has been documented in birds and crocodilians. Infected animals should be isolated. Oral and cloacal shedding of virus in alligators and birds usually lasts for up to 2 weeks, however in some cases shedding may last much longer, for example viral shedding was documented up to 93 days after diagnosis in a naturally infected American crow. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: WNV is firmly established in avian and mosquito populations worldwide. The virus is endemic, and transmission is reinitiated annually in the summer within temperate areas of North America and Europe. Therefore, animals housed outdoors in endemic or at-risk areas will be at a continual risk.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: -  Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome is characterized by a unique constellation of pulmonary, hematological, and reticuloendothelial pathological findings - mediated by vascular endothelial damage. -  Findings may include pleural effusions, alveolar edema and fibrin, and an interstitial mononuclear cell infiltrate. Immunoblast type cells in the lungs, blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, liver, and spleen. Hematological findings include left-shifted neutrophilic leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, hemoconcentration in severe cases, and circulating immunoblasts. Diagnosis: Detection of hantavirus-specific IgM antibodies at the earlier stage of infection or a 4-fold or greater increase in hantavirus-specific IgG antibody titer and detection of hantavirus antigen by immunohistochemistry in serum. Other tissues including lung, spleen, kidney, liver and heart can be used for immunohistochemistry (IHC) and reverse transcriptase-PCR (RT-PCR) as post-mortem options. Material required for laboratory analysis: Tubes with coagulation activator are required to separate the serum, once obtained, it should be stored frozen.

Non-human primate HBVs are species-specific, and infect chimpanzees, orangutans, gorillas, gibbons, and woolly monkeys. The viruses are rarely reported or experimental in other primates (macaques, baboons, spider monkey, vervet monkey, and ruffed lemurs). - o Species-specific rodent orthohepadnaviruses also infect woodchucks, various ground squirrels, and arctic squirrels. secao: Clinical signs: Infection can result in:
texto: -  Acute transient or fulminant hepatitis, with fever, anorexia, lethargy, nausea, vomiting, icterus, abdominal discomfort, ascites. Increases in alanine transferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) documented in several species. -  Asymptomatic infection or mild disease and clearance of the virus with lifelong immunity. -  Chronic hepatitis leading to liver failure or hepatocellular carcinoma. Increases in ALT and AST possible. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Hepatitis, hepatic necrosis, hepatic fibrosis is seen in humans, gibbons, and wooly monkeys, but rarely in other primates. Chronic infections can lead to hepatic cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma in humans, woodchucks, and, to a lesser degree, in ground squirrels and ducks. A progression to hepatic cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma has not yet been reported in non-human primates. Diagnosis: Increased ALT and AST on biochemical analysis. Since the genome of human and nonhuman primate hepatitis B viruses are similar, human Hepatitis B testing is applicable in non-human primates. Guidelines for the interpretation of serologic markers can be found at: CDC or HepB foundation.

texto: surface antigen. - o It is a protein on the surface of hepatitis B virus; it can be detected in high levels in serum during acute or chronic hepatitis B virus infection, and indicates infectiousness. - o HBsAg is the antigen used to make hepatitis B vaccine. -  anti-HBs = Hepatitis B surface antibody. - o The presence of anti-HBs is generally interpreted as indicating recovery and immunity from hepatitis B virus infection. - o Anti-HBs also develop when successfully vaccinated against hepatitis B. -  anti-HBc = Total hepatitis B core antibody = IgG & IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen. - o Appears at the onset of symptoms in acute hepatitis B and persists for life. The presence of anti-HBc indicates previous or ongoing infection with hepatitis B virus in an undefined time frame. HBsAg+ and HBsAB- indicates active, acute, or chronic infection. -  IgM anti-HBc = IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen. Positivity indicates recent infection with hepatitis B virus (<6 mos). Its presence indicates acute infection. Material required for laboratory analysis: Serum for liver enzyme analysis and serology testing; serum or whole blood EDTA or ACD for PCR testing.

One triple antigen (Prehevbrio) recombinant vaccine is FDA-approved and dosed at 0 and 1 month. - o There are also multiple combination vaccines approved by FDA in the USA for humans that include hepatitis B virus protection. - o All current US vaccines provide life-long immunity in humans. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: 1:10 bleach; The virus can survive up to 7 days even on surfaces contaminated by dried blood/bodily fluids. Notification: None. Hammond (2011, 2013, 2018) Susceptible animal groups: All mammals (dogs - increased incidence in Bernese Mountain Dogs in Europe, horses, cattle appear less susceptible), some birds (birds are usually asymptomatic, and may be a reservoir host). Causative organism: Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato (s.l.) & sensu stricto (s.s.) (gram-negative spirochete); B. burgdorferi s.s. is the cause of Lyme disease in the US, but B. mayonii has recently been identified as the cause of Lyme disease in the Midwest US. B. afzelii and B. garinii (cause of neuroborreliosis in horses) are the most common s.l. subspecies in Europe. Different strains may explain varied clinical signs depending on region; tick vector: Ixodes sp. (I. scapularis,I. ricinus, I. pacificus). Zoonotic potential: Yes, tick bite only; tick must be attached for at least 24 hours.

varied clinical signs depending on region; tick vector: Ixodes sp. (I. scapularis,I. ricinus, I. pacificus). Zoonotic potential: Yes, tick bite only; tick must be attached for at least 24 hours. Distribution: Temperate areas worldwide, with highest seroprevalance in Pacific coast, New England, mid-Atlantic, and upper Midwest regions. Increasing distribution of ticks due to climate change. Incubation period: 60-90 days. Clinical signs: Shifting leg lameness, joint swelling, arthritis (knee/elbow most common), lymphadenopathy, anorexia, fever, myocarditis, CNS signs, renal syndrome (dogs). Chronic weight loss, acute skin sensitivity, uveitis and neuroborelliosis seen in horses. Only 5-10% of infected animals are expected to show clinical signs. In humans there is often a rash (erythema migrans, aka "bull's eye" rash) at the site of tick attachment. B. mayonii can also cause nausea and vomiting, and large widespread rashes. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates in kidneys that can lead to glomerulonephritis (dogs), liver, cerebrum, meninges, and lungs. Synovitis also seen with inflammatory cells and fibrin deposits.

lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates in kidneys that can lead to glomerulonephritis (dogs), liver, cerebrum, meninges, and lungs. Synovitis also seen with inflammatory cells and fibrin deposits. Diagnosis: Serology (ELISA, IFA, EIA, modified Western blot)-several weeks of infection may be required before samples are positive. Lyme multiplex assay (Cornell) detects antibiotics to outer surface proteins. Two-tiered serologic testing in humans. PCR (lower sensitivity), or culture of organism from urinary bladder (difficult), kidney, spleen, skin, and other organs with evidence of clinical signs of disease. History of exposure and response to treatment. Current research with metabolomics. Material required for laboratory analysis: Serum, whole blood, tissue, CSF (in addition to serum) in horses with neurologic signs. Relevant Diagnostic lab: Standard diagnostic laboratories can test for serologic evidence of Lyme disease; patient-side ELISA SNAP® test (4Dx Plus, IDEXX, Westbrook, ME, USA); VetScan FLEX4 Rapid Test (Abaxis, Inc., Union City, CA) and the VetScan canine rapid Lyme test (Abaxis, Union City, CA, USA). Culture of organism requires special growth media.

Westbrook, ME, USA); VetScan FLEX4 Rapid Test (Abaxis, Inc., Union City, CA) and the VetScan canine rapid Lyme test (Abaxis, Union City, CA, USA). Culture of organism requires special growth media. Treatment: Doxycycline x 30d (contraindicated in young animals) or minocycline x28d (minocycline has better nervous system penetration-common in horses); oxytetracycline in horses; amoxicillin (preferred for doxy-sensitive or juvenile dogs); cefovecin (used with joint lesions); azithromycin; ceftriaxone (especially for neurologic disease); cefotaxime; penicillin G; tinidazole (if biofilms suspected). Drug combinations recommended for resistant colonies. The effect from antibiotic treatment should be apparent in 1-3 days, however recrudescence is possible. Better chance of resolution if treatment initiated early, however post treatment Lyme disease syndrome has been reported in humans and dogs with chronic Lyme symptoms that may take months to resolve. Prevention and control: Tick prevention (topical and oral, recommend to give year-round). Remove ticks within 48hr (minimum time needed to transmit the organism).

Lyme disease killed and recombinant subunit vaccines are available for dogs only. Surface lipoproteins OspA and OspC current candidates for new vaccines. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Standard disinfectants, such as 1% sodium hypochlorite, 70% ethanol, heat, and UV light, are appropriate (Borrelia sp cannot survive free-living in the environment). Notification: Reportable in humans (US), but not in animals. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animals: Tick control. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: None.

Animals affected | Transmission | Clinical Signs | Treatment | Prevention & Control Many species of Artiodactyla, including bovids, cervids, giraffids, suids Sheep, goats & blue and black wildebeest are common carrier species and subclinical; though clinical disease in sheep has been reported | Transmitted only between carrier species and clinically susceptible animals; the latter do not transmit MCF to their conspecifics Direct or indirect contact with bodily fluids (nasal and ocular secretions); inhalation primary route, but ingestion also possible Fomites, water, rangeland, feed Carriers: in utero transmission is common in wildebeest, less so in sheep | Mucous membrane ulceration and inflammation, high fever, oral and nasal exudates, corneal opacities, and lymphadenopathy ; additional signs may include neurologic signs, diarrhea, arthritis, skin lesions, or sudden death | No specific antiviral treatment Treatment of secondary infections and supportive care are usually ineffective | Separate clinically susceptible species from known carrier species in known infected areas to prevent direct transmission Prevent fomite transmission Use precautions to prevent aerosol transmission Br

clinically susceptible species from known carrier species in known infected areas to prevent direct transmission Prevent fomite transmission Use precautions to prevent aerosol transmission Breed virus- free Òcarrier speciesÓ Severity? High fatality rates in susceptible species; susceptibility to individual viruses varies between species; up to 25% of cattle may develop chronic disease with a waxing and waning course; up to 5% may clinically recover, but most eventually die; reservoir hosts remain infected for life Zoonotic? No Current update by Brian G. Stockinger (2025) Reviewed by Gretchen Cole (2026) Susceptible animal groups: Cervidae, Bovidae, Giraffidae, Suidae. Causative organism: Herpesviruses classified in the genus Macavirus. At least 10 viruses have been identified that are categorized within the MCF virus group. Some have been associated with MCF in clinically susceptible species. * = most important. - ∞ *Alcelaphine herpesvirus 1 (AlHV-1; classic African MCF/wildebeest-associated), carried by wildebeest, predominant cause of MCF in Africa; susceptible species = Cervidae and Bovidae.

important. - ∞ *Alcelaphine herpesvirus 1 (AlHV-1; classic African MCF/wildebeest-associated), carried by wildebeest, predominant cause of MCF in Africa; susceptible species = Cervidae and Bovidae. - ∞ Alcelaphine herpesvirus 2 (AlHV-2), identified in but non-pathogenic in Jackson's hartebeest; clinically susceptible species = Barbary red deer (Cervus elaphus barbarus). - ∞ Caprine herpesvirus 2 (CpHV-2), carried by domestic and exotic goats, considered endemic in domestic goats; clinically susceptible species = white-tailed deer, moose, Sika deer, pudu, and some antelope species. - ∞ Caprine herpesvirus 3 (CpHV-3), previously called "malignant catarrhal fever virus-white tailed deer" (MCFV-WTD), goat likely carrier; susceptible species = North American deer. - ∞ Ibex-MCF virus, carried by Nubian ibex (Capra nubiana); susceptible species = anoa, bongo, pronghorn, and duikers. Prior to a case in a captive bongo (Tragelaphus euryceros) the virus was not considered pathogenic. - ∞ *Ovine herpesvirus 2 (OvHV-2; sheep-associated), carried by domestic and wild bighorn sheep, considered endemic in domestic sheep; susceptible species = ruminant species and swine.

pathogenic. - ∞ *Ovine herpesvirus 2 (OvHV-2; sheep-associated), carried by domestic and wild bighorn sheep, considered endemic in domestic sheep; susceptible species = ruminant species and swine. The major cause of MCF in animals outside Africa. European breeds of cattle (Bos taurus), are relatively resistant, but Bali cattle, bison, and some cervid species such as Pere David's deer are highly susceptible. - ∞ Gazelle Dorcas gammaherpesvirus 1 and Gazelle Dorcas gammaherpesvirus 2; similar to Rusa unicolor equina gammaherpesvirus detected in dik-diks and Bovidae gammaherpesvirus 2 in black bucks. Other herpesviruses categorized in the same group as the pathogenic MCF viruses have been identified in aoudad, roan antelope, musk ox, oryx, chamois, and gemsbok, but do not yet appear to cause disease under natural conditions.

Distribution: Disease may occur worldwide in situations in which clinically susceptible species are in contact with carrier species. Incubation period: Incompletely understood. Two weeks to a few months in most cases. Varies depending on several factors such as amount of virus transmitted and host. In field outbreaks, the incubation period for bison is about 40 to 70 days. Cattle have become ill in as few as nine days, while other evidence suggests that some cattle may be subclinically infected for 20 months or more before developing the disease. The latter case could be due to a long period of subclinical infection followed by viral reactivation leading to clinical disease. Cattle have become infected 11-73 days after the administration of blood from OvHV-2 infected sick cattle.

- ∞ Vary with susceptibility of affected species. Most clinical cases described in cattle. Virus attacks blood vessels in multiple organs. Highly susceptible species may present peracutely with no clinical signs but sudden death, though this may be preceded by a brief period of weakness, depression, or diarrhea. Acute disease may involve high fever and a loss of appetite. Other clinical signs may include mucous membrane inflammation and ulceration, oral and ocular/nasal exudates, corneal opacities (common in domestic cattle), and lymphadenopathy. Neurologic signs, diarrhea, hematuria, arthritis, and skin/hoof lesions may also develop. Sudden death has also been reported in Dorcas gazelle (Gazella dorcas)). - ∞ Bison: often die rapidly with minimal clinical signs until near death. Common terminal findings include inhalation pneumonia and an edematous corneoscleral band but the latter is hard to visualize antemortem. - ∞ Cervids: peracute in highly susceptible species of deer but less susceptible cervids may have disease course lasting up to three weeks. - ∞ Domestic sheep: Systemic necrotizing vasculitis or "polyarteritis nodosa" may be associated with OvHV-2.

of deer but less susceptible cervids may have disease course lasting up to three weeks. - ∞ Domestic sheep: Systemic necrotizing vasculitis or "polyarteritis nodosa" may be associated with OvHV-2. - ∞ Free-ranging bighorn sheep: muscle atrophy, marked weight loss, and bilaterally symmetric alopecia with hyperpigmentation and crusting over the face, medial surfaces of the pinnae, dorsal trunk, distal limbs, perineal area, and tail was associated with OvHV-2. - ∞ Moose, captive: cerebral lymphocytic vasculitis and panuveitis were associated with CPHV-2. - ∞ Variation in illness may be due to stressors that increase virus shedding in the carrier and/or susceptibility in the incidental host, or environmental conditions (e.g., high humidity) that increase virus survival or concentration - ∞ Carrier species do not typically develop clinical signs. Rare clinical cases attributed to OvHV-2 are thought to result from unusually high virus replication.

virus survival or concentration - ∞ Carrier species do not typically develop clinical signs. Rare clinical cases attributed to OvHV-2 are thought to result from unusually high virus replication. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: May vary with disease severity and course, but often include "inflammation and epithelial necrosis in the gastrointestinal, respiratory, and urinary tracts, with lymphoproliferation, infiltration of nonlymphoid tissues (particularly the renal cortex and periportal areas of the liver) by lymphoid cells, and vasculitis."

- ∞ Detection of viral DNA in tissues. - ∞ PCR (polymerase chain reaction) is the method of choice for strain-specific viral detection and should be used to confirm suspected cases of MCF in all clinically susceptible species. PCR tests are available for all MCF viruses known to cause disease. - ∞ Serological tests for antibodies include competitive inhibition ELISA (cELISA), immunoperoxidase test (IPT), virus neutralization (VN), and others. cELISA is used for detection of antibodies to all viruses in the MCF-group. Detection of antibodies indicates infection, not necessarily disease. Recommended for screening of latent/subclinical infections in both clinically susceptible species and carrier hosts. - ∞ In susceptible species such as cattle, bison, and deer detection of MCF antibodies indicates nonspecific infection by a member of the MCF virus group, but is not diagnostic of disease; lack of antibodies when performing cELISA usually indicates lack of infection, except for very early stages of infection <1 week before antibodies can be produced; in acute cases seroconversion may not occur prior to death.

cELISA usually indicates lack of infection, except for very early stages of infection <1 week before antibodies can be produced; in acute cases seroconversion may not occur prior to death. - ∞ cELISA-positive but PCR-negative animals are most likely latently infected with a level of virus in the blood below the assay detection threshold. - ∞ High levels of MCF viral DNA in tissues can be used to corroborate suspect clinical disease in carrier species that would normally be expected to test positive on blood PCR. - ∞ MCF multiplex PCR (broader specificity) may be considered when MCF is strongly suspected based on clinical, diagnostic, and epidemiologic evidence but common MCF PCR tests are negative; an unknown MCF virus may be involved.

- ∞ Antibody testing by cELISA: serum or plasma. - ∞ Antemortem detection of viral DNA by PCR: whole blood in EDTA. - ∞ Postmortem detection of viral DNA by PCR: fresh or fresh frozen lymph node or lung are preferred, but spleen, liver, and intestine are acceptable; preferred fixed tissue samples (vasculitis): lymph node or spleen; but lung, brain, kidney, and intestine among others are also acceptable.

- ∞ Separate clinically susceptible species from carrier species such as wildebeest, domestic and exotic sheep, and domestic and exotic goat species. Bovids, particularly bison and water buffalo, are highly susceptible to MCF. Exotic members of the Bovidae family such as bongo antelope have died from MCF traced back to an exotic goat species. Wildebeest-associated MCF has occurred in domestic cattle in the U.S. when the two species were housed together. - ∞ Cervids should not be mixed with sheep, goats, or wildebeest. - ∞ Prevent direct contact and fomite transmission. Transmission of the wildebeest-associated form (AlHV-1) and the sheep-associated form (OvHV-2) is believed to occur primarily from direct contact with infected body fluids or secretions, or via fomites such as water sources, feeders, caretakers, and birds. Calving is considered a high-risk period transmission period. - ∞ Use precautions to prevent aerosol transmission. Transmission of the disease over relatively short distances has occurred, indicating that direct contact is not necessary, but the distance needed to prevent airborne transmission is unknown.

Transmission of the disease over relatively short distances has occurred, indicating that direct contact is not necessary, but the distance needed to prevent airborne transmission is unknown. Aerosol transmission is a significant mode of transmission of OvHV-2 in domestic sheep. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Herpesviruses causing MCF are typically "fragile and quickly inactivated in harsh environments" so common disinfectants are likely effective. Many common disinfectants can inactivate MCF viruses. However, if heavy organic debris is present the OIE recommends 3% sodium hypochlorite. Notification: The wildebeest-associated and sheep-associated forms are reportable diseases under USDA-APHIS-VS National Animal Health Reporting System. MCF clinical signs may appear similar to foreign animal diseases such as rinderpest, BVD/mucosal disease, bluetongue, and foot and mouth disease. Reportable in many U.S. states - consult state authorities for more specific information. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: Currently none.

and foot and mouth disease. Reportable in many U.S. states - consult state authorities for more specific information. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: Currently none. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Clinically susceptible species should be physically separated from and not introduced to carrier species. In addition, separate keeper staff and equipment should be used to prevent fomite transmission. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: See prevention and control measures.

secao: Carnivore protoparvovirus 1 (formerly canine parvovirus & feline panleukopenia)
texto: Animals affected | Transmission | Clinical Signs | Treatment | Prevention & Control Canids, felids, hyaenids, mustelids, procyonids, ursids, viverrids, and possibly sea lions | Ingestion, primarily (fecal- oral); may also be transmitted oronasally and transplacentally | Vomiting and diarrhea that can result in dehydration and death Immune- suppression, leukopenia Respiratory or neurologic signs | Symptomatic treatment to prevent dehydration and prevent or treat secondary bacterial infections | Vaccination or strict isolation of naïve populations Prevention of contamination of environment & disinfection Control can be managed with quarantine for at least 30 days Severity? Non-clinical or mild to severe including death; depends on immune status of animal

-  Canine parvovirus 2: Tara M. Harrison (2011, 2013) -  Feline panleukopenia: Ray Wack (2011, 2013) Susceptible animal groups: Carnivores, such as felids, canids, procyonids, mustelids, ursids, hyaenids, and viverrids. Causative organism: Carnivore protoparvovirus 1 (CPPV-1) belongs to the genus Protoparvovirus of the family Parvoviridae, and can cause life-threatening pathogenic infections in many carnivores. Parvoviruses are non-enveloped, DNA viruses. According to the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses, numerous phylogenetically similar viral strains that infect carnivore species are classified under CPPV-1, including feline panleukopenia, canine parvovirus (including the variants CPV2a, CPV-2b, and CPV-2c), mink enteritis virus, and raccoon parvovirus. Zoonotic potential: None. Distribution: Worldwide. Incubation period: Typically 2-7 day incubation period, but can range from 4-10 days, rarely up to 14 days.

-  Canids: puppies are most likely to suffer severe disease and death. However any unvaccinated canid, of any age, can become infected with CPV-2. Clinical signs range from non-clinical to profound depression, lethargy, and inappetence; enteric parvoviruses cause signs of gastroenteritis such as vomiting and severe diarrhea that can be foul-smelling and include mucus, fibrin casts, and blood; may also see pyrexia and dehydration. -  Felids: most cases are subclinical in felids > 1 yr of age or those with protection from maternal antibodies. Most cases with illness are < 1 yr of age. Peracute cases may result in death. Acute cases present with fever, anorexia, depression, vomiting, diarrhea, hematochezia, severe dehydration, septic shock, and DIC. In transplacental infections, ataxia and tremors with normal mentation are observed in kittens due to cerebellar hypoplasia. Retinal lesions are also possible. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: The virus replicates in and destroys rapidly dividing cells, especially in bone marrow, lymphoid tissue, and gastrointestinal tract mucosa.

also possible. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: The virus replicates in and destroys rapidly dividing cells, especially in bone marrow, lymphoid tissue, and gastrointestinal tract mucosa. Feline parvovirus (panleukopenia): total white counts of <1000-2000/ml and neutrophils <200/ml and possible concurrent lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and anemia. Canine, feline, and other enteric parvoviruses: anemia and hypoproteinemia possibly due to blood and protein loss through the gastrointestinal tract; segmental reddening, hemorrhage, and a granular appearance of the serosa of the small intestine; lymphoid depletion; necrosis and loss of crypts with subsequent villous atrophy, blunting and fusion in the small intestine; involution of the lymphoid tissues in the small intestine, lymph nodes, spleen and thymus; bone marrow may be hypocellular. Eosinophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies are rare. Transplacental infection may result in cerebellar hypoplasia, retinal dysplasia, embryonic resorption, fetal mummification, abortion, or stillbirth. Diagnosis: For canids, testing should be performed on acutely infected or recently exposed or high risk individuals.

dysplasia, embryonic resorption, fetal mummification, abortion, or stillbirth. Diagnosis: For canids, testing should be performed on acutely infected or recently exposed or high risk individuals. In-house fecal ELISA tests are quite specific and sensitive for currently circulating strains of canine parvovirus, and are reportedly useful for feline panleukopenia. Some strains of CPV-2 can infect domestic cats as well as dogs. As with any test, false results are possible, and negative results can occur later in the course of disease. Weak false positives may also reportedly occur due to recent vaccination. However, this is uncommon, so positive results should be taken seriously even in recently vaccinated dogs. Shedding can be intermittent, therefore testing more than one animal, or one animal on sequential days is suggested. Other possible tests are latex agglutination, and hemagglutination which is not a specific test. Virus can be detected in serum by hemagglutination and IgG IFA; virus may be detected in tissues using virus isolation, hemagglutination, PCR, immunohistochemistry (IHC) and electron microscopy.

Virus can be detected in serum by hemagglutination and IgG IFA; virus may be detected in tissues using virus isolation, hemagglutination, PCR, immunohistochemistry (IHC) and electron microscopy. Serology is a useful tool to assess risk or to further clarify the need for quarantine of individual dogs. Necropsy (both gross and histopathology) are very useful, especially in a "herd" health situation when mortality is present. A presumptive diagnosis may be made from characteristic gross and histologic lesions and confirmed with positive IHC labeling within the damaged small intestinal crypts and in the epithelial cells of the tongue; tongue can be useful for PCR, IHC, or FA testing in canines and felines if there is marked autolysis in the small intestine. Material required for laboratory analysis: Enteric parvoviruses: feces, small intestine >> tongue, systemic lymphoid tissues. Serum can also be used, but may not be helpful for diagnosis. Serology can be used to document successful vaccination using hemoagglutination inhibition or indirect immunofluorescence testing.

Serum can also be used, but may not be helpful for diagnosis. Serology can be used to document successful vaccination using hemoagglutination inhibition or indirect immunofluorescence testing. Relevant diagnostic laboratories: Most commercial and academic diagnostic laboratories can test for enteric parvoviruses; several in-house diagnostic tests are also available for enteric parvovirus. -  Washington Animal Disease Diagnostic Lab, Pullman, WA., USA; 509-335-9696; waddl@vetmed.wsu.edu - [ Cornell University's Animal Health Diagnostic Center, Ithaca, NY, USA; 607-253-3900](https://ahdc.vet.cornell.edu/) Treatment: Enteric parvoviruses: isolate infected animal; provide supportive care to treat dehydration and electrolyte imbalance; prevent secondary bacterial infections, especially in animals with leukopenia. Provide antiemetics if vomiting, analgesia for abdominal pain, and nutritional support. Leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypoalbuminemia, and hypokalemia are negative prognostic indicators in felids with panleukopenia.

-  Vaccination is the cornerstone of parvovirus prevention. In the absence of maternal antibody interference, a single modified live vaccine can confer protection within 3-5 days. Revaccination must be performed, especially in high risk situations such as shelters. Both inactivated-adjuvanted and modified live vaccines are available, although the use of modified live vaccines in non-domesticated animals may produce disease and is typically not recommended. - o Most cats produce a robust long lasting immunity following illness or vaccination. Vaccinated queens generally transfer protective levels of antibodies. The first vaccination is usually given at 6-9 weeks of age with booster vaccines given every 3-4 weeks with the last dose being administered when the kitten is > 16 weeks old, to ensure that interfering maternal antibodies do not inactivate the modified live virus or block vaccine response. A booster should be given 1 year later. Unvaccinated adults should be given a total of 2 doses of the vaccine 3-4 weeks apart. Vaccine titers suggest that triennial or longer booster intervals are effective after the initial series.

later. Unvaccinated adults should be given a total of 2 doses of the vaccine 3-4 weeks apart. Vaccine titers suggest that triennial or longer booster intervals are effective after the initial series. Greater than 95% of domestic cats respond to primary vaccination series with protective titers that may last more than 7 years. A few non-domestic cats have been documented to be non-responders, so determination of titers is recommended. - o Killed vaccines are often used in non-domestic cats due to rare cases of vaccine induced disease with modified live vaccines, though modified live vaccines are available. Pregnant, immunosuppressed, sick cats, or kittens < 4 weeks of age should not be vaccinated with a modified live product. - o Fel-O-Vax PCT + Calicivac (Elanco) is a commonly used killed vaccine given as a 1 ml dose regardless of the size of the cat. A 0.5 ml dose Fel-O-Vax vaccine has also become commercially available recently. -  Control: Parvoviruses shed in all secretions in the acute phase and in the feces for up to 6 weeks following recovery.

ml dose Fel-O-Vax vaccine has also become commercially available recently. -  Control: Parvoviruses shed in all secretions in the acute phase and in the feces for up to 6 weeks following recovery. The virus can survive for months in cool, moist areas protected from sunlight, and are very stable when frozen; can persist in feces for 6 months at room temperature and may remain viable in the natural environment for 9-12 months. Susceptible animals should not be with or in close proximity to positive animals until they have been vaccination and/or demonstrate protective antibody titers. Recovered animals should be bathed prior to exposure to juveniles for whom antibody protection cannot be assured. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Transmission on fomites is common, thus stringent infectious disease control is required. Parvovirus must be mechanically removed or can be killed by one of the few effective disinfectants.

Transmission on fomites is common, thus stringent infectious disease control is required. Parvovirus must be mechanically removed or can be killed by one of the few effective disinfectants. Disinfection using formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde, potassium peroxymonosulfate (Trifectant or Virkon-S), Rescue TM , or chlorine solutions, such as 0.1755% sodium hypochlorite solution; for bleach, 5% household bleach can be used but should be freshly diluted at 1:32 (1/2 cup per gallon). Foot baths can also be used with sodium hypochlorite solutions to prevent spread. Like all disinfectants, bleach must be used and stored correctly to be effective. Application should be only to pre-cleaned surfaces free of organic matter. Independent studies have shown that quaternary ammonium disinfectants do not reliably kill parvovirus. Notification: Not required. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Do not introduce non-infected animal to infected animal; non-infected animal should be vaccinated prior to exposure to previously infected animal whenever possible.

animals to infected animal: Do not introduce non-infected animal to infected animal; non-infected animal should be vaccinated prior to exposure to previously infected animal whenever possible. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Adequate husbandry practices using an approved disinfectant; in many environments parvovirus may be endemic and it may be difficult to restore a disease-free environment. If the virus is present endemically in other wildlife vectors or in a captive setting, appropriate vaccination and disinfection may assist in controlling potential outbreaks. Quarantine of infected animals for a minimum of 30 days may also help to control an outbreak and restore a disease-free state. Multiple swabs for PCR and identification of parvovirus DNA may be collected from infected and exposed animals to assure viral shedding has stopped.

Causative organism: Foot and mouth disease virus (FMDV) Aphthovirus in family Picornaviridae. Multiple serotypes (O, A, C, SAT 1, SAT 2, SAT 3, Asia 1); O is most common. While most strains affect all susceptible hosts; some strains primarily affect certain species (e.g., the pig O Cathay strain); Immunity to one serotype does not protect from other serotypes. Zoonotic potential: Human infections seem to be very rare, with mild clinical signs and no public health significance. Many of these infections were reported in people exposed to large amounts of virus in vaccine plants, although cases also occurred after drinking FMDV-contaminated raw milk for several days. Distribution: Endemic in parts of Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. Incubation period: 2-14 days.

Clinical signs: Fever (2-3 days); vesicles followed by erosions/ulcers on the tongue, lips, oral mucosa, teats and between the hooves; abundant stringy saliva if mouth is significantly affected; decreased appetite, lameness, abortion; sudden death from myocarditis in newborns; rare instances of sudden death in adults, especially in some severely affected wildlife species. The pattern of illness varies between species, and some species (e.g., sheep) can have minimal signs. Shedding may occur before the onset of clinical signs. Cattle may be persistently infected in the pharynx, but no evidence that they transmit infection. African buffalo can be long term shedders and transmit the virus. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Blanched foci to vesicles to complete ulceration with fibrin can be seen in the oral cavity and tongue. Interdigital redness, vesicles or ulceration and similar on coronary bands are seen. Vesicles or erosions may also be found on udder, occasionally other sites.

Myocardial pallor or streaking may be observed; young animals with myocardial lesions may not have vesicles. Lesions are species dependent, less severe in sheep and goats than cattle or swine. Location of lesions can also vary between species. Diagnosis: Grossly, it is indistinguishable from other vesicular diseases (vesicular stomatitis, swine vesicular disease, Seneca virus A, vesicular exanthema of swine). Other differential diagnoses include diseases with mouth and/or foot signs such as traumatic stomatitis, bovine viral diarrhea, bluetongue, malignant catarrhal fever, contagious ecthyma, and epizootic hemorrhagic disease of deer. Lab detection of FMDV is based on virus isolation, antigen ELISA, and RT-PCR. Serology tests for detecting exposure include virus neutralization and various ELISA assays, e.g., those that detect antibody to structural proteins and those that detect antibody to nonstructural proteins.

Material required for laboratory analysis: Before collection of samples, proper authorities should be contacted. Send appropriate samples under secure conditions to authorized laboratories as directed by the Veterinary Officials. Preferred samples include epithelium from un-ruptured or freshly ruptured vesicles, esophageal-pharyngeal (probang) samples. Other samples may include myocardium from heart failure deaths, milk and other secretions and excretions. For suspect carriers, esophageal-pharyngeal fluids should be submitted.

secao: Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan:
texto: -  Surveillance in zoos during an outbreak will be determined by the Veterinary Officials (Federal, State, or Tribal) depending on the epidemiology of the outbreak. - [ USDA-APHIS-VS District Offices Points of Contact for Field Operations.](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/contact/animal-health) - [ Foot-and-Mouth Disease: The Red Book FAD PReP October 2020 : see plans for zoos.](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/animal_health/emergency_management/downloads/fmd_responseplan.pdf) -  Secure Zoo Strategy, Zoos and Aquarium All Hazards Partnership. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: No animals should be introduced into the zoo until the disease is brought under control or it is demonstrated that the zoo is free of infection and the animal to be introduced is also free of infection. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Surveillance to demonstrate absence of infection and absence of virus circulation, according to the WOAH Terrestrial Code. Time to regain FMD free status varies with method of eradication and surveillance (e.g., use and type of vaccination).

Susceptible zoological mammal groups: - Artiodactylids (pygmy hippopotamus, antelope hybrid, alpaca - Perissodactylids (tapir, rhinoceros) - Non-human Primates (all families from lemurs to great apes) - Elephants - Felids (tigers, lions, black leopard, clouded leopard, cheetah) - Rodents (capybara, crested porcupine) - Macropods (Goodfellow's tree kangaroo) Causative organism: Encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV) is a non-enveloped, positive-sense, singlestranded RNA virus in the genus Cardiovirus A within the family Picornaviridae. There are three serotypes: EMCV-1, EMCV-2, and EMCV-3. It is primarily a myocardiotropic virus but can also exhibit epitheliotropism. Zoonotic potential: Human infection occurs relatively often, though many cases are asymptomatic and go unrecognized. When clinical signs develop, they may include fever, headaches, neck stiffness, vomiting, and occasionally delirium. Transmission is typically via the fecal-oral route.

and go unrecognized. When clinical signs develop, they may include fever, headaches, neck stiffness, vomiting, and occasionally delirium. Transmission is typically via the fecal-oral route. Distribution: Worldwide in both free-ranging and captive populations. In the US, cases are primarily reported in states bordering the Gulf of Mexico. Rats and mice are the natural hosts of the virus, while pigs are the most commonly and severely affected domestic animals. Seasonality of infection has occurred with incidence peaking in colder months of the year, corresponding to the tendency of rodents to shelter indoors. Incubation period: Viremia can occur within 24 hours post-infection. The virus enters through M cells in the intestinal Peyer's patches, likely replicates in macrophages, and spreads via the lymphatic system. EMCV is adapted to evade the host's immune defenses. Disease development is associated with cytokine-driven inflammatory response; strains that elicit a stronger response are more likely to cause clinical illness after the incubation period. In asymptomatic cases, limited disease is likely due to reduced host inflammatory stimulation.

that elicit a stronger response are more likely to cause clinical illness after the incubation period. In asymptomatic cases, limited disease is likely due to reduced host inflammatory stimulation. Clinical signs: Many infections are nonlethal and likely subclinical. When present, nonspecific signs include lethargy, hyporexia to anorexia, recumbency, colic, ataxia, listlessness, and dyspnea. Signs of acute heart failure may occur, particularly in primates and artiodactylids. The most common presentation, however, is sudden death without prior clinical signs.

- Gross lesions: - o Cardiovascular: pericardial effusion, pale foci or streaks in the myocardium, cardiomegaly, petechia or ecchymoses on the heart, or soft cardiac consistency - o Respiratory: Severe pulmonary edema, pulmonary congestion, foam in the trachea or bronchi, pulmonary emphysema, or dark mottling of the lungs. - o Nervous system: Meningeal congestion when involved. - Histologic lesions: - o Lymphocytic and/or histiocytic necrotizing and hemorrhagic myocarditis, markedly edematous and congested lungs, cerebral edema and hyperemia, cerebral congestion; perivascular meningeal hemorrhage, lymphohistiocytic infiltrates, satellitosis, and neuronal necrosis.

- Histologic appearance of affected tissues combined with clinical presentation is highly suggestive of EMCV. - For confirmation, qRT-PCR is rapid and requires only a small sample (heart tissue is best because it has the highest viral load). - Other diagnostic options include virus isolation (heart, brain, splenic tissue) with electron microscopy, ELISA, genome sequencing, and immunohistochemistry (IHC). - Serology is typically unhelpful due to the rapid clinical course; however, in prolonged cases, both serum neutralization and hemagglutination inhibition assays can be used. - Note: EMCV strains emerge rapidly and can circulate concurrently, increasing the risk of false negatives on PCR. Interpret negative PCR tests cautiously and consider parallel testing via a second technique.

- Virus Isolation: Heart, brain, or splenic tissue - RT-PCR: Heart tissue best, next best choice blood but can use samples from wide variety of tissues including brain, liver, lung, kidney, lymph nodes, pericardial effusion, or nasal/oral/rectal/vaginal swabs. Samples that are small or autolyzed can still be used. If patient is a rodent, then consider testing GI tract/GI material.

- Consistent and long-term rodent control and prevention of rodent access to animal enclosures and food sources are critical for prevention. Hygienic feeding practices are important. If rodent feces are detected, increase rodent control measures and change feeding practices, such as not leaving food bowls available overnight. In enclosures with heavy contamination of rodent feces, removal of soil and substrate should be considered. - Do not feed meat from peracute or acute mortalities to other animals until EMCV infection has been ruled out. - Commercial vaccines are not available. Vaccine research is ongoing, and recent trials have shown some efficacy with both inactivated and live attenuated vaccines. Currently, the USDA allows the production and use of autogenous product from an affected institution's viral isolates at that institution only. - [o https://vaxxinova.us.com/](https://vaxxinova.us.com/)

- EMCV, and picornaviruses in general, are stable in the environment. - Frequent disinfection is required with appropriate disinfectants that target picornaviruses. - o Sodium hypochlorite, acetic acid, sodium carbonate, sodium hydroxide, formaldehyde, ethylene oxide, or potassium peroxymonosulfate with sodium chloride. Notification: None. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: None.

secao: Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak:
texto: - Remove all evidence of rodent feces in the environment - Clean the affected animal's living spaces with an approved disinfectant (see above) - Increase rodent control - Re-evaluate animal feeding strategies. - Any survivors of infection, both rodent and non-rodent, may become carriers and can potentially resume shedding the virus under stress.

Causative organism: Double-stranded DNA enveloped virus in the family Poxviridae, subfamily Chordopoxvirinae, genus Orthopoxvirus which includes smallpox (Variola virus-irradicated 1980), monkeypox, buffalopox and rabbitpox (vaccinia virus), ectromelia, camelpox, horsepox, raccoonpox, skunkpox, volepox, and Uasin Gishu disease. Multiple strains of cowpox exist. Cowpox viruses are categorized into 5 clades and in 2023 there were 96 individual fully sequenced viral genomes of cowpox viruses identified in the United States National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) database. Zoonotic potential: Yes. Smallpox vaccination confers protection against cowpox as well and there is concern cowpox may become more prevalent in humans with the cessation of routine smallpox vaccination since the 1970's. Recently, cats and pet rats are the most common source of human infection. Less common sources include cattle (last reported zoonosis from cattle was 1976) and an Asian elephant.

since the 1970's. Recently, cats and pet rats are the most common source of human infection. Less common sources include cattle (last reported zoonosis from cattle was 1976) and an Asian elephant. Distribution: Endemic in various rodent (voles, rats, mice) reservoir hosts in Great Britain, Scandinavia, European mainland, and adjacent western Asiatic countries. Incubation period: 3-10 days.

-  Skin lesions usually progress through characteristic macule, papule, vesicle, and pustule phase before becoming scabbed. Generally mild self-limiting cutaneous pox lesions in humans and most animal species but can become generalized and/or cause necrotizing pneumonia in certain species or immune-compromised individuals. Strain, route and dose of virus causing infection may influence the course of disease. -  Humans: Generally localized lesions on hands, face, arms, or other points of contact with infected animal. Infection may cause lymphadenopathy and flu-like symptoms. Lesions typically resolve in 6-8 weeks without secondary bacterial infections which can extend the process by several weeks. Systemic infections and fatalities may occur in immunecompromised individuals. Previous vaccinia vaccination for smallpox should confer at least partial immunity. -  Animals: Mild localized pox lesions to generalized lesions with ulcerations, including the conjunctiva, oral cavity, and esophagus. Oral lesions may cause anorexia. An uncommon disease in cattle, but lesions most typical on udder and teats of cows and mouths of suckling calves.

the conjunctiva, oral cavity, and esophagus. Oral lesions may cause anorexia. An uncommon disease in cattle, but lesions most typical on udder and teats of cows and mouths of suckling calves. Infection may cause pyrexia and lymphadenopathy. Pulmonary disease is rare in most species but is more common in felid species. Pulmonary involvement has also been seen in giant anteaters. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Epitheliotropic virus causing necroproliferative and ulcerative multifocal to coalescing lesions. The lesions undergo the classical poxvirus cascade of macules, papules, and later collapse of the lesion from the center giving the lesion a targetoid appearance. The lesions then scab over and are slow to heal. Histologically, affected epithelial cells demonstrate ballooning degeneration and may have eosinophilic homogenous intracytoplasmic inclusions. The affected cells often swell and rupture leaving spaces filled with neutrophils and debris (pustules). These lesions with intraepithelial intracytoplasmic inclusions have also been identified in the pulmonary tract and oral cavity.

In an outbreak in captive banded mongooses, inclusions were also present in hepatocytes, enterocytes and in cells with histiocytic and fibroblastic morphology. Diagnosis: Histopathology shows large homogenous eosinophilic intracytoplasmic A- type inclusion bodies (ATIs) in epithelial cells undergoing ballooning degeneration. ATIs associated with cowpox viruses and ectromelia virus (a mouse associated orthopoxvirus), are often, but not always, present. Electron microscopy of fresh or frozen lesion material will typically demonstrate morphologically distinct orthopoxvirus particles (approximately 250nm x 350nm, brick-shaped virions with tubular surface projections). Cell culture, PCR and DNA sequence analysis are used to define the specific poxvirus causing the lesions. Serologic testing is available to determine if exposure to an orthopoxvirus occurred. Material required for laboratory analysis: Biopsies of lesions-fresh/frozen and formalin fixed.

Swabs from ulcers may also be utilized for molecular techniques of identification. Relevant Diagnostic lab: Laboratories capable of performing electron microscopy of biopsy samples can identify to the level of orthopoxvirus. Sequencing of viral DNA is required for more specific identification. Treatment: Lesions are generally self-limiting, but in some severe cases supportive care and antibiotics for secondary infections are indicated. Systemic treatment with the antiviral drug cidofovir has been used with some success in the treatment of some poxvirus infections, but severe side effects have been reported in humans (e.g. nephrotoxicity). A compounded topical cream preparation of cidofovir is available as well. Interferon omega (Virbagen Omega) was utilized as a treatment in a giant anteater in the United Kingdom. In severe, unresponsive cases euthanasia should be considered before secondary complications cause significant morbidity.

Omega) was utilized as a treatment in a giant anteater in the United Kingdom. In severe, unresponsive cases euthanasia should be considered before secondary complications cause significant morbidity. Prevention and control: Control of rodents to the extent possible in endemic areas. Isolated affected animals if possible. Vaccination of susceptible zoo animals with Modified Vaccinia virus Ankara (MVA) is authorized in some European countries. There is an FDA licensed second generation vaccinia vaccine (ACAM2000) in the United States with limited use to designated military personnel and laboratory workers. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Removal and incineration or burial of organic material. Sunlight, heat and humidity leads to more rapid inactivation of virus, but virus may persist for months or longer in scabs or crusts, if frozen, or present in cool, dry locations. Fairly resistant to disinfectants, but phenolics, quaternary ammonium compounds and iodophors can be effective disinfectants with proper concentration and contact time. Organic debris will decrease disinfectant efficacy. Steam sterilization may also be utilized for disinfection.

and iodophors can be effective disinfectants with proper concentration and contact time. Organic debris will decrease disinfectant efficacy. Steam sterilization may also be utilized for disinfection. Notification: May be reportable is some jurisdictions. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: Currently none. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Maintain infected animals in a quarantine situation until lesions have healed and scabs have come off. If feasible, may want to bathe infected animal in order to remove all virus from fur. In endemic areas, may want to vaccinate susceptible species. Recovered animals should have immunity to the virus. Surviving infected brown rats have demonstrated continued viral shedding in feces and urine for more than a month after recovery. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Wait for all scabs to be lost from an infected animal. Remove bedding and biological material and incinerate or dispose of with other appropriate method. Disinfect environment with phenolic or quaternary ammonia disinfectants to the extent possible.

-  BTV: Ruminants: sheep, goats, cattle, bison, deer, antelope, bighorn sheep, North American elk, camelids, greater kudu, muntjac, topi; perinatal infection in Grant's gazelle, gemsbok, sable, Cape buffalo, ibex, hartebeest, addax. Many other ungulates serologically positive without evidence of disease. - o Clinical signs (including mortality) common in sheep, occasional in goats, and rare in cattle. - o White-tailed deer, pronghorn and bighorn sheep can suffer high levels of mortality and severe disease. - o Seropositivity in a variety of large African carnivores. Report of infection and death in 2 Eurasian lynx fed ruminant fetuses and stillborns in area of BTV infections. BTV contaminated vaccines administered to dogs resulted in abortion, heart failure and death. -  EHDV: Ruminants: white-tailed deer most severely affected, then pronghorn, less frequently in mule deer, and North American elk/wapiti. - o Black-tailed deer, red deer, wapiti, roe deer, fallow deer and other cervids, bison, black and white rhinoceros, black bear have been found seropositive.

-  BTV: Where Culicoides vectors are present (generally between latitudes of 50°N and 35°S, but range is expanding); vertical and horizontal transmission has been documented, but has been rarely documented. Mostly southern and western USA but expanding into northern and eastern areas. -  EHDV: Disease in North America, Australia, Asia, Africa; seropositive animals in South America.

-  Infections resulting in disease do not always occur with these viruses, asymptomatic and nonfatal infections can occur -  Sick and dead animals are often found near/in water -  BTV: Variable; species and serotype dependent. - o Sheep: pyrexia, ptyalism, depression, dyspnea, panting, hyperemia and edema of muzzle, lips, tongue, ears, ulcerations and erosions in mouth, sloughing of hooves, abortion, loss of wool 3-4 weeks post infection. Recrudescence possible, severity partially dependent on serotype. - o Cattle: pyrexia, rarely hyperemia, vesicles or ulcers in mouth, hyperemia of coronary band, dermatitis, hydranencephaly or cerebral cysts in calves. Extended viremia. - o Pronghorn and white-tailed deer: hemorrhage (similar to EHDV) and sudden death.

in mouth, hyperemia of coronary band, dermatitis, hydranencephaly or cerebral cysts in calves. Extended viremia. - o Pronghorn and white-tailed deer: hemorrhage (similar to EHDV) and sudden death. -  EHDV: Three distinct syndromes in deer: - o Peracute: fever, anorexia, weakness, swelling of head and neck, respiratory distress; death within 8-36 hours - o Acute/classical: multi-organ hemorrhage, ptyalism, rhinorrhea, oral and GI ulcerations; mortality may be high - o Chronic: ill thrift with gradual recovery; may have hoof damage/slough or enough scarring from rumen ulcerations to cause emaciation - o Typically subclinical in cattle, but clinical signs include fever, oral ulcers, salivation, lameness associated with coronitis, and weight loss (similar to many FADs). Fetal resorption and hydranencephaly possible; death uncommon in North America, although lameness and unthriftiness may be prolonged.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: -  BTV and EHDV: Gross lesions associated with these viruses can appear similar in affected animals, but can also vary. Sheep: edema of face and ears, crusty exudates on nostrils, hyperemia of coronary bands, ulcers and erosions of oral cavity +/- necrosis and cyanosis; hyperemia, hemorrhage and edema throughout internal organs. Hemorrhage at base of pulmonary artery. Deer: early disease results in pulmonary and subcutaneous edema (head, neck). With progression, multisystem hemorrhage occurs, primarily in the GI tract and heart. Hemorrhage at the base of the pulmonary artery (at the level of the tunica media), and hemorrhage on the serosal surface of the abomasum are considered pathognomonic lesions. Coronitis, coronary band hemorrhage and laminitis may occur. -  EHDV: Additionally, reported in mule deer, edema and necrosis of the testes/epididymis have been observed, associated with poor antler growth and velvet retention. . -  Histologic findings include widespread vasculitis with thrombosis, endothelial swelling, hemorrhages, degenerative changes, and necrosis in many organs.

-  BTV: Limit vector exposure, reduce number and alter habitat to decrease suitability for primary vectors. Pyrethroids or organophosphates effective against Culicoides, frequent applications required, typically administer in axillary, abdominal areas. USDA Nationally approved vaccine for sheep available with BTV 10 specific MLV throughout US (regulated combo of serotypes 10, 11, 17 available in CA only; 17 available in Texas). Vaccination recommended in spring prior to vector season in endemic areas; contraindicated in pregnant ewes and during outbreaks. Quarantine of imported animals, serologic screening, and vector control during transport are important for preventing introduction into BT-free areas. -  EHDV: Limiting vector exposure, as above. No commercially available vaccines available but autogenous EHD inactivated vaccines are used in farmed cervids. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Vector borne, unlikely to contaminate environment. However, sodium hypochlorite or 3% sodium hydroxide are effective if disinfection is warranted. Notification: Required in certain states; check with AVIC or state veterinarian.

environment. However, sodium hypochlorite or 3% sodium hydroxide are effective if disinfection is warranted. Notification: Required in certain states; check with AVIC or state veterinarian. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Seronegative animals (two negative test results >28 days apart with no vector exposure between), vaccinated animals or naturally immune animals (positive serologic test for all applicable serotypes >60 days prior) pose minimal risk for introduction. Introduction of an actively infected animal to a naïve population/area should be avoided. A viremic animal should become negative on PCR or VI prior to being introduced, which should take no longer than 60 days. During that time, the viremic animal should be kept without vector access and treated with insecticides (both animal and environment). Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Seasonal in endemic areas, unlikely to be eradicated once established in vector population. OIE has firm guidelines for being classified as a BTV free country.

disease-free status after an outbreak: Seasonal in endemic areas, unlikely to be eradicated once established in vector population. OIE has firm guidelines for being classified as a BTV free country. Infection by one serotype of either virus usually offers lasting immunity for that serotype, but with limited cross protection against other serotypes. Experts who may be consulted: NVSL, OIE, state veterinarians, and state wildlife veterinarians.

Rotaviral enteritis also documented in poultry and wild birds, ferrets, rabbits, guinea pigs, felids, canids, camelids, equids, and domestic pigs. -  Rotaviruses, especially of Group A, are the most common cause of severe diarrhea in children under 5 years of age. Rotavirus infections are considered species-specific, but re-assortment of the virus between species may occur. Causative organism: Rotaviruses (family Reoviridae) are generally named after the species in which it was first found: Bovine Rotavirus, Porcine Rotavirus, Feline Rotavirus, Canine Rotavirus, etc. Much diversity exists in these viruses due to their genomes' ability to mutate, reassort, and rearrange. Common animal rotavirus serotypes differ from prevalent human strains. Rotaviral isolates are grouped according to antigens present using A - E. Those rotaviruses common in veterinary species differ from prevalent human isolates, with Group A being the most prevalent cause of illness in humans; Group C can also cause outbreaks.

Zoonotic potential: Animal rotaviruses are reservoirs for genetic exchange with human rotaviruses, although zoonotic transmission of whole virions appears to be uncommon. Distribution: Worldwide. Incubation period: Variable - from 15h to 5d. Clinical signs: Enteritis resulting in diarrhea is nearly always the presenting sign, sometimes pale yellow or mucoid in character. Lactose-intolerance may be present due to the lack of lactase secretion by enterocytes-an important complication in nursing animals. Other clinical signs may include fever, inappetence, dullness, and progressive dehydration causing metabolic acidosis, which if severe enough can lead to death. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Gross lesions include thinning of the intestinal walls with sequestration of fluid into the small intestine leading to marked distention of the intestines and abdomen. In young animals, non-digested milk may be present in the intestine.

Depending on the strain's virulence, lesions may present in only localized areas of the jejunum or may be throughout the small intestine and into the large intestine. Rotaviruses infect mature enterocytes on the villi surface in the small intestine, leading to villous atrophy and blunting with club-shaped, stumpy villi that are often fused. Crypt epithelium is often hyperplastic while trying to recover the lost villous enterocytes. Columnar epithelium is lost and replaced with cuboidal or squamous epithelium.

-  Electron microscopy (EM) can be used as a screening tool to identify virus in the feces. Comparative levels with nonclinical animals are used in cattle to support diagnosis. Antigen detection can be performed via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), commonly used to diagnose rotavirus infection. -  Enzyme immunoassays (EIA) point-of-care tests exist for human medicine that have been validated in detecting bovine rotavirus. Latex agglutination testing can also be used to detect Group A rotavirus antigen. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR), including reverse-transcriptase qPCR can both detect rotavirus and differentiate between species. Indirect fluorescent assay (IFA) can detect antigen in tissue, generally using post-mortem samples. Serology is generally noncontributory, as rotavirus exposure is often widespread and results are nonspecific.

-  In ruminants, colostrum often contains antibodies (IgA) to rotavirus in herds where rotavirus is naturally circulating, but the calf's antibody concentrations decline sharply after one week. - Vaccination of the dam 1-3 months prior to calving increases circulating antibodies in the milk and helps reduce rotavirus in calves. Oral bovine rotavirus vaccine (combined with coronavirus) - a modified live vaccine - can be used in newborn calves, but reversion to virulence is possible in nondomestic bovids. -  In species without viable vaccine, prevention and control are best achieved by reducing fecal contamination of the environment through routine cleaning and removal of feces, disinfection of enclosures and all material the animal contacts. Isolation of sick individuals and quarantine of new animals is important to reduce exposure of naïve animals to shed virus. In production animals, the all-in/all-out technique is used to reduce exposure and contamination. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Rotaviruses are hardier than coronaviruses and other diarrheal viruses.

Causative organism: The disease rabies is caused by the rabies virus (family Rhabdoviridae, genus Lyssavirus) and non-rabies Lyssaviruses, such as Australian Bat Lyssavirus, Duvenhage virus, European Bat Lyssavirus, and Mokola virus. Zoonotic potential: Bites or scratches of infected animals; saliva into open wounds and mucous membranes. Distribution: Worldwide, except Antarctica. Several countries have been declared canine rabies-free because of either successful elimination programs or thanks to island status and enforcement of rigorous quarantine regulations. Virus can be shed for a few days prior to the onset of clinical signs and during illness. Clinical signs: Animals will show inappetence, cranial nerve deficits, ataxia, salivating, drooping of lower jaw, acute behavioral changes, such as altered vocalization, aggression, docility, coma, and progressive paralysis. Humans experience pain, paresthesia, and intense pruritus at the bite site; fever, myalgia, malaise and mood changes that progress to paresthesia, paresis, seizures, coma, and many other neurologic signs. Necrotic tonsillitis, necrotic bronchitis, bronchiolitis and alveolitis are commonly seen. Focal areas of necrosis are often found in the liver, spleen, lymph nodes and adrenal glands. - Rabies diagnosis should be performed in accordance with the established national standardized protocol for postmortem rabies testing by a qualified laboratory that has been designated by the local or state health department. Euthanasia should be accomplished in such a way as to maintain the integrity of the brain so that the laboratory can recognize the anatomical parts. Rabies viral antigen is typically widespread in the brain of rabid animals, though may spread unilateral. It is therefore critical to examine a complete cross section of the brainstem. Rabies diagnosis in animals is accomplished through the direct fluorescent antibody test. Brain tissues examined must include medulla oblongata and cerebellum. - Serological tests are used to monitor antibody titers in response to rabies vaccination. - Human antemortem testing requires a minimum of four samples to rule out rabies. Samples required include saliva, nuchal skin biopsy, serum and cerebral spinal fluid and brain biopsy. Nuchal skin biopsy for immunofluorescent antibody staining is the most reliable test of rabies infection during the first week.

Material required for laboratory analysis: Except in the case of very small animals, such as bats, in which whole animals should be collected, only the head or brain (including brain stem) should be submitted to the laboratory. Brain tissues examined must include multiple regions. To facilitate laboratory processing and prevent a delay in testing, any animal specimen being submitted for testing should preferably be stored and shipped under refrigeration and not be frozen. Chemical fixation of tissues should be avoided to prevent significant testing delays and because it may preclude reliable testing.

For parenteral vaccines, killed virus vaccine products only are recommended in exotic mammals, with the exception of a recombinant nonadjuvanted modified live canarypox vaccine approved for ferrets. - Vaccination is primary means of prevention. Rabies in humans can be prevented either by eliminating exposures to rabid animals or by providing exposed persons (without a prior history of vaccination) with prompt local treatment of wound washing for 15 minutes combined with the administration of human rabies immune globulin and a series of 4 doses of vaccine. - Though not nationally notifiable, some state health departments have made animal bites and use of postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) reportable within their jurisdictions. Individuals that have been previously vaccinated and have a potential rabies exposure require prompt wound care and a series of 2 doses of vaccine.

Other biting animals which might have exposed a person to rabies should be reported immediately to the local health department. If the owner is unwilling, strict isolation for 6 months is indicated. Rabies vaccine should be administered upon entry into isolation or 1 month prior to release to comply with pre-exposure vaccination recommendations. Animals maintained in USDAlicensed research facilities or accredited zoological parks should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis. Rabies virus may be excreted in the saliva of infected animals during illness and/or for only a few days prior to illness or death. A healthy animal which was previously vaccinated that bites a person should be confined and observed daily for 10 days; administration of rabies vaccine is not recommended during the observation period to avoid confusing signs of rabies with possible side effects of vaccine administration. If signs suggestive of rabies develop, the animal should be euthanized and the head submitted for testing.
