texto: -  Mammals: Many species of domestic animals especially goats and sheep. Cattle, pigs, horses, dogs, and cats have higher resistance to melioidosis. Non-domestic reports include marine mammals, camels, alpacas, mules, zebra, deer, kangaroos, bears, & non-human primates. Hamsters and guinea pigs can be infected in the laboratory. -  Birds: parrots, penguin -  Reptiles: crocodiles, snakes, soft-shelled turtles -  Tropical fish. Causative organism: Gram negative, flagellated, bipolar-shaped saprophytic bacteria. Zoonotic potential: Humans can be infected by ingesting contaminated food, inhalation, or direct contact of the contaminant with open wound. Intrauterine and mammary transmissions have also been observed. Arthropod borne transmission has also been described. Distribution: The organism is ubiquitous throughout southeast Asia, northern Australia, and the South Pacific. Its distribution is predominantly tropical and subtropical with "hyperendemicity" in the top end of the Northern Territory of Australia and northeast Thailand.

Its distribution is predominantly tropical and subtropical with "hyperendemicity" in the top end of the Northern Territory of Australia and northeast Thailand. The true boundaries of its endemicity are ambiguous due to movement of the organism and its ability to travel to and exist in temperate regions (southwest Australia and France), where it may cause sporadic disease and outbreaks. Reports of possible autochthonous melioidosis have also come from India, Pacific islands, Central and South America, the Caribbean, Africa, and the Middle East. Even within an endemic region, extremely local/focal hot spots may be seen. Incubation period: In natural infections, the incubation period in humans can vary from days to months or years. The medical onset time of the disease is usually in the range of 1-21 days (means 9 days). Abscesses may be carried without clinical signs which can be found in some resistant animal species such as pigs and cattle. In marine mammals the disease often occurs peracutely after a heavy rainfall in endemic areas during the rainy season.

Clinical signs: Called "The Great Mimicker," melioidosis has a wide range of clinical presentations, including fulminating septicemia, and chronic and local suppurative infections. Moreover, relapsing melioidosis can also cause the fulminating sepsis in a patient who underwent insufficient eradication phase of treatment. The most common site of infection is acute respiratory form and sepsis through hematogenous dissemination. The chronic septicemia can present as intermittent febricula with chronic respiratory infection. Local infection can be seen as lameness, osteomyelitis, mastitis, orchitis, aortic aneurysms which may possibly induce fulminating septicemia or chronic infection. Subclinical infections are common in animals. Abscesses may be found in asymptomatic animals at slaughter. The clinical presentation varies widely by species. -  In goat and sheep, a severe febrile reaction accompanied by anorexia, lameness and yellow thick exudate from the nose and eyes is seen.

In horses, neurologic disease, respiratory symptoms, or colic and diarrhea have been described. -  Neurological signs include circling, nystagmus, blindness, hyperaesthesia and mild tetanic convulsions have been reported in cows, goats, camels and horses. Septicemia or extensive involvement of the vital organs can be fatal. -  Camels are highly susceptible and can present symptoms of pyrexia, severe depression, septic arthritis, anorexia, mucopurulent nasal discharge with nervous signs. -  Non-human primates mostly show generalized lethargy, progressive cachexia and respiratory distress with nasal purulent discharge. -  Most cases in captive marine mammals have been characterized by acute septicemia with pyrexia, anorexia, and lethargy followed by death. Respiratory distress was noticed only in a few animals immediately before death.

Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: At necropsy, the major findings are multiple abscesses containing thick, caseous greenish-yellow or off-white material. These abscesses are generally not calcified. The regional lymph nodes, lungs, spleen, liver and subcutaneous tissues are most often involved, but abscesses can occur in most organs. In animals with respiratory disease, fibrinous pleuritis and exudative bronchopneumonia, consolidation and/or abscesses may be found in the lungs. Suppurative lesions including nodules and ulcers may also be found on the nasal mucosa and septum, as well as on the turbinate bones. These nodules may coalesce to form irregular plaques. Meningoencephalitis, severe enteritis, suppurative polyarthritis and other syndromes have also been reported.

Splenic abscesses are often found in asymptomatic pigs at slaughter. Diagnosis: The gold standard method is isolation and identification of the organism from blood, lesions, or discharges. The organism is readily cultured on routine diagnostic media such as MacConkey's agar and blood agar. The selective media Ashdown's agar can help increase the sensitivity and specificity of this technique. Blood culture should be taken before starting treatment whenever possible. The unique characteristic of Burkholderia pseudomallei colony is earth odor. Serologic screening tests include indirect hemagglutination, ELISA, microagglutination tests, and complement fixation. Serological end points are not available for each wildlife species, and seroconversion may take days to weeks, limiting the utility when making clinical decisions in acutely ill animals.

Treatment: The medical treatment takes several months, and in veterinary patients usually consists of both an acute induction phase followed by prolonged eradication phase.

Treatment: The medical treatment takes several months, and in veterinary patients usually consists of both an acute induction phase followed by prolonged eradication phase. The acute phase typically requires intravenous antibiotic therapy multiple times per day, although in some species and individuals other routes may be used such as intramuscular injections in birds. Ceftazidime is the most common agent used for acute intravenous therapy. The eradication phase takes several months and generally consists of oral therapy, although long-acting injectable antibiotics have also been used. Specific treatment and diagnostic strategies for various taxa are described in the 9 th Edition of Fowler's Zoo and Wild Animal Medicine, Chapter 46: Update on Melioidosis in Zoo and Wild Animals. Prevention and control: In endemic or contaminated areas, contact between the animal and soil or rain water should be minimized. Providing safe drinking water is important in endemic areas. Ultraviolet light, chlorine, and ozone can be used to sterilize water. Carnivores and omnivores should not be allowed to eat contaminated carcasses.

Causative organism: Campylobacter spp. (various). Zoonotic potential: Yes. Distribution: Surfaces (wet cutting boards or utensils) where raw or partially cooked meat (particularly poultry) is prepared; surface waters and mountain streams exposed to feces from cattle and wild birds; surfaces in contact with feces from infected agricultural animals, pets, wild, zoo and lab animals. Incubation period: 2-5 days, and may be up to one week. Clinical signs: Clinical signs are host-specific; cross-infection is possible and range from non-clinical to severe. Diarrhea tends to be watery or may be bloody; fever, abdominal cramps, nausea, and vomiting may also be present; other illnesses, such as abortion, stillbirths or infertility may occur in cattle and sheep.

texto: -  Enteric campylobacteriosis: Biopsy specimens from people have shown acute colitis with inflammatory infiltrates of the lamina propria and crypt abscesses. Organisms can stably colonize the small and large intestine, although most animals show cecal and colonic lesions with typhlocolitis; marked inflammation of lamina propria, dominated by neutrophilic polymorphonuclear and mononuclear cells that sometimes extend into submucosa; crypt abscesses and damage to the crypt epithelium is common; a compromised epithelial surface also been observed in most species. -  Bovine and ovine genital campylobacteriosis: Abortion occurs most frequently in late pregnancy with occasional infertility. Liver shows typical gray, necrotic foci 1-2 cm in diameter; fetuses usually edematous and body cavities contain reddish fluid; fetal membranes edematous and cotyledons pale and necrotic but lesions do vary. Curved bacteria in stains of cotyledon impressions or fetal abomasal fluid. Gram negative organisms found in wet preps of abomasal fluid examined by dark-field or phase-contrast microscopy.

Diagnosis: Bacterial culture of fresh feces; darkfield examination of abomasal contents or culture of placenta or abomasal contents or in uterine discharge. Material required for laboratory analysis: Fresh fecal samples in enteric transport kit and storage at 4°C. Relevant Diagnostic lab: Laboratories capable of bacteriologic culturing on selective culture media incubated under microaerobic conditions, and temperatures allowing growth of non-thermotolerant species. Campylobacter species are difficult to isolate and suboptimal conditions for isolation will yield false-negative results. Variations in laboratory practices have been reported, also suggesting variations in specimen handling and processing, which likely influence recovery and detection of Campylobacter species. Treatment: Usually no medical treatment is necessary. Rehydrating levels of fluids should be administered during diarrheal disease. Appropriate antibiotics, such as erythromycin, may be a consideration in some cases.

Prevention and control: Raw poultry meat should not be prepared on a cutting board then used unwashed for other food items, especially when not cooked after handling. Appropriate hygiene in food preparation should include separate cutting boards for proteins and produce. Unpasteurized milk and untreated surface water and mountain streams should be avoided. Wash hands using soap and running water after contact with animals, their enclosures, and other surfaces that are in contact with feces from animals. Animals infected with genital campylobacteriosis should not be utilized for breeding. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: After cleaning gross contamination, diluted bleach (15ml in one quart of water) applied to dry or wiped dry after 10 minutes.

-  Animals: Clinical signs are mostly neurologic and caused by muscle paralysis. A symmetrical, ascending weakness starting from the rear limbs and progressing to the forelimbs is typical. Cranial nerve deficits are usually present and may include decreased palpebral reflex, decreased gag or swallowing reflex, ptyalism, decreased jaw tone, mydriasis, and sluggish pupillary responses. Respiratory or cardiac paralysis can occur and usually causes death. -  Humans: Three types of botulism: food-borne, wound, and infant. - o Food-borne botulism is caused by consumption of toxin-tainted food. In these infections, signs can include gastrointestinal issues such as nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain; symmetric, descending flaccid paralysis, and drooping palpebrae; and dry mouth, slurred speech, and muscle weakness. Descending paralysis of the respiratory muscles - potentially fatal, arms and legs may occur within 24 hours in severe cases. - o Wound botulism is caused by a wound that is contaminated, usually from toxins in the soil. Signs are consistent with food-borne illness, but usually without gastrointestinal signs.

Signs are consistent with food-borne illness, but usually without gastrointestinal signs. - o Infant botulism is seen only in infants less than one year of age and caused by spores germinating in the intestinal tract. Signs include constipation, poor suckling reflexes, peripheral weakness ("floppy baby" syndrome), and in severe cases, respiratory distress and death. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Most post mortem or histologic findings are the result of muscle paralysis. Mammals with wound botulism may have lesions, but the wounds are generally not obviously or grossly infected.

-  History of exposure and clinical signs. The toxin can be hard to find in feed or in tissues, so most diagnosis is done by eliminating out other differentials. -  Cultures from wounds or tissues can be taken to potentially isolate the organism. The toxin can also be isolated from serum, feces, vomitus, or samples of food that were ingested. -  ELISA testing can detect neurotoxin, but each subtype of toxin must be evaluated individually. -  Real-time PCR of botulism neurotoxin genes. -  Bioassays: - o Mouse bioassay; Serum or an extract of contaminated material is injected alone and in combination with a type-specific antitoxin into the mice. Survival of the group of mice protected with antitoxin and death of the other group from signs consistent with botulism confirms the presence of botulism toxin. This test is considered the standard and most reliable method of identifying botulism toxin. Reported sensitivity in equine 32% with a specificity of 97%, similar studies have not been performed in non-domestic species. Positive results are highly suggestive of botulism, but a negative result does not rule a diagnosis.

-  Vaccines are available for humans and animals with high risk of exposure. -  To ensure food is properly stored and prepared, botulism toxin is destroyed by heating food to 80 ℃ for 30 minutes or to 100 ℃ for 10 minutes. Wounds should be kept clean and avoid contamination as much as possible. For wildlife, prompt removal of carcasses that could be infected is critical as decaying carcasses are known to support toxin production. Maggots feeding on decaying carcasses are sources of infection for many waterfowl as the maggots are unaffected by the toxin, but effectively concentrate it. Waterfowl consume the maggots and become infected. Stagnant water should be avoided as this creates an environment for Clostridium botulinum bacteria to grow and for spores to germinate. -  Use of PPE is recommended when performing necropsy on suspected cases of botulism. Disease has been described in three laboratory workers performing necropsy on an animal that died of botulism. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Clean areas with diluted bleach (0.1%) when possible. Sunlight inactivates the toxins within 1-3 hours. Adding chlorine to water if possible will destroy toxins as well.

Horses, guinea pigs, primates, sheep, and mice are most susceptible, followed by goats and cattle. Elephants, kangaroos, camelids, giraffe, and rabbits have also been infected. Carnivores are considered less susceptible, although disease is occasionally reported in domestic dogs and has been seen in a maned wolf. Avian species are largely considered to be resistant.

Carnivores are considered less susceptible, although disease is occasionally reported in domestic dogs and has been seen in a maned wolf. Avian species are largely considered to be resistant. There is one report of naturally acquired tetanus in a gyrfalcon, but all other avian cases have been experimentally induced. Animals can become infected be through contaminated wounds, postpartum, and after surgical procedures. Neonatal tetanus is seen in animals born without passive immunity, usually through infection of the umbilical stump.

-  Clostridium tetani is a Gram-positive, anaerobic bacillus that may develop a terminal spore, giving it a "drumstick" or "safety pin" appearance. C. tetani is ubiquitous in soil worldwide; however, it is most prevalent in warm humid regions. It can also be found in animal and human feces, but it is not believed to be a component of normal intestinal flora. -  In the presence of oxygen, it produces spores and may live in the soil in spore form for months to years. In an anaerobic wound, the spores germinate and multiply, producing two major toxins: a potent neurotoxin known as tetanus toxin (TeNT), formerly called tetanospasmin, and tetanolysin, a compound that causes local tissue destruction and is thought to contribute to an environment of anaerobic necrosis that favors continued bacterial growth. -  Tetanus toxin is disseminated by retrograde axonal transport to the spinal cord and/or brainstem, where it binds to inhibitory interneurons that regulate motor neuron activity. TeNT prevents the release of glycine and GABA, removing negative control on the motor neurons which then fire excessively, leading to uncontrollable muscle contraction and spasm. Zoonotic potential: None.

prevents the release of glycine and GABA, removing negative control on the motor neurons which then fire excessively, leading to uncontrollable muscle contraction and spasm. Zoonotic potential: None. Tetanus is acquired through contact with spores in the environment and is not transmitted from animal to animal or person to person. Distribution: Worldwide. Found in soil, dust, and animal feces. Enzootic areas exist, mainly in warm humid regions, such as West and Central Africa, Southeast Asia, India, and in the southern USA. Incubation period: Ranges from 3 to 30 days after contamination of a deep wound or surgical site that provides anaerobic conditions. Clinical signs: Signs often begin with localized rigid extension of muscles in the region of the infected wound. Initial signs of generalized tetanus include limb spasticity, extensor rigidity, neck stiffness, protrusion of the nictitans, erect ears, salivation, and risus sardonicus (lips drawn back and forehead wrinkled due to contraction of the facial muscles).

extensor rigidity, neck stiffness, protrusion of the nictitans, erect ears, salivation, and risus sardonicus (lips drawn back and forehead wrinkled due to contraction of the facial muscles). Signs may progress to include difficulty swallowing, restriction of jaw movements proceeding to trismus (lock jaw), generalized rigidity, spasms of skeletal muscle and exaggerated reflexes. Equids often assume a "sawhorse stance" with tail stiff and extended. In the most severe cases, prolonged recumbency with rigid extension of all limbs, pyrexia, sweating, seizures, opisthotonos, and tachycardia are seen. Death is caused by respiratory failure due to spastic paralysis of the diaphragm and other muscles involved in respiration and/or autonomic dysregulation, resulting in bradyarrhythmias and hypo- or hypertension. Mortality ranges from 50100% depending on species, timing of intervention, and circumstances of infection. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: No specific lesions are seen on gross necropsy or histopathology. If the site of C. tetani introduction was a wound, it is often healed prior to death.

Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: No specific lesions are seen on gross necropsy or histopathology. If the site of C. tetani introduction was a wound, it is often healed prior to death. It may be possible to see secondary aspiration pneumonia or other non-specific signs such as pulmonary edema and atelectasis. Diagnosis: Prior existence of a wound and characteristic clinical signs are the basis for diagnosis. Direct microscopic examination of wound material may be useful. Attempting to culture C. tetani from the wound is generally not successful. PCR to detect toxin genetic material from the wound or blood is available but has low sensitivity. Material required for laboratory analysis: Wound tissue or blood. Relevant Diagnostic lab: None are suggested since diagnosis is primarily based on clinical signs. PCR testing for TeNT toxin on whole blood or serum, or wound tissue, can be performed by some laboratories, but is not readily commercially available and is low sensitivity. Gram stain and/or anaerobic culture of tissue from wound could reveal Clostridium (low sensitivity).

-  The principles of treatment are to eliminate the causal bacteria with antibiotics, neutralize the toxin with antitoxin, maintain hydration and electrolyte balance, treat muscle spasms and anxiety, and minimize stimulation. Wounds should be cleaned and debrided. Animals who have previously received tetanus toxoid vaccination should be given a booster. -  Antibiotic therapy with high doses of penicillin, cephalosporins, or metronidazole are effective against C. tetani. -  Tetanus antitoxin is hyperimmune serum generated by either a horse or human to bind and destroy the tetanus toxin. Antitoxin can be used to neutralize unbound circulating toxin, but it cannot remove toxin already bound to nerve endings or bound within the CNS. It can be given intramuscularly or intravenously, but IV administration can cause anaphylaxis, so pretreatment with diphenhydramine is recommended. -  If tetanic spasms are occurring, supportive care should be provided, including maintenance of hydration, minimization of sensory stimulation, and airway support if needed.

is recommended. -  If tetanic spasms are occurring, supportive care should be provided, including maintenance of hydration, minimization of sensory stimulation, and airway support if needed. -  Treatment may include muscle relaxants such as benzodiazepines and methocarbamol, tranquilizers such as phenothiazines, and/or barbiturate sedatives. Prevention and control: Active immunization with tetanus toxoid is recommended in susceptible species due to ubiquitous presence in environment. Two doses of tetanus toxoid should be given 4-8 weeks apart with boosters given one year later and every 2-5 years thereafter. Consideration of age at first vaccination is important to ensure that maternal antibodies do not interfere. Revaccination is recommended in the event of a significant wound or a surgical procedure. Vaccination is not contraindicated in pregnant animals. Passive immunization with antitoxin should be reserved for cases with high-risk wounds and no previous active immunization, unvaccinated patients who must undergo surgical procedures, and neonates in high-risk situations.

Clinical disease has infrequently been reported in some birds. Causative organism: Coxiella burnetii (obligate intracellular Gram-negative coccobacilli). Zoonotic potential: Yes (called Query fever in humans). Approximately 50% of human infections are asymptomatic. Symptoms of acute-onset infection include flu-like symptoms (fever, headache, chills, sweating, and fatigue) and occur usually 2-6 weeks after exposure. Most cases are self-limiting in 1014 days, but some may require antimicrobial therapy. Approximately 30-50% of those developing acute clinical disease develop pneumonia, and a smaller proportion can develop hepatitis, myocarditis and meningoencephalitis. A chronic form of Q fever (mostly endocarditis) is seen in <5% of people that developed acute symptomatic infections, months to years after the initial presentation. Distribution: Global. Incubation period: Depends on number of infective organisms, but usually 2-3 weeks in humans.

Clinical signs: Often subclinical in domestic ruminants. Clinical disease usually consists of abortion, stillbirth, endometritis, mastitis and infertility. Often sporadic abortions in herds can be seen that are followed by recovery without complications. Abortion storms are also reported. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Necrotizing placentitis with large number of organisms in trophoblasts, but otherwise it is non-specific. Metritis and mastitis can also be seen. Adequate personal protective equipment must be worn during manipulation of birth fluids, placenta and aborted fetuses (N-95 respirator, gloves, protective outerwear).

-  Serology: IFA antibody tests can be used to screen for exposure or to identify recent infection using paired sera. Antibodies to phase I antigens predominate in chronic infection, whereas those to phase II antigens predominate in acute infection. Complement fixation test and ELISA are also available. Antibodies to both phase I and phase II antigens can persist for several years after the initial infection. -  Other means of diagnosis include: direct isolation using cell culture (which requires highly specialized facilities), PCR, histopathology and immunohistochemical staining of placenta/aborted tissues for organisms. Special stains include: Stamp, modified Ziehl-Neelson, Gimenez, Giemsa, or modified Koster stain in order to detect organisms, but diagnosis using this method should be supported with serologic test results and/or molecular diagnostic. -  For more in-depth information about the diagnosis of Q fever, please see the diagnostic section in the CDC's MMWR Diagnosis and Management of Q fever-United States, 2013. Material required for laboratory analysis: Placenta is the tissue of choice to submit.

Other specimens include vaginal discharge, milk, feces, semen and tissues from aborted fetuses (liver, lung, stomach content). At risk personnel (contact with birth products, reproductive organs, infected carcasses, and fur or wool) should wear adequate protective equipment to protect against small droplet and aerosol exposure.

texto: E. phagocytophila, and Human Granulocytic Ehrlichial Agent are now considered to be the same species  Anaplasma phagocytophilum. Zoonotic potential: Yes, via vectors or mechanical transmission. Distribution: Almost every state in the US has reported a case of ehrlichiosis. Most human cases occur in the south-central and southeastern US. E. canis is endemic in southern, eastern, south-central and in southwest US, and is mainly transmitted by the brown dog tick Rhipicephalus sanguineus. E. ewingii is found predominantly in southern and mideastern US and is mainly transmitted by the lone star tick Amblyomma americanum. E. chaffeensis occurs predominantly in the southeastern US and is also transmitted by A. americanum. Globally, Ehrlichia has been reported in South America, Asia, Africa, and Europe.

-  Humans: 5-10 days after a tick bite. -  Dogs: 8-20 days. -  It is estimated that the infected tick must be attached to the host for 24-48 hours for transmission to occur. Ehrlichia can remain alive in the developing tick for up to 5 months. Acute infection develops 1-3 weeks after transmission and lasts ~2-4 weeks. After ~6-9 weeks, the organism is eliminated in an immunocompetent animal or a parasitemia develops with no clinical signs in the subclinical phase which can last from weeks to years or mild to severe clinical signs. If the animal cannot mount an effective immune response, the animal becomes chronically infected.

-  Generally non-specific, multi-systemic: fever, depression, lethargy, thrombocytopenia, anemia, anorexia, weight loss, lymphadenopathy; hepatocellular enzyme abnormalities, possibly gastrointestinal signs (vomiting, diarrhea), polymyositis, polyarthritis, rash, ocular signs (uveitis or retinal petechiae), reproductive disorders, and neuropathies. -  Clinical signs depend on the strain of Ehrlichia, dose of infection, species, immunological status of host, and concurrent infections with other tick-borne parasites. -  In dogs, the acute phase is generally mild and causes immune-mediated platelet destruction and manifesting in lethargy, anorexia, lymphadenopathy, fever, and is often associated with the presence of ticks. In the subclinical phase, dogs appear normal with a somewhat reduced platelet count and elevated globulin levels; this phase can last months to years. In the chronic phase, clinical signs recur with up to 60% of infected dogs presenting with abnormal bleeding due to reduced platelet numbers; elevated globulin levels are almost always seen; uveitis, neurological effects, and glomerulonephritis can also result; most dogs do not show full pancytopenia.

-  History of exposure and clinical signs (diagnosis of subclinical disease based on anamnesis, geographic location, persistent antibody titers, mild thrombocytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinemia). -  Morulae (intracytoplasmic bacterial aggregates) in monocytes on blood and buffy coat smears (Romanowski stain); however, often only seen in a small percentage of blood smears of infected dogs, and only found in the bloodstream for a few days in the acute stage. -  Serology - o Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA), e.g. IDEXX "snap 4DX" (includes Lyme disease and heartworm tests; detects E. canis, not E. ewingii) - not quantitative. - o Detection of E. canis serum antibodies with indirect Immunofluorescence Antibody Test (IFA), antibodies can be detected as early as 7 days post-infection, although animals may not be seropositive until 28 days post-infection. It takes 6-9 months after infection for titers to drop. Serologic cross-reactions may occur with other rickettsial agents. - o With ELISA and IFA, a positive test only indicates exposure and does not imply active infection. A titer >1:80 is considered positive.

PCR remains positive for several weeks after infection has cleared, as it does not distinguish between live and dead organisms. Distribution: Endemic countries are on the African continent south of the Sahara, Madagascar, various small islands in the Indian and Atlantic Oceans, and islands in the Caribbean. A foreign animal disease for US, concern of entry is high due to illegal wildlife trade with infected ticks and the potential for domestic ruminants and white tailed deer in the US to serve as host species. Ticks on tortoises from Africa can carry infected ticks. Incubation period: This period varies with species infected, route of infection, and strain of E. ruminantium. In domestic cattle, incubation is 12 days after intravenous injection of E. ruminantium "vaccine". The period is shorter (e.g., 7 days) when more virulent strains are used. Incubation period of tick transmitted heartwater is 18-21 days. Clinical signs: Severity ranges from subclinical infection to peracute disease. Clinical signs range from mild transient fever in subclinical cases to death without premonitory signs in peracute cases - i.e., presenting as sudden death. The acute form is characterized by rapid onset of fever (41.5 o to 42 o C), tachypnea, inappetence, petechiation on serosal and mucosal surfaces, and neurologic signs (e.g., hyperesthesia, high-stepping or unsteady gait, twitching eyelids, head pressing, chewing, abnormal tongue movement, individual muscle tremors).

Incubation period: generally, 3-5 days, but 1-21 days possible Pathophysiology: F. tularensis is usually invading and replicating in vector-derived cells and hemolymph, and in macrophages within the host. Cytokines, such as interferon-gamma and tumor necrosis factor, produced by T-cells are critical for activation of macrophages and cell-mediated and protective immunity. Yet, F. tularensis proliferates in macrophages without destroying the host cell. It has also developed good survival and adaptation strategies using surface proteins to suppress innate immune response, which makes it harder to diagnose and control it within the host. New research has discovered that F. tularensis is also able to invade erythrocytes. The high hemoglobin and iron content in erythrocytes could influence the virulence gene expression in F. tularensis. Yet, erythrocytes do not support replication of the pathogen and, therefore, do not seem to be a major contributor to the pathogenesis of tularemia. Confirmation of results would likely be carried out by the CDC's National Center for Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases (NCEZID), 800-232-4636. Treatment: Streptomycin is considered the treatment of choice in humans with tularemia. Chloramphenicol is added to streptomycin for meningitis in humans. Other chemotherapeutics, such as gentamicin, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, and fluoroquinolones, have been used successfully. Tetracyclines and chloramphenicol are bacteriostatic and require a longer treatment period of at least 14-21 days.

Due to frequent treatment relapses or failure, combined with increase in resistance against commonly used products, alternative chemotherapeutics and newer chemotherapeutic generations, such as glycocyclines, ketolides, and new generation fluoroquinolones are currently investigated and show promising results. A live attenuated vaccine strain of F. tularensis type B was developed in the Soviet Union for immunization of humans. Although this live vaccine serum (LVS) strain was also shown to be effective against the type A strain and oral infection, this vaccine was not fully effective against infection acquired by inhalation.

-  The genus Helicobacter was created in 1989 with approximately 20 species currently described across all taxa. The essential property of almost all Helicobacter spp. is the presence of sheathed flagella, and in most species, possession of strong ureolytic (urease producing) ability, particularly those associated with gastric mucosa. Considerable diversity in cell morphology is present with respect to cell length, number and location of flagella, and presence of periplasmic fibrils. H. pylori has a global distribution and infects human gastric mucosa (predominately the gastric cardia) with evidence for infection in cats. The most commonly described pathogenic species of Helicobacter include: H. pylori (human), H. heilmannii (cat, dog), H. felis (mouse model), Helicobacter acinonychis (formerly H. acinonyx; persists in the gastric fundus in cheetah), H. mustelae (domestic ferrets) and H. enhydrae (southern sea otter). H. acinonychis lacks the cag pathogenicity island (PAI), but is otherwise the most closely related Helicobacter to H. pylori.

H. mustelae (domestic ferrets) and H. enhydrae (southern sea otter). H. acinonychis lacks the cag pathogenicity island (PAI), but is otherwise the most closely related Helicobacter to H. pylori. The PAI is the characteristic component causing the human neutrophilic inflammatory response, but has not been associated with Helicobacter spp. infecting cheetah. Multiple strains of H. acinonychis have been reported, but the demographic of these strains within North America and other populations of felids is poorly understood. -  The urease produced by Helicobacter and the flagella allow the organism to survive in the gastric environment over a wide spectrum of pH, penetrate into gastric mucous layer, and reach the gastric epithelium where it can then attach to cells. Both cellular immune response and humoral response to H. pylori are believed to contribute to disease pathogenesis. -  In cheetah, gastritis is associated with single species or multi-species infections of Helicobacter spp. (H. pylori-like, H. heilmannii, H. felis, or H. acinonychis (formerly H. acinonyx)).

-  In cheetah, gastritis is associated with single species or multi-species infections of Helicobacter spp. (H. pylori-like, H. heilmannii, H. felis, or H. acinonychis (formerly H. acinonyx)). Helicobacter-associated gastritis causes morbidity and mortality in captive cheetah, but this reaction to Helicobacter spp. is not seen in free-ranging cheetahs when infected with the same Helicobacter spp. It has been hypothesized that immunomodulation caused by chronic stress (elevated glucocorticoids) or other factors may play a role in the pathogenesis of cheetah gastritis. Pet cats are frequently colonized by H. heilmannii without substantial correlation between infection and degree of gastritis. Differences in the pathogenicity of Helicobacter spp. across taxa are apparent, making understanding the pathogenesis, epidemiology and treatment difficult. -  An occurrence of natural infection with H. pylori in a group of cynomolgus monkeys was associated with chronic active gastritis and gastric erosions. Zoonotic potential: The exact route of transmission of H. pylori among people is unknown. Several routes of transmission of H. pylori have been proposed including fecal-oral, oral-oral, gastro-oral, and via respiratory droplets. In humans, familial associated spread from person-to-person is suspected. Under controlled laboratory conditions, human sourced H. pylori has been shown to infect nonhuman primates. However, H. pylori occurring naturally in monkeys (or other species) are unlikely to represent a major route of transmission to humans, since close contact between nonhuman primates and humans is typically limited. H. pylori has been cultured from feline salivary and gastric sections, and H. pylori DNA has been found in in feline feces and dental plaque raising the possibility that H. pylori could be transmitted from cats to humans via saliva, vomit, or feces. In developing countries, it is suspected that H. pylori may have an environmental reservoir (e.g. untreated water or contaminated food). Transmission of Helicobacter and subsequent clinical disease between humans and animals is poorly studied, but veterinarians should be careful and take personal protective precautions for potential exposure. In humans, H. pylori is associated with gastric cancer and is a known carcinogen of the stomach. Human medical endoscopists and endoscopy nurses have significantly higher rates of H. pylori than other medical professionals. Because of this, appropriate precautions using proper personal protective equipment (gloves, masks) should be used by veterinary staff conducting endoscopy, performing dental procedures, handling saliva or fecal material.

-  H. pylori is the most common bacterial infection in the world affecting people, with estimates that it infects half of the people worldwide, but causes clinical disease in only a small percentage of those infected. The discrepancy between infection and clinical disease is a problem for physicians; it is difficult to discern when to treat patients. To help with this challenge, standardized human medical guidelines recommend only treating people suffering from peptic ulcer disease or mucosally associated lymphoma. -  The distribution of Helicobacter spp. in animals is poorly understood and under studied. Hand raised cheetah have been found to be Helicobacter negative until introduced to other cheetah (personal comm. S. Citino). But it can be assumed that most cheetah (free-ranging and captive) have been exposed to various Helicobacter spp. of varying strains.

-  Clinical signs range across taxa, but most are consistent with gastrointestinal signs. -  Cheetah with Helicobacter-associated gastritis display partial or full anorexia as the most common clinical sign leading to vomiting, regurgitation, diarrhea with undigested meat in feces, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), acquired lower esophageal sphincter dysfunction, acquired hiatal hernia, and weight loss. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Helicobacter-associated gastritis cannot be identified by gross evaluation of the stomach by endoscopy. Gastric ulcers can be identified via ante-mortem endoscopy evaluation or post-mortem gross evaluation, but further testing is needed to identify Helicobacter. As a spiral shaped bacterium, cytology can be helpful when diagnosing Helicobacterassociated gastritis. Histopathologic and immunological findings in cheetah with Helicobacterassociated gastritis are described as florid lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltrates within the gastric lamina propria and glandular epithelium, parietal cell apoptosis, leading to gland hyperplasia, goblet cell metaplasia, fibrosis and atrophy of the glandular fundus.

Cheetahs with severe gastritis have larger numbers of active B cells and plasma cells. Diagnosis: Rapid urease test, C-13-urea breath test (UBT), serology, gastric biopsy with histopathology (rec. minimum 5 biopsies for submission for gastritis & helicobacter evaluation), and touch cytology are all highly accurate invasive diagnostic tests for gastric Helicobacter organisms, whereas culture and polymerase chain reaction are the only means to identify Helicobacter to the species level. Material required for laboratory analysis: Stomach (multiple fundic biopsies recommended for cheetah, ferret, dogs, and cats) biopsies (full thickness with mucosa) for histopathology, once initial diagnosis and grading of gastritis has been performed, non-invasive C-13-urea breath test (UBT) can offer an alternative to repeated biopsies for therapeutic monitoring.

-  Triple therapy with a proton pump inhibitor (PPI), in combination with amoxicillin and clarithromycin is the established treatment for H. pylori. Metronidazole is used in the place of amoxicillin as part of the triple therapy for penicillin hypersensitive patients. Metronidazole is an important treatment for Helicobacter, but resistance among strains of H. acinonychis and H. pylori have been reported. For human cases of H. pylori, resistance to metronidazole has been reported in up to 80%, and resistance to clarithromycin in 2-10% of strains cultured. Resistance to one antibiotic, when triple therapy is attempted reduces the efficacy of therapy up to 50%. For H. pylori, quadruple therapy incorporating a bismuth compound with a PPI, tetracycline and metronidazole has been a choice for rescue therapy if triple medication course is not successful. Ranitidine-bismuth citrate has been shown to over-come metronidazole and clarithromycin resistance, and can be used in place of a PPI for rescue therapy as studied in humans. The exact mechanism by which PPI exert their effect on H. pylori eradication is not clear, but it is suspected that the potent acid suppression creates an optimal pH for bacterial growth and cell division allowing the key antibiotics amoxicillin and clarithromycin to act more effectively on the bacterium. H. pylori resistance to amoxicillin is not often reported, but amoxicillin is less effective when used alone on H. pylori than clarithromycin or metronidazole. -  Because treatment of Helicobacter requires the use of several medications, compliance is a significant challenge to success. Resistance of H. pylori toward levofloxacin is rising worldwide, due to a point mutation reducing quinolone susceptibility. Because the quinolones are used for second line therapy when triple or quadruple courses are ineffective, a major concern for human medicine exists. -  Personal protective equipment such as wearing barrier gloves and hand washing is recommended to prevent exposure. -  Proper cleaning of endoscopy equipment requires use of a detergent (enzymatic cleaner) and - brush (mechanical cleaning over manual cleaning preferred) to remove blood, mucus, and tissue from the endoscope channels prior to disinfection. The World Congresses of Gastroenterology recommends that endoscopes be soaked in 2% activated glutaraldehyde for at least 10 minutes after cleaning to prevent transfer of Helicobacter between patients. -  Sterilization of biopsy forceps, or the use of disposable biopsy forceps is preferred to prevent transfer of Helicobacter. Typically, as biopsy forceps penetrate the gastric mucosa, they are difficult to clean and pose a significant risk for cross transfer among patients. -  Common reservoir species ("host-adapted") such as rodents can have high prevalence of infection - as high as 90%. Generally, these animals do not develop disease or clinical signs, except perhaps mild signs at initial infection. Reservoir hosts may shed the organism for a few weeks or intermittently for several years due to chronic renal infection and biofilm formation in the renal tubules. Specific sequence types may circulate among specific reservoir host species; wildlife and rodents are often implicated in this role during outbreaks. Reservoir situations, increasing contact with humans through urbanization and conversion to an omnivorous diet is associated with increased prevalence for some taxa, such as Phalangeridae (brush-tail possum). Additional reservoirs, including birds and reptiles, have been identified, but as of yet have unclear relevance. -  Acute infections can occur in susceptible species ("non-host-adapted" or incidental hosts) and include most managed zoological species and humans; following infection with the organism, they develop moderate to severe illness. Fatality can occur, especially in untreated individuals.

These animals generally do not become carriers. Once infection has resolved, especially if these animals are treated, prolonged shedding is not typical, although chronic kidney damage may be incurred in survivors. -  Published literature assessment identified that 10-20% prevalence had been reported in most mammalian families, although families Muridae, Canidae, and Bovidae were overrepresented. -  Species from Felidae appear more resilient, but recent assessments are that domestic felids are detected more often with sub-clinical disease than recognized previously, and author has personal experience with clinical disease in two large exotic felids. -  Although original association of this organism with black rhinoceros and hemolytic anemia was considered, it has not been proven. -  Free-ranging California sea lions have a marked predisposition to infection with severe renal disease which presents as cyclic epizootics.

hemolytic anemia was considered, it has not been proven. -  Free-ranging California sea lions have a marked predisposition to infection with severe renal disease which presents as cyclic epizootics. Infection has been identified in other pinnipeds, but not in cetaceans, and a recent case cluster of sea otters was documented with clinical renal disease. Causative organism: Leptospira spp. (250 + serovars) are spirochete bacteria which share a common lipopolysaccharide (LPS) antigen but differ by surface agglutinating antibodies that allows classification with a current move towards sequencing rather than serotyping. Currently, some of the most common pathogenic leptospiral serovars for US mammals are identified as (L. kircshneri) Grippotyphosa, L. borgpetersenii (Hardjo) and Ballum, and (L. interrogans) Pomona, Bratislava, Icterohaemorrhagiae, and Autumnalis. There is a move away from serotyping to sequence types. Zoonotic potential: Infectious to people from animals; though generally comes from a common point source (i.e., rodents, contaminated water) when both human and non-host-adapted animal are involved.

Zoonotic potential: Infectious to people from animals; though generally comes from a common point source (i.e., rodents, contaminated water) when both human and non-host-adapted animal are involved. Distribution: Considered as the zoonoses with the most worldwide distribution and re-emerging; moist environments most conducive, especially prevalent in tropical countries; occupational and leisure activity risk factors; autumn seasonality observed. Incubation period: usually 7-14 days, up to 21 days.

-  Endothelial cell damage contributes to pathology and clinical signs. Initial signs are nonspecific, and many infected animals do not become clinically, or severely, ill. The first signs in humans are mild to moderate flu-like signs with fever, anorexia, malaise and fatigue. Other clinical signs are much more severe and related to systemic infection with signs of acute kidney injury. Concurrent azotemia (elevated BUN, creatine, and SDMA with or without hyperphosphatemia) may be accompanied by evidence of hemorrhage due to vasculitis or coagulopathy. Some infected animals (10-20%) develop a cholestatic hepatopathy with icterus, increased activity of serum liver enzymes, and hyperbilirubinemia. Abortion may occur in pregnant animals. -  As specific taxon focus, equids tend to present with recurrent uveitis rather than renal or hepatic disease; however, reports of acute pulmonary distress resulting from leptospirosis has been reported in foals. Recurrent uveitis is associated with biofilm formation in the eye. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: These findings are specific to the body system infected and presenting clinical signs at time of illness.

Usually, it is evidence of acute kidney injury. Acute hepatitis or chronic hepatic disease is observed in those animals which had icterus. Scarring ("white spots") in the kidneys of suids and canids has been observed macroscopically in chronic cases.

-  Can be challenging, and treatment generally must begin before diagnosis is conclusive. Combination of test samples (e.g., urine, whole blood, and serum) and modalities is recommended. -  Serum: - o The gold standard is microscopic agglutination testing (MAT), but it cannot differentiate between vaccine and natural antibody production. A positive status is assigned to a test result >1:100 in an unvaccinated animal, but this low seroconversion requires a four-fold rise in titer over 2-4 weeks for diagnostic support. In a clinically ill animal with consistent clinical signs, a single serologic status of 1:800 or above is strongly suggestive of leptospirosis. Serovar cross-reactivity is common, so the serovar with the highest titer is the most likely causative agent. Seronegative results do not discount infection. - o New canine specific tests include indirect ELISA and commercial lateral flow assays that are IgM-specific or detect both IgG and IgM. A point-of-care IgM assay on serum (IDEXX SNAP Lepto Test) has been developed.

tests include indirect ELISA and commercial lateral flow assays that are IgM-specific or detect both IgG and IgM. A point-of-care IgM assay on serum (IDEXX SNAP Lepto Test) has been developed. -  Urine: - o direct observation with (silver or fluorescent antibodies (FA)) or without (darkfield microscopy) stain enhancement has been reported as useful, leptospires must be present in sufficient numbers. - o PCR of urine detects specific gene unique to pathogenic serovars. - o Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) are reported in development.

-  Serum, and urine are the most common samples. Whole blood and serum can be submitted for PCR or whole blood for culture. Of note, whole blood collected in EDTA is acceptable for culture and PCR, but is less sensitive than whole blood collected in sodium heparin although this anticoagulant inhibits molecular detection. -  Post-mortem tissues - ideally kidney - can be submitted for histology using special silver stains, culture, PCR, or FA. Due to the fastidious nature of Leptospira, cultures are often unrewarding, so additional diagnostic methodologies are recommended.

-  Pest control and exclusion of other carriers from contact with collection animals can be important. -  Killed whole cell bacterins vaccines are available for domestic pigs, cattle, and dogs, but they are serovar specific and circulating serovars can vary regionally. Therefore, vaccine choice may be most appropriate for outbreak control or in areas with high risk of exposure. Serologic testing can be monitored in these situations and during transfers between facilities. -  Once an animal is confirmed infected, - o prompt treatment will minimize or may eliminate shedding. - o In the treatment interval, appropriate staff PPE and personal hygiene is to be utilized. - o Consideration of drainage of the area should be made in this control measure. - o If the situation were to occur in a contact program area, it is recommended to exclude guests until the situation is treated, and leptospiruria is confirmed resolved. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Any standard disinfectant technique would be appropriate for cleaning of this organism. Large volumes of infected urine should be treated 1:1 with 10% bleach.

disinfectant for housing facilities: Any standard disinfectant technique would be appropriate for cleaning of this organism. Large volumes of infected urine should be treated 1:1 with 10% bleach. Notification: In the US, Hawaii is the only state currently maintaining this disease as reportable in animals (2023). Centers for Disease Control and local health authorities should be alerted for human cases, especially clusters. USDA apprises WHO of leptospirosis issues in certain production species. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Infected animals should be maintained as isolated as possible from other mammals until treatment interval is completed. PCR testing on urine would be helpful to confirm that the infected animal was no longer shedding. Serologic monitoring of co-housed or adjacently housed animals would be considered prudent. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Serologic monitoring of adjacent areas would be considered prudent following return of infected animal to collection to assess for exposure.

Over 11 serotypes.) Zoonotic potential: Zoonotic potential exists when handling aborted tissues or removing infected brain during necropsy. Food-borne illness most common and at-risk groups are pregnant, elderly, and immune-compromised people. CDC delineates intestinal (acute) and invasive illness (starting within 2 weeks after eating contaminated food). Distribution: Worldwide, more frequent in temperate and colder climates Incubation period: Approximately 10 days - 3 weeks, but clinical signs have been within 5 hours of exposure in poultry. but clinical signs have been within 5 hours of exposure in poultry. Clinical signs: Several forms are possible: -  Encephalitic form (adult ruminants, occasionally pigs): a.k.a. "Circling Disease". Early signs of depression, anorexia, disorientation, decreased milk production, fever which can progress to seizures, unilateral trigeminal and facial nerve paralysis, circling, cerebellar signs [ear droop, deviated muzzle, flaccid lip, lowered eyelid on affected side(s)], salivation, deviated muzzle, flaccid lip, and death. -  Encephalitic form (poultry): ataxia, lateral recumbency with leg paddling, twisting and backward retraction of neck, paralysis. -  Abortion (all species, especially ruminants): fever, hypo- to anorexia, late-term abortions & stillbirths. Retained placentas with secondary metritis. -  Septicemic form (typically neonates and monogastrics): diarrhea, focal hepatic necrosis, death. -  Septicemic form (poultry, rare): lethargy, depressed mentation, diarrhea, death.

-  Encephalitic form: few gross lesions (some congestion of meninges), histologic lesions consistent with encephalitis or meningoencephalitis with micro-abscessation and organisms present (predilection for pons, medulla oblongata, brain stem and cranial spinal cord). -  Septicemic form: evidence of sepsis, miliary hepatic necrosis, frequently marked hemorrhagic gastroenteritis -  Septicemic form (poultry): myocardial inflammation and necrosis, hepatic necrosis, splenomegaly -  Abortion form: third trimester abortion common, gross lesions are placentitis (most severe lesion), metritis, and subtle fetal infection. Histologic lesions are suppurative and necrotizing placentitis and small necrotic foci in any fetal organ, especially liver, with fetal necrotizing colitis not common but very supportive of listeriosis. Gram-stain and culture of abomasal contents may be positive for bacteria. Maceration of the fetus can occur with retained abortions. The herd and dam generally do not present with the encephalitic or septicemic forms concurrent with the abortion form.

-  Pre-mortem: Clinical signs, lumbosacral CSF tap for cytology and culture. CSF will have increased protein concentration (0.6-2.0g/L) with mild pleocytosis composed of large mononuclear cells. IFA and PCR testing specific for Listeria monocytogenes are available. - o Aborted placenta and fetus are specimens of choice, dam usually non-clinical. - o Serology not routinely done due to low specificity. -  Post-mortem: culture of affected tissues* (very suggestive if grows at 4°C from brain tissue), IFA affected tissues*, gram-stain (gram-positive pleomorphic bacteria, not always diphtheroid coccobacillus), immunohistochemistry of brain tissues. - o *Affected tissues include brain (pons & medulla), nasal discharge, placenta & associated fluids, abortus, urine, feces. Milk, meat, silage, and other sources can also be cultured - o Primary bacteria isolation enhanced under microaerophilic conditions. -  DDx: Trichomoniasis, pregnancy toxemia (ewes)*, ketosis (cattle)*, BSE, histophilosis, polioencephalomalacia, sporadic bovine encephalitis, lead poisoning, rabies, brain abscess (cestode).

-  DDx: Trichomoniasis, pregnancy toxemia (ewes)*, ketosis (cattle)*, BSE, histophilosis, polioencephalomalacia, sporadic bovine encephalitis, lead poisoning, rabies, brain abscess (cestode). - o *Facial and ear paralysis are absent -  DDX encephalitic form in poultry: Marek disease, Newcastle disease (neuro signs usually followed by high flock mortality, lesions in visceral organs) Material required for laboratory analysis: Aborted fetuses and placentas; brain (pons & medulla oblongata), CSF, milk, and feces. Cold enrichment method for culture may be necessary. Wear gloves and protective clothing when handling tissues. Relevant diagnostic laboratories: As the diagnosis is mostly post-mortem, all diagnostic labs should be able to perform testing. Remember to request cold enrichment method* if initial culture results do not correspond to clinical presentation. *may take 3 months to get results Treatment: Dependent on prompt diagnosis at early stage of disease as death can occur within 24-48 hours of onset of clinical signs. High doses of penicillin(first choice), oxytetracycline, ceftiofur, erythromycin (not in dairy cattle), trimethoprim/sulfonamide.

-  Good hygiene standards should be maintained, including rodent, wildlife, and insect control. -  Reduce fecal contamination of feed and monitor sewage contamination. Discard spoiled feed and hay. Improve sanitation of pens, water supply, pasture, food refrigerators, and housing facilities. Limit access of wild birds (as possible vector for bacteria) if possible. -  Isolate aborting females. -  Pasteurization of milk for human consumption or bottle feeding, but may not be 100% effective. -  Listeria vaccine developed for oncology patients. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Susceptible to many common disinfectants (sodium hypochlorite, povidone iodine, chlorhexidine, 70% ethanol, glutaraldehyde +/- quaternary ammonium). Good hygiene standards should be maintained. Heat and autoclaving also kills organism. Notification: Reportable to local health authorities upon disease confirmation - see specifics for each state. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None defined. Most measures are currently for prevention of Listeria introduction into the human food supply.

specifics for each state. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None defined. Most measures are currently for prevention of Listeria introduction into the human food supply. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Organism can be shed intermittently in milk (without signs of mastitis), feces, and vaginal secretions for >1 month but no recommended measures for reintroduction. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Segregate affected animals, remove affected silage or feed. Disease may continue to be sporadic as is found in the soils. Non-tuberculous mycobacteria - Mycobacterium avium, M. intracellulare, M. marinum, M. fortuitum, M. chelonae, M. porcinum, M. farcinogenes, M. smegmatis, M. scrofulaceum, M. xenopi, M. kansasii, M. simiae, M. genavense, and others Slender, nonmotile, acid-fast bacilli that are classified as slow growing or rapidly growing. Zoonotic potential: Yes. Many of these bacteria species may infect people who have a genetic predisposition or diminished immune function. Typically, they are not transmitted between humans or between animals and humans. Most infections are acquired from environmental sources, but infection may result secondary to abrasions, cuts, or similar disruption to surfaces.

-  Ubiquitous worldwide -  In zoo or aquarium environments, habitats can develop higher mycobacterial loads if positive animals have been shedding in these confined spaces over a period of time, increasing risk to non-infected animals housed in the same environment. Incubation period: Typically, two weeks to greater than 2 months, however the Runyon Group IV (M. chelonae, fortuitum, smegmatis) are rapid growing and need less than 7 days for incubation.

-  Variable clinical signs are observed which depend on species infected and site of infection. -  Asymptomatic to acute death presentations are possible. -  Other signs include: lethargy, emaciation, and other non-specific signs of illness; non-healing ulcers, abscesses, and granulomas; enlarged abdomen and ascites; cough, dyspnea, pneumonia; mastitis; lymphadenopathy; and lameness due to bone infections (particularly amphibians).

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: -  Gross: Granulomas in multiple organs, cutaneous ulcers and/or abscesses, ascites, pneumonia, mastitis, lymphadenitis, osteomyelitis, tenosynovitis, arthritis -  Histologic: Granulomatous inflammation, with macrophages often presented as an epithelioid appearance, and/or acid-fast positive bacilli

-  Cytology or histopathology: acid-fast bacilli can be demonstrated -  Culture: may take up to eight weeks -  Polymerase chain reaction (PCR): direct testing of specimens as well as speciation of cultured organisms. Allows identification of resistance markers to help guide antimicrobial therapy.

-  Due to possibility for development of antibiotic resistance, ongoing amplification of mycobacterial organisms and contamination of the environment, risk to other animals housed in environments with high mycobacterial loads, and safety concerns for personnel in close contact with affected animals, treatment may not be recommended. -  Treatment when attempted should be based on antimicrobial susceptibility testing but empirical treatment options include: aminoglycosides, quinolones, and macrolides in combination for multimodal therapy. Consider consultation with NVSL on current recommendations for therapy of cultured strain prior to implementing empirical treatment to reduce risk of antibiotic resistance. -  Radical surgical excision of cutaneous lesions in conjunction with long-term antibiotic therapy has been described.

-  Once diagnosed, excellent sanitation measures and permanent quarantine of known positive animals should be implemented. -  Increased diagnostic screening in species with known high susceptibility including but not limited to: tree kangaroos (Dendrolagus spp.), whistling ducks (Dendrocygna spp.), African clawed frogs (Xenopus spp), sea horses and sea dragons (Syngnathidae family). -  Appropriate wound care and prevention of wound contact with potentially contaminated water, soil, and feed will minimize these infections. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: EPA-listed Tuberculocidal products. *Organisms in biofilms will be more resistant to disinfectant - mechanical removal of the biofilm is required to remove organisms. Notification: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria are not federally reportable. Some states may require reporting. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None required

secao: Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak:
texto: -  Due to ubiquitous nature of the etiologic agents, chronic profile, and inability to diagnose - carrier state, disease-free status is not possible. -  For environments with a high incidence of disease, remediation after removing known positive animals can help limit transmission cycle and reduce risk. For aquatic systems, this may involve replacing all pipes/life support elements that have a biofilm harboring organisms, and for terrestrial environments replacement of soil/substrate may be required.

- Birds, with the orders Anseriformes, Gruiformes, and Galliformes most commonly affected groups; although multiple other taxa including Sphenisciformes are susceptible as well. - Some mammals, such as pigs, mink, tapir, and rabbits. Causative organism: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) or Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare complex (MAIC) describe a suite of mycobacterial species, subspecies, and serotypes that share several growth characteristics and species-specific antigens. M. genavense can also cause disease in birds. Zoonotic potential: Yes; there is potential, however humans appear to be highly resistant unless immune compromised. Distribution: Worldwide. However, in North America the distribution favors the North Temperate Zone. Incubation period: There is not a definitive incubation period because the resultant disease is dependent upon immune response to exposure. Exposure does not guarantee disease, and immunocompromised or stressed animals are more at risk. Typically, an animal suffering from disease caused by Mycobacteria may have had the disease for many years before signs are recognized or it is an incidental finding on necropsy.

are more at risk. Typically, an animal suffering from disease caused by Mycobacteria may have had the disease for many years before signs are recognized or it is an incidental finding on necropsy. Clinical signs: Emaciation, weakness, lethargy, hepatosplenomegaly, difficulty breathing, coughing. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Emaciated carcasses, hepatosplenomegaly, nodular disease in affected organs. Nodules are typically white to yellow and solid to soft or crumbly in consistency. Liver, spleen, lung and intestines are most affected but joints, skin, and respiratory tract may also show lesions.

- Elevated white blood cell counts >60,000 can be an indicator of mycobacteriosis. - Computed tomography (CT) is an effective antemortem screening tool to identify the tubercule-type granulomas but is less useful for plaque-like lesions. Antemortem screening can also be performed via coelomoscopic examination focusing on the liver, spleen and intestines. Biopsy or aspirate any plaque-like lesions or granulomas. A general biopsy of the liver may also be helpful. Gastric lavage or bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) can be utilized to screen for respiratory disease. - Acid fast positive organisms in lesions on histopathology or cytology (touch prep of lesions or FNA) are suggestive of infection, but this is not a definitive test since other organisms can be acid fast positive. Historically, acid fast staining of the feces was utilized as a routine screening test, though it should be noted this is unlikely to detect organisms unless samples contain more than 10,000 organisms/mL (i.e. only in cases of advanced gastrointestinal tract shedding). Active shedding of organisms may only occur in later stages of the disease, and may be intermittent in nature.

10,000 organisms/mL (i.e. only in cases of advanced gastrointestinal tract shedding). Active shedding of organisms may only occur in later stages of the disease, and may be intermittent in nature. - Confirmatory diagnosis is attained through a combination of microbiological and molecular diagnostic methods. - o Culture is the gold standard, though time consuming. - o PCR assays detect the actual disease-causing organism and can be performed on organisms isolated through culture or other directly from clinical samples depending on the lab and assay. PCR on fecal samples or cloacal swabs may be of limited value due to unreliable organism shedding, environmental contamination, and PCR fecal inhibitors. - Tuberculin testing is not recommended. - ELISA assays detect specific antibodies for M. avium in serum and help determine exposure.

- PCR or Culture of fresh/frozen tissue samples, tissues with lesions imbedded in paraffin blocks (PCR only), gastric lavage or BAL samples, or other clinical samples depending on the lab and assay. - Acid Fast staining of slides from a suspect nodule, feces or touch prep of affected tissues; formalinized tissue for histopathology examination. - Post mortem sampling includes liver, spleen and lungs and/or suspect areas.

- Try to maintain a clean environment and be diligent in screening via quarantine, necropsy and testing. - Design habitats that do not encourage the accumulation of Mycobacteria in the environment (e.g. avoid chronically wet soil such as at soil-water interfaces; limit use of acidic soils; scrub pool surfaces to disrupt biofilms when cleaning; prevent contact with wild birds; avoid aerosolization of water droplets from fountains, hose spraying, or waterfalls). - Remove animals from the environment that are known to be positive. - Limit stress in susceptible species (e.g. reduce number of moves between enclosures, avoid overcrowding, choose social situation that reduce aggression)

It is also effective against a glutaraldehyde resistant M. chelonae but at a concentration of 5000 ppm for 15 minutes, or at 2500 ppm for 60 minutes. Note that this product may not be available in the US. Notification: None. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: If an animal is known to be infected, euthanasia may need to be considered. It is not recommended to mix a known infected animal with a healthy animal unless the risk for infection is considered acceptable. Studies show that there is an increased incidence of disease when an animal is housed with a known positive. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: As this bacterium is ubiquitous, this condition is unachievable.

Efforts should be concentrated on decreasing the environmental load of this bacterium, and reducing stress or otherwise enhancing the immune response for those living in the contaminated environment through good nutrition and proper husbandry. Screening of all deaths for mycobacteria, having sentinel animals in the enclosure, and periodic liver biopsies have all been done.

Miliary patterns of granulomas may be present in some species. Primarily affected organs are lungs and lymphoid system, especially retropharyngeal and tracheobronchial lymph nodes. Many other Mycoplasma spp. exist and new ones are being identified in connection with disease syndromes in mammals, birds, and reptiles. Mycoplasma mycoides cluster - sheep, goats, cattle, others. M. bovis - bison and bovids. Some Mycoplasma spp. may be minimally or non-pathogenic (e.g. M. iguana and M. insons in iguanas). Causative organism: Mycoplasma spp. are bacteria with no cell wall and complex growth requirements making traditional culture mediated isolation difficult. Many of the organisms associated with disease have not been fully characterized because identification has been by molecular methods. Mycoplasma mycoides cluster organisms cause contagious bovine pleuropneumonia, contagious agalactia of sheep and goats, and contagious caprine pleuropneumonia and are considered foreign animal diseases in the United States. M. agalactiae is the major cause of contagious agalactia of sheep and goats, but has only been reported sporadically in the United States.

M. agalactiae is the major cause of contagious agalactia of sheep and goats, but has only been reported sporadically in the United States. Within a Mycoplasma species, some strains may vary in pathogenicity as well as in the clinical syndrome that develops. For example, some strains M. bovis are linked to calf pneumonia while others will generally cause mastitis. A subcategory of mycoplasmas is the hemoplasmas, obligate red blood cell pathogens such as Mycoplasma ovis in sheep, M. suis in swine, and novel species in raccoons. Disease caused by hemoplasmas is not considered to be mycoplasmosis. Note: name changes are being considered for many organisms in the genus. Some species may be classified as Mesomycoplasma, Mycoplasmopsis, or Metamycoplasma. Zoonotic potential: Marine mammal workers have acquired skin infections suspected to be Mycoplasma spp. Humans have their own complement of Mycoplasma pathogens and many of those may infect non-human primates. Distribution: Worldwide, often host species specific. Incubation period: 2 to 4 weeks, possibly longer.

texto: - ∞ Generally, mycoplasmas cause one or more of three clinical syndromes: - o Lymphocytic pneumonia where secondary infection with additional bacteria is common (members of the Pasteurellaceae for example) - o Polyarthritis - o Mastitis - o Additionally, otitis media and conjunctivitis may occur with some species - ∞ Species propensities include: - o In bighorn sheep and mountain goats, signs typically consist of coughing, respiratory distress, otitis, sinusitis, loss of body condition; death is possible in all age classes on first exposure, death in neonates and weanlings in subsequent years, population declines, and poor recruitment. Conjunctivitis occurs with some Mycoplasma spp. - o In birds the predominant sign is mild to severe conjunctivitis; death in some cases. - o In tortoises the predominant signs are nasal discharge (clear to mucopurulent), conjunctivitis, edema of the eyelids, infection often becomes chronic, and may end in death. A fatal multisystemic disease attributed to M. alligatoris has been identified in American alligators and related caimans. - o Additional species (black vultures, skunks, crocodiles) signs consist of polyarthritis, and stomatitis.

Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Mycoplasmas are susceptible to most commonly used disinfectants, including Virkon S, quaternary ammonium compounds, or household bleach (1:20 in water). They can be circular or bar shape, which aggregate and form pinion teeth on the surface of red blood cells. -  Mycoplasma haemofelis (formerly Hemobartonella felis and Eperythrozoon felis). Additionally, tachycardia, anemia, decreased hemoglobin, slight to moderate icterus, vomiting, and splenomegaly may be seen. -  PCR is the most reliable diagnostic test as Mycoplasma spp. cannot grow in culture media. -  Blood smear (from fresh uncoagulated sample) evaluation by direct microscopy should be done before starting treatment. These smears should be examined daily for 5-7 days since parasitemia is cyclic. Parasites are found on the surface of the erythrocyte (extracellular) or free in the smear. It is recommended to use Giemsa, Wright-Giemsa, May-GruenwaldGiemsa, or Wright-Leishman stains to be able to differentiate this organism from stain precipitate, refractile artifacts, and Cytauxzoon; the latter is intracellular, normally found in the center and occurring singly. -  Direct Coombs' test may be positive in some species during the acute phase. Material required for laboratory analysis: Microscope, blood smear slide, and stain. Blood in EDTA and standard blood shipment supplies to submit for PCR. Relevant Diagnostic lab: Most commercial veterinary laboratories can examine blood smears and submit a sample for PCR testing.

-  Tetracyclines & fluoroquinolones. In one study, infected, domestic cats were treated with doxycycline (5mg/kg q 12h orally) for 28 days, and those that remained positive (PCR testing) were then treated with marbofloxacin (2mg/kg q24h orally) for 14 days. All cats remained negative after marbofloxacin treatment. Therefore, the recommendation is 28 days of doxycycline treatment and if the agent persists, treat secondarily with marbofloxacin. -  If severe anemia is present, consider glucocorticoid treatment, e.g. prednisolone. Prevention and control: Prevent and eliminate arthropod vectors (flea and tick control). Blood for transfusion should be PCR tested. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Standard cleaning and disinfection if areas contaminated with blood. Notification: Currently none.
