-  Capillarids of many genera (e.g., Capillaria, Eucleus, Calodium, Pearsonema) occur in mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish. -  Trichuris spp. occurs in mammals, primates, ruminants, carnivores, suids, and rodents. Zoonotic potential: Yes, some species of Trichuris, Capillaria hepatica and C. philippinensis. Distribution: Worldwide, although parasites of concern will vary by location and species. Incubation period: Variable but tends to be longer than many other parasites. Prepatent period is three months in many intestinal Trichuris. Clinical signs: Clinical cases and fatal disease are rare. Many low parasite burdens can be asymptomatic, and infections are frequently asymptomatic in hoofed stock. In clinical animals, weight loss, colitis, diarrhea, hematochezia, or melena can be present. Capillaria tend to infect airways, nasal cavity, or the urinary bladder such as air sacculitis or pneumonia from Eucolies spp. Or Pearsonema spp. In the urinary system. Capillaria hepaticum causes hepatic cirrhosis and C philippenensis is found in the tissues of fish, causing an intestinal infection when affected raw fish are consumed.

Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Trichuris spp. can be observed embedded in the wall of the colon of carnivores and ungulates and found in the neutral pH forestomach of some leaf-eating monkeys (e.g., Colobus). Capillaria hepatica induces cirrhosis of the liver. It is usually identified on post mortem. Other capillarids can cause nasal, bronchial, intestinal, hepatic, and urinary infections, and findings will vary according to parasitic and host species and site of parasitism. Diagnosis: Centrifugation fecal floatation can be performed for identification of infection. However. The eggs (bipolar plugs) are very dense and require correct floatation solution - good choice is Sheather's with specific gravity of 1.27 - and centrifugation to recover them. Eggs are shed intermittently, so repeated fecals may be necessary. For pulmonary species, BAL, and for urinary tract infections, urine sedimentation.

Ova of different capillarids that infect the same host (e.g., carnivores) can be distinguished by structure of patterns of egg case. Biopsies of affected areas - gastrointestinal tract or liver - can be used. Material required for laboratory analysis: Fecal sample, colon or gastric biopsy, hepatic biopsy, BAL. Relevant Diagnostic lab: These diagnostics are readily available, as in-house fecal floatation or any laboratory performing fecal exams or histopathology. Treatment: Fenbendazole and other benzimidazoles, milbemycin oxime, and pyrantel pamoate can be used. Variable sensitivity to ivermectin has been noted. Due to its long prepatent period, it is appropriate to treat monthly for 3 treatments. Prevention and control: Quarantine measure and treatment before introduction is best. Chronic treatment may be required. Environmental control and preventing recontamination are critical.

Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Eggs are very resistant to destruction and may remain infective in the soil for long periods of time. Remove fecal material promptly from enclosures. Dirt floored enclosures are almost impossible to disinfect. Dig out dirt or use fire to sterilize. Notification: None. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Many facilities manage chronically infected groups with varying levels of problems. Many use chronic anthelmintic treatment. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Treat for a minimum of 3-4 months. Clear animals while held in cement floored facility before introducing to a clean group in a clean environment. Continue long term monthly fecal screening and environmental sanitation.

- ∞ DH: No clinical signs. - ∞ Larval metacestode infections of IH/AH are initially subclinical and signs may not develop during the host's life span. - ∞ Clinical signs are related to metacestode location, which is most often the liver and lungs. As metacestodes develop, signs may include lethargy, abdominal pain, abdominal enlargement (due to hepatomegaly or mega cysts), inappetence, and respiratory signs. Hepatic signs include cholangitis, biliary obstruction, jaundice, and weight loss. Cyst rupture lead to peritonitis and death. - ∞ EM is most likely to cause disease; metacestode growth can be very rapid and lethal within few months in rodents or have a long asymptomatic period (5-15 yrs) in humans and great apes.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: - ∞ DH: Adult cestodes (body length: 1.2 - 11 mm) are found in the small intestine of DH with EG (and relatives) primarily in the upper third and EM in the middle third. - ∞ IH/AH: In cystic echinococcosis, the formation of fluid-filled cysts is primarily in hepatic and pulmonary tissues, but can occur in any other organ. In alveolar echinococcosis, primary location is almost exclusively hepatic. EG, EE, EOr, EC, EF and EOl are usually associated with a single cyst. Similar to a metastasizing neoplasm, EM and EV form masses of small cysts. Viable protoscoleces may be present within cysts. Diffuse polyserositis.

- Antemortem: Imaging may be used to identify and classify fluid-filled cysts in IH/AH (see Table 2.5, Eckert et al. 2001) along with a cytologic exam of FNA. Fecal diagnosis in DH is difficult due to the small size of gravid proglottids (1-2mm) and inability to differentiate from eggs of Taenia species. Fecal coproantigen ELISA and confirmatory Echinococcus PCRs have been developed for DH. Serum antibody ELISAs (Em2+ antigen) have been developed but Taenia false positives may occur and species validation is limited. Immunoblotting (as used in human - serology) also yields high diagnostic sensitivity and specificity for AE in primates. Percutaneous drainage of cysts may reveal the presence of protoscoleces. Minimally invasive surgical techniques in combination with ultrasound provide real time screening as a field technique (Campbell-Palmer et al. 2015) - Postmortem: Fluid-filled cysts may be seen at necropsy (primarily hepatic and pulmonary). In IH/AH, histopathology may reveal the presence of protoscoleces within brood-capsules or in hydatid sand. In DH, the scraping, filtration and counting technique can be used to extract cestodes from the intestines.

Genotyping by PCR by mitochondrial DNA sequences. Material required for laboratory analysis: metacestode tissue (protoscoleces), serum (IH/AH); feces, small intestine (DH); FNA (or biopsies) for PCR analysis. Treatment: In humans, treatment options for cystic echinococcosis include surgical removal of cysts and ultrasound-guided partial removal of cyst fluid and injection of a parasiticidal agent (PAIR - puncture, aspiration, injection, re-aspiration). Alternatively, anthelmintics (benzimidazoles, preferred albendazole) can be used for IH/AHs treatments variate from 10-24 months, life-long with alveolar echinococcosis. Degenerating cysts may not require treatment and monitoring would be an option. Prevention and control: Infective material (eggs in feces) can be decontaminated by extreme temperatures (70°C for 12 hrs.; -80°C for 48 hrs.). Metacestodes in infected organs of IHs are susceptible to ordinary freezing and boiling.

material (eggs in feces) can be decontaminated by extreme temperatures (70°C for 12 hrs.; -80°C for 48 hrs.). Metacestodes in infected organs of IHs are susceptible to ordinary freezing and boiling. When handling infective material, personal protective equipment should be worn to reduce the risk of human exposure. Ensure the DH's diet does not include potentially infected organs and carcasses. Prevent scavenging and predation by susceptible mammals. Decontaminate foliage or branches used for environmental enrichment. Fresh outdoor produce (vegetables) from EM endemic areas can be problematic for potential IH/AH. Pet and feral dog population management and deworming. Education of animal care workers, dog owners and other at-risk human populations. Anthelmintic baiting of foxes (50mg praziquantel/bait). EG95 vaccine has been shown to be protective against EG in sheep, goats, cattle and tammar wallabies. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Chemical disinfection is unreliable but 3.75% bleach (NaOCl) solution for 1 hr. (metal surface) or 2-3 hrs. (concrete) may be effective for EM. Notification: OIE reportable disease and USDA should be notified.

- ∞ Order Oxyurida; Superfamily Oxyuroidea; Family Oxyuridae. - o Enterobius sp. infect humans, great apes, & Old World monkeys. - o Trypanoxyuris sp. & Oxyuronema sp. infect New World monkeys. - o Lemuricola sp. infect Strepsirrhini primates (lemurs, lorises, pottos, and galagos). - o Skrjabinema sp. infect sheep, goats, & wild ruminants. - o Oxyuris equi infects equids, and O. karamoja infects African rhinoceroses and elephants. - o Passalurus ambiguus is common in the colon and cecum of lagomorphs. - o Syphacia sp., Aspiculuris sp., and Dentostomella sp. infect laboratory rodents, although no oxyurid is described in guinea pigs. - ∞ Multiple oxyurid (family Pharyngodonidae) have been described in herbivorous & omnivorous reptiles, as well as larval anurans. - ∞ Oxyurids can also infect fish & invertebrates, +/- birds (may be seen as pseudoparasites in some sp.). Zoonotic potential: Yes, but limited. Distribution: The order Oxyurida (pinworms) inhabits the posterior gut of vertebrates and some arthropods. Oxyurid host diversity is unique, as no other nematode groups have parasitized both vertebrates and invertebrates to the same degree.

- ∞ Enterobius sp.: prepatent period 30-60 days. - ∞ Oxyuris sp.: pre-patent period of ~5 months. - ∞ Passalarus ambiguus: prepatent period 56-64 days. - ∞ Syphacia sp.: prepatent period of 8-15 days. - ∞ Aspiculuris sp.: prepatent period 21-25 days. - ∞ Pharyngodonidae sp.: pre-patent periods highly variable, often undetermined. Clinical signs: Pinworms feed on bacteria in the hindgut or cecum, rather than feeding on host tissue. Therefore, effects on hosts are low with minimal-no pathogenicity. Main clinical signs are pruritus of the perianal region, irritability, and rarely intestinal impaction in reptiles with high parasite burdens. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Parasites are most commonly an incidental finding on routine fecal ova and parasite examination, but rarely do they occur in large enough numbers to cause noticeable gross pathology. Occasional reports of infections in lizards and turtles severe enough to cause intestinal impaction. Hemorrhagic enteritis has been reported in Ateles spp. infected with Oxyuronema atelophorum.

- ∞ Routine fecal O&P examination (both direct & floatation). "Scotch tape preparation" from anus/perineum, and anal swabs. PCR amplified DNA has recently been demonstrated to be more sensitive than fecal O&P examination in some species. - ∞ Gold Standard: Examination of cecal and colonic contents at necropsy. Material required for laboratory analysis: Egg masses from perineum or from fecal examination or worms and eggs recovered from cecal or colonic contents at necropsy. Relevant Diagnostic lab: Any laboratory equipped with light microscopy and basic supplies for fecal O&P examination can detect oxyurids. PCR capabilities are a useful adjunct.

- ∞ Benzimidazoles (fenbendazole, oxfendazole, etc.,) & pyrantel are the primary treatment options. - o Fenbendazole medicated feed is commonly used for laboratory rodents. - o A single dose of oxfendazole was as effective as multiple doses of fenbendazole in green iguanas. - ∞ Topical emodepside + pyrantel (Profender®) was successful in captive tortoises. - ∞ Avermectins (Ivermectin, etc.,) are often used, though may have decreased efficacy especially as a sole agent. Prevention and control: Detection on routine fecal ova and parasite examinations, and on scotchtape preparations on symptomatic individuals, and follow-up treatment on infected individuals should allow for control of the organisms. Good hygiene of enclosures should help to prevent re-infection. Eggs have been shown to be present on laboratory workers hands as well as in the dust found around cages, on air vents, and in animal room ventilation systems (the eggs are small enough to become airborne). Filter-top cages or individually ventilated cages, therefore, may be useful to prevent airborne transmission in laboratory rodent facilities.

Strict sanitation and hygienic measures should be adequate to prevent zoonotic transmission of Enterobius spp. between apes and man. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Eggs may be resistant to routine disinfectants. Heat disinfection of cages and cleaning implements (100 o C = 212 o F) is effective in killing eggs. Ethylene oxide gas, formaldehyde vapors, and 75 mg/L chlorine dioxide have also been recommended. Mechanical removal by washing/laundering fabric, washing and scrubbing of enclosures, vacuuming, and heat disinfection, where possible, is recommended. Notification: This disease is not ordinarily reportable. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: Currently none. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Routine anthelminthic treatments.

S. haematobium infects humans, and hybridizes with S. bovis to infect cattle. Although S. mansoni can infect rodents and non-human primates, humans are believed to be its primary mammalian reservoir. Causative organism: Schistosoma japonicum, S. mansoni, S. haematobium (main species). Zoonotic potential: Yes, via a snail vector. Humans are the most common host for S. mansoni and S. haematobium, but S. japonicum infects many domestic and wild mammals that can serve as reservoirs of the fluke. Old World monkeys, including baboons and vervet monkeys, are hosts for S. mansoni. These host species are commonly found around human settlements and share water sources with humans.

- ∞ S. mansoni: Africa, Arabian Peninsula, South America - ∞ S. japonicum: China, Philippines, Indonesia - ∞ S. haematobium: Africa, Arabian Peninsula. - ∞ S. mekongi: Cambodia and Laos - ∞ S. intercalatum: Central/West Africa - ∞ S. guineensis: West Africa Incubation period: 14-84 days (although signs due to the acute phase of infection may be immediate). Clinical symptoms: S. japonicum and S. mansoni (acute phase): fever, nausea, cough, diarrhea (chronic phase): anemia, bloody diarrhea, gastro-esophageal bleeding, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, cirrhosis, cachexia, ascites, portal hypertension, pulmonary hypertension. S. haematobium: hematuria, dysuria, ureteral obstruction, hydronephrosis, squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Portal and periportal hepatic fibrosis, hepatosplenomegaly, gastroesophageal varices, granulomatous hepatic inflammation, mesenteric lymphadenopathy, colonic ulceration, urinary bladder and ureteral fibrosis, hydronephrosis. Human gnathostomiasis is caused by migrating immature third-stage larvae (L3) after eating raw or inadequately cooked freshwater fish or other intermediate hosts such as snakes, frogs, and chickens causing cutaneous, visceral or ocular larva migrans. However, two alternative routes of infection have been suggested; ingestion of water containing infected copepods (thus taking the place of a second intermediate host) or by penetration of the skin of food handlers by L3 from infected meat. Various species of Thelazia also can affect human eyes and it is transmitted by non-biting flies that feed on lacrimal secretion directly into the eyes. Distribution: Global, more common in warm climates. Incubation period: Variable, typically weeks to months; the life cycle includes an obligate arthropod intermediate host, including house or stable flies, cockroaches, coprophagous beetles, and crickets. Incubation period: Under ideal conditions, the third stage infective larvae develop in a week, but the process is quite temperature dependent. States reporting the highest incidence in 2010 included Minnesota, Wisconsin, New York, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and Connecticut. Norway, UK, Sweden, Switzerland, and Germany have reported infections in ruminants, dogs, and people. Infections in camels in Iran is reported with regional variation. Infections in wild felids have been reported in Brazil and Africa.

-  Group 1 - Clinical signs are highly variable, ranging from subclinical infection in calves under a year to severe peracute disease in adult naïve cattle, characterized by significant production losses (milk or weight gain), bull infertility, severe anemia, icterus, inappetence, dehydration, constipation, dark yellow urine, weight loss, pyrexia, abortion and death. The acute form generally occurs in cattle from 1-3 years old, with similar but more moderate clinical signs. All recovered animals become persistent carriers and reservoirs of infection for life. -  Group 2 - Humans (A. phagocytophilum): Clinical disease is associated with acute parasitemia of which the duration and severity is variable. Co-infection with other pathogens results in greater severity of symptoms. Genetic variants of A. phagocytophilum and be associated with mild or flu-like clinical signs or rash in 10% of patients. The aged and immunosuppressed show more severe signs. These signs include headache, pyrexia, chills, myalgia, nausea, ataxia, organ failure, susceptibility to opportunistic infections, neuritis or respiratory complications.

Hepatic and mediastinal lymph nodes may appear brown and the gall bladder distended with thick brown or green bile. Serous effusions may occur in body cavities, edema, petechial hemorrhages in the epi- and endocardium often accompanied by severe gastrointestinal stasis. During acute rickettsemia, the organism has been demonstrated in the alveolar macrophages, Kupffer cells, and other tissue macrophages. Sites of persistence in-between recurrent rickettsemia remain to be established.

Blood transfusions, electrolyte solutions, and hematinic drugs may be beneficial in later stages of the disease. Convalescent period of up to 3 months. Cattle remain immune for life but become persistent carriers. -  Group 2 - Treatment may be difficult as clinical signs often do not appear until the disease has progressed. Testing for co-infections with other tick-borne organisms is recommended. Tetracycline antibiotics (usually doxycycline in humans and dogs) for 10-14 days (or at least until 3 days after fever subsides). A marked improvement is usually seen in 24-48 hours.

Universal vaccines are not available that are effective for geographically diverse strains for A. marginale or A. phagocytophilum. In California, a modified live vaccine (Anavac®) is available for cattle <11 months but lacks efficacy and is rarely used. -  Identification of regional vectors are important to control zoonotic anaplasmosis. -  Clinical signs are consistent with gastrointestinal irritation and typically are watery mucoid diarrhea. Following ingestion of the cysts, excystation occurs in the small intestine, then the trophozoites colonize the large intestine and cecum. If invasion occurs through the mucosa, extraintestinal disease has been reported, including to the liver, lung, and bone. -  Suids are mostly asymptomatic unless the parasite invades the mucosa, and this only occurs when prior mucosal damage enables its entry. Similarly, cercopithecine monkeys are rarely symptomatic. In great apes, chimpanzees are typically asymptomatic or present mild clinical signs of diarrhea, which may be simply unformed feces. Asymptomatic chimpanzees may recrudesce with diarrhea when stressed by other illnesses. B. coli may compete with commensal protozoa, such that perturbation of the normal gastrointestinal microflora may facilitate infection or recrudescence. In gorillas, ulcerative colitis; severe diarrhea; and potentially, abdominal abscessation or colonic fistulation have been noted. Post-mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Ulcerative colitis with large numbers of characteristic B.

severe diarrhea; and potentially, abdominal abscessation or colonic fistulation have been noted. Post-mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Ulcerative colitis with large numbers of characteristic B. coli organisms in the colonic contents or invading the colonic mucosa. Diagnosis: Direct examination of feces by saline smear allows diagnosis. While flotation can be utilized, cysts are the only form detected routinely by this method, and sedimentation may assist in concentration of the organism. Lugol's iodine staining may assist in identification of the organism. Detection of trophozoites (30-150 µm x 25-120 µm) in diarrhea is most common; this stage is a distinctive ovoid with an elongated end, peripheral short cilia, and containing a large cytostome. This stage also has a distinctive spiraling motility with uniform ciliate beating. The infective cyst form (4565 µm) is usually found in formed feces, is round, and contains the ciliated organism within a transparent double wall. Both forms have a large, kidney-shaped nucleus. At necropsy, scrapings of the colonic and cecal mucosa can be performed for evaluation and staining with H&E.

Material required for laboratory analysis: Feces. Relevant Diagnostic lab: Any diagnostic laboratory with routine parasitologic capabilities should be able to diagnose this infection. The required diagnostic methods, such as fecal flotation, are readily available in-house in any laboratory performing routine fecal exams. Treatment: Antiprotozoals (e.g., tetracyclines, iodoquinol, 5-nitroimidazole compounds (e.g., metronidazole and secnidazole), and paromomycin) are recommended in clinical cases. Symptomatic care during clinical disease may be necessary in severe cases. Starch-rich diets support of the organism's replication and may account for the increased susceptibility of managed as opposed to free-ranging great apes. Prevention and control: Carrier animals should be managed separately from susceptible animals whenever possible. For example, co-housing of cercopithecine monkeys with gorilla should be considered cautiously.

Excellent sanitation should be practiced between carrier animal enclosures and susceptible animals as this parasite has a directly infective life cycle. That said, this approach should include pest control as some roach species have been demonstrated to carry the protozoan within their gastrointestinal tract. Treatment of carrier animals to reduce environmental contamination should be considered. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: B. coli trophozoite cannot survive for in a dry environment, and generally is expected not to survive beyond 48 hours; it is susceptible to acidic environments. Regular removal of feces assists with reduction of environmental contamination. However, cysts can survive outside body for two weeks or more at ambient temperatures and are highly resistant to disinfection. Bleach (sodium hypochlorite) at routine disinfection concentrations is not sufficient to destroy the cyst stage. Notification: None.

In lizards, enteritis is more common (C. varanii is an intestinal parasite). Birds are often diagnosed with either enteritis or respiratory tract infections (often C. meleagridis or C. bayleyi). -  Two morphologic forms of Giardia exist: trophozoites and cysts. The trophozoite, a motile form, is binucleated, pear shaped, and flagellated. Diagnosis of Giardia infection can be - difficult in that cysts are shed intermittently and are delicate, and artifacts (grass pollen, yeast, etc.) mimic to varying degrees the morphology of Giardia cysts. Microscopy of fresh feces may identify motile trophozoites that appear as a face with the two nuclei forming the eyes and median bodies forming the mouth. Mix a drop of fresh liquid feces with a drop of normal saline. Trophozoites are not often found in semi-formed or firm feces. Trophozoites have a concave ventral surface and a rapid "falling leaf" motion which may be the only motion visible may be the flagella. Duodenal fluid aspiration and examination of the sediment for motile trophozoites requires either endoscopy or exploratory laparotomy to obtain duodenal fluid, making this an impractical means of diagnosing Giardia. -  Zinc sulfate fecal by centrifugation is better than zinc sulfate fecal flotation but due to intermittent shedding of cysts, the sensitivity is approximately 70%.

Fecal ELISA tests identify Giardia specific antigens from trophozoites, avoiding the problem of intermittent cyst excretion in the feces. False negative ELISA results are not common; but a negative fecal ELISA does not eliminate the possibility of Giardia infection in an animal with appropriate clinical signs. Positive test results can occur in asymptomatic dogs and cats since some animals may harbor the organisms without having clinical signs. -  IDEXX Laboratories has an in-house, quick SNAP Giardia test that is ELISA-based. Immunofluorescence (IFA) test identifies cysts. In one study, this test was the best single test for detecting subclinical giardiasis. Material required for laboratory analysis: Feces. Treatment: Fenbendazole and metronidazole have been used, although high doses have been associated with neurological dysfunction.

Furazolidone (Furoxone® Suspension, SmithKline Beecham, 4 mg/kg BID for 7 days) is available as a suspension and is convenient to administer to cats and small dogs and has been shown to be effective in cats. Quinacrine (6.6 mg/kg BID For 5 days) has been shown to be 100% effective in dogs. Approximately half of the dogs treated developed minor and reversible anorexia, fever, or lethargy. Quinacrine has been shown to improve clinical signs in cats but not to eliminate infection; however, quinacrine is not currently available in the US. Albendazole is effective in dogs and cats but can lead to bone marrow suppression. Reports of a combination of praziquantel (5.4-7 mg/kg) febantel (26.8-35.2 mg/kg) and pyrantel (26.8-35.2 mg/kg) for 3 days was effective in reducing cyst excretion. -  Domestic and wild canids are the main hosts. Domestic dogs are historically the most important reservoir, but lagomorphs and other rodents have served as reservoirs in outbreaks, while non-human primates have shown reservoir potential experimentally. In Texas and OK, woodrats in the genus Neotoma are the main reservoir. -  Humans are commonly infected. -  Infection is becoming recognized in more mammalian species including domestic and nondomestic carnivores, primates, lagomorphs, and marsupials. Opossums and some rodents are commonly infected, although usually asymptomatic. Causative organism: Protozoal organisms Leishmania donovani (Asia, Middle East, Africa) and L. infantum (Asia, Middle East, Europe, South America). Zoonotic potential: Transmission occurs via sandfly bites; dogs are usually the reservoir host. Humans are accidental hosts and not considered important in the epidemiology of the disease. Dog to human and human to human transmission does not seem to occur. Distribution: Europe, South America, Africa, Middle East, Asia. Dogs in North America are occasionally infected.

-  Humans: Fever, weakness, lethargy, weight loss, muscle wasting, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, pallor; anemia & thrombocytopenia are common. -  Dogs: lymphadenopathy, onychogryphosis, weight loss, conjunctivitis, alopecia. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Inflammation and parasites found in macrophages of infected organs; specific findings vary with parasite and host species, chronicity of disease, and immune status of host. Diagnosis: Gold standard: demonstration of intracytoplasmic parasites (amastigote form) in splenic or bone marrow aspirates. Serologic tests include an IFAT, ELISA (rK39 antigen most promising), DAT, and immunochromagraphic test strip. Cross-reaction with T. cruzi can complicate serologic diagnosis. Numerous blood and bone marrow PCR protocols are also often used. Material required for laboratory analysis: Depends on diagnostic method; could include bone marrow, lymph node, or splenic aspirates or blood.

-  Humans: Liposomal amphotericin B is first choice. Meglumine antimoniate is less expensive but has more adverse effects. Miltefosine is a newer oral drug that has shown good efficacy in India. Paromomycin also may have some efficacy. -  Dogs: Allopurinol, meglumine antimoniate, and liposomal amphotericin B have all been used; a complete cure is usually impossible, and euthanasia is often recommended. Prevention and control: Prevention of vector bites is key - insecticide use (sprays, nets, delamethrinimpregnated collars, and pour-ons). Culling of dogs is not effective based on evidence reviews. Studies show that vectors are differentially attracted to infected dogs. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Control of the disease is based on control of the insect vector. Notification: Not a nationally notifiable disease in the US; it is notifiable in a few states such as Texas. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None.

- ∞ Avian: Plasmodium spp. infections have been reported in the majority of avian orders. Subclinical infections are common in many species, including ratites and flamingos. Species that have been relocated from habitats without malaria, or in areas where the vector or parasite have been introduced are especially vulnerable, e.g. penguins, other captive Arctic or Antarctic species, species from Hawaii or other islands, etc. Among raptors, gyrfalcons and snowy owls are most susceptible to clinical disease. Penguin chicks, juveniles, and naïve adults are at highest risk, and stressors such as molt, chick rearing, or poor husbandry increase mortality. It is possible that some passerine species may be reservoir hosts for virulent hemoparasitic infections in other avian species. Global prevalence in wild birds is estimated to be 16%. - ∞ Reptile: Reptile infections have been documented mainly in tropical countries, primarily in lizards, chelonians, and some snakes, but has not been reported in crocodilians. - ∞ Mammal: Infection of mammals is most common in tropical countries.

Diversity of affected mammals is greatest in Africa, where Plasmodium has been detected in primates, rodents, ungulates and bats. Humans and non-human primates are infected mainly in tropical Africa, Asia and South America. Mosquito-transmitted human malarial cases occur rarely in the southern USA but is not considered endemic. Infection with Plasmodium spp. is common in free-living western gorillas, chimpanzees, orangutans, and gibbons. One report in wild and captive capybaras in South America has been documented. A single fatal case of Plasmodium infection in a wild-caught Leadbeater's possum in Australia has been reported. Causative organism: Plasmodium spp. (Plasmodiidae, Haemosporida) >200 species. P. relictum is the most pathogenic species infecting birds. Zoonotic potential: The species of Plasmodium infecting non-human primates are often identical or closely related to human pathogens, and mosquito-mediated cross-species transmission has been documented.

No zoonotic risk exists from avian or reptilian species. Distribution: Worldwide, except Antarctica due to absence of mosquitoes and low temperature. Incubation period: Plasmodium requires two host species - sporogony occurs in an invertebrate host, and schizogony occurs in avian, mammal, or reptile host erythrocytes or tissue. In birds, peak infection typically occurs 6-12 days after parasites first appear in the blood. Chronic infections may persist throughout a bird's life.

- ∞ Avian: Cases in most adapted avian species are often of low virulence and asymptomatic. Importantly, the same lineages of Plasmodium sp. cause diseases of markedly different severity in different avian hosts, which should be taken in consideration in conservation projects. Susceptible non-adapted avian species (e.g. penguins and some endemic Hawaiian birds) present with lethargy, dyspnea, anorexia, vomiting, ruffled feathers, pale mucous membranes, anemia (hematocrit may fall by more than 50%) and regenerative hemolytic anemia, or may be found dead. Hemolysis and catabolism of hemoglobin leads to production of excess biliverdin, leading to green coloration of feces. Severe infection may induce neurological signs, including motor incoordination, seizures, and partial or total paralysis. Mortality rates in penguins have been documented as high as 50-80% (typically due to infection with P. relictum or P. elongatum). - ∞ Reptile: Infections are often nonpathogenic, but reptiles may present with variable levels of anemia and reduced exercise tolerance. Infections may impact behavior and physiology of some reptile species, including reduced clutch sizes.

Juvenile lizards have presented with acute death. - ∞ Primates: Plasmodium spp. infection in apes is typically subclinical. Gibbons have been reported to experience mild cyclic depression, and confiscated orangutans have shown clinical improvement with antimalarial treatment. Several Plasmodium species have been reported in wild lemurs, but clinical disease has not been described. - ∞ Bats: Infection with Plasmodium spp. in free-ranging bats has been reported, with no reports of associated clinical disease

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: - ∞ Avian: Patients present with hemolysis, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, pulmonary edema, hydropericardium with granulocytic interstitial pneumonia, mononuclear hepatitis, granulocytic splenitis, and myocarditis. Exoerythrocytic meronts can be found in macrophages and endothelial cells, especially of lungs, heart, liver and spleen. Extramedullary - hematopoiesis and hemosiderosis are seen in the liver and spleen, along with deposition of birefringent hemozoin (malarial pigment, digested hemoglobin) granules. - ∞ Reptile: Severe hemolytic anemia. Reduced testicle size of some male lizard species, and reduced clutch size of some female lizard species. - ∞ Mammal: Primate: Virulence of different species and strains vary markedly in different hosts. Hepatosplenomegaly is a common finding at necropsy. Macroscopic pathology of the brain and endocardium might show hemorrhage. Microscopic pathology usually shows sequestration of pigmented parasitized red blood cells in the vessels of the cerebrum, cerebellum, heart, kidney and other organs. The spleen and liver contain abundant pigment (hemazoin) within macrophages and parasitized red blood cells.

The spleen and liver contain abundant pigment (hemazoin) within macrophages and parasitized red blood cells. During acute infections, the kidney often has evidence of tubular necrosis. Diagnosis: Gold standard diagnosis is via identification of intracellular red blood cell parasites on a Giemsa-stained thin blood smear; however, it is difficult to detect low intensity chronic infections by microscopy. PCR is more sensitive and can detect subclinical infections, but may not identify low level parasitemias and may fail to detect co-infections. Small subunit ribosomal ribonucleic acid and mitochondrial cytochrome b genes are definitive targets for malarial parasite ID and used to determine genetic relationships. Immunoblotting can be used to ID antibodies to Plasmodium but only to the level of parasite genus. A serological test (ELISA) is available for P. relictum in penguins. At necropsy, impression smears of lung, liver or spleen may demonstrate gametocytes of Plasmodium.

Identification of the species is based on molecular analysis and morphologic features of the intraerythrocytic gametocytes and meronts. PCR with DNA sequencing can be used to confirm infection and speciate the organism. Material required for laboratory analysis: Giemsa-stained blood films (microscopy) and whole blood or tissue (i.e. liver and/or spleen) for PCR are most often used. Relevant Diagnostic lab: Any laboratory performing complete blood counts is capable of diagnosing Plasmodium spp. on blood smears. DNA testing (PCR) is available at several laboratories including UF ZMDX and Zoologix.

- ∞ Avian - Chloroquine phosphate, primaquine phosphate, pyrimethamine-sulfadoxine combinations, mefloquine, and atovaquone - proguanil hydrochloride - can be used to treat canaries, penguins, raptors and wild passerines. Sulfamonomethoxine suppresses parasitemia but does not protect from mortality if given after circulating parasites are present, sulfachloropyrazine reduces mortality but has no effect of parasitemia. Halofuginone delays parasitemia with only minor suppression in turkeys. Mefloquine, and atovaquone - proguanil hydrochloride are highly efficient for blood stages, but does not affect exoerythrocytic (tissue) stages. - ∞ Reptile - Data on use of antimalarial drugs in reptiles are largely lacking. Chelonians have been treated with chloroquine and primaquine; however, use of chloroquine was ineffective at decreasing burden in a Boettger's lizard - ∞ Primates - Drugs which are used for human malaria treatment can be used for treatment of malaria in primates (chloroquine phosphate, quinine sulfate plus doxycycline or malarone, and other drugs). Prevention and control: Housing susceptible species indoors. Vector (e.g. mosquito) control.

-  Australian marsupials (particularly Macropodidae), prosimians (lemurs), New World primates (particularly the genera Callithrix, Leontopithecus, Saguinus, Saimiri), meerkats, bovids (gazelle [dama, Cuvier's, slender-horned], gerenuk, dik dik, & Saiga antelope), pronghorn, mustelids (black footed ferrets, southern sea otters), delphanids (spinner, Hector's & Maui), and pinnipeds (California sea lions, harbor seals, & Hawaiian monk seals). -  Hawaiian crows, other endemic island birds, and canaries. -  Cattle, rats, horses, Old World monkeys, and turkeys are reported as relatively resistant to clinical disease. -  Usually asymptomatic in most felids. Pallas' and sand cats are an exception, and a dam's positive immune response prior to pregnancy does not prevent congenital disease.

secao: Causative organism: Obligate intracellular coccidian Toxoplasma gondii.
texto: -  Felids are the definitive host and are the only taxa known to shed infective oocysts, the product of sexual reproduction of the parasite, in feces. Oocysts passed in feces become infective after 1-5 days in the environment. Felids can shed millions of oocyts over 1-3 weeks. -  Other mammals and birds are most frequently infected by ingestion of oocysts that once shed from the felid host may survive for months to years in the environment. Once ingested by an intermediate host, the organism forms rapidly asexually dividing tachyzoites in host tissues - that are the cause of clinical signs. Tachyzoites can then transform into thin-walled tissue cysts containing slowly asexually dividing bradyzoites. The life cycle is completed when felids ingest the tissue cysts from prey species whereupon male and female gametocytes in the felid gut fuse to make an oocyst. There is also mounting evidence that the parasite may modulate host behavior facilitating its transmission to the definitive host. For instance, rats with asymptomatic infection lose their fear of cats making them more susceptible to predation.

Zoonotic potential: In the USA, an estimated 22.5% of the population has been infected with toxoplasmosis, and up to 95% prevalence in some other parts of the world. Transmission can occur from ingestion of oocysts passed in cat feces (e.g. cleaning pet litter boxes, gardening/contact with contaminated soil, contaminated produce), ingestion of undercooked meat, transplacentally, or rarely through blood transfusions and organ transplants. -  Most infections are asymptomatic or cause mild self-limiting flu-like symptoms. -  Infections acquired during pregnancy can cause abortion, congenital defects, or more severe disease in the child.

secao: Causative organism: Obligate intracellular coccidian Toxoplasma gondii.
texto:  Most infections are asymptomatic or cause mild self-limiting flu-like symptoms. -  Infections acquired during pregnancy can cause abortion, congenital defects, or more severe disease in the child. Clinical signs in children, including ocular disease, seizures, and mental health disorders, may not be present until later in life. -  Infections in immunocompromised persons may be severe, and recrudescence of an otherwise asymptomatic chronic infection can occur with immunosuppression. Distribution: Worldwide. There is a clear relationship between presence of cats in an ecosystem and presence of Toxoplasma gondii. Runoff water infected with oocysts can introduce the organism to ocean environments.

-  In felids, typically subclinical, although a transient mild diarrhea may occur. -  In species sensitive to the disease, animals are often found dead with no clinical signs observed prior to death. If present, clinical signs may vary depending on the organs affected. Reported clinical signs include respiratory signs (dyspnea, tachypnea, coughing), gastrointestinal signs (diarrhea), general signs (depression, anorexia, behavioral changes), lymphadenopathy, muscle weakness, neurologic signs (blindness, ataxia, dysphagia), ocular disease (keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis, endophthalmitis, cataracts), and abortion. Serum biochemical abnormalities may include elevated muscle and liver enzymes.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: -  Gross: Affected animals may have no gross lesions. If present, gross lesions may include congestion, hemorrhage, organomegaly, pulmonary edema, or necrosis of any affected organs. -  Histologic: Multifocal, multi-organ necrosis is often associated with acute toxoplasmosis. Focal necrosis of affected organs may be associated with free and intracellular tachyzoites (2µm x 6µm crescent-shaped structures with pointed anterior and rounded posterior). Brain (encephalitis with microglial nodules and perivascular cuffing), myocardium (myocarditis), and lung (interstitial pneumonia) are frequently affected. Tissue cysts measuring 5-100µm in diameter can be found in any tissue, but frequently occur in the brain, eye, and muscle. Cysts have thin (<0.5µm) elastic walls and contain up to hundreds of 7µm x 1.5µm crescent-shaped bradyzoites. Diagnosis: Observation of tachyzoites or bradyzoites in affected tissues with cytology or histopathology.

texto: elastic walls and contain up to hundreds of 7µm x 1.5µm crescent-shaped bradyzoites. Diagnosis: Observation of tachyzoites or bradyzoites in affected tissues with cytology or histopathology. Multiple serologic tests capable of detecting IgG and IgM antibodies are available including ELISA, Western blot, direct agglutination test (DAT), modified agglutination test (MAT), latex agglutination test (LAT), and indirect hemagglutination test (IHAT). A single positive serologic test indicates exposure to the organism. In young animals, transfer of maternal antibodies can produce positive serology results. Active infections are generally characterized by a high positive IgM titer with subsequent seroconversion and development of an IgG antibody titer > 32 or by a 4-fold increase in paired IgG titers taken 2-4 weeks apart. PCR and immunohistochemical staining can also be used to detect Toxoplasma antigen in tissues. Material required for laboratory analysis: Formalin-fixed affected tissues can be used for histopathology and immunohistochemical staining. Fresh tissues for cytology, and fresh or frozen tissue can be used for PCR. Serum is needed for the serologic tests.

-  Controlling exposure to cat feces is very important part of prevention. In regions with no endemic felids, elimination of all felids from wildlands and prevention of importation. Feral cats are a common source of infective oocysts in the environment; although, in habitats with native felids, disentangling the role of domestic vs wild felids becomes difficult. Contamination of food and bedding materials with cat feces may be a source of infection in situations where felids are not known to be present near the affected animal. -  Vaccine, live attenuated, developed for livestock; efficacy is variable in other species. -  Meat containing tissue cysts can be rendered non-infective by cooking to 67 ℃ or freezing to -12 ℃ for at least 24 hours. -  Control of intermediate hosts (e.g. rodents) can help prevent transmission to carnivores. -  Prophylactic treatment of queens or kittens has been recommended to reduce morbidity and mortality in Pallas' and sand cats. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Resistant to most disinfectants, but is usually susceptible to boiling water, formalin, and iodine. Notification: None.

Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Animals introduced to the environment where felids are shedding oocysts are at risk of contracting toxoplasmosis. Non-felid warm blooded species that are infected with toxoplasmosis do not pose a risk to other individuals in the environment unless their tissue is ingested. Vertical transmission between females and their offspring is possible in all mammalian species when the infection occurs during gestation. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Once an individual becomes infected with toxoplasmosis, it can remain infected for life. Toxoplasma organisms can remain dormant in tissue cysts where they are protected from the host's immune response. Episodes of immunosuppression can result in a recrudescence of clinical disease.

Hamer (2013) Susceptible animal groups: All mammal species are considered to be susceptible to Trypanosoma cruzi, including more than 150 species of 24 families that have been reported to be infected. -  Disease is best described from humans, nonhuman primates, and dogs; the degree to which other domestic or wild animals present disease upon infection is unknown. Many species of wild and domestic mammals serve as reservoirs for T. cruzi in North and South America. -  There have been no reports of infection in birds, amphibians, or reptiles. Causative organism: Trypanosoma cruzi is a flagellated protozoan parasite that maintains many life stages. The parasite is spread hematophagously and through triatomine bugs (also known as kissing bugs or cone-nosed bugs). -  Trypomastigotes are the abundant blood form that circulates in the mammalian host after infection. After ingesting trypomastigotes from the blood of a vertebrate host, the bug's hindgut contains epimastigotes. -  Metacyclic trypomastigotes appear in the insect's rectum 8-10 days after infection.

After ingesting trypomastigotes from the blood of a vertebrate host, the bug's hindgut contains epimastigotes. -  Metacyclic trypomastigotes appear in the insect's rectum 8-10 days after infection. These metacyclic forms pass in the feces and can enter the body of a vertebrate host through the bite, scratched skin, or mucous membranes. Consumption of the vector is suspected to be a route of infection in non-human primates. -  Amastigotes are the reproductive form of the parasite, and develop in muscle and other tissue cells. Repeated binary fission causes amastigotes to lyse the host cell and burst free; these can then attack other host cells. -  Pseudocysts of parasites may form in muscle cells. Zoonotic potential: High in areas of South and Central America, where kissing bugs maintain domestic cycles and colonize human dwellings. In contrast, the housing structures in North America are generally less able to be colonized by bugs, and therefore zoonotic potential is reduced relative to areas with domestic cycles. Distribution: Chagas' disease in humans or animals can occur wherever there is overlap among kissing bug vectors, the T. cruzi parasite, and vertebrate reservoir hosts - it is endemic across most of South, Central America, and Mexico, and is increasingly recognized across the southern USA. -  In the USA, 11 species of kissing bugs occur, and are predominantly distributed across the southern half of the country and range as far north as the California/Oregon border and New Jersey. -  Six million people are estimated to be infected across the Americas, and vector eradication campaigns have assisted in reducing the disease burden. -  An increasing number of studies document local transmission to animals and humans in the southern US where kissing bugs occur.

-  Once the metacyclic trypomastigotes enter the host, an acute local inflammatory reaction may occur. In humans, within 1-2 weeks of infection, the parasites spread to lymph nodes and multiply within phagocytic cells. The intracellular amastigotes multiply and pseudocysts may form. Within days, some organisms may transform to trypomastigotes and burst free from the pseudocyst. A generalized parasitemia can occur, followed by parasite invasion of many tissues within body. -  May be up to several months if contaminated blood from transfusion is the source of infection.

-  Acute: In humans and dogs, the initial acute phase of infection may be asymptomatic or undetected; regional or generalized lymphadenopathy, fever, myalgia, headache, hepatosplenomegaly, edema, rash, vomiting, diarrhea, or anorexia may occur. Humans may note a lesion (chagoma) where the parasite enters the body. There are usually no electrocardiographic (ECG) changes during the acute phase; however, sudden death from acute myocarditis is a concern. -  Chronic: may develop in a subset of patients who survive the acute phase of infection. In chronic disease, cardiac abnormalities may be noted including right bundle branch block and left anterior hemi-block, atrioventricular conduction abnormalities, and arrhythmias. Cardiomegaly may be noted on radiographs. In dogs, systolic dysfunction is indistinguishable from dilated cardiomyopathy. Weakness and exercise intolerance may be noted. Humans infected with some strains of the parasite may also have complications of the digestive system, including megaesophagus and megacolon.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: -  Gross cardiac changes may include cardiomegaly and focal thinning of the myocardium including apical aneurysm. Dilatation and thinning of the wall of the esophagus and colon may occur. -  Histologically, examination of the heart may reveal unruptured pseudocysts with no inflammatory response, or ruptured pseudocysts with characteristic infiltration of lymphocytes, monocytes, and/or polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Histologic examination often fails to reveal amastigotes, yet lymphoplasmacyic inflammation can be seen.

-  Microscopy (blood smear or buffy coat) may identify the trypomastigotes (blood stage of the parasite) during acute infections; the organism has a single flagellum and a large kinetoplast at the posterior end of the cell and appears as a characteristic 'C' shape in Giemsa stains of bloodsmears. -  PCR can be used to amplify the DNA of the parasite from a blood sample. -  Serologic tests may be of limited utility during acute infections. Because the level of circulating parasites decreases within months, parasites are undetectable in blood by most methods during the chronic phase of disease. During chronic disease, serologic tests are used to detect antibodies to the parasite. To increase sensitivity and specificity, a standard serodiagnostic approach is to apply two or more tests that use different techniques or different antigens. Two commonly used techniques are enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and immunofluorescent antibody test (IFA). Some serological tests are cross-reactive and will also detect antibodies to Leishmania species. Rapid immunochromatographic 'dipstick' assays have not been validated in animals.

The only parasitological techniques useful in the chronic phase of disease are xenodiagnoses and hemoculture. Tick-borne infection is by far the most common mode of infection, but blood transfusion, blood exposure, organ transplantation, and maternal-fetal transmission can all occur. B. microti, divergens, venatorum, and crassa-like cause the majority of disease in humans. B. duncani and B. motasi round out the top 6 causes of human babesiosis. Human infection is typically mild or inapparent but can cause significant illness in immuneintact persons, though illness tends to be more severe in immune-compromised persons, especially in splenectomized individuals. When co-infections with other tick-borne diseases occur, human illness is much more severe. Distribution: Babesia spp. distribution is shaped by the range of its primary tick vectors, but the geographic distribution of Babesia spp. that affect birds are not fully understood. -  B. bovis and B. bigemina are transmitted by Rhipicephalus microplus and R. annulatus respectively and found in Mexico and occasionally southern Texas and California.

Incubation period for humans is reported as 1-6 week from beginning of tick feeding. Chronic infections may recrudesce if an animal is stressed or becomes immunocompromised for any reason, including malnutrition. Clinical signs: Nonspecific clinical signs include fever, anorexia, depression and lethargy, lymphadenopathy. Erythrocyte destruction by the parasite and host immune response results in mild to severe hemolytic anemia, icterus, hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, splenomegaly. In rare cases where Babesia-infected erythrocytes obstruct brain capillaries, neurologic signs may be noted. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Pathologic findings may include icterus, generalized lymph node enlargement, hepatomegaly and splenomegaly (due to red pulp hyperplasia), abomasal mucosal ulcerations, hemorrhage into the intestinal tract, and dark red kidneys (hemoglobinuric nephrosis).

Edema and hemorrhage of tissues such as the cardiac muscle, intestinal serosa, and lymph nodes may be observed, as well as fluid in the body cavities and pericardial sac. The bladder is frequently distended with dark red urine. For fulminating ruminant infections, Giemsa-stained brain crush smears are helpful to detect parasitized erythrocytes in brain capillaries. Also, the spleen often contains large numbers of parasitized cells, which may be appreciated on impression smears taken from cross sections of the spleen. Postmortem of stressed animals may show high parasitemias, but this does not necessarily implicate babesiosis as the sole cause of death. Diagnosis: Microscopic visualization of piroplasms within erythrocytes in Giemsa, Wright's or DiffQuick®-stained thin or thick whole blood smears. Piroplasms become more difficult to find on blood smears after the acute phase of infection passes. Serologic tests (cELISA, IFA, CFT), nucleic acid probes and PCR are also available.

Gross splenomegaly is a common finding, particularly in naïve or unnatural hosts. Impression smears of spleen may be made for the identification of parasitized cells. Material required for laboratory analysis: Whole blood (EDTA) for smears and PCR, serum for serological testing. Relevant Diagnostic lab: Several veterinary diagnostic laboratories offer serologic and PCR testing for B. bovis, B. bigemina, B. caballi, B. equi, B. canis, and B. gibsoni. Research labs with Babesia expertise are good options to work up samples. Treatment: Treatment is most successful in the early phase of the disease. Chemotherapy may not completely eliminate infection and may be unsuccessful in the later stages of the disease. Imidocarb dipropionate (1mg/kg IM), diminazene aceturate (3mg/kg IM), phenamidinediisethionate (8-13 mg/kg), and amicarbalide diisethionate (10 mg/kg IM), have been used to treat babesiosis in artiodactylids.

Similarly, imidocarb, diminazene, and phenamidine have also been utilized to treat B. canis and B. gibsoni. Primaquine phosphate is a preferred treatment in felids and birds. Quinine and clindamycin, or atovaquone and azithromycin are used to treat zoonotic babesiosis and might be tried for other species and infections, if needed. In addition to specific therapy, supportive care with fluids, blood transfusions, iron, and antibiotics may be important as well. Prevention and control: Free-ranging animals sharing zoo habitats are often already infected with Babesia as well as vector ticks; therefore, outbreak control should center on control of the tick vector. Elimination or reduction of tick infestation may be accomplished via application of acaricides, prophylactic use of chemotherapeutics, range burning, prolonged pasture rest, and repellents.

Additionally, care should be taken to prevent accidental transmission through the transfer of infected blood between animals via routine surgical or vaccination procedures. Vaccines of noninfectious material have been developed, and although they do not prevent infection, they do ameliorate the severity of disease. Additionally, differences in strain antigenicity limit vaccine cross-protection. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities Disinfectants are generally not effective in preventing the spread of babesiosis; however, standard biosecurity measures should be undertaken to avoid infected blood transfusions. R. sanguineus, the vector for canine babesiosis, is typically found indoors in kennels and other housing situations; such facilities should be treated with appropriate acaricides. Notification: Babesiosis caused by B. bovis, B. bigemina, B. equiand B. caballi are reportable diseases and state and federal authorities must be notified immediately of infection.

Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: Equine piroplasmosis is considered a foreign animal disease in the U.S., therefore any equids imported must be serologically screened by the National Veterinary Services Laboratory using the competitive enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (cELISA) prior to importation. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Animals that have been treated for and survive infection should be considered chronic carriers. The most important means of preventing transmission is through vector control. A premunition approach may be an alternative strategy for introducing naïve animals into endemic areas for conservation purposes. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Disease-free status may not be realistic, particularly where wildlife is involved in the maintenance of endemicity.

Aleutian mink disease virus (AMDV) has now been reclassified as Carnivore amdoparvovirus 1 within the genus Amdoparvovirus. For many years it was the sole member of the genus Amdovirus within the family Parvoviridae, subfamily Parvovirinae. Novel amdoparvoviruses have recently been discovered in various small carnivore species including free-ranging gray fox, farm-raised raccoon dogs and arctic foxes, free-ranging striped skunks, and zoohoused red pandas (Carnivore amdoparvoviruses 2-5, respectively), and at least in some cases appear to cause similar disease in their respective hosts. Zoonotic potential: Carnivore amdoparvovirus 1 (formerly AMDV) is not considered zoonotic.

Carnivore amdoparvovirus 1 (formerly AMDV) can be detected in blood by PCR in most animals within 10 days post-infection. Viral replication reached its peak around 10 days post-infection thus incubation period is considered short. Infections in adult animals are typically persistent (life-long). Clinical signs: Disease presentation can vary from subclinical to fatal. Aleutian phenotype mink are particularly susceptible.

texto: short. Infections in adult animals are typically persistent (life-long). Clinical signs: Disease presentation can vary from subclinical to fatal. Aleutian phenotype mink are particularly susceptible. In adults, disease results from persistent infection with an exuberant immune response resulting in plasmacytosis, hypergammaglobulinemia and deposition of antigen-antibody complexes in tissues (type 3 hypersensitivity). In mink kits, virus replicates in type II pneumocytes resulting in interstitial pneumonia. -  In adults: Plasmacytosis, hypergammaglobulinemia, and immune complex deposition can cause damage in various tissues and organ systems, most often manifesting as glomerulonephritis and arteritis. Clinical signs can include lethargy, inappetence, cachexia, fever, oral/gastrointestinal hemorrhage, infertility, and abortions. Progression can lead to chronic kidney disease and renal failure. -  In kits: Acute pneumonia with lethargy, dyspnea, death.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: - Gross: Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, renal changes (varying from swelling, petechiation to atrophy and pitting), enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, hemorrhages (arteritis), oral ulcers (uremia). In kits, rubbery, non-collapsing lungs, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly. Infected ferrets may have few or no gross lesions. - Histologic: Plasma cell infiltration in the kidneys, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and bone marrow; bile duct proliferation; membranous glomerulonephritis and fibrinoid arteritis; lymphoplasmacytic meningitis. In kits, acute interstitial pneumonia, hyperplasia of type II pneumocytes, hyaline membranes, +/- intranuclear inclusion bodies. Diagnosis: Presumptive diagnosis is based on clinical signs and hypergammaglobulinemia. Common testing modalities: counterimmunoelectrophoresis (CIEP), lateral flow ELISA, and PCR. Tissue biopsies usually done post-mortem. Material required for laboratory analysis: Blood; serum for CIEP/ELISA; urine, saliva, feces, tissues for PCR.

Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Clean environment with 10% bleach solution. Steamclean pens and spray with 2% sodium hydroxide. African cercopithecoid monkeys including Patas monkey (Erythrocebus patas), vervet monkeys (Cercopithecus aethiops) and baboons (Papio spp.) are suspected to be the natural reservoirs for simian hemorrhagic fever virus, the best characterized simarterivirus. Currently, SHFV is thought only to affect Asian macaques of diverse species, including: rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta), bonnet macaque (M. radiata), cynomolgus macaque (M. fasicularis), stump-tailed macaque (M. arctoides), Assam macaque (M. assamensis) and Southern pig-tailed macaque (M. nemestrina). Causative organism: Simian hemorrhagic fever is caused by simian arteriviruses, including simian hemorrhagic fever virus (SHFV), simian hemorrhagic encephalitis virus (SHEV), and Pebjah virus (PBJV). Zoonotic potential: Humans exposed to the disease in primates and swine have become seropositive but have no apparent or clinically mild infection. It is unknown how infection would affect immunecompromised people, pregnant women, or children. Distribution: Philippines (and animals recently imported from Philippines), China, Bangladesh. Geographic distribution may be larger depending on the reservoir distribution. Incubation period: 7-14 days.

- ∞ In primates, RESTV infection may present with non-specific signs such as anorexia, lethargy, or sudden death. Other reported signs include fever, cough, nasal discharge, swollen eyelids, splenomegaly, and renomegaly. Some animals develop hemorrhagic manifestations, including - diarrhea or melena with frank blood, bleeding from external orifices, and petechial to suffusive hemorrhages. Laboratory findings may show elevated LDH, BUN, ALP, AST, and CPK levels, along with evidence of DIC (elevated fibrin degradation products and thrombocytopenia). High viral loads have been detected in urine and nasopharyngeal washes. - ∞ In swine (Sus scrofa domesticus), the disease ranges from subclinical or mild febrile illness to severe respiratory distress and sudden death. Clinical signs include coughing, nasal discharge, pulmonary edema, and interstitial pneumonia, though hemorrhagic signs have not been observed.

- ∞ In primates, gross lesions include maculopapular rash, splenomegaly, widespread petechial hemorrhages, duodenal hemorrhage, and interstitial pneumonia. Histologically, findings include lymphoid necrosis, hepatic and adrenal cortical necrosis, interstitial nephritis, and amphophilic cytoplasmic inclusion bodies in multiple tissues. Viral replication occurs primarily in tissue macrophages and interstitial fibroblasts, and to a lesser extent in endothelial cells, hepatocytes, adrenal cortical cells, and renal tubular epithelium. - ∞ In swine, lesions are predominantly respiratory, including lung consolidation, pulmonary edema, alveolar and interstitial infiltrates, peribronchiolitis, and inflammation of the nasal turbinates and trachea. Lymphadenopathy, especially in mandibular and tracheobronchial nodes, is common. Viral replication is most prominent in respiratory and lymphatic tissues, with no evidence of hemorrhagic disease.

Causative organism: Marburg virus (MARV) is the causative agent of several human cases of hemorrhagic fever that occurred in Marburg, Germany. This RNA virus is classified in the family Filoviridae of the order Mononegavirales, and is related to Ebola virus.

Distribution: Natural virus circulation and human cases (isolated or during outbreak) are restricted to Africa (geographical range of the reservoir), although imported monkeys caused a human outbreak in Europe in 1967 and several infected travelers have imported the disease outside the endemic zone. Incubation period: Usually 8-10 days (range 5-21 days).

-  Early signs are similar to influenza and malaria, and the onset of disease is sudden. -  Humans: Fever, headache, chills, and myalgia, sometimes followed around the fifth day by possible maculopapular rash on the chest, abdomen, and back. As the illness progresses, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, chest pain, sore throat, jaundice, weight loss, and pancreatitis are observed. Many patients develop some form of bleeding and often from multiple sites. Shock, renal failure, liver failure, and multiple organ dysfunctions occur in the most severe cases and usually preceded death. Case fatality rate ranges from 23% to more than 80% in recent outbreaks. In recovered humans, complications such as orchitis, recurrent hepatitis, uveitis, transverse myelitis, have been reported. -  Animals: Lymphopenia and elevation of liver enzymes are characteristic. Thrombocytopenia is frequent. Although duikers are susceptible to Ebola virus, a related filovirus, little is known about the host range of Marburg virus. Complications in the few recovering animals are not reported.

Other clinical signs noted include epistaxis, diarrhea, encephalitis, shock and death. - ∞ Humans: Fever, headache, severe muscle pain, prostration, inflammation of conjunctiva, vesicular eruptions on the soft palate, tussis, vomition, diarrhea, dehydration and bleeding. Decreased platelets, red blood cell and white blood cell counts are noted. Patients sometimes recover after 1-2 weeks but usually a biphasic illness with a second wave at three weeks with above clinical signs and, for some, encephalitis. Fatality rate of 3-10%. Diagnosis: Serology (convalescent phase), RT-PCR, qRT-PCR, IgM capture ELISA, virus isolation and serology.

Causative organism: Macacine herpesvirus 1 (McHV-1), also called herpes B virus or B virus. Strains endemic to different macaque species are genetically distinct and may have differing pathogenicity to non-macaque hosts. Zoonotic potential: Yes, but in infections in people are rare. -  Since B virus was identified in 1932, approximately 50 human infections have been reported, although many were incompletely documented In one review of 28 confirmed cases, at least 18 patients died. All confirmed cases in humans have involved exposure to captive rhesus macaques, most in occupational settings, except for one exposed to macaques at a tourist site. Macaques involved in confirmed transmissions are usually asymptomatic and may have been seronegative at the last screening or even at the time of the exposure prior to seroconversion.

Distribution: Worldwide, with macaque species as carriers. Incubation period: < 2 days to 5 weeks, usually 5-8 days.

-  Macaques: 80-100% of sexually mature rhesus macaques in both laboratory and free-ranging settings are seropositive for B virus, especially in large social groups. Prevalence varied from <20% to 98% in free-ranging and laboratory populations of cynomolgus macaques. Prevalence in other macaque species is less well studied. Macaques of any species rarely have clinical signs indicating infection or recrudescence; however, they will occasionally have herpes-like skin mucosal pustules. In large social groups, shedding increases during periods of stress, including the breeding season. -  Humans: Sometimes there are herpes-like skin/mucosal lesions associated with the point of infection accompanied by pain and itching and erythema. Most cases present with fever, and encephalitis manifesting in neurologic signs including: dysphagia, ataxia, confusion, paresthesia and paralysis. Latency is established and reactivation has been documented up to 54 years after the initial infection.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: -  Macaques: Most often, histological evidence of acute infection is present without gross pathology. The virus often remains latent in the trigeminal or sacral nerve ganglia, from which culture or PCR may be used to detect the virus. If oral or genital lesions are present there may be vesicle formation with leukocytic invasion of the area; when keratinized cells overlying the vesicle slough, a plaque of necrotic fibrinous material remains overlying the base of the ulcer. Intranuclear inclusions can be seen in tissues showing recent signs of degeneration. -  Humans: Few reports of histological findings have been documented. Inclusion bodies are not typically found. Reported findings include severe inflammatory and degenerative changes in the spinal cord, particularly in the cervical cord and brainstem; the thalamus and hypothalamus may also be infected.

-  Macaques: Initial screen is a multiplex assay, and the confirming test utilizes immunoblots purchased from B-virus reference lab. A negative antibody titer does not indicate the animal is not infected, only that it is not currently producing antibodies. Rising titers may be associated with viral shedding period. Diagnosis is often based on Western blot or virus neutralizing antibodies as well as virus isolation. PCR has been developed as well. -  Humans, an exposed person: Collection of acute (as soon as feasible after exposure, and after the appropriate cleansing protocol has been completed) and convalescent (3 weeks post-exposure) serum is advisable, and should be submitted for serologic testing.

-  For serology: 0.5-2.0 ml serum in plastic tube. Store and ship at -20˚C or with dry ice. -  For virology: Swabs of vesicle or other lesions. Place swab in 1-2 ml viral transport media, store at -80˚C. CSF, autopsy samples of brainstem, biopsies from the site of inoculation: place in plastic storage/shipment tubes. Ship samples on dry ice according to US Department of Transportation regulations.

- Rodents: The virus is widespread through reservoirs in wild populations. Cattle present no correlation between presence of virus and specific lesions. Horses present conjunctivitis, oculonasal discharge, and cough. In finches, affected birds present respiratory disease and death. Humans and non-human primates are usually subclinical. After reactivation or immunocompromised non-human primates can present with generalized infection which may include necrotizing meningitis, neuritis, enterocolitis, and interstitial pneumonia. In humans, severe permanent disabilities in children can occur when primary infection occurs during pregnancy, or when acquired in AIDS patients, organ transplant and cancer chemotherapy. These clinical signs range from malaise to permanent hearing loss, and include mental retardation; gastrointestinal, pulmonary, and auto-immune disease; and death.

Distribution: Worldwide, but now it is considered a foreign disease in the US as it was eliminated in 2000. Causative organism: Poliovirus types 1, 2 and 3, family Picornaviridae, subgroup Enteroviridae. Zoonotic potential: Yes, but humans are the only natural host and primary reservoir. Distribution: Historically, the disease was present worldwide. Western Hemisphere declared free of indigenous poliovirus since September 1991, with the last case of endemic polio in the US in 1979. Eradication status was achieved through the global efforts of WHO, UNICEF, and an international contingent spearheading the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) and widespread use of polio immunization and surveillance in humans in 1988. Complete global eradication is still an active goal of these organizations, and incidence and transmission have continued to dramatically decline with continued use and distribution of vaccine. Global efforts have led to eradication of 2 of the 3 wild poliovirus (WPV 2 and 3) serotypes.

Currently, two countries maintain an endemic status of WPV 1 strain: Afghanistan and Pakistan; WPV1 outbreaks linked to Pakistan strain were detected in two southeast African countries in 2021 and 2022. Variant Polioviruses are now the main cause of polio outbreaks around the world, with over 600 cases of circulating VDPV type 2 (cVDPV type 2) reported in 2022. A majority of these cVDPV2 cases have been reported from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Yemen, and Nigeria. Outbreaks are more likely in under-immunized countries. Incubation period: Differs depending on the type of polio but ranges from 3 to 35 days. Non-paralytic disease has an incubation period of 3 to 6 days; paralytic disease has incubation period of 7 to 21 days. Virus can be shed in the feces for 3 to 6 weeks post- exposure or after vaccination with oral polio vaccine (OPV).

Clinical signs: Although acute flaccid paralysis is the most noteworthy and potentially severe of the clinical signs described, poliovirus infection in humans can be highly variable and clinical signs are categorized based on presentation. Most human infections are asymptomatic (72%). About 24% of infections result in minor disease including those of the upper respiratory tract, gastrointestinal disturbances, and flu-like signs with associated fever and muscle aches. In 1-2% of cases, signs are more severe including meningitis, muscle weakness or flaccid paralysis of a single limb to quadriplegia, and respiratory failure with 0.1% of all reported polio cases resulting in the paralytic form in humans. Death occurs, but rarely, at 2-5% in children and 15-30% in adults that contract the paralytic form of this disease. A post-polio syndrome may occur in 25% to 40% of human cases as well, which develops decades after the initial infection.

Inactivated (IPV) and oral polio (OPV) vaccines are available for human use, but since 2000, only IPV has been used in the US to minimize vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP) incidence. The World Health Organization recommends that all children be fully vaccinated. Current recommendations for childhood coverage are a series of 4 IPV vaccines at 2, 4, 6-18 months, and 4-6 years of age. Naïve adult vaccine recommendations and vaccine information for travelers to endemic countries are also available through the CDC website. OPV is still used in several other countries. Routine polio vaccination with OPV or IPV of great apes in human care has been recommended historically but is currently at the discretion of the animal's holding facility. Risk of exposure is low due to human vaccine eradication efforts.

The reservoir and full host range is unknown, but African rodents are suspected in transmission. Old and New World primates and rodents have shown susceptibility to experimental and natural infection. Virus recovery from naturally infected animals has been limited to a clinically ill rope squirrel (1985, Democratic Republic of Congo), a dead infant mangabey (2012, Tai National Park, Cote d'Ivoire), and wild chimpanzees (2019, Tai National Park, Cote d'Ivoire). Viral testing during the 2003 U.S. outbreak identified infection in imported rope squirrels, dormice, and African giant pouched rats, and in exposed prairie dogs. Prairie dogs appear very susceptible to infection. Chinchillas, coatimundis, giant anteaters, shrews, and hedgehogs have also been documented as susceptible to infection. Serological evidence of monkeypox virus infection has been detected in non-human primates and rodents (especially squirrels) in Africa.

Experimentally infected rope squirrels and Gambian pouched rats shed large quantities of virus. Experimentally infected marmosets and ground squirrels developed typical clinical signs and shed virus. In 2022, a possible anthropozoonotic infection occurred in a pet dog owned by 2 symptomatic individuals; however, the reviewer comments that the authors of that report may be in the process of retracting it. Causative organism: Monkeypox virus (Orthopoxvirus, family Poxviridae). Two clades: Clade I (formerly known as Central African or Congo basin clade) and Clades IIa and IIb (formerly known together as West African clade). Clade II viruses are generally less pathogenic than that clade I viruses, but still can cause severe illness. Transmission: Contact with an infected animal, human, or contaminated materials through broken skin, respiratory tract, or mucous membranes.

Transmission: Contact with an infected animal, human, or contaminated materials through broken skin, respiratory tract, or mucous membranes. -  Animal-to-human: bite, scratch, wild game meat preparation, needle sticks; direct contact with infected fluids or lesion material; indirect contact (contaminated bedding). Cutaneous transmission implicated in the 2003 U.S. outbreak. -  Human-to-human: Mpox can spread during close contact, including direct contact with rash/scabs of infected person, as well as contact with upper respiratory secretions (snot, mucus), and areas around anus, rectum, or vagina. Direct contact can happen during prolonged face-toface contact. The risk is considered low for getting Mpox by touching objects, fabrics, or surfaces that have been used by someone with Mpox. A person with Mpox can spread it to others from as early as 1-4 days prior to the onset of symptoms until the rash has fully healed with a new fresh layer of skin.
