-  The majority of TB cases reported in non-human primates (NHP) are caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tb). -  M. bovis, M. africanum; and other species from the M. tb complex have infected NHP, but are less commonly identified. -  M. avium subsp. avium and other nontuberculous or atypical mycobacteria species can also infect NHPs. Zoonotic potential: Yes (and anthropozoonotic), but there is scant evidence of direct primate-tohuman transmission. Distribution: Worldwide: all NHPs should be considered susceptible. However, a recently published review suggests that there is little evidence of disease or mortality caused by M. tb sensu stricto in the different species of African apes both under human care and free ranging populations.

Incubation period: Variable from weeks to months; animals can develop latent infections with reactivation in weeks, months or even years later. Development of disease is dependent on organism, route of infection, dose, and immunologic status of animal. Susceptibility, morbidity, and mortality are variable for different species. Clinical signs: The clinical signs are often nondescript and ill-defined. Tuberculosis can imitate a multitude of diseases such as pneumonia, neoplasia or fungal infections. The clinical spectrum of signs range from asymptomatic to multi-symptomatic; the profile is highly dependent on the route of exposure, the system involved, and the infecting agent. General signs can include a roughened hair coat, anorexia, depression, lethargy, fever (low grade; intermittent or persistent), weight loss, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and local or general lymphadenopathy which may or may not have draining tracts. A chronic or paroxysmal cough and dyspnea indicate pulmonary involvement, which mirrors acute bronchitis, or pneumonia.

Neurological presentation with signs including anisocoria or ataxia may implicate meningitis or central nervous system involvement, and paresis to paralysis can indicate a peripheral neurological component that may be a result of spondylitis.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: -  At necropsy, tuberculosis indications vary with the duration and degree of disease. Organs of predilection are the lung and adjacent hilar lymph nodes. Dissemination occurs to the spleen, kidney, liver and associated lymph nodes. Additional sites less frequently seen include omentum, ovary, cerebrum, spinal column, peripheral lymph nodes skin and mammary gland. The extent of the lesions can range from no detectable lesions to wide dissemination of caseous granulomas varying in size from pinpoint to large coalescing lesions. Appearance of lesions within the lung can be focal, coalescing or cavitary. Lesions in parietal pleural with adjacent adhesion may be caused by collapse of large granulomas expelling contents into the adjacent airway in a process referred to as cavitation. -  Nontuberculous mycobacteria can cause a variety of post-mortem findings, for example, granulomatous enteritis (siamang gibbon, M. a. intracelulare) and multifocal subcutaneous nodules (black bearded saki monkey, M. kansasii). Underlying immune suppression should be considered in cases of non-tuberculous mycobacteria in non-human primates.

-  Ante-mortem - o Intradermal tuberculin skin test (TST): Mammalian Old Tuberculin (MOT) produced by Symbiotics, Inc. is currently the only USDA approved tuberculin for non-human primates in the USA. Intradermal injection of 0.1 ml of MOT is performed using a 27 gauge or smaller needle in the palpebrae. In small primates such as marmosets and squirrel monkeys, reduced dose (0.05ml) may be considered. Injection sites are observed at 24, 48 and 72 hours post injection for signs of a delayed Type II hypersensitivity reaction (hyperemia, edema, and induration). Grading systems can be found in the Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Tuberculosis in Nonhuman Primates. The test is interpreted as suspect when moderate swelling is observed and positive when palpebral swelling is present in conjunction with droop. A minimum of two weeks should occur between skin tests. Detection of positive animals is difficult in early infections and in advanced stages of disease animals may be nonresponsive. An immunologically competent animal is required for the test to be effective.

of positive animals is difficult in early infections and in advanced stages of disease animals may be nonresponsive. An immunologically competent animal is required for the test to be effective. False positives may occur due to trauma during administration of antigen or nonspecific response caused by cross reactivity with nontuberculous Mycobacteria or previous exposure to Freund's Complete adjuvant. A comparative TST - using biologically balanced purified protein derivatives (PPD) of M. bovis and of M. avium - placed into separate palpebrae or at separate sites on the thorax or abdomen is useful in differentiating nonspecific sensitization. Palpation of the injection sites should be performed with abdominal skin testing. Limitations to testing can be challenged by the immunocompetency of the animal, quality and purity and volume of the tuberculin injected, skill in administration, thorough recording of bruise or palpebral trauma, visual access in group settings, accurate interpretation at all time periods, inadequate interval between tests or lack of documentation. All of these can jeopardize a surveillance program.

Additional diagnostics such as imaging and laboratory testing can augment TST results and should be considered in suspect cases. - o Diagnostic imaging: Thoracic radiographs or CT scan may help identify pulmonary lesions or lymph node enlargement. - o Bacterial culture is the gold standard to confirm presence of mycobacterial organisms. Further identification can be performed via biochemical analysis and 16s rDNA sequencing. Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) may also be used to confirm the presence of mycobacterial DNA. In vitro gamma interferon (IFN-γ) release assays (IGRA) or antibody detection platforms can be used in conjunction with TST or to supplement other testing methods. PRIMAGAM (Prionics USA, Inc., NE, USA), a commercial IFN-γ assay, and PrimaTB STAT PAK (Chembio Diagnostic Systems, Inc. NY, USA), a commercial serologic assay, were used previously to augment TST results, but are not currently available.

The development of additional non-human primate-specific IFN-γ based diagnostics is ongoing. - o T-SPOT.TB (Oxford Immunotec, Oxford, UK) Cell Mediated Immunity IFN-γ assay for use in macaques. - o Response is to M. tuberculosis-specific antigens and shows some promise for the diagnosis of latent and active infections. - o A Monkey-IGRA (mIGRA) assay was recently developed using QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube test (QIAGEN, MD, USA) Cell Mediated Immunity IFN- γ assay, in combination with the monkey IFN- γ ELISA pro kit system (Mabtech, Inc., OH, USA). This test also shows promise for diagnosis of active and latent TB infections in macaques. - o TB-Plex (Charles River Laboratories, MA, USA) commercially available TB multiplex assay that detects TB antibodies in non-human primate serum or plasma.

Additional laboratory tests such as culture and PCR, with a genome sequence analysis, should be performed if TB is suspected.

-  Culture or PCR may be conducted on ante-mortem or post-mortem samples including fresh or frozen tissues containing lesions or granulomas, blood, feces, discharge, or bronchoalveolar - and gastric lavage fluids. PCR may also be performed on formalin-fixed tissues containing lesions. -  Culture and speciation: To optimize isolation, it is recommended that the samples be centrifuged at 3,500 rpm for 30 minutes in sterile polypropylene conical tubes. Success of isolation is dependent on quality of specimen, appropriate processing and culture techniques. The process requires 4- 8 weeks for isolation and longer to speciate. Microbiological staining: Specimens include lesions or granulomas in lymph nodes (i.e., broncho-alveolar) and bronchioalveolar or gastric lavage. Fine needle aspirates, impression smears or tissue suspensions that are air dried in a thin layer on slides that is heat fixed and stained for the appearance of acid fast bacilli. -  IFN-γ assays are typically run on fresh heparinized whole blood. -  Products Available: - o AFB Kinyoun Kit (Polysciences, Inc.): stain of slides for acid-fast bacilli. - o T-SPOT.TB ( Oxford Immunotec, Oxford, UK): heparin PBMCs

-  Non-human primate colonies should be maintained closed and have minimal direct contact with public. Establish a routine surveillance program using the skin testing to identify infected animals; additional diagnostics may augment TST. Segregate or cull positive animals during confirmation. Identify designated quarantine area for all new nonhuman primates; hold animals for a minimum of 30 days and retest using TST. Animals of unknown source or high risk animals should be quarantined for longer duration for retest. -  Humans are the primary reservoir for M. tuberculosis. Personnel screening and biosecurity protocols can be used to mitigate zoonotic and anthropozoonotic transmission. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: All primate primary housing, clinics and caging should incorporate tuberculocidal products. The Environment Protection Agency Antimicrobials Division Test oversees the testing of these products for efficacy. Consideration for product selection will depend on surfaces, caging, and equipment needing tuberculocidal products. Notification: Disease may be reportable to USDA or OIE, depending on species of Mycobacteria.

Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Cull all positive animals or treat extremely valuable animals in isolation. - ∞ Family: Enterobacteriaceae; genus: Shigella; four species: - o Shigella dysenteriae - serogroup A; - o Shigella flexneri - serogroup B; - o Shigella boydii - serogroup C; - o Shigella sonnei - serogroup D. - ∞ Infection and transmission occurs mainly via fecal-oral route through contaminated food, water or direct contact; in humans, person-to-person transmission is the most common route. Arthropods, such as houseflies can function as mechanical vectors. - ∞ Shigella bacteria are able to invade intestinal mucosa cells, cytotoxins (Shiga -toxin) may also be produced. Zoonotic potential: High. Distribution: Worldwide. Originally, a common problem encountered mostly in under-developed regions Incubation period: 1-6 days. Clinical signs: Lethargy, abdominal cramps, and severe painful diarrhea that may be watery, and potentially with mucus, pus or blood. Loss of appetite is common. Vomiting may occur. When more than one NHP is affected, concern for enteric pathogen(s) should be highly suspected. Fever is possible. Gingivitis has been reported in macaques. Reactive arthritis, neuritis, vulvovaginitis, conjunctivitis, and hemolytic uremic syndrome may be sequela.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: - ∞ Most common findings during gross necropsy; signs of erosive colitis, gastroenteritis, enteritis. The colonic mucosa may appear bright red (with erosions) or black (if necrotic). Possibly hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, miliary white foci in the liver, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy. - ∞ Histopathologic findings include: suppurative necrosis of cryptic or surface enterocytes in lower small intestines, sometimes in cecum and colon, depending on bacterial species involved. Possible necrotizing hepatitis.

- ∞ Fecal cytology may be useful as a first-line diagnostic tool, but definitive diagnosis requires PCR or culture of fresh fecal material. - o Culture is not recommended as the only first line screening test due to difficulty isolating the organism, and decreased sensitivity compared to PCR. - o However, culture is required for antibiotic susceptibility testing. - o In culture, Shigella has a very similar appearance to E. coli. - ∞ High-through put sequencing may be available to rapidly discern between several enteric pathogens, although a human laboratory may be needed for this testing. - ∞ Intermittent shedding in asymptomatic carriers can make screening difficult. Material required for laboratory analysis: Feces, rectal swabs. For post-mortem sampling, organ tissue may be used (intestine, colon) Relevant Diagnostic lab: Any laboratory that is set up for culture and/or PCR methods can be used for first screening for Shigella. Veterinary diagnostic labs may have access to sequencing to allow for rapid diagnosis. A local health department may be contacted to determine the availability of sequencing although human labs may not be willing to accept NHP samples.

- ∞ Treatment should include oral rehydration at suggested osmolality of 250-310 mOsm. Suggested oral hydration may be apple juice diluted 1:1 with water, Pedialyte, watermelon - and fruits with high water content. Animals may have cramping and abdominal pain, therefore, reluctance to drink and take oral medication is often a factor. If the animal does not appear to be drinking enough to accommodate for losses, consider intravenous and subcutaneous fluids. - ∞ Other treatments may include antibiotics, ondansetron (a serotonin receptor agonist that may help reduce abdominal cramping), analgesics, anti-emetics. Lactobacillus may help to promote non-pathogenic flora. Antibiotics given to asymptomatic animals is controversial due to the risk of contributing to antimicrobial resistance. Sulfasalazine may be used to manage reactive arthritis. - ∞ Anti-motility drugs (eg. loperamide) are contraindicated, as they may inhibit the body's ability to clear the bacteria. Antibiotic therapy should be based on antimicrobial sensitivities, when available.

drugs (eg. loperamide) are contraindicated, as they may inhibit the body's ability to clear the bacteria. Antibiotic therapy should be based on antimicrobial sensitivities, when available. The choice of antibiotics should be based on an antibiogram of the culture; however, a recommended first-line antibiotic in human medicine is ciprofloxacin, second line drugs include azithromycin, pivmecillinam, ceftriaxone. Due to rapid mutation and changing resistance patterns, it is advised to consult current guidelines: https://www.cdc.gov/shigella/treatment/index.html. Prevention and control: Asymptomatic carriers with intermittent shedding may make eradication and control of shigellosis difficult. Preventative control programs should include a good sanitation protocol and animal collection management. The existence of multiple Shigella serotypes and their growing resistance to antibiotics stress the urgent need for the development of a low-cost vaccine that is protective across all serotypes. No vaccine is yet officially available.

Testing potentially contaminated feed, water sources, and habitat surfaces with PCR can help to prevent exposure. Quarantine protocols to identify potential asymptomatic carriers (history of exposure at previous institution). Public health and food safety officials may be able to assist with source investigations using source genome sequences. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: Culture and serotyping of Shigella of any animals potentially in contact with infected animals and asymptomatic carrier in a collection with shigellosis outbreak. It is recommended to consult with the CDC and/or the local Health Department for staff considerations and public health contact investigation. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Do not introduce any unexposed/ naive animal to the affected animal(s). This would likely be a case-by-case and joint veterinary/animal management decision. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: An outbreak may be considered resolved after animals return to full health and test negative for Shigella.

texto: -  Mammals: - o Pinnipeds: Sinusitis, rhinitis, bronchopneumonia. O. attenuata adults primarily occupy the nasopharynx, while O. diminuata are found in the lungs. Causative organism: Anatrichosoma is a genus of nematodes belonging to the family Trichuridae. -  Anatrichosoma cutaneum and A. cynomolgi have been found in nasal and cutaneous lesions in wild-caught and captive primates and are the presumed cause of most human and domestic animal cases. A. buccalis has been found in the oral mucosa of opossums, and was suspected in one human case cluster. -  A. ocularis, A. gerbilis, and A. haycocki have been reported in wild or wild-caught tree shrews, gerbilid and murid rodents, and dasyurid marsupials, respectively. -  Adult female Anatrichosomes tunnel through the epidermis, laying embryonated ova which reach the surface through normal exfoliation. Ova are released directly into the environment or swallowed during grooming and passed in feces. Adult males reside in the dermis. -  Mechanism of infection is unknown. Experimental direct infection has been unsuccessful, suggesting an indirect life cycle, but no intermediate host has been identified. Free immature A. haycocki were found in the intestine of dasyurid hosts, suggesting an enteric route of infection.

Lesions have recurred after treatment in captive primates, suggesting either reinfection or incomplete response to treatment. Zoonotic potential: Rare. Eight human cases reported (Asia, Europe, USA); US cases in 2010 and 2014 all had oral lesions and history of travel to Mexico. Exposure route unknown, although the 2014 patients had placed live wild-collected snails on their faces as a skincare treatment. Distribution: Documented in wild animals from the Americas, the Middle East, Africa, India, Asia, and Australia, and in humans and domestic animals in the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia. Incubation period: Unknown; clinical lesions are associated with migration of adult worms.

-  Cutaneous (A. cutaneum, A. cynomolgi): Nodules or track-like lesions with ulceration, apparent predilection for glabrous skin. Severe ulcerative pododermatitis in domestic cats. -  Nasal (A. cynomolgi, A. cutaneum): Nodules or tracks in the nasal mucosa of primates, minimal local inflammation. -  Oral (A. buccalis): Nodules or tracks in the oral mucosa. Minimal local inflammation in opossums, mucosal ulceration in suspected human cases. -  Gastric (A. gerbilis): Nodules or tracks in the gastric mucosa of gerbilid and murid rodents. -  Ocular (A. ocularis): Adults within the corneal or conjunctival epithelium of tree shrews, minimal local inflammation. -  Glandular (A. haycocki): Adults within the paracloacal glands or encapsulated in the lumen of the cloaca of Antechinus spp., minimal local inflammation. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Adults and ova embedded in epithelial tissue on histopathology. Diagnosis: Cytology or biopsy of lesion, mucosal swab, skin scrape, or fecal flotation. Best is identification of adults or eggs in tissue. Ova are Trichuris-like, brown, bioperculate and larvated, approximately 78 x 35 um.

-  Avermectins and benzimidazoles have effectively resolved clinical lesions in reported cases, recurrence is infrequently reported. -  Primates: Fenbendazole 10-25 mg/kg PO once daily for 3-10 days. -  Domestic cat: Ivermectin 0.3 mg/kg SC weekly for 4 weeks. -  Human: Mebendazole 100 mg PO twice daily for 20 days or albendazole 400 mg PO once daily for 3 days. Prevention and control: The mechanism of infection is unknown. However, control of feral animals and wildlife in exhibit areas, sanitation and hygiene with regular removal of feces from enclosures, and routine prophylactic deworming are expected to be beneficial. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: None specified; expect sensitivity as for Trichuris spp. and Capillaria spp. Notification: None required. secao: Causative organism: Bertiella spp. (cestode, family Anoplocephalidae).
texto: -  Australian marsupials (B. trichosuri). Zoonotic potential: Yes. Human infection (via accidental ingestion of the intermediate host), can occur in those having close contact with the environment of definitive hosts (especially primates) and is most common in children. Distribution: Africa, Asia, South America, Australasia. Incubation period: Unknown. Clinical signs: Typically none. Humans have been reported to experience intermittent diarrhea, abdominal pain, anorexia, and weight loss. Increased leaf swallowing behavior has been reported in wild chimpanzees. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: The adult tapeworm may be found in the small intestine. Diagnosis: Identification of eggs or gravid proglottids in feces, identification of adult worm at necropsy. Free eggs from gravid segments or feces are 40-46µm long and 36-40µm wide in B. mucronata and 48-60µm long and 40-60µm wide in B. studeri. Material required for laboratory analysis: Feces. Relevant diagnostic laboratories: Any veterinary diagnostic laboratory with a parasitologist on staff. Treatment: Praziquantel.

-  Wild: Avoid contact with soil in proximity of definitive hosts. Proper hygiene practices and food safety in endemic areas. -  Captivity: quarantine, screen all animals for infection and treat accordingly. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Commonly used disinfectants are generally not effective in killing tapeworm eggs or larvae. Recent research has demonstrated that sodium hypochlorite is effective in killing Taenia spp. eggs, but its effectiveness against Bertiella spp. eggs is currently unknown. Notification: None. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Eliminate infection in positive animals prior to introduction to other animals. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: N/A. Experts who may be consulted: While no specific researchers are currently reporting expertise in this parasite, parasitology staffs at veterinary colleges would be a good option; it would be prudent to consider Australian veterinary colleges due to parasite location. References: 1. | Beveridge I.

Originally compiled by Ginger L. Takle (2011); updated by Karen Terio (2013, 2018) Susceptible animal groups: Great apes, Old World monkeys, suids, camelids, ruminants, rodents, canids, elephants. Causative organism: Most reports do not speciate but instead just list Oesophagostomum spp.; identified host to species relationships are: -  Primates - Oesophagostomum bifurcum, O. stephanostomum, and other species. -  Ruminants - O. columbianum, O. venulosum, O. radiatum and other species may be found in wild ruminants. -  New and Old World camelids - O. venulosum and other species. -  Suids - O. dentatum, O. brevicaudum, O. quadrispinulatum, and other species may be found in wild suids. -  Elephants - O. aceleatum, O. columbianum. -  Fox - O. muntiacum. -  Cane rats - O. venulosum. Zoonotic potential: Yes, Oesophagostomum bifurcum and O. stephanostomum are zoonotic. Distribution: Worldwide, but most commonly occurs in the tropics and subtropics. Incubation period: Ova passed in feces hatch and develop into infective L3 in approximately 2-7 days, depending on environmental conditions.

but most commonly occurs in the tropics and subtropics. Incubation period: Ova passed in feces hatch and develop into infective L3 in approximately 2-7 days, depending on environmental conditions. After ingestion, the L3 burrow into the intestinal wall forming cystic nodules to granulomas within the submucosa, muscularis and mesentery in which the nematodes molt into fourth-stage larvae (L4). The L4 can then remain in the nodules or return to the intestinal lumen where they develop to the adult stage. Generally, pre-patent period is considered 3242 days.

-  Primates - Clinical signs can range from intermittent diarrhea to inappetence, severe mucoid bloody diarrhea, pale mucous membranes, weakness, lethargy, weight loss, vomiting, abdominal pain, and death. -  Ruminants and Suids - fetid diarrhea, anorexia, weakness, emaciation, and death. If chronic infection is present, clinical signs may be seen that are consistent with decreased intestinal motility, stenosis, or intussusception. -  Elephants, fox, and cane rats - none reported to date. Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Oesophagostomum spp. are also known as nodular worms due to their gross appearance. The L3 penetrate deep into and encyst in the lamina propria, submucosa, muscularis of the small and large intestine and in some cases the adjacent mesentery. Granulomas (nodules) form around the larvae and can be 5-50mm in diameter. These granulomas may contain reddish brown fluid and a central nematode. In some sections, inflammation is associated with migration tracts and abdominal adhesions, or peritonitis may be present. Mesenteric lymph nodes are often enlarged. Diagnosis: Identification of ova on routine fecal examination or by PCR.

with migration tracts and abdominal adhesions, or peritonitis may be present. Mesenteric lymph nodes are often enlarged. Diagnosis: Identification of ova on routine fecal examination or by PCR. Ova can be confused easily with 'hookworm' eggs; identification of larvae or adults during intestinal biopsy or at necropsy. Material required for laboratory analysis: Fecal sample, larvae or adult worms, nodular intestinal tissues. Relevant Diagnostic lab: Any diagnostic laboratory with routine parasitological capabilities should be able to diagnose this infection as fecal flotation is an effective test. Treatment: Macrocyclic lactones (ivermectin, eprinomectin), pyrantel pamoate, monepantel or benzimidazoles (albendazole) can be administered. Recent reports of resistance to ivermectin and albendazole in some populations. Where possible, surgical excision of the nodules may be performed. Prevention and control: Quarantine of new animals, parasite monitoring program, isolation and treatment of affected animals, proper sanitation and waste removal can assist with prevention. Freeliving larval stages (L1- infective L3) survive in the environment (moisture and temperature dependent).

Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Commonly used disinfectants can be used after removal of feces from the area. Notification: None. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Treat infected or potentially infected animals prior to introduction to non-infected animals. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: Negative fecal examinations can be used to identify persistent infections that should be resolved before introductions. Experts who may be consulted: Parasitologists are well versed in this disease.

-  Almost exclusively snakes of the Boidae and Pythonidae families. Koch's postulates have been satisfied with experimental infections of Python regius and Boa constrictor. -  There is one report of Wagler's pit vipers (Tropidolaemus wagleri) with respiratory signs that were reptarenavirus PCR-positive. -  Histopathological inclusions have been reported in palm vipers (Bothriechis marchi), Eastern kingsnakes (Lampropeltis getulus), and corn snakes (Elaphe guttata). Causative organism: Family Arenaviridae, genus Reptarenavirus; this etiological agent has only recently been identified. -  It seems that pathogenic and non-pathogenic reptarenaviruses exist, and pathogenic ones can affect species differently. Arenaviral coinfections may be common in snakes clinical for IBD. -  Older literature suspected a retrovirus was causative. Zoonotic potential: No.

-  Highly variable - infected animals can be asymptomatic or develop severe disease, which can include anorexia, regurgitation, neurological signs (disorientation, ataxia, head tremors, opisthotonus, inability to right itself, and flaccid paralysis), or secondary bacterial infections (stomatitis and pneumonia). -  Pythons are reported to have a more acute, severe, and CNS-involved disease progression without regurgitation or other gastrointestinal signs -  Boas, especially boa constrictors, commonly have regurgitation, anorexia and CNS signs. Boas can maintain high levels of viremia and accumulated widespread intracytoplasmic inclusions without clinical signs, and may have more chronic disease course. -  Lymphoproliferative disorders have recently been associated with IBD in boa constrictors.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: -  Eosinophilic to amphophilic intracytoplasmic (IC) inclusions in H&E-stained tissue sections; composed of ∼68 kDa reptarenaviral nucleoprotein (NP). -  Cells with inclusions can frequently be observed in the absence of associated inflammation. -  Tissue tropism can be diverse. Within the CNS, inclusions may be observed in neurons and glial cells. With acute neurologic disease (e.g. pythons), inclusions are often limited to the CNS. With chronic disease (e.g. boa constrictors), inclusions can be seen in epithelial cells (enteric, respiratory, and renal), hepatocytes, pancreatic acinar cells, and mononuclear cells. Diagnosis: As detailed above, finding IC inclusions or virus by PCR in a live python can be challenging; less so for a boa. -  Ante-mortem, diagnostic options include: - o Light microscopy exam of a peripheral blood smear for IC inclusions in WBCs with H&E or Wright Giemsa stain, - o Arenavirus RT-PCR at University of Florida of an esophageal swab or whole blood sample, - o Tissue biopsies (esophageal tonsils, liver, kidney) obtained via endoscopy with IC inclusions seen on H&E stain +/- Arenavirus RT-PCR at University of Florida.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: swab or whole blood sample, - o Tissue biopsies (esophageal tonsils, liver, kidney) obtained via endoscopy with IC inclusions seen on H&E stain +/- Arenavirus RT-PCR at University of Florida. -  For post-mortem, histopathology and/or PCR on brain, kidney, liver, pancreas are recommended. -  Of note, immunohistochemical testing of blood and tissues for NP used to be available at University of Florida, but has been discontinued. Material required for laboratory analysis: Blood, esophageal swabs, serum or biopsies from the liver, tonsils or gastric mucosa. Contact laboratory for handling and shipping instructions.

-  Quarantine of all incoming snakes for a minimum of 90 days. Good hygiene, prevention of exposure to infected animals, pest control and removal of infected animals. See below for disinfection recommendations. -  Snakes suspected of IBD should be isolated. Diagnostic samples mentioned above should be collected and submitted for evaluation. Infected snakes should be euthanized and necropsied. -  One report vaccinated four Boa constrictors with either inactivated virus or recombinant NP, which resulted in strong antibody responses. Three of the four vaccinated snakes seemed to sustain challenge with the same reptarenavirus; however, neither of the two snakes rechallenged with different reptarenaviruses remained uninfected. Suggested Disinfectant for Housing Facilities: Arenaviruses are an enveloped RNA virus; they can be inactivated by most detergents and disinfectants including 1% sodium hypochlorite, phenolic compounds, 3% acetic acid, lipid solvents and detergents (e.g. sodium dodecyl sulfate [SDS]), formaldehyde, and glutaraldehyde (2%).

and disinfectants including 1% sodium hypochlorite, phenolic compounds, 3% acetic acid, lipid solvents and detergents (e.g. sodium dodecyl sulfate [SDS]), formaldehyde, and glutaraldehyde (2%). Arenaviruses, in general, are inactivated with heating to 5660°C (122-140°F), exposure to gamma or UV irradiation, exposure to pH less than 5.5 or greater than 8.52, autoclaving, incineration, and boiling.

Measures Required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measure Required for Introducing Animals to Infected Animal: Not recommended. Conditions for Restoring Disease-Free Status after an Outbreak: Sick snakes should never be introduced into an established collection. It is unknown what percentage of snakes with reptarenavirus infection will develop clinical signs and how many will remain clinically healthy.

Causative organism: Chelonid alphaherpesvirus 5 (ChAHV5; family Herpesviridae, subfamily alphaherpesvirinae, genus Scutavirus) is the suspected etiological agent of fibropapillomatosis. -  The virus has been isolated from FP tumors, as well as animals without lesions, suggesting that other factors may be involved in lesion development. FP lesions can be transmitted using cell-free tumor extracts, and ChAHV5 has been isolated in 3-dimensional tissue cultures. -  Viral variants appear to cluster based on geographic origin, rather than host species: western Atlantic (Florida, Barbados, Texas); Atlantic (Puerto Rico, Gulf of Guinea); midwest-Pacific (Hawaii, Australia, Indonesia); and eastern Pacific (Costa Rica, California). -  Other factors including warm water temperatures, natural biotoxins, co-infections, immunosuppression, proximity to shallow/inshore waters of coastal habitats, and other ecological factors have been associated with FP lesion occurrence. Zoonotic potential: None.

co-infections, immunosuppression, proximity to shallow/inshore waters of coastal habitats, and other ecological factors have been associated with FP lesion occurrence. Zoonotic potential: None. Distribution: Worldwide, but primarily circumtropical. Prevalence of disease varies spatially and temporally (0 - 92%). It may be associated with eutrophic coastal ecosystems with high human population densities and agricultural run-off. The disease was first documented in 1938. Reported increase in prevalence in the late 1950's, especially in specific areas such as the Florida Keys and Indian River Lagoon, Florida, and Hawaii. Prevalence seems to be decreasing in Hawaii while increasing in other regions.

-  Clinically apparent FP developed 15 - 43 weeks after experimental inoculation. Initiation of tumor growth was positively correlated with water temperature. -  Inoculated turtles developed antibodies to CFPHV in < 1 year if they developed tumors. Turtles that did not develop tumors, did not seroconvert.

-  Focal to multifocal flat, plaque-like, or raised exophytic, verrucous masses that are white/grey/black and vary in diameter from 0.1 to >30 cm. Cutaneous lesions are typically located on the head, neck, and limbs but may also develop on the cornea, sclera, conjunctiva, and surface of the carapace and plastron. Many fibropapillomatous lesions will resolve spontaneously, particularly smaller tumors. Number and severity may increase with curved carapace length (CCL) then decrease as CCL increases further. -  Internal fibromas are less common, can affect all internal organs, and are generally associated with "end-stage" fibropapillomatosis. -  When tumors are numerous or large in size, they may impinge on function of affected structures as well as disrupt the turtle's ability to swim, dive, and forage which leads to progressive debilitation and death. Secondary bacterial and/or fungal infections associated with larger or ulcerated masses.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: -  Fibropapillomas are raised, sessile or polypoid masses with verrucous or smooth surfaces. Internal tumors can be found in the oral cavity, glottis, heart, lungs, liver, gall bladder, kidneys, skeletal muscle, and gastrointestinal tract, and are generally described as fibromas, myxofibromas, and fibrosarcomas of low-grade malignancy. -  Common histological descriptions include cytoplasmic vacuolation, ballooning degeneration of epidermal cells, and benign papillary epidermal hyperplasia (especially in the stratum spinosum) supported by thick stalks of proliferating fibrovascular stroma characterized by disorganized collagen fibers. Perivascular mononuclear cell inflammation is often observed in the deeper layers of the dermis. Eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions and mitoses are rare.

-  Presence of skin or oral masses consistent in appearance with fibropapillomas. -  Endoscopy, laparoscopy, radiography, ultrasonography, CT, MRI, and coeliotomy can be useful diagnostic modalities for identifying visceral tumors. -  Definitive diagnosis requires compatible histopathology findings. Further support of a diagnosis occurs if intralesional DNA of ChAHV5 are detected by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) from tissue obtained from tumors. In situ hybridization (ISH) can be used to detect ChAHV5 in nuclei of infected epithelial cells. Material required for laboratory analysis: Formalin-fixed tissue for histology & frozen tissue for PCR. Relevant diagnostic laboratories: All histopathology labs can assess tissues for compatible lesions. -  Herpesviral PCR and sequencing, University of Florida Zoo Med Diagnostic Lab, Gainesville, Florida, USA.

-  Supportive care (appropriate temperature, good water quality, low stocking density, fluid therapy, adequate nutrition, and, as needed, systemic antibiotics). -  Surgical excision; CO2 laser-mediated tumor removal surgery followed by second intention healing is usually recommended. Recurrence of surgically removed lesions reported in up to 50% of cases. Acyclovir has been found anecdotally to be useful. Tumors on and around the eyes are most important to remove. -  Electrochemotherapy using intralesional bleomycin sulfate injections is reported; complete resolution took up to 10 months. Controlled studies on improved outcomes are lacking. -  Turtles with internal tumors may require euthanasia. Prevention and control: Currently no prevention and control measures for wild populations are available. In captivity, fibropapillomatous turtles should be quarantined from unaffected turtles, including by a separate water system. Some turtle rehabilitation centers will not accept turtles affected by fibropapillomas. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Standard disinfectants effective for herpesviruses should be effective against ChAHV5. Notification: Not required.

turtles affected by fibropapillomas. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Standard disinfectants effective for herpesviruses should be effective against ChAHV5. Notification: Not required. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: None. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: Unaffected individuals should not be introduced to affected turtles. Conditions for restoring disease-free status after an outbreak: None known. It is probable that affected turtles are ChAHV5 carriers for life. Experienced marine turtle rehabilitation facilities consider release of animals if they remain tumor-free for an extended period of time (up to one year) after surgical removal and are otherwise healthy, although sufficient long-term housing is rarely available in large stranding events to accommodate this approach.

Causative organism: Scutavirus testudinidalpha, previously known as Testudinid herpesviruses (TeAHVs) (and prior known as tortoise herpesviruses) have four currently known genotypes: TeAHV1, -2, -3 and -4. Of them the only genotype 3 (Scutavirus testudinidalpha3) is recognized at the species level by the International committee on taxonomy of viruses (ICTV). The name of Testudinid alphaherpesvirus 3 and in general of Testudinid alphaherpesviruses and/or Testudinid herpesviruses are still in use as common name, including their acronym (TeHV3-TeAHV3).

The name of Testudinid alphaherpesvirus 3 and in general of Testudinid alphaherpesviruses and/or Testudinid herpesviruses are still in use as common name, including their acronym (TeHV3-TeAHV3). In diseased individuals, TeAHV1, -2 and -3 have been detected or isolated. The TeAHV3 genotype includes at least two genogroups (A, B) that might be characterized by distinct virulence but both lethal. Genogroup A is the most common, genogroup B is putatively the most virulent. TeAHV4 has been detected also in a clinically ill leopard tortoise (Stigmochelys pardalis).

- ∞ TeAHV1 and -3 have been detected worldwide; more commonly in the genus Testudo but also in several other tortoise species not autochthonous of the Eurasian area. - ∞ TeAHV2 was originally detected only in the USA in desert tortoises (Gopherus agassizii). Recently, the same genotype was detected in a Gopherus berlandieri from Spain. Detection of herpesvirus-like particles had been reported several decades ago in Gopherus agassizii kept in Spain. - ∞ TeAHV4 has been detected in the US in a clinically healthy, imported Bowsprit tortoise and in in a captive-bred leopard tortoise co-infected with Mycoplasma sp. in Europe. Both Bowsprit and leopard tortoises are African tortoises. It is likely that at least for some of the genotypes, the current area of distribution might only partially overlap with their original ones because of the extensive movements that the species have undergone especially because of the pet trade. Incubation period: Following experimental infection in Greek tortoises, the first clinical signs were recorded 7 to 12 days post inoculation. The overall course of the disease lasted 2.5 weeks.

Incubation period: Following experimental infection in Greek tortoises, the first clinical signs were recorded 7 to 12 days post inoculation. The overall course of the disease lasted 2.5 weeks. In Hermann's tortoises experimental inoculation of the virus (genotype 3) was followed by the occurrence of clinical signs within 20 days from inoculation.

- ∞ The disease originally was called "stomatitis and rhinitis disease" or "running nose" and it was named after its most common clinical signs that include a diphtheronecrotic stomatitis and a glossitis with nasal, oral and eye discharge. The discharges are generally clear, intermittent and recurrent. Monolateral or bilateral recurrent conjunctivitis is also common. Cervical edema and epistaxis in severe cases has been reported. The oral plaques have been shown to develop and eventually fully regress in the survival animals within a 2.5 weeks period of time during an experimental transmission study in Greek tortoises. Following the loss of the crusts covering the healing plaques, no scar can be detected after the resolution of the oral lesions. A band of chalky white material can be observed along the rim of the external aspect of the mandible after the oral discharge has resolved. Respiratory and neurological signs might follow along more general signs such as lethargy and anorexia. Not all the clinical signs described above can be detected in the same diseased individuals and some infected tortoise might not develop obvious clinical signs at all.

Similar clinical signs were observed also in a more recent transmission study carried out with TeAHV3 in Herman's tortoises. - ∞ It is important to consider that none of the clinical signs described above are specific for TeAHVs, since similar oral plaques have also been described in tortoises infected with less common iridovirus and virus X (topivirus-tortoise picornavirus). However, from an epidemiologically stand point, the presence of diphtheronecrotic plaques is overrepresented in Testudo spp infected with TeAHV3 (there is a single report of similar plaques in Testudo spp following Ranavirus infection). Additionally, nasal discharge and conjunctivitis, in absence of stomatitis, are commonly described in tortoises infected with Mycoplasma agassizii (an etiologic agent of the upper respiratory tract disease-URTD).

Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings: Classic gross lesions include diphtheronecrotic plaques over the mucosa of the oral cavity and the tongue, occasionally extending over the mucosa of the esophagus and of the trachea up to the lung. Hepatomegaly and enteritis have also been described. The histologic hallmark of the disease is the presence of eosinophilic to amphophilic intranuclear inclusions in most of the epithelial tissues. Inclusions can also be observed within the central nervous system either associated or not with inflammation. Inclusions are likely to be detectable for a limited time during the initial phase of the disease. Diagnosis: The clinical diagnosis relies on the detection of the clinical signs described above. The clinical diagnosis requires the confirmation by laboratory testing. Multiple molecular and serological tests are available for the diagnosis of Testudinid herpesvirus infection.

Multiple molecular and serological tests are available for the diagnosis of Testudinid herpesvirus infection. - ∞ Serology - The available serological tests comprise an ELISA and a serum neutralization test (SNT), while the molecular diagnostic tests comprise multiple PCR protocols for the partial amplification of different herpesvirus genes. The ELISA test has been developed to detect TeAHV3 exposure and it has been validated for Greek and Hermann's tortoises. The test detects the large majority of the antibody developed by the host against the virus after seroconversion. Although the test can detect the exposure to TeAHV3 relatively early following the infection, for a reliable diagnosis it is recommended to test a suspected individual two times no less than 8 weeks a part. A modified version of the same test has been shown to be able to detect TeAHV2 exposure in desert tortoises, although in this format the test has not been fully validated.

SNT similarly to the ELISA, allows the detection of the exposure of an individual to a Testudinid herpesvirus due to the presence of circulating antiTeAHVs antibody (serum neutralizing in this case) following seroconversion. This test can be applied to any species of tortoise, and it requires live virus to be carried out. SNT can detect seroconversion to TeAHVs 2-5 weeks after the ELISA test. For this reason, it is suggested to test the suspected animals two times 10-12 weeks apart for a reliable detection of the occurred seroconversion when using the SNT. Both ELISA and SNT show comparable specificity and sensitivity. - ∞ Molecular diagnosis - Several PCR protocols have been developed for the diagnosis of TeAHVs infection. A PCR test targeting the partial sequence of the viral DNA polymerase gene is available for the specific detection of TeAHV1. Another protocol has been developed for the detection of the partial sequence of the helicase gene of TeAHV3.

The same protocol also allows the detection of the homologous gene of the TeAHV1 genotype following a specific modification of the test conditions. A PCR test directed to the amplification of the partial sequence of the ribonucleotide reductase (RR) (large subunit) of TeAHV3 has also been developed. This test can also amplify the homologous gene portion of TeAHV2, although a specific PCR protocol is also available for the partial amplification of TeAHV2 RR. Finally, a PCR protocol, not specifically developed for TeAHVs but more in general for the detection of the members of the family Herpesviridae is also available and allows the detection of all the 4 genotypes of TeAHVs known up to date (partial amplification of the DNA polymerase gene; the target is a different region from that used for TeAHV-1 amplification).

Recently, a PCR protocol has been developed to differentiate viral strains belonging to distinct genogroups (A, B) within the TeAHV3 genotype, which might be associated with distinct virulence. - ∞ Histopathology - routine histopathologic diagnosis of TeAHVs infection is more often considered a post-mortem diagnostic method. It is based on the detection of the classic intranuclear inclusions. An immunohistochemistry and an in-situ hybridization method are also available for the detection of TeAHVs antigen and DNA in tissue, respectively and can be - used to enhance the sensitivity of the histopathological diagnosis. Electron microscopy is also commonly used to detect the presence of the virus in tissues. - ∞ Viral isolation - Viral isolation of TeAHV1 and -3 can be performed on reptilian cell cultures (TH-1 cells, subline B1, ATCC CCL-50). Classic cytopathic effects include cell rounding with cell detachment and lysis (plaque formation).

- ∞ Serology - 0.2-0.5 ml serum in plastic tube. Store at 4ºC and ship refrigerated. - ∞ Virology - Pharyngeal swabs are collected for live animals. For dead animals, it is helpful to send the entire carcass if available or 1 g portions of each organ, ideally. If this approach is not possible, the head (including the tongue) of the suspected individual can be submitted. Place samples in viral transport media with antibiotic (2-3 ml for swabs and 5 ml per each tissue sample). Store the samples at 4ºC for very short-term storage and -80ºC for long-term storage. Ship samples refrigerated or on dry ice accordingly. Preserve the entire carcass and the head at 4ºC and ship refrigerated immediately. - ∞ Molecular diagnostic - Same samples described for virology but in this case viral transport media is not required. Samples can be stored and shipped also as described for the virology samples, with the exception that for molecular diagnostic the samples can be stored also at - 20ºC if -80ºC freezers are not available. If only formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues are available, whole tissue block(s) can be used.

If not possible, please send 3 sections 20μ-thick each (per tissue block) in a plastic tube (DNAse- and RNAse-free). The samples do not need to be refrigerated but should protected from light. - ∞ Histopathology - The entire carcass is preferred if the carcass can be stored at 4ºC and shipped immediately refrigerated. - ∞ Tortoises showing clinical signs consistent with TeAHVs infection should be isolated from clinically healthy individuals and tested for the presence of TeAHVs (PCR, virus isolation) and for the exposure to the virus by ELISA or SNT. All clinical animals should also be treated with antiviral drugs and supportive therapy as appropriate. Serological tests need to be repeated after 8 (ELISA) or 10-12 weeks (SNT) for all the tortoises showing clinical signs that tested negative at the first sampling. - ∞ Clinically healthy exposed animals should be closely monitored and tested for viral exposure similarly to what described above. - ∞ Serologically and/or PCR positive animals that have recovered from the disease and clinically healthy animals that have seroconverted (and/or have tested positive by PCR) following viral exposure should be considered carrier for life. Circumstantial evidence does not completely rule out vertical transmission at the moment. - ∞ Preventive measures include: - o All the tortoises entering established collections should be tested for the presence and exposure to the virus ideally both by molecular and serological tests. Viral isolation is also recommended.

o All the tortoises entering established collections should be tested for the presence and exposure to the virus ideally both by molecular and serological tests. Viral isolation is also recommended. Animals should be tested during the quarantine period, which ideally should last no less than 6 months. Molecular diagnostic tests and viral isolation are relevant in the acute stage of the disease and during viral recrudescence when the virus is actively replicating. Serological tests are relevant especially after the acute stage of the disease, during the latency of the virus, when seroconversion has occurred, and no active viral replication can be detected. Testing an animal during the acute stage of the disease with serological tests only is likely to provide a false negative result, since seroconversion has not occurred yet. However, this is still recommended since some diseased animals might not be showing a primary infection, but differently a recrudescence of the infection and so they might have already seroconverted. Additionally, for naïve negative animals this would be considered the "pre-immune" serum.

Clinically healthy infected animals that have survived the acute stage of the disease are likely to shed the virus only sporadically and this can determine a high rate of false negative animals if tested solely by PCR and/or virus isolation at that time. More frequent viral shedding occurs in infected animals post brumation. It is recommended to repeat two serological tests no less than 8 or 10-12 weeks apart when running the ELISA test or the SNT, respectively. Occasional "non-reactors" do exist. - o It is very important to avoid mixing of different tortoise species due to evidence of different species-specific resistances/sensitivity to TeAHVs. Mixing of different species might be fatal for the less resistant species. - o It is important to avoid overcrowding since close contact between tortoises is considered to enhance the transmission of TeAHVs. - o Contaminated soil might contain viable virus for 2-4 up to 9-24 weeks according to the season of the year.

Exposure to full sunlight of the contaminated soil might reduce the viability of the virus present. - o Disposable gloves and shoe cover should be changed when moving from pen to pen and when touching different tortoises. An appropriate hands disinfectant is also recommended. - o A veterinary health check should be performed ideally every 6 months. For tortoises from temperate climates a health check performed before and after brumation is critical. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: Any proven virucidal compound may be used to disinfect contaminated instrument and/or pen furniture. Notification: TeAHVs associated diseases are not reportable at the moment. Measures required under the Animal Disease Surveillance Plan: N/A. Measures required for introducing animals to infected animal: If a seronegative animal is introduced to a seropositive animal, it should be expected that the seronegative animal will seroconvert eventually.

Zoonotic? No Current update by Garrett Fraess (2026) Reviewed by Randy Junge (2026) Susceptible animal groups: All snakes, especially Viperidae. Species specific susceptibility is likely - experimental infection resulted in severe disease in corn snakes, mild disease in ball pythons. Paramyxovirus also reported in Gila monster, tegu, and caiman lizards. Rarely, tortoises with pneumonia have had ferlaviruses isolated. Causative organism: Ophidian paramyxovirus - divided into four genetic clusters (genogroups) - A, B, C, and Tortoise. In experimentally infected corn snakes, Type A is the least pathogenic, with Type B as the most pathogenic. The genus Ferlavirus is named after Fer-de-Lance virus (FDLV), which was the first OPMV isolated from the snake. FDLV is considered the type species of the genus. Zoonotic potential: None.

The genus Ferlavirus is named after Fer-de-Lance virus (FDLV), which was the first OPMV isolated from the snake. FDLV is considered the type species of the genus. Zoonotic potential: None. Distribution: Outbreaks have been documented in multiple private and zoological collections worldwide; seroconversion and outbreaks have been documented in wild specimens and importance of which remains uncertain. Outbreaks are more common from January through May. Incubation period: Seroconversion may take 8 weeks but the incubation period has been documented to be as long as 10 months in some specimens. Five experimentally infected rattlesnakes developed clinical signs in a few days, and died within 22 days of infection. Clinical signs: Acute death, respiratory compromise, blood or exudate in the oral cavity or nares, neurologic signs, including head tremors, star gazing, abnormal posture, flaccid paralysis, convulsions, and loss of righting reflex. In more chronic cases: anorexia, regurgitation, cachexia, lethargy, and abnormal feces. As with other paramyxoviruses, OPMV causes immunosuppression, so secondary infections are common, especially with Salmonella spp.

secao: Post mortem, gross, or histologic findings:
texto: - ∞ No pathognomonic lesions occur with this disease. Hyperplasia of ciliated cells in the lungs and Type II pneumocytes result in a severely thickened air-blood barrier which dramatically reduces lung function. Inflammatory cell infiltration and exudation/edema worsen this compromise. Rare eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions may be seen. - ∞ CNS involvement entails encephalitis with multifocal gliosis, moderate ballooning of axon fibers in the brain stem and spinal cord. Hepatic necrosis or multifocal pyogranulomatous inflammation is often observed. Hyperplasia of pancreatic ducts and acinar cells with cystic dilatation has been observed. The salivary glands can be affected by ductular dilatation, flattening of the ductular epithelium, and accumulation of cellular debris and secretory material in the lumen. - ∞ Gross findings range from no lesions to respiratory lesions including pulmonary congestion, hemorrhage, respiratory exudates, and pneumonia, pancreatic hyperplasia, and hepatic necrosis and granulomas may all be macroscopically evident. Diagnosis: Recommended antemortem diagnostic is PCR of oral/choanal swabs or tracheal/pulmonary lavage samples.

- ∞ All aquatic turtles, captive & free-ranging are likely susceptible. - ∞ Consistent lesions (epithelial inclusion cysts of the shell; described further below), with the pathogen identified by PCR, culture, or GMS stain, have been reported in the following genera: Actinemys, Apalone, Chelus, Clemmys, Emydoidea, Emydura, Graptemys, Heosemys, Hydromedusa, Podocnemis, Pseudemys, and Trachemys. - ∞ Macrochelys temminckii have been found to be PCR positive with dermatitis; not shell disease. Causative organism: Emydomyces testavorans is a keratinophilic fungi belonging to the order Onygenales and is newly reported. Other primary reptilian fungal pathogens of the order Onygenales are Nannizziopsis spp., Paranannizziopsis spp., and Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola. Zoonotic potential: None. Reviewed by Matt Allender (2026) Distribution: North America. Incubation period: Unknown. Clinical signs: The shell can appear to have bleaching of epidermis in early stages of the disease. Can progress to pitting or ulceration of the shell with pockets of tan to black friable debris and bone loss that can be full thickness.

to have bleaching of epidermis in early stages of the disease. Can progress to pitting or ulceration of the shell with pockets of tan to black friable debris and bone loss that can be full thickness. However, this pathogen can be insidious with fairly normal appearing shells on the surface with advanced lesions found via computed tomography (CT). This advanced imaging modality is highly recommended to screen turtles, determine severity, and plan for surgery. Some animals may have dermatitis of the palmar/plantar feet, ventral neck, and cloaca.

- ∞ Postmortem/gross findings: Bleaching of epidermis, loss of normal architecture with pitting or ulceration, pockets of tan to black friable debris, loss of bone resulting in softening or pliability of the shell, and deep penetrating lesions may be appreciated during gross necropsy. - ∞ Histologic features: Epidermal ulceration, epithelial inclusion cysts characterized by necrotic bone and keratinaceous debris surrounded by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, fibrin deposition, granulocytic to granulomatous inflammation, osteonecrosis, peripheral reactive bone proliferation and fibroplasia associated with narrow, septate branching fungi are characteristic findings.

- ∞ Antemortem: combination of typical examination findings, radiographs or computed tomography (CT) showing radiolucency consistent with osteolysis, and qPCR indicating presence of Emydomyces testavorans associated with lesions. For qPCR, a combined oralcloacal-shell swab correlated with infection best as compared to shell swabs or oral-cloacal swabs alone. Testing of water is most sensitive for detection of DNA if multiple animals are involved. CT least sensitive in early disease. - ∞ Postmortem: characteristic gross and histologic findings in association with positive qPCR.

- ∞ Sterile swabs and scrapes or tissue samples contained within a cryovial, or red top tube can be submitted for qPCR. - ∞ Sample transport studies for this fungus have not been conducted yet; common convention is that samples be moistened with sterile saline in cryovial, but it has been found that sterile saline reduced detection ability in turtles with ranavirus compared to dry swabs.

- ∞ Aggressive debridement of all diseased keratin, bone, and necrotic material followed by covering the exposed areas with terbinafine-impregnated bone cement will usually allow the affected area of shell to heal over several months with replacement of the cement patches monthly. Infected cavities and cysts may not be detectable without CT scanning and may not be fully accessible for debridement in areas with full thickness shell lesions. - ∞ Topical terbinafine ointment and immersion baths may be used on skin and superficial shell infections. Terbinafine baths (1-2g/L) three times weekly for extended periods appear promising in early studies. - ∞ A pharmacokinetic study shows promise for achieving fungicidal plasma concentrations of terbinafine when administered every 24 or 48 hours via earthworm bioencapsulation. Previous studies of systemic antifungal treatment including terbinafine administered by nebulization, orally or subcutaneous implant and voriconazole by injection did not achieve a consistent fungicidal concentration or proven clinical efficacy. - ∞ Housing of freshwater turtles in brackish water using biofiltration system +/- UV may be beneficial.

injection did not achieve a consistent fungicidal concentration or proven clinical efficacy. - ∞ Housing of freshwater turtles in brackish water using biofiltration system +/- UV may be beneficial. - ∞ Clearing infections completely is unlikely and recurrence of new lesions at different locations on the shell months or years later may occur. Prevention and control: The biology and epidemiology of E. testavorans is almost completely uncharacterized and environmental persistence is unknown. However, the use of biofiltration systems to maintain water quality rather than the conventional more sterile, dump-and-fill practices, promotes a more diverse microbiome and is associated with reduced incidence of Emydomyces associated shell disease. Emydomyces may be found on clinically normal turtle shells so preshipment or quarantine qPCR testing of shell swabs / scrapes may prevent introduction into a collection. Any turtle with a history of Emydomyces-associated shell disease should be considered persistently infected since clearance of infection may not be possible at this time.

secao: Compiled by Krista Keller (2023) Reviewed by Jean Paré (2023)
texto: Susceptible animal groups: Nannizziopsis spp. historically exhibit host-pathogen relationships. -  Chameleons, geckos: N. dermatitidis -  Bearded dragons, green iguanas: N. chlamydospora, N. draconii, N. guarroi -  Five-lined skink: N. pluriseptata -  Australian lizards: N. barbatae -  Lizards, snakes, turtles: N. arthrosporioides -  Corn snakes (experimentally): N. guarroi -  Saltwater and freshwater crocodiles, and likely other crocodilians: N. crocodilii Causative organism: Nannizziopsis spp are keratinophilic fungi belonging to the order Onygenales. Other primary reptilian fungal pathogens of the order Onygenales are Emydomyces testavorans, Paranannizziopsis spp., and Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola. Many genera in this order were part of the previously named complex CANV (Chrysosporium anamorph of Nannizziopsis vriesii); this terminology is outdated and should not be used. Zoonotic potential: One case report found a human tongue lesion was associated with Nannizziopsis arthrosporioides; otherwise, Nannizziopsis spp. that infect humans (N. obscura, N. hominis) are genetically distinct from reptile associated isolates. Distribution: Global. Incubation period: Unknown.

Clinical signs: The classic appearance of infection in lizards includes a yellow crusty lesion with ulceration beneath, however, lesions can be dark in color as well. Infection in crocodiles may be a dark, well-circumscribed lesion. Spread to coelomic organs has been documented in multiple species and clinical signs may be associated with the organ of involvement.

-  Postmortem/gross findings: Ulcerative cutaneous lesions that may progress to deeper structures, +/- fungal granulomas within coelomic organs. -  Histologic features: Epidermal ulceration, pyogranulomatous inflammation, pyogranulomas within coelomic organs. Special stains may identify fungal elements (typically hyphae) within inflammation.

-  Swabs or impression smear of the lesion can be observed microscopically for cytology. Within a background of pyogranulomatous inflammation, fungal elements like aleurocondian and arthroconidia (basophillic rectangular to ovoid structures with slight halo around cell wall) and hyphae (basophillic often branching chains that septation may or may be able to be appreciated) may be observed. -  Sterile swabs and scrapes or tissue samples contained within a cryovial, or red top tube can be submitted for fungal culture, panfungal PCR, microbe specific PCR, or next generation sequencing.

-  In lizards, there are many reports of treatment failure, suspected antifungal toxicity (azoles), and infection recrudescence (or reinfection). -  Minimum inhibitory concentrations of several antifungals for 4 strains of N. guarroi have been published and can be used to drive antifungal therapy (ketoconazole 2,000 ng/mL, posaconazole 1,000 ng/mL, voriconazole 250 ng/mL, nystatin 4,000 ng/mL, terbinafine 30 ng/mL). - o There are no published treatment trials for infection in any species. - o Clinicians are urged to use published MIC data or to obtain MIC data from cultured specimens to guide therapy. - o Of note, nystatin may only be useful topically, ketoconazole may cause adverse effects, and itraconazole could be effective for non-guarroi Nannizziopsis species. -  Many topical products have been used in literature. Enilconazole should be used with great caution in crocodilians, as it is associated with development of terminal gout. Prevention and control: N. guarroi exhibits prolonged persistence in the environment, thus environmental disinfection may reduce reinfection. N. guarroi has not been documented from clinically normal lizards.

Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: A disinfection study in N. guarroi proved that 10% dilution of commercial bleach with a 2-minute contact time is effective. Ineffective disinfectants include chlorhexidine, potassium permanganate, ethanol, and ammonia. Unpublished data indicates that F10 does not disinfect against N. guarroi. Given the favorable MICs of terbinafine against N. guarroi, nebulizing environments may be beneficial and less labor intensive than traditional disinfection with bleach. There are no studies evaluating effective disinfection for other species of Nannizziopsis available. Incubation period: Based on challenge studies, cutaneous lesions can develop as quickly as 4 days following inoculation. Natural infection likely takes weeks or months to present.

-  Early ophidiomycosis typically presents as one or more displaced, discolored, swollen, vesicular, or necrotic scales at the site of infection. As the affected scale(s) undergo inflammatory and necrotic changes, serocellular crusts develop. When crusts and necrotic scales slough off, erosions and ulcers remain. If O. ophidiicola invades deeper than the epidermis, underlying granulomas can develop, which present as nodules or localized swellings. Lesions can progress from focal scale abnormalities into large, coalescing patches of affected scales. Over time, additional cutaneous lesions can appear at distant sites on the body. Infection can invade locally into skeletal muscle, bone, eyes, heat pits, and even viscera, creating significant disfiguring lesions that contribute to morbidity and mortality and predispose the snake to secondary infections. Systemic dissemination to multiple internal organs (lungs, liver, kidneys) has also been reported, and is proposed as one reason for treatment failure. Antemortem identification of animals with disseminated infection is extremely difficult.

Snakes with ophidiomycosis tend to shed at greater frequency compared to uninfected snakes, and also tend to have more problems with dysecdysis. Non-specific clinical signs of ophidiomycosis may include anorexia and lethargy. -  Early cutaneous lesions may be difficult to visually identify, especially on snakes with a highlycontrasting skin pattern. Palpating the skin can be quite helpful for detecting subtle scale abnormalities.

-  Postmortem/gross findings: displaced, discolored, edematous, swollen, vesicular, or necrotic scales, cutaneous or subcutaneous granulomas, +/- granulomas involving tissues underlying or adjacent to cutaneous lesions. Visceral granulomas may also be present if the infection is disseminated. In advanced or chronic cases, fat bodies may be reduced in size. -  Histologic features: cutaneous lesions are characterized by necrotizing heterophilic and granulomatous dermatitis. Serocellular crusts, epidermal ulceration, and edema are common. Granulomatous and heterophilic inflammation may also be present in the dermis and underlying tissues deep to cutaneous lesions. Epidermal and dermal granulomas can occur. Intralesional hyphae are up to 5 μm in diameter, have parallel walls, acute-angle branching, and transverse septa. Along the surface of lesions at the air-tissue interface, cylindrical, approximately 2 x 4 μm, fission arthroconidia may be present; these can occur in dense aggregates. Grocott's or Gomori methenamine silver or periodic acid-Schiff stains are useful to identify fungal elements and characterize fungal morphology.

-  Antemortem: a combination of consistent physical examination findings and qPCR indicating the presence of Ophidiomyces ophidiicola DNA associated with lesions. qPCR can be performed on skin biopsies, shed skin, or skin swabs. Swabbing technique can significantly influence the sensitivity of skin swabs for O. ophidiicola detection; optimally the entire surface of a snake's body should be aggressively swabbed 8 - 10 times to maximize detection probability. Separate skin lesion swabs may also be tested to improve diagnostic sensitivity. - o DNA extraction for O. ophidiicola should incorporate a lyticase digestion step. Omission of this step reduces diagnostic sensitivity. Ensuring that diagnostic laboratories incorporate lyticase digestion into DNA extraction protocols is recommended to reduce the risk of false negatives. - o Fungal culture can be performed, but is relatively time consuming and O. ophidiicola is frequently out-competed in culture. Histopathology can be used to confirm the presence of a fungal infection, but follow-up culture or PCR is necessary for the ultimate diagnosis of ophidiomycosis. - o O.

-  Nebulization with a 2 mg/mL solution of terbinafine in saline for 30 minutes every 24 hours achieves fungicidal plasma concentrations in cottonmouths (Agkistron piscivorous) and anecdotally appears effective in several species. Treatment should be continued until three consecutive skin swabs (each collected one month apart) test negative for O. ophidiicola using qPCR. -  Slow-release subcutaneous terbinafine implants at a dose of 75-190 mg/kg achieve fungicidal plasma concentrations for 6+ weeks in cottonmouths. Treatment should continue until three consecutive negative qPCR tests are obtained as described above. -  Treatment duration typically ranges from weeks to months. -  Surgical debridement of cutaneous lesions is not recommended due to poor healing and the potential for hematogenous spread of fungal elements. -  Survival is reduced for snakes with ophidiomycosis if maintained at low temperatures and/or brumated. Infected snakes should be kept at the upper end of their preferred optimum temperature zone (POTZ) to augment immune response and survival rates. -  Housing in easily disinfectable hospital enclosures is recommended during treatment.

Enclosures, bowls, hide boxes, and other furniture should be regularly disinfected with an appropriate compound and contact time to reduce the environmental O. ophidiicola burden. -  Clearing O. ophidiicola appears possible when the infection is confined to the skin. However, recrudescence of infection weeks to months after apparently successful treatment has been observed in snakes with disseminated ophidiomycosis.

-  O. ophidiicola has growth characteristics consistent with a soil fungus, although its environmental persistence is currently unknown. Organic material from enclosures housing infected snakes should be removed and autoclaved or incinerated prior to disposal. All snakes and lizards co-housed with a confirmed ophidiomycosis case should be quarantined, tested via qPCR, and monitored closely for the development of clinical signs. -  A good biosecurity program is important for preventing the spread of ophidiomycosis within a collection. Gloves should be worn and changed between exhibits. Boots and snake handling equipment (e.g. tongs, tubes, pillowcases, etc.) should be disinfected between individuals. -  Pre-shipment or quarantine qPCR testing of skin swabs or shed skin may prevent introduction into a collection. Any snake with a history of ophidiomycosis could be considered persistently infected since clearance of infection may not be possible in animals with disseminated infection. The prevalence and epidemiology of disseminated O. ophidiicola infection is currently unknown.

Causative organism: Paranannizziopsis spp. are keratinophilic fungi belonging to the order Onygenales. Other primary reptilian fungal pathogens of the order Onygenales are Nannizziopsis spp., Emydomyces testavorans, and Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola. Many genera in this order were part of the previously named CANV complex (Chrysosporium anamorph of Nannizziopsis vriesii); this terminology is outdated and should not be used. Zoonotic potential: No human cases reported. Distribution: North America, Australia, New Zealand Incubation period: Unknown.

-  In chameleons, disease has also presented as grey to black skin lesions, subdermal masses and swollen toes. -  Disease in snakes appears to be more severe. Skin lesions vary from yellow to brown, black, white, and grey with dysecdysis, significant epidermal ulceration and variable myositis/fasciitis. -  Spread to coelomic organs has not been documented in any species, however osteomyelitis has been reported in snakes and in a single tuatara.

-  Postmortem/gross findings: - o All species: ulcerative dermatitis that may invade deeper structures, - o Chameleons: subdermal masses and swollen toes, - o One tuatara: subdermal masses. -  Histologic features: Epidermitis and dermatitis, variable necrosis with heterophilic exudate and pyogranulomatous inflammation. Fungal elements are often seen on H&E-stained sections but may be more evident with special stains that may identify fungal elements. Typically, these are branching septate hyphae; arthroconidia and aleuroconidia may also be seen within epidermis, dermis, inflammation and crusts. -  Co-infection with bacteria both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria is reported.

-  Cytologic or histologic evaluation may identify fungal elements (hyphae, conidia). -  Paranannizziopsis spp. can be readily grown, albeit slowly, in fungal culture on selective media; identity of colonies must be confirmed with sequencing or MALDI-TOF. -  Consensus fungal PCR with sequencing -  Real-time pan-Paranannizziopsis PCR with sequencing. -  Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP). -  Paranannizziopsis has been isolated from asymptomatic tuatara, histopathology is recommended to confirm Paranannizziopsis is the causative organism and not an incidental finding

-  Swabs or impression smears of the lesion can be observed microscopically for cytology, though this may lead to false negatives. -  Lesion crusts and biopsies can be submitted for culture, histologic evaluation, and molecular testing. Soaking biopsy specimens in an antibiotic such as enrofloxacin for 5 minutes may help reduce bacterial contamination and improve diagnostic yield of fungal cultures. -  Sterile swabs and scrapes or tissue samples contained within a cryovial, or red top tube can be submitted for fungal culture, PCR, or next generation sequencing.

-  P. australasiensis has been detected via LAMP in soil samples from environments with and without clinically affected animals present, and also from clinically normal tuatara and lizards. Effective quarantine, testing and enclosure disinfection protocols, potentially including substrate testing and change, may reduce reinfection. -  Recurrence after apparent clinical cure has been documented, though it is unclear if this is recrudescence of asymptomatic infection or a true re-infection. Any reptile with a history of Paranannizziopsis infection may pose a risk on introduction to unaffected animals. -  Autoclaving and disposal of substrate from enclosures housing affected animals may be indicated to reduce the likelihood of reinfection. Suggested disinfectant for housing facilities: No disinfection studies have been conducted on Paranannizziopsis species. Extrapolation from disinfection studies in related Onygenalean fungi (Nannizziopsis guarroi and Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola) suggest that a 2-minute contact time with 10% commercial bleach or 70% ethanol may be effective. Causative organism: There are currently four genera of haemogregarines (Apicomplexa: Adeleorina) reported from reptiles. -  Haemogregarina are intraerythrocytic parasites that are most commonly reported from aquatic turtles. Leeches are the only known vectors for aquatic turtle parasites. Numerous other hosts, such as alligators, snakes, and tortoises have reported Haemogregarina spp. infections. However, these reports are based on morphologic data from only intraerythocytic stages, which is insufficient for genus-level distinction and identification. The absence of morphologic data for other life stages and vectors is a common problem among all genera and "species" of hemogregarines of reptiles that has hindered appropriate classification. -  Hepatozoon are intraleukocytic parasites that infect a wide range of reptiles - as well as mammals and birds.

Many species infecting terrestrial reptiles previously classified within Haemogregarina were transferred to Hepatozoon, and so this change should be considered for a correct and up-to-date diagnosis. These are transmitted by blood-feeding arthropods. -  Karyolysus are intraerythrocytic parasites of lacertid lizards including the genera Lacerta and Podarcis, among others. These parasites are transmitted via blood-feeding mites (e.g,, Ophionyssus). -  Hemolivia are intraerythrocytic parasites of tortoises and lizards - and a few amphibians. The arthropod vector are hard ticks within the genera Hyalomma and Amblyomma. Zoonotic potential: None. Distribution: Worldwide depending on the range of appropriate hosts and vectors. Incubation period: Highly variable. It is also unknown for most species as most species have only been detected in naturally infected hosts that have unknown histories. Generally, in experimental trials, parasites are not observed in the blood for several weeks.
