A metastrongylid nematode (Angiostrongylus chabaudi) is occasionally detected in the right ventricle and pulmonary arteries of European wildcats (Giannelli et al., 2016). Recently it was found in two domestic cats in Italy (Varcasia et al., 2014; Traversa et al., 2015). It is postulated that cats are occasional hosts for A. chabaudi because small and non-fertile parasites were detected and L1 larvae were not found in the faeces of infected cats (Giannelli et al., 2016). Moreover, pathological findings consistent with Angiostrongylus infection were not evident, and thus, this parasitic infection is not thought to be clinically relevant in domestic cats (Giannelli et al., 2016). The life cycle of Angiostrongylus vasorum, the metastrongylid species affecting dogs and wild canids, involves slugs and snails, and infection occurs by oral ingestion of infected molluscs carrying infectious L3 larvae but the intermediate host of A. chabaudi is still not known (Giannelli et al., 2016).

Dirofilaria immitis is worldwide distributed in tropical and temperate regions and endemic in some countries in Europe and North and South America. Conversely, D. repens is frequently reported from Europe and Asia, infrequently from Africa and has not been found in the Americas, Australia and Japan (Yilmaz et al., 2019). In Europe, endemic areas of both species exist in Mediterranean countries (Italy, Spain, France, Greece, and Turkey) but recent extension within these countries as well as to Central and Eastern Europe (Switzerland, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands, Croatia, Serbia, Hungary, Czech Republic, Poland, and Russia) was documented (Traversa et al., 2010; Genchi et al., 2011; Mórchon et al., 2012). This spread is particularly concerning with D. repens as this is currently considered an emerging zoonosis in Europe (Capelli et al., 2018). Increasing mosquito abundance and seasonal activity as well as increased travelling of infected dogs are causing the spread of filarial infection. Global rising of temperatures also lengthens the seasonal timeframe adequate for maturation of larvae in the infected mosquitoes up to throughout the year (Simón et al., 2014).

of filarial infection. Global rising of temperatures also lengthens the seasonal timeframe adequate for maturation of larvae in the infected mosquitoes up to throughout the year (Simón et al., 2014). However, climatic differences concerning humidity also impact on the risk of exposure for susceptible hosts, particularly when the canine population is not undergoing massive chemoprophylactic treatment (Montoya-Alonso et al., 2016). According to predictive models developed for dirofilariosis, summer temperatures in Europe are able to support the life cycle of larvae in mosquitoes even in colder regions, such as UK, in case of the presence of infected reservoirs (Genchi et al., 2005; 2009; 2011). Thus far, Estonia is the northernmost European area where D. repens life-cycle has been demonstrated, and a human case was diagnosed even in Finland (Capelli et al., 2018). The true prevalence of feline HWD is difficult to evaluate because of diagnostic difficulties, but infection is detected in the same areas as canine HWD at about 9-18% of the rate in unprotected dogs (Venco et al., 2011a). Despite the low parasite load (1-6 adult worms per cat), severe pathological changes are found early in cats and they can be lifethreatening. Pulmonary endo-mesoarteritis with occlusive medial hypertrophy are observed as soon as immature worms arrive in the pulmonary vessels (about 3 months post-infection [p.i.]) (Dillon et al., 2007; 2014). Early death (3-4 months p.i.) of juvenile heartworms usually occurs soon after they arrive in the pulmonary arteries, otherwise they survive about 2-4 years followed by self-cure in most cases (Venco et al., 2008). Early or end-stage parasite death can be associated with acute severe lesions (severe pulmonary thromboembolism and eosinophilic inflammatory response in lungs) causing the so-called heartworm-associated respiratory disease (HARD) characterized by acute onset of dyspnoea and interstitial pattern on lung radiography (Dillon et al., 2007; García-Guasch et al., 2013; Dillon et al., 2014). In experimental studies, the inflammatory response due to the death of immature adult heartworms is associated with chronic myofibrocyte proliferation histologically evident in lungs up to 18 months after infection (Dillon et al., 2017).

Pulmonary arterial disease is associated with exposure to D. immitis and is considered more severe compared to dogs due to the increased activity of pulmonary intravascular macrophages in cats (Browne et al., 2005; Dillon et al., 2008). In one case, pathological changes of the arterial wall caused fatal artery dissection of the pulmonary artery (Figures 3-5) (Biasato et al., 2017). Sometimes sudden death is reported in apparently healthy cats as a consequence of severe pulmonary thromboembolic or haemorrhagic pathology, including haemothorax due to pulmonary artery dissection (Alho et al., 2016; Biasato et al., 2017; Diakou et al., 2019). According to experimental studies, an acute systemic anaphylaxis could be involved in this hyperacute course of feline HWD secondary to the release of large quantities of D. immitis antigens from dead parasites. The usual clinical signs are severe respiratory insufficiency, hypotension, vomiting and diarrhoea (Lister and Atwell, 2006; Lister et al., 2007). Most cats have, however, a less severe, transient and chronic course of HWD with mild to moderate respiratory signs, due to chronic bronchoalveolar inflammation (epithelial infiltration and proliferation of smooth muscle cells in bronchioles), persisting even after the parasite death.

Various further clinical manifestations, such as chronic vomiting, anorexia, and cachexia, are also reported and can be the most evident clinical signs (Dillon et al., 2000). Caval syndrome is rarely observed in cats but can arise when 1-2 worms are located in the right side of the heart causing tricuspid regurgitation (Figure 1). Aberrant migrations (e.g. in body cavities, central nervous system, femoral artery) are rare but more frequently reported in cats than in dogs and are responsible for effusions or neurological manifestations (e.g., blindness, ataxia, paraparesis, monoparesis, seizures) (McCall et al., 2008; Simón et al., 2012; Favole et al., 2013; Oldach et al., 2018). Acute-onset pelvic limb monoparesis due to femoral thromboembolism was caused in a cat by an adult 13 cm female HW extending from caudal abdominal aorta into the right external iliac and femoral arteries (Oldach et al., 2018).

due to femoral thromboembolism was caused in a cat by an adult 13 cm female HW extending from caudal abdominal aorta into the right external iliac and femoral arteries (Oldach et al., 2018). Interestingly, HWD had been diagnosed in this cat three years before when it was evaluated for cough and successfully treated with prednisone (Oldach et al., 2018). Laboratory diagnosis may reveal eosinophilia on complete blood count and on bronchoalveolar lavage cytology. Changed concentrations of acute phase proteins have been described (Dillon et al., 2014; Venco et al., 2015; Silvestre-Ferreira et al., 2016). Hyperglobulinaemia, hypoalbuminaemia and proteinuria can occur in cats with HWD irrespective of their parasite burden (Atkins et al., 2011).

Dirofilaria repens infection is often subclinical in infected hosts; however, subcutaneous nodules or dermatitis are associated with the presence of adult worms in dogs (Venco et al., 2011b). An adult parasite or some microfilariae were incidentally found, respectively, in the subcutaneous tissue of an asymptomatic cat during elective surgery and in the blood of a stray queen and in some of her 8-week old kittens (Mazurkevich et al., 2004; Długosz et al., 2016). Microfilaraemia or positive D. repens-specific PCR were found in cats with papular and crusting dermatitis (Tarello, 2011). Recently, D. repens adult worms were detected in a cat that was presented with 3 large (around 2 x 2 cm) firm and infiltrating subcutaneous nodules on the lateral thoracic wall and forelegs associated with axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy (Figures 6, 7) (Manzocchi et al., 2017). Moderate absolute eosinophilia was the only clinicopathological abnormality found and eosinophilic lymphadenitis (Figure 8) was detected on cytological evaluation of the enlarged lymph nodes (Manzocchi et al., 2017). The rare and short-term occurrence of microfilaraemia and the low number of adult worms make it difficult to diagnose HWD in cats, compared to dogs. A multistep approach, combining mainly antigen and antibody tests and diagnostic imaging, is required to overcome the limitations of each single diagnostic technique (Jones et al., 2014) (Figure 9). Moreover, HARD can already occur during early death of parasites and this explains the possibility of discordant results between different tests even in symptomatic cats. Anti-D. immitis antibody detection and thoracic radiography for detecting compatible pulmonary lesions are sensitive methods to have early information about possible feline HWD. However limitations of antibody detection are due to lower sensitivity in asymptomatic cats as time passed, and to antibody persistence for some time in cats that self-cure.

A positive antigen test or the ultrasound visualization of filarial worms are confirmatory but their sensitivity is inadequate for excluding HWD in case of no antigen and worm detection. Rarely microfilariae are evidenced in blood (Knott test or millipore filter), but they have to be differentiated from those of D. repens in countries where both species are found (e.g. in Europe). In contrast to dogs, both microscopical detection of microfilariae and ELISA or immunochromatographic (IC)-based tests that detect circulating antigens of adult D. immitis females have low sensitivity in cats (McCall et al., 2008; Simón et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2014; Venco et al., 2015). Albeit rarely, microfilariae of both species can incidentally be detected on feline routine blood smears and further investigations are always required for their identification (Długosz et al., 2016).

rarely, microfilariae of both species can incidentally be detected on feline routine blood smears and further investigations are always required for their identification (Długosz et al., 2016). When microfilariae are detected using routine techniques (modified Knott test or millipore filtration), morphometric identification, cytochemical stain or PCR are needed to differentiate D. immitis and D. repens microfilariae in countries where both species are found (e.g. in Europe) (Venco et al., 2015). Feline HWD is usually associated with the presence of few pre-adult or adult worms. When no or only one adult female worm is present, a false negative result is obtained on ELISA or IC antigen tests (Berdoulay et al., 2004). However, heat pre-treatment of feline and canine serum or plasma samples improves the sensitivity of these commercial antigen assays in cats (and dogs) carrying only few adult female worms by releasing antigens blocked within circulating immune-complexes (Little et al., 2014; Velasquez et al., 2014; Gruntmeir et al., 2016; Little et al., 2018).

In order to underline the low negative predictive value of antigen assays in cats it is suggested to record any negative result as "no antigen detected" instead of "negative" (Jones et al., 2014). Anti-D. immitis antibodies are found about 2 months p.i. and they confirm exposure to D. immitis early irrespective of the parasite load (Prieto et al., 2002). However, a risk of false positive results exists because of antibody persistence even in cats that have cleared the parasites (Berdoulay et al., 2004). False negative results are also possible (particularly in asymptomatic cats), and a wide range of sensitivities exist among the different tests (Jones et al., 2014). The combined use of antigen and antibody testing increases diagnostic accuracy of testing for feline HWD but negative results on both tests still cannot exclude a diagnosis in suspected HARD cases.

Thoracic radiography is always indicated for the diagnosis of HWD because of suggestive changes and for prognostic reasons (Venco et al., 2015). Suggestive abnormalities include a vascular pattern (enlargement, loss of tapering, tortuosity, and truncation of the right or both caudal pulmonary arteries on ventro-dorsal thoracic radiography) and patchy infiltrates around the caudal lobar arteries resulting from plasma leakage and perivascular inflammation (often peripheral in caudal lobes) (Figure 10) or a diffuse broncho-interstitial pattern (Venco et al., 2015). Radiographic changes can be the only detected abnormality in suspected HARD cases, but lungworm disease should be excluded in these cats as a differential diagnosis for the radiographic changes (Pennisi et al., 2015).

Pulmonary thromboembolism, arterial changes and bronchial collapse are common findings when cats with HWD undergo computed tomography (CT) or angiography investigations of the thorax (Dillon et al., 2014; Panopoulos et al., 2018). The body wall of adult HW appears as double hyperechoic parallel lines ("railway lines") because of reflection of ultrasound waves by the cuticle of the worm (Figure 11). However, diagnostic sensitivity is operator-dependent, quantification of the worm burden is difficult and false negative as well as false positive evaluations are possible (Venco et al., 2015).

In these cases, the right side of the heart, pulmonary arteries, and ectopic sites, including the brain and spinal cord in case of neurological signs, must be carefully examined for adult worms (McCall et al., 2008; Simón et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2014). Parasite-species-specific PCR assays are available for discriminating D. immitis and D. repens (Favia et al., 1996). A panfilarial-6-species PCR has been developed and, in some cats, DNA of filarial worms not yet reported in feline hosts was detected (Rishniw et al., 2006; Manzocchi et al., 2017).

There is no adulticidal drug approved for the treatment of feline HWD, and adulticide therapy is not recommended in asymptomatic cats because self-cure occurs in most cases in 18-48 months (Venco et al., 2008; Jones et al., 2014). Infected cats should be followed up by thoracic radiography, echocardiography, and antigen and antibody testing for decision making regarding treatment and to detect selfcure. Prednisolone (2 mg/kg/24 hour declining over a few weeks) should be given to cats with respiratory signs that test positive on antigen and/or antibody testing (Jones et al., 2014). In asymptomatic cats with suggestive radiographic changes, prednisolone treatment should also be applied, and treatment should be followed up by the same clinical, radiographic and antigen/antibody testing method (Jones et al., 2014). Improvement of radiographic changes associated with previous positive antigen tests becoming negative are markers of recovery despite the persistence of positive antibody tests (Jones et al., 2014). Hyperacute cases of HWD require intensive care unit stabilization because of the risk of respiratory failure and shock.

Adulticide therapy used in dogs (melarsomine) is not safe in cats and carries a high risk of pulmonary thromboembolism and anaphylactic reactions following parasite death in treated cats (Jones et al., 2014; Alho et al., 2016). Surgical procedures to mechanically remove the adult parasites have been proposed in symptomatic cats for retrieving worms visualized from the right heart and main pulmonary arteries, but they have to be removed intact to avoid anaphylaxis (Iizuka et al., 2009; Jones et al., 2014). Surgical removal of an adult heartworm migrated to the femoral artery was successfully obtained by direct access to the worm from the arteriotomy site (Oldach et al., 2018).

Jones et al., 2014). Surgical removal of an adult heartworm migrated to the femoral artery was successfully obtained by direct access to the worm from the arteriotomy site (Oldach et al., 2018). Slow kill protocols combining monthly administration of heartworm-preventative drugs combined with a one-month course of doxycycline therapy are used in dogs when melarsomine is contraindicated and is reported in cats (Diakou et al., 2019), but their efficacy and safety are unknown and therefore these protocols are not recommended (Savadelis et al., 2017). Nevertheless, all cats diagnosed with HWD should also undergo monthly application of preventative drugs (see below). In a cat affected by subcutaneous dirofilariosis, nodules containing adult worms and microfilariae have been successfully removed surgically (Manzocchi et al., 2017). There is no adulticidal drug approved for the treatment of feline subcutaneous dirofilariosis.

Because of the unpredictable and potentially fatal course of HWD in cats and the lack of safe and effective treatments in endemic areas, all cats - irrespective of their access to outdoors - should be given monthly chemoprophylaxis from 2 months of age all year long for killing infective larvae in the L3-L4 stages (Jones et al., 2014). Although a recent study found that outdoor cats had a 3-fold increased risk of being D. immitis antigen-positive, it is known that about one third of all antigen-positive cats actually live indoors (Levy et al., 2017). The same recommendation is given for cats that live in areas that do not have heartworm but that are travelling to endemic areas. Chemoprophylaxis should be performed within 30 days of arrival in the risk area (European Scientific Counsel Companion Animal Parasites, 2012; European Society of Dirofilariosis and Angiostrongylosis, 2017). Unfortunately, awareness of the importance of feline HWD prevention seems to be low and is often neglected, especially in cat shelters, for economic reasons (Polak and Smith-Blackmore, 2014; Levy et al., 2017; Genchi et al., 2019).

importance of feline HWD prevention seems to be low and is often neglected, especially in cat shelters, for economic reasons (Polak and Smith-Blackmore, 2014; Levy et al., 2017; Genchi et al., 2019). Adequate preventative treatment covering the whole of the transmission season is crucial for effective prevention, and a year-round approach is often the best option because of climatic differences concerning humidity having a great impact on the risk of exposure for susceptible hosts (Montoya-Alonso et al., 2016). Five preventative drugs are currently available for cats and are monthly given orally or topically as spot-ons (Baker et al., 2014; Dillon et al., 2014; Little et al., 2015; McTier et al., 2019) (table 1). Antigen- or antibodypositive cats can be safely given preventative therapy, but both tests should be carried out before starting chemoprophylaxis to obtain a risk assessment for HWD in cats living in endemic areas (Jones et al., 2014). Selamectin administration was not effective in preventing subcutaneous dirofilariosis in one cat but this apparent failure could have been due to it being stopped before the end of transmission season (Manzocchi et al., 2017).

There is great interest in dirofilariosis because of the increasing number of human case reports in endemic areas. Immature D. immitis worms can reside in a branch of pulmonary artery of humans and induce the development of pulmonary nodules (Simón et al., 2012). Dirofilaria repens can cause dermatitis or subcutaneous, submucosal, mammary, genital, omental, ocular or lung nodules, which can be misdiagnosed as malignancy (Pampiglione et al., 2001). The disease is sporadic and in Europe D. repens is responsible for human dirofilariasis more frequently than D. immitis, even in areas of high endemicity of the latter species (Simón et al., 2012; Capelli et al., 2018). Italy, France, Czech Republic, Serbia, Greece, and Ukraine are the countries where human dirofilariasis caused by D. repens is more frequent (Capelli et al., 2018). Epidemiological studies detecting antibodies in people found that rates of infection are similar as those of dogs in an endemic area (Simón et al., 2012).

titulo: Domestic Cat Hepatitis B Virus infection
texto: - Domestic Cat Hepatitis B Virus (DCHBV) is a feline hepatitis B-like virus first reported in 2018 in Australia, classified as a novel species in the genus Orthohepadnavirus, within the family - Since its initial identification, DCHBV has been detected in feline populations worldwide with molecular prevalence rates ranging from less than 1% to over 18%. - Like human hepatitis B virus, DCHBV is linked to chronic hepatitis and hepatocellular carcinoma in cats. However, the full clinical impact of DCHBV on feline health is still under investigation. - DCHBV can establish persistent infection in clinically healthy cats with high viral DNA loads in blood samples. - Continuous viral shedding from multiple mucosal surfaces (oral, nasal, rectal, and vaginal swabs) suggests potential horizontal transmission. - Current diagnosis relies on viral DNA detection via conventional PCR, or real-time quantitative PCR in whole blood, serum, or liver tissue samples. - Tools for antibody detection are essential to identify all infected cats and to establish the stage of infection or earlier exposure and clearance although they are currently restricted to research laboratories.

titulo: Domestic Cat Hepatitis B Virus infection
texto: Domestic Cat Hepatitis B Virus (DCHBV) has emerged as a significant pathogen in feline medicine that shares several similarities in genome organisation and pathogenic potential with human hepatitis B virus (HBV) (Aghazadeh et al., 2018). DCHBV was first identified and characterised in Australia in 2016 (Aghazadeh et al., 2018). Its discovery was serendipitous, occurring during a high-throughput transcriptomic sequencing study aimed at investigating gene expression alterations in a seven-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat presenting with lymphoma and concomitant feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) infection. On pairwise nucleotide comparison of the complete genome, the Australian strain was taxonomically assigned to the genus Orthohepadnavirus (family Hepadnaviridae) and formally classified as a novel species designated Orthohepadnavirus felisdomestici (Magnius et al., 2020). Since its discovery, DCHBV has been shown to be geographically widespread and common across domestic cat populations (Beatty et al., 2025). DCHBV has been detected in both the blood and liver tissue of cats (Shofa et al., 2022).

texto: The family Hepadnaviridae comprises small hepatotropic enveloped viruses, with a partially double-stranded circular DNA genome of approximately 3.0-3.4 kb in length (Seeger and Mason, 2015). Based on their divergent genomic sequences and narrow host range of infections, the hepadnaviruses are currently classified into five different genera: Parahepadnavirus, Metahepadnavirus, Herpetohepadnavirus, Avihepadnavirus, and Orthohepadnavirus (Magnius et al., 2020). The genus Orthohepadnavirus, whose members infect mammals, includes at least 12 species, with HBV as the type species of the genus (Magnius et al., 2020). The species demarcation criterium in the genus is more than about 20% nucleotide sequence divergence of complete genomes. The prototype species, HBV, is a critical global health burden, accounting for approximately 1.1 million deaths annually, predominantly due to cirrhosis and HCC (WHO, 2026).

Circular genome plot was generated using Geneious Prime version 2026.1. DCHBV displays similarities with HBV, presenting different genotypes and sub-genotypes. Phylogenetic analysis based on the full-length genome sequences currently available on databases, revealed the existence of at least two distinct genotypes (A and B) of DCHBV, characterised by an inter-genotypic nucleotide divergence of approximately 10.8% (de Oliveira-Filho et al., 2025). Genotype A is the globally dominant lineage, which has been identified across Australia, Southeast Asia, Europe, and the United States. Within this large cluster, DCHBV sequences fell into three well-defined geographic sub-clades, proposed as clades A1, A2 and A3 (Diakoudi et al., 2025; Pellegrini et al., 2026). Genotype B represents a more sporadically detected lineage that includes five strains.

While HBV DNA serves as a proxy for active viraemia during both acute and chronic phases, many patients eventually suppress viral replication through immune control or functional clearance. Furthermore, in such cases, the virus is not eliminated but persists in the liver as covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA). Consequently, DNA-based testing cannot identify all infected patients, necessitating the use of alternative markers. Antibodies against the viral core protein (anti-HBc) are particularly valuable in this context: they emerge early during infection (IgM) and typically persist throughout the host's lifetime (IgG), serving as a definitive record of exposure (Kao, 2008). Drawing on these parallels with HBV, an in-house enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was developed to detect anti-DCHBV core IgM and IgG, utilizing a recombinant core protein (DCHBVc) produced in a baculovirus-insect expression system. The application of this test confirmed the limitations of molecular testing. For instance, in a cohort of 256 cats, only 9.8% tested positive for DCHBV DNA, whereas 25% tested seropositive for anti-DCHBVc antibodies (Fruci et al., 2022).

Notably, 84.2% of these seropositive young cats displayed IgM antibodies, a hallmark of early acute infection. Taken together, these findings highlight that DCHBV exposure is far more widespread than previously thought and underscore the critical role of serology in capturing the full epidemiological landscape of the virus, beyond identifying the stage of infection.

Although many studies suggest that cats aged 2-10 years are at higher risk due to cumulative horizontal exposure, others have found no significant correlation with age.

texto: While the transmission dynamics of HBV are well-defined, the natural routes of DCHBV transmission are still being elucidated. HBV is transmitted most commonly from mother to child during birth and delivery, in early childhood, as well as through contact with blood or other body fluids during sex with an infected partner, unsafe injections or exposures to sharp instruments (WHO, 2026). Like HBV, DCHBV DNA has been identified in body fluid specimens, including those collected from auricular, nasal, oral, rectal and vaginal swabs, suggesting the potential for horizontal transmission of the virus within the feline population (Wardhani et al., 2023; Wardhani et al., 2025; Pellegrini et al., 2026; Kato et al., 2026). Increasing evidence suggests that DCHBV infection in young cats can lead to prolonged high-level viraemia and continuous viral shedding from multiple mucosal surfaces (Wardhani et al., 2025; Pellegrini et al., 2026).

A 12month longitudinal study on four naturally infected juvenile cats revealed for two cases a high-titre persistent viraemia of up to 1.39 x 10 10 DNA copies/mL, with the lack of spontaneous clearance and the absence of seroconversion to protective anti-surface (anti-DCHBVs) antibodies, throughout the follow-up period (Pellegrini et al., 2026). This occurs alongside a delayed or incomplete serological response, suggesting an "immune-tolerant" phase, similar to that seen in HBV infection. This state characterizes young viraemic cats as potential "silent spreaders", capable of transmitting the virus through horizontal, vertical, and sexual routes (Pellegrini et al., 2026). The first recorded outbreak of DCHBV was recently documented in a feline shelter in Japan, exhibiting an unprecedented molecular prevalence rate of 26.59% (Kato et al., 2026).

texto: Following the identification of a novel hepadnavirus in domestic cats, research has rapidly expanded to delineate its host range. Recent evidence indicates that DCHBV can be transmitted to domestic dogs (Diakoudi et al., 2022; Choi et al., 2022; Fruci et al., 2023). The detection of DCHBV sequences in domestic dogs was initially unexpected, as hepadnaviruses are generally display narrow host specificity. Nevertheless, molecular surveillance has confirmed canine susceptibility. In an initial survey of 635 canine serum samples in Italy, Diakoudi et al. (2022) identified DCHBV DNA in 6.3% of the cohort. Genomic sequences retrieved from these dogs exhibited approximately 98% nucleotide identity with DCHBV strains circulating in Italian cats, suggesting active viral transmission among these domestic carnivores. However, geographic variations in prevalence appear significant. In Hong Kong, a survey of 501 canine blood samples identified DCHBV DNA in only 0.4% of the population assessed (Choi et al., 2022). Furthermore, a robust large-scale study by Oliveira-Filho et al. (2025), which screened 2,123 canine sera from Brazil and Germany, failed to detect DCHBV DNA.

These data demonstrate unequivocally that hepadnaviruses genetically and antigenically related to DCHBV circulate within canine populations. However, while an aetiopathogenetic link between DCHBV and feline liver disease is emerging, the clinical significance of this infection in dogs remains unknown. An expansion of the known host range for DCHBV was recently established following its identification in the endangered Iberian lynx. A survey on serum and liver samples collected from 191 Iberian lynxes examined post mortem in 2017-2023 throughout the Iberian Peninsula revealed a remarkably high seroprevalence of 32.3% for anti-DCHBVc antibodies, while viral DNA was detected in 0.5% of screened liver samples (Diakoudi et al., 2025).

texto: The pathobiology of DCHBV in cats is still uncertain, but the possible parallels with HBV might contribute to understanding the biology of this feline virus recently detected. The natural history of HBV infection and the spectrum of the disease are diverse and variable in severity, evolution and prognosis, ranging from acute asymptomatic and self-limiting forms to symptomatic disease and to progressive chronic hepatitis B (Fattovich, 2003; Liaw and Chu, 2009). A substantial proportion of patients develops cirrhosis and HCC, whereas others have lifelong quiescent viral activity not requiring antiviral therapy (Seto et al., 2018). The clinical impact of DCHBV on feline health is currently under investigation, but evidence indicates it likely plays a pathogenic role in feline liver disease similar to HBVinduced pathology in humans (Pesavento et al., 2019; Piewbang et al., 2022; Cavasin et al., 2025; Capozza et al., 2023a) (Fig. 3). Viraemia is expected during acute and chronic stages of infections but, in overtly healthy cats, viral DNA might be below the limits of detection in the blood (Fruci et al., 2022). In these cases, the presence of antiDCHBVc antibodies alone might be compatible with a phase of inactive carrier, as observed in overtly healthy individuals with occult HBV infection. On the other hand, the concomitant antibody seroconversion to DCHBVs antibodies in non-viraemic cats might be a marker of recovery from infection (Fruci et al., 2023; Pellegrini et al., 2026). Hence, a panel of widely available antibody serological markers will be essential to determine the stage of DCHBV infection. Currently, diagnostic testing for DCHBV is not widely accessible to practitioners, as these assays are largely restricted to research laboratories; however, it is hoped that diagnostic availability will improve in the future with more commercial facilities offering PCR and antibody testing. DCHBV viraemia has been linked with elevated serum levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), suggesting hepatocellular injury (Lanave et al., 2019).

texto: Currently, there is no specific treatment for DCHBV infection other than supportive care for the management of any associated inflammatory liver disease. A link between DCHBV and liver injury could justify the need for the development of novel antivirals and vaccines for cats. Unfortunately, many nucleoside/nucleotide analogues used in the treatment of HBV infection in humans are unacceptably toxic to cats (Hartmann, 2015; Beatty et al., 2025). Whether novel approaches to targeting HBV, such as capsid inhibitors or entry inhibitors, might be effective in cats, remains an unknown but exciting prospect. Detection of post-clearance neutralising antibodies in cats (e.g., anti-DCH surface antibodies) could support the development of a subunit vaccine, as is used in HBV prevention (Fruci et al., 2023; Pellegrini et al., 2026). As vaccines become commercially available, molecular tests to investigate the biology of DCHBV infection in cats remain the most effective strategy for its management. DCHBV molecular screening should be included among agents to be tested in veterinary diagnostic panels in cases where hepatic disease is clinically suspected and when testing blood donors.

Recent studies have demonstrated that DCHBV can establish persistent infection, with high viral DNA loads associated with prolonged viraemia (Wardhani et al., 2025; Pellegrini et al., 2026; Kato et al., 2026). Furthermore, high viral shedding rates in nasal, oral, rectal and vaginal swabs (Wardhani et al., 2023; Wardhani et al., 2025; Pellegrini et al., 2026; Kato et al., 2026) and the clinical observation of shelter outbreaks (Kato et al., 2026), underscores the need for effective infection control measures. In multicat facilities, implementing rigorous testing, quarantine protocols, and enhanced sanitation of shared spaces will help to mitigate the risk of DCHBV spread. Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies to elucidate the natural history of infection, with particular emphasis on deciphering the mechanisms underlying DCHBV-induced hepatic injury and its potential involvement in oncogenesis.

Encephalitozoon (E.) cuniculi is a common obligate intracellular microsporidian parasite of rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus), which is increasingly recognised as a pathogen of cats and other mammalian species. Objectives: to review the literature on E. cuniculi in cats and provide recommendations for feline clinical conditions in which E. cuniculi should be considered as a possible differential diagnosis. Conclusions: E. cuniculi should be considered in cases of feline uveitis and cataract formation. It is not significantly associated with either chronic kidney disease or meningoencephalitis. E. cuniculi infection is more common in stray or feral cats than in pet cats. Serological tests for antibody detection in blood are easy to perform and can be useful for diagnosis, but their specificity is low as antibodies have been found in apparently healthy cats. PCR appears more sensitive than histopathology for diagnosis, and is more sensitive when performed on cataractous lenses compared to aqueous humour, although ease of sampling is an obvious limitation. E. cuniculi is a potential zoonotic infection, posing a special risk to immunocompromised humans from infected rabbits. Encephalitozoon cuniculi is a common obligate intracellular microsporidian parasite of rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus), which is increasingly recognised as a pathogen of cats and other mammals. These unicellular microsporidia were previously considered "primitive" protozoa; however, more recent insight gained through molecular phylogenetic analysis is indicating that these organisms are not primitive but instead degenerate, and that microsporidia are related to the fungal Kingdom, either as a basal branch of the Fungi or as a sister group (Han and Weiss, 2017). Four species have been identified by PCR and sequencing: strain I is the rabbit strain; strain II is the mouse strain, strain III is from the dog (Didier et al, 1995) and strain IV is from the cat (Benz et al, 2011 and Benz personal communication) . In rabbits, E.

Mice appear to be the major reservoir of infection for cats (Benz et al, 2011). Cats are most likely to become infected by ingestion of mice rather than rabbits, since of 11 infected cats in Austria, seven were infected with the mouse strain (strain II), and the remaining four were infected with what is now known as the cat strain (strain IV) (Benz et al, 2011). Cats, like humans, may also be infected by consuming water or food contaminated with infective spores (Wang et al., 2018). Oral and nasal transmission has been described in rabbits (Harcourt-Brown and Holloway, 2003), but it is unknown if direct transmission occurs in cats. Two uninfected cats that had been in direct contact with infected ones tested negative for blood antibodies in one study (Benz et al., 2011). In utero infection is seen in rabbits (Baneux and Pognan, 2003), but it is unknown if transmission by this route occurs in the cat (Benz et al., 2011). Rebel-Bauder et al. (2011) reported a case of generalised encephalitozoonosis in a kitten with cerebellar hypoplasia, which could have been related to in utero infection.

Benz et al (2011) speculate that vertical transmission is necessary for cataract formation in the cat because vertical transmission is presumed to play an important role in the mechanisms by which the microsporidium enters the lens in rabbits and mink: the presumption is that the organism would be unable to infect a lens which already had a fully formed capsule.

In cats, ocular signs have been associated with E. cuniculi infection (Fig. 1). Detection of antibodies in blood by Western blot or IFAT remains the major means of pre-mortem clinical diagnosis in animals. As the IFAT is quick and easy to perform, it is recommended for routine use in the diagnosis of feline encephalitozoonosis (Künzel et al., 2014). However, antibodies have been detected in cats that appeared to be clinically healthy, which has to be borne in mind when interpreting positive results: a positive result supports a diagnosis of encephalitozoonosis, but is not confirmatory.

Histopathology and cytology are aided by immunohistochemistry. Five tentative positive results were achieved by cytological examination of material removed from cataractous lenses (Benz et al., 2011). Spores were detected in 15 of 19 samples of cataractous lens material with immunohistochemical staining (Benz et al., 2011). E. cuniculi spores are difficult to observe when the samples are stained with haematoxylin and eosin, particularly when there is an inflammatory reaction and tissue damage. The spores are easily mistaken for other microorganisms, such as fungi (yeasts), protozoa and bacteria. Modified trichrome stain (MTS) and Gram stain, detected by light microscopy, and calcofluor white stain, detected by ultraviolet light microscopy, are the best stains for detecting spores of E. cuniculi in paraffin-embedded tissues. These stains were superior to Warthin-Starry, Ziehl-Neelsen, Giemsa and periodic acid-Schiff reaction for identifying spores without background 'noise' or monochromatic interference. In addition, these stains allow individual spores to be discerned in paraffin-embedded tissues.

MTS allows observation of the polar tube, polaroplast and posterior vacuole, the most distinctive parts of the spore (Rodriguez-Tovar et al., 2017). Leipig et al. (2013) recommended that confirmation of pathogenic E. cuniculi infection in rabbits should include standard histology of the predilection sites in combination with a specific aetiological assay, preferably real-time PCR. Presumably the same is true for diagnosis of E. cuniculi infection in cats.

There is no commercially available vaccine to prevent E. cuniculi infection in rabbits or cats. It is noteworthy, however, that an experimental vaccine containing inactivated spores was shown to induce a long-lasting antibody response in rabbits (Sobottka et al., 2001). However, it is unknown whether antibodies are protective in this infection. Where cats and rabbits are kept together, the main method of prevention of infection is by maintenance of excellent hygiene. Heat or steam cleaning will be the most effective means of eliminating E. cuniculi spores. Rabbits suspected to be infected should be tested and treated. The safest option for individuals - both cats and humans - that consume rabbit meat is for E. cuniculi-free sources to be used. However, the prevalence of E. cuniculi is extremely high in rabbits kept for meat: 100% of 13 rabbit farms in Italy contained seropositive rabbits (Lonardi et al., 2013), and active E. cuniculi infections were determined in 85.9% and 56.3% of rabbits in commercial and household farms, respectively, in the Czech and Slovak Republics (Neumayerová et al., 2014).

cleaned then disinfected with sodium hypochlorite (household bleach), ensuring a contact time of at least 16 min (Wolk et al., 2000), followed by rinsing with boiling water or steam cleaning. Similar precautions are recommended for pig meat, which Sak et al. (2019) recently reported can also contain E. cuniculi spores. Exposure to 70% ethanol for 15 min inactivated microsporidian spores in fish (Leiro et al., 2012), and so is likely to be effective for cleaning hands and utensils following the preparation of rabbit or pig meat (although use of disposable gloves would be more practical in the case of hands). The ABCD recommends that immunosuppressed cats should not have any contact with infected rabbits or their urine and faeces.

- Dirofilaria immitis is a zoonotic mosquito-borne nematode causing heartworm disease (HWD) in cats. - The life cycle involves an intermediate mosquito host, and dogs and wild canids are reservoir hosts. - Cats, ferrets, other mammals, and humans are imperfect hosts as, after inoculation, only a low number of L3 immitis larvae develop to adults in a small percentage of infected individuals. - Cats are however susceptible to disease and HWD is potentially lethal. - Heartworm-associated respiratory disease (HARD) is characterised by acute onset of dyspnoea and signs of severe respiratory insufficiency. - Sudden death can be associated with severe pulmonary thromboembolism, eosinophilic inflammatory response in the lungs, or arteria dissection (tear). - Most symptomatic cats have a less severe and chronic course of HWD with mild to moderate respiratory signs. - Self-cure occurs frequently, usually 18-48 months after infection, but lesions may persist after parasite death. - Diagnosis in cats is more difficult compared to dogs and needs a multistep approach based on diagnostic imaging and serological tests.

Filarial worms (Spirurida, Onchocercidae) are vector-borne nematodes infecting animals and humans worlwide. The Dirofilaria genus include species primarily infecting wild and domestic animals but some of them are reported in humans (Perles et al., 2024). Dirofilaria immitis and Dirofilaria repens are mosquito-borne zoonotic species causing in cats heartworm disease (HWD) and subcutaneous dirofilariosis, respectively. Feline subcutaneous disease due to D. repens is treated in a separate ABCD GL. Dogs and some wild carnivores (fox, jackal, coyote, wolf, eurasian badger) are parasite reservoir hosts. Cats and wild felids, other carnivores (ferrets, raccoons, ursids, sea lions) and humans can be infected (McCall et al., 2008; Simón et al., 2012; Otranto and Deplazes, 2019). Dirofilaria spp. host the Gram-negative bacterium Wolbachia pipientis, a obligatory mutualist symbiont which plays an important role in the biology and pathogenicity of filariae (Sironi et al., 1995).

spp. host the Gram-negative bacterium Wolbachia pipientis, a obligatory mutualist symbiont which plays an important role in the biology and pathogenicity of filariae (Sironi et al., 1995). Wolbachia pipientis bacteria are always found in every filarial species known to harbour Wolbachia, and are transmitted vertically from female worms to the next generation of nematodes and are responsible for long-term survival and reproduction of filarial worms. In fact, W. pipientis is involved in moulting, embryogenesis and survival of filariae, and the filariae provide amino acids for W. pipientis bacterial growth (Simón et al., 2012). Dirofilaria immitis adults (females 25-30 cm long by ~1 mm wide; males 12-20 cm by 0.7-0.9 mm) reside in pulmonary arteries and right heart chambers (Fig. 1) (McCall et al., 2008; Simón et al., 2012). Aberrant migrations of larval stages can occur in cats and they and/or adult individuals can be found in unusual tissues (i.e. erratic locations). Fig. 1. Dirofilaria immitis is distributed worldwide, from tropical to cold climate regions (Dantas-Torres et al., 2023), and is endemic in some countries in Europe, North and South America, and the Far East (Oi et al., 2014; Genchi and Kramer, 2020; Morchón et al., 2022; Murillo et al., 2023; Chocobar et al., 2024; Hattendorf and Lühken, 2025). In the past, data regarding geographical distribution were mostly from regional epidemiological studies and case reports in dogs for D. immitis (Genchi and Kramer, 2020). Both filarial species affecting cats were historically reported in Mediterranean endemic areas (Italy, Spain, Portugal, France, Greece, and Turkey) and hyperendemicity (persistent, high levels of disease occurrence) of D. immitis was well known in North Italy (Genchi et al., 2011; Mórchon et al., 2012; Genchi and Kramer, 2020). In the twenty-first century, nationwide studies in Mediterranean countries and epidemiological investigations in other countries provided more extensive data and changes in geographical distribution emerged; D.

century, nationwide studies in Mediterranean countries and epidemiological investigations in other countries provided more extensive data and changes in geographical distribution emerged; D. immitis distribution expanded in endemic countries and it also spread to central and eastern Europe (Switzerland, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgary, Hungary, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Poland, Ukraine, and Russia) and other Mediterranean countries (Algeria, Tunisia, Israel) within years (Traversa et al., 2010; Genchi et al., 2011; Mórchon et al., 2012; Genchi and Kramer, 2020; Morchón et al., 2022; Carbonara et al., 2025a). Hyperendemicity has been reported in some South Europe islands such as the Canary and Balearic Islands in Spain (Montoya-Alonso et al., 2022), Kythnos in Greece (Carbonara et al., 2025a), and Linosa in Italy (Brianti et al., 2022). At the same time, canine HWD prevalences in historical endemic-hyperendemic foci in Western Europe were found to be stable or lowering due to the awareness of owners and vet practitioners of the canine disease risk and availability of chemoprophylactic drugs (Genchi and Kramer, 2020; Morchon et al., 2022).

Introduction of new competent mosquito species (Ae. albopictus, Ae. koreicus), increasing mosquito abundance and seasonal activity, as well as increased travelling of infected dogs, have caused the spread of filarial infections worldwide (Genchi and Kramer, 2020). Global temperature rising also lengthens the seasonal timeframe adequate for maturation of larvae in the infected mosquitoes up to throughout the year (Simón et al., 2014). Climatic differences concerning humidity also impact on the risk of exposure for susceptible hosts, particularly when the canine population is not undergoing massive chemoprophylactic treatment (Montoya-Alonso et al., 2016). The long-lasting life cycle of filarial worms involves an intermediate mosquito host (the same for D. repens) that become infected by taking a blood meal from reservoir hosts carrying in blood an adequate number of circulating L1 larvae (microfilariae) (Fig. 2). Culex pipiens, Aedes vexans, Aedes caspius and Aedes albopictus are the main mosquito vector species hosts in Europe (Cancrini et al., 2006; 2007; McCall et al., 2008; Simón et al., 2012; Vismarra et al., 2025). They feed on humans, cats, dogs and other vertebrates; however, the reservoir role is played by dogs and some wild canids, as cats and humans and other vertebrates are scarcely microfilaraemic. In susceptible mosquitoes, larvae moult up to the L3 stage; these larvae are infective for the definitive hosts (Simón et al., 2012). Italy is the European country where Ae. albopictus is most abundant, and Italian geographical areas with suitable habitats for Ae. albopictus correlated with the majority of D. immitis antibody-positive cats detected in a national study (Genchi et al., 2024). Cats are imperfect hosts to Dirofilaria worms with many important differences between the parasite life cycles in cats and dogs. After inoculation, only a low number of L3 larvae develop to the adult stage in a small percentage of cats, and this takes about 8 months for D. immitis (Simón et al., 2012). Moreover, the production of L1 larvae (microfilariae) occurs only rarely (only 20% of cats with mature female and male worms) and, when microfilariae production does occur, it lasts only for a few months in feline blood and at a low load (McCall et al., 2008; Simón et al., 2012; Panarese et al., 2021).

Despite the low parasite load in cats (1-6 adult worms per cat), severe pathological changes can be found early in HWD which can be life threatening. First, pulmonary endo-mesoarteritis with occlusive medial hypertrophy is observed as soon as immature worms arrive in the pulmonary vessels (about 3 months post-infection [p.i.]) (Dillon et al., 2007; 2014). Immune response causes early death (3-4 months p.i.) of most juvenile heartworms soon after they arrive in the pulmonary arteries, otherwise they survive about 2-4 years followed by self-cure in most feline cases (Venco et al., 2008). Early or end-stage parasite death can be associated with acute severe lesions (severe pulmonary thromboembolism and eosinophilic inflammatory response in lungs) causing the so-called heartwormassociated respiratory disease (HARD), characterised by acute onset of dyspnoea and an interstitial pattern on lung radiography (Dillon et al., 2007; García-Guasch et al., 2013; Dillon et al., 2014). According to experimental studies, an acute systemic anaphylaxis can occur in a hyperacute course of feline HWD secondary to the release of large quantities of D. immitis and Wolbachia antigens from dead parasites.

The immune response is considered responsible for differences of feline HWD compared to dogs. The strong feline immune response evidenced in both spontaneous and experimental infections interfere with the development of larvae and promotes death of worms (Prieto et al., 2002; Morchon et al., 2004). Immune response can also interfere with heartworm fertility as adults transplanted from cats to dogs can resume their ability to produce microfilariae (American Heartworm Society, 2024). Immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies, against somatic antigens from D. immitis L3 stage larvae and against synthetic peptides derived from adult worm molecules, are respectively found one and two months after experimental infections, and persist at least for months (Prieto et al., 2002; Morchon et al., 2004). Antibodies trigger an acute inflammatory reaction to immature stages and dead larvae are phagocytised by pulmonary intravascular macrophages enhancing inflammation (Prieto et al., 2002; Dillon et al., 2008). A strong IgG immune response against the Wolbachia endosymbiont is detected in both spontaneous and experimental infections with D. immitis (Morchon et al., 2004).

When experimentally infected cats receive prophylactic treatment against L3 larvae, anti-D. immitis antibody levels rapidly decrease, while an increased level of anti-Wolbachia antibodies is detected (Morchon et al., 2004). Large amounts of bacteria probably stimulate the immune system when they are released during larval moults and/or larval death (Morchon et al., 2004). Clinical signs decline or disappear as worms mature and adult worms seem to be better tolerated, until they die and trigger a second acute severe inflammatory reaction (Venco et al., 2015). Cats that are antibody-positive to D. immitis, irrespective to clinical signs, have a 6-fold higher risk to be hypersensitive to one or more of 20 tested common environmental allergens, with hypersensitivity to Dermatophagoides farinae being most frequent (García-Rodríguez et al., 2023).

Sometimes sudden death is reported in apparently healthy cats as a consequence of severe pulmonary thromboembolic or haemorrhagic pathology, including haemothorax due to pulmonary artery dissection (Alho et al., 2016; Biasato et al., 2017; Diakou et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2026). The so-called HARD is characterised by acute onset of mixed dyspnoea and signs of severe respiratory insufficiency. Hypotension and signs of systemic anaphylaxis, vomiting, and diarrhoea can be associated with parasite death (Litster and Atwell, 2006; Litster et al., 2007; Panarese et al., 2021). Most symptomatic cats have, however, a less severe and chronic course of HWD with mild to moderate respiratory signs, that can persist for some time even after the parasite death (Carbonara et al., 2025b). Various further clinical manifestations, such as chronic vomiting, anorexia, and cachexia, are also reported and can be the most evident clinical signs (Dillon et al., 2000). Caval syndrome is rarely observed in cats but can arise when worms located in the right side of the heart cause tricuspid regurgitation (Kulmer et al., 2021; Carbonara et al., 2025b) (Fig. 1).

Diagnosis of HWD in cats is more elusive compared to dogs. The rare and short-term occurrence of microfilaraemia and the low number of adult worms can make it difficult to diagnose HWD in cats. A multistep approach, combining mainly antigen and antibody tests and diagnostic imaging, is required to overcome the limitations of each single diagnostic technique in symptomatic cats (Venco et al., 2015; American Heartworm Society, 2024) (Fig. 6). Moreover, HARD can occur during spontaneous early death of parasites and this explains the possibility of discordant results between different tests even in symptomatic cats. The discrepancies between clinical, radiological, ultrasound, and serological findings are due to different chronologies in the development of the parasite, host immune response and pathology. It is therefore suggested to record negative heartworm serological test results as "no antigen detected" and "no antibody detected" rather than as "negative" (American Heartworm Society, 2024). Unfortunately, even in a historically endemic country like Italy, the diagnostic approach of veterinarians managing suspected cases of both HWD and subcutaneous filariosis is varied, and they mostly do not follow available guidelines (Genchi et al., 2023). This means that currently both diseases are probably underdiagnosed. No data are available regarding adherence to the recommendation of including Dirofilaria serological tests in annual health check of cats.

Thoracic radiography is always indicated for the diagnosis of HWD, because of frequent suggestive changes, and for prognostic reasons (Venco et al., 2015; Falcón-Cordón et al., 2024). Suggestive abnormalities include a vascular pattern (enlargement, loss of tapering, tortuosity, and truncation of the right or both caudal pulmonary arteries on ventro-dorsal and dorso-ventral thoracic views) and patchy infiltrates around the caudal lobar arteries resulting from plasma leakage and perivascular inflammation (often peripheral in caudal lobes) (Fig. 7) or a diffuse broncho-interstitial pattern (Venco et al., 2015; Alberigi et al., 2020; Carbonara et al., 2025b; Kim et al., 2026). Radiographic changes can be the only detected abnormality in suspected HARD cases, particularly when HARD occurs in an early phase of infection. However, lungworm disease should be excluded in these cats as a differential diagnosis for the radiographic changes (see the ABCD Guidelines for lungworm disease and Pennisi et al., 2015). Follow-up thoracic radiographic evaluation is recommended in the monitoring of disease. Fig. 7. Thoracic radiograph (left lateral view) of a cat with acute dyspnoea caused by HWD.

Pulmonary thromboembolism, arterial changes and bronchial collapse are common findings when cats with HWD undergo CT or angiography investigations of the thorax (Dillon et al., 2014; Panopoulos et al., 2018). In symptomatic early phases of spontaneous infection, bronchial remodelling can be evidenced with thoracic CT examination and bronchial dilatation with no arterial enlargement is detected by measuring specific CT ratios (García-Rodríguez et al., 2025; 2026).

Filariae can be easily recognised by ultrasound examination when they are in the right heart chambers, the main pulmonary trunk or distal caudal vena cava (Diakou et al., 2019; Alberigi et al., 2020; Kulmer et al., 2021; Carbonara et al., 2025b; Kim et al., 2026). The body wall of adult HW appears as double hyperechoic parallel lines ("railway lines") because of reflection of ultrasound waves by the cuticle of the worm (Fig. 8). Diagnostic sensitivity is operator-dependent, and quantification of the worm burden is difficult and false negative, as well as false positive, evaluations are possible (Venco et al., 2015). To increase the sensitivity of the test, caudal pulmonary arteries should be carefully followed to their bifurcation within the lung fields (American Heartworm Society, 2024). Severe right chamber dilatations are rarely seen at diagnosis (Kulmer et al., 2021). Tricuspid insufficiency can be detected, even after parasitological cure, probably due to pulmonary hypertension caused by arterial hypertrophy and myofibrosis (Dillon et al., 2014; Kulmer et al., 2021; Carbonara et al., 2025b). Necropsy is the only diagnostic method available in cases of sudden death of cats with HWD (Fig. 3) but it also can confirm the disease when negative results of antemortem diagnostic methods are obtained in suspected cases (Biasato et al., 2017; Mosley et al., 2023). In these cases, the right side of the heart, pulmonary arteries, and ectopic sites, including the brain and spinal cord in case of neurological signs, must be carefully examined for adult worms (McCall et al., 2008; Simón et al., 2012; American Heartworm Society, 2024).

Nelson and Johnson, 2024). Heat treatment of serum samples prior to carrying out an antigen test has to be done at an external laboratory because specific heat treatment conditions are needed (i.e. 103°C for 10 mins incubation followed by centrifugation) (European Society of Dirofilariosis and Angiostrongylosis, 2017); heat-treated serum is not suitable for antibody detection tests. In dogs, heat treatment may cause false positive results towards other filarial worms (e.g. D. repens and Acanthocheilonema dracunculoides) but no similar information is available in cats (Szatmári et al., 2020; Sobotyk et al., 2021). In order to underline the low negative predictive value of antigen assays in cats it is suggested to record any negative result as "no antigen detected" instead of "negative" (American Heartworm Society, 2024).

Anti-L3 antibodies against D. immitis are found as early as one month p.i. and they confirm exposure to D. immitis early, irrespective of the parasite load (Prieto et al., 2002). An indirect ELISA assay using somatic antigens of adult worms has also been developed (Perles et al., 2025). Availability of commercial assays vary among countries and a wide range of sensitivities exist among different tests (American Heartworm Society, 2024). In the USA the preferred antibody test for the American Heartworm Society is the Heska (an Antech company) antibody test, but this test is not available in Europe, where the only anti-D.immitis antibody test is available at IDEXX reference laboratory. The risk of false positive results exists because of antibody persistence even in cats that have cleared the parasites (Berdoulay et al., 2004). Importantly, antibody cross-reactivity between D. immitis and D. repens exists and serological tests actually detect antibodies against any Dirofilaria spp. (Perles et al., 2025).

There is no adulticidal drug approved for the treatment of feline HWD, and adulticide therapy is not recommended in cats because selfcure occurs in most cases in 18-48 months (Venco et al., 2008, 2015; American Heartworm Society, 2024; Kim et al., 2026). Moreover, adulticide and surgical therapy are risky in cats and an increase in survival time has not been demonstrated in treated cats. Infected cats, with no clinical and radiographic signs of pulmonary lung disease should be followed up by thoracic radiography, echocardiography, antigen and antibody testing for decision-making regarding treatment and to detect self-cure (Venco et al., 2015). Usually spontaneous elimination of infection in antigen-positive cats is followed by clearance of antigenaemia over some months (Kim et al., 2026). Medical treatment is based on clinical signs and is not evidence based. Prednisolone (1-2 mg/kg/24 hour tapering over a few weeks) should be given to cats with respiratory signs that test positive on antigen and/or antibody testing (American Heartworm Society, 2024).

Prednisolone (1-2 mg/kg/24 hour tapering over a few weeks) should be given to cats with respiratory signs that test positive on antigen and/or antibody testing (American Heartworm Society, 2024). In asymptomatic cats with suggestive radiographic changes, prednisolone treatment should also be applied, and treatment should be followed up by the same clinical, radiographic and antigen/antibody testing method (American Heartworm Society, 2024). Improvement of radiographic changes associated with previous positive antigen tests becoming negative are markers of recovery despite the persistence of positive antibody tests (American Heartworm Society, 2024). Hyperacute cases of HWD require intensive care unit stabilisation because of the risk of respiratory failure and shock (Venco et al., 2015). Adulticide therapy used in dogs (melarsomine) is not safe in cats and carries a high risk of pulmonary thromboembolism and anaphylactic reactions following parasite death in treated cats (American Heartworm Society, 2024).

in dogs (melarsomine) is not safe in cats and carries a high risk of pulmonary thromboembolism and anaphylactic reactions following parasite death in treated cats (American Heartworm Society, 2024). Adult parasites visualised by echocardiography in the right heart and main pulmonary arteries, have been surgically removed through the jugular vein (Iizuka et al., 2009; Kulmer et al., 2021). However, worms have to be retrieved intact to avoid anaphylaxis (American Heartworm Society, 2024). Surgical removal of an adult heartworm that had migrated to the femoral artery was successfully obtained by direct access to the worm from the arteriotomy site (Oldach et al., 2018). A slow kill protocol, combining monthly administration of heartworm-preventative drugs combined with a one-month course of doxycycline therapy, is used in dogs when melarsomine is contraindicated; this has also been reported in cats (Diakou et al., 2019) but its efficacy and safety are unknown and therefore this protocol is not recommended (Savadelis et al., 2017; American Heartworm Society, 2024). Nevertheless, all cats diagnosed with HWD should also undergo monthly application of preventative drugs (see below).

The prognosis is guarded in feline HWD. Death can occur suddenly, even in asymptomatic cats, or associated with the development of HARD (Kim et al., 2026). A guarded prognosis is resolved when (self) cure is confirmed through serological tests becoming negative and diagnostic imaging findings resolving. Antibody positivity can however persist and can be due to repeated L3 exposure, even in cats under preventative regimen. The prognosis in the case of atypical localisation of D. immitis depends on the tissue(s) involved.

Apart from a comprehensive approach to mosquito control (USA Environmental Protection Agency website, 2025), the corner stone of HWD prevention in cats is chemoprophylaxis (European Society of Dirofilariosis and Angiostrongylosis, 2017; American Heartworm Society, 2024; European Scientific Counsel Companion Animal Parasites, 2024). Prevention of host mosquito bites is an adjunctive strategy in dogs, but it is not possible in cats because of toxicity of permethrin (Bessant and Sparkes, 2010). Because of the unpredictable and potentially fatal course of HWD in cats, diagnostic difficulties and the lack of safe and effective treatments, all cats in endemic areas should be given monthly chemoprophylaxis from 2 months of age - all year long - for killing infective larvae in the L3-L4 stages (American Heartworm Society, 2024). Although outdoor cats have a 3-fold increased risk of being D. immitis antigen-positive, it is known that variable percentages of antigen seropositive cats (15-32%) actually live indoors (Levy et al., 2017). Chemoprophylaxis is also recommended for cats that do not live in heartworm area but that are travelling to endemic heartworm areas.

A chemoprophylactic drug should be administered around 30 days after exposure, even in the case of a shorter duration (less than one month) of stay in the risk area (European Scientific Counsel Companion Animal Parasites, 2025; European Society of Dirofilariosis and Angiostrongylosis, 2017). In case of stays longer than one month in a risk area, a monthly regimen of chemoprophylactic administration is required. Unfortunately, veterinarian awareness of the importance of feline HWD prevention is still low and is often neglected, even more so in cat shelters for economic reasons (Polak and Smith-Blackmore, 2014; Levy et al., 2017; Genchi et al., 2019; 2023). Adequate preventative treatment covering the whole of the transmission season is crucial for effective prevention, and a year-round approach is the best option.

Chemoprophylaxis theoretically could be restricted to 1-2 months after the end of the mosquito transmission season in colder countries but this is a risky regime, and is not recommended in endemic areas because of annual climatic variability (temperature and humidity) and the possibility of winter survival of mosquitos in urban heat islands (Montoya-Alonso et al., 2016; European Society of Dirofilariosis and Angiostrongylosis, 2017; American Heartworm Society, 2024). Macrocyclic lactones are used for HWD chemoprophylaxis as they are effective in killing L3-L4 stages. Currently, four macrocyclic lactone drugs are licensed for cats: milbemycin oxime, moxidectin, selamectin and eprinomectin. Some formulations include isoxazoline systemic insecticides (fluralaner, sarolaner, esafoxolaner) that are known to kill mosquitos after they feed on treated hosts, although they are not licensed for this effect.

This effect is epidemiologically less important than in dogs as microfilaraemia is infrequent in cats. Ivermectin, the first oral macrocyclic lactones used to prevent HWD in dogs, can also be given to cats but it is not widely available in Europe as oral formulations suitable for the administration of the low dosage required in cats (24-71 μg/kg) (European Scientific Counsel Companion Animal Parasites, 2024). Almost all currently licensed drugs available for cats are given monthly, topically as spot-ons or orally (Baker et al., 2014; Dillon et al., 2014; Little et al., 2015; McTier et al., 2019) (table 1). Antigen positive or antibody positive cats can be safely given preventative therapy, and chemoprophylaxis is part of their treatment. Serological (antigen and antibody) tests should be carried out before starting chemoprophylaxis to obtain a risk assessment for HWD in cats living in endemic areas and discriminate false lack of efficacy (American Heartworm Society, 2024).

Macrocyclic lactone resistance has been confirmed in USA since 2011 where resistant strains are spreading from hyperendemic regions (Prichard, 2021; Curry et al., 2025). There was no demostration of resistance in dog clinical samples studied in Europe (Curry et al., 2022). Resistance is genetically based, inherited between parasite generations and there is concern that it could spread to other parts of the world due to dog and mosquito migration (Curry and Prichard, 2022). Phylogenetic analysis of Wolbachia isolates from susceptible and resistant D. immitis worms shows that the Wolbachia bacteria isolates divide according to the susceptible/resistant status of the D. immitis worms (Shin et al., 2020), suggesting the possible involvement of Wolbachia in D. immitis resistance. Suboptimal doses and prolonged intervals between treatment administrations play a role in the genesis of resistance.

There is great interest in human dirofilarioses because of the increasing number of cases reported in endemic areas (Perles et al., 2024). Immature D. immitis worms can reside in a branch of the pulmonary artery of humans and induce the development of pulmonary nodules (Simón et al., 2012). The disease is sporadic and in Europe D. repens is responsible for human dirofilariasis more frequently than D. immitis, even in areas of high endemicity of the latter species (Simón et al., 2012; Capelli et al., 2018). Epidemiological studies detecting antibodies in people found that the rates of infection in humans are similar to those of dogs in endemic areas (Simón et al., 2012). Importantly, Ukraine is likely the only European nation with a mandatory case registration system, along with a national register for Dirofilaria human infections, since 1975. This system reported, between 1997 and 2012, 1,465 cases of D. repens infection and a limited number of cases due to D. immitis (Pękacz et al., 2025). In contrast, between 2000 and 2019, only 576 clinical cases of Dirofilaria spp. were reported worldwide outside of Ukraine, 72% caused by D. repens and 7% by D. immitis (Simón et al., 2021).

- The domestic cat is the main host of feline herpesvirus (FHV) although other felids can be infected. - Prevalence of infection is high especially in large populations and in shelters. - FHV infection causes acute upper respiratory and ocular disease, which is particularly severe in young kittens. Corneal dendritic ulcers are considered a pathognomonic manifestation of FHV ocular infection. - Following the acute phase of the disease, almost all cats undergo a latent infection, which can lead to recurrent clinical signs, mainly ocular diseases (conjunctivitis and keratitis) after intermittent reactivation. However, reactivation can also be asymptomatic. - The preferred method to detect FHV in biological samples is PCR and taking samples at different sites (e.g. conjunctival, oro-pharyngeal and nasal swabs) significantly increases the detection rate. - Trifluridine (topical) and Famciclovir (systemic treatment) are the preferred antiviral drugs for treatment of acute FHV ocular diseases, but other antiviral drugs are available. - Cellular immunity plays an important role in protection against the disease and antibody testing is not useful to predict protection.

Only modified live and inactivated parenteral vaccines are available and there is no difference in efficacy regarding the disease. All the vaccines are combined with FCV. - Maternal antibodies interfere with the response to vaccination until eight weeks of age on average. Two vaccinations at an interval of two to four weeks are generally recommended for primary vaccination, irrespective of the vaccine type. After the first annual booster, three-years interval boosters should preferentially be given when the risk of infection is considered as low. In shelters or high-risk situations, annual boosters can be considered.

The agent of the feline viral rhinotracheitis is distributed worldwide and belongs to the order Herpesvirales, family Herpesviridae, subfamily Alphaherpesvirinae, genus Varicellovirus. The new (actual) name of this virus is Felid alphaherpesvirus-1 (however for practical purposes, it is named FHV all along this guidelines). Another feline herpesvirus belonging to the Gammaherpesvirinae subfamily of Herpesviridae (FcaGHV1: Felid Gammaherpesvirus 1) and described in cats (Troyer et al., 2014) is not related to FHV. Although only one serotype[1] is described for FHV, the virulence can differ between viral strains (Gaskell et al., 2007); differences can also be observed by restriction endonuclease analysis (Hamano et al., 2004; Thiry, 2006). However, a recent molecular study failed to correlate viral genomic polymorphisms and severity of clinical signs (Lewin et al., 2020). The genomic double-stranded DNA of FHV is packaged into an icosahedral capsid surrounded by a proteinaceous tegument and a phospholipid envelope, which contains at least ten glycoproteins. [1] Serotype: antigenic property allowing different strains to be distinguished by serological methods.

Serotype should be differentiated from genotype, which refers to characterization by molecular methods. In the feline host, FHV replicates in epithelial cells of the conjunctiva, cornea and the upper respiratory tract, and in neurons. The neuronal infection enables the virus to establish lifelong latency after primary infection. FHV is related antigenically to canine herpesvirus and phocid (seal) herpesviruses 1 and 2; there is no known cross-species transfer (Gaskell et al., 2006). The virus is inactivated within 3 hours at 37°C and is susceptible to most commercial disinfectants, antiseptics and detergents. At 4°C, it remains infectious for about five months, at 25°C for about one month, and it is inactivated at 56°C in 4-5 minutes (Pedersen, 1987).

The domestic cat is the main host of FHV, but FHV has been isolated also from other felids, including cheetahs and lions, and antibodies have been detected in pumas (Carmel et al., 2017; Chaber et al., 2017; Witte et al., 2017). Clinical signs have been described after infection in wild felids, including dermatitis in cheetahs. Cheetahs especially are very sensitive to FHV, including development of serious clinical signs after being vaccinated with modified-live vaccines (Pennings et al., 2020). In healthy small populations, the prevalence of viral shedding is usually less than 10% of cats, whereas in large populations, especially those containing cats with visible clinical signs, up to 50% can shed virus (Coutts et al., 1994; Binns et al., 2000; Zapirain et al., 2004; Helps et al., 2005; Berger et al., 2015; Fernandez et al., 2017). The highest positivity rates (25 to 50%) are generally observed when cats with acute upper respiratory tract disease (URTD) are sampled (Schulz et al., 2015; Fernandez et al., 2017; Zirofsky et al., 2018).

positivity rates (25 to 50%) are generally observed when cats with acute upper respiratory tract disease (URTD) are sampled (Schulz et al., 2015; Fernandez et al., 2017; Zirofsky et al., 2018). The results of prevalence studies depend on the diagnostic method used to diagnose FHV infection; PCR detection of FHV DNA is more sensitive than virus isolation, which was the technique used in many older studies. One multicentric Spanish study, exploring the prevalence of different pathogens in healthy and diseased cats by PCR, found that FHV was detected in 6% of healthy cats, 28% of cats with URTD and 24% of cats with conjunctivitis (Fernandez et al., 2017). In another study in Switzerland, 9% of asymptomatic cats tested positive for FHV by PCR (Berger et al., 2015). In shelters, the risk is higher, and with increasing time spent at a shelter facility, the rate of shedding increases: 4% of cats are shedders upon entering the shelter and after one week this increases, with 50% of the cats shedding (Pedersen et al., 2004).

The low initial prevalence of shedding likely reflects the intermittent nature of viral excretion during latency, while the high rates after one week are likely due to both new infections in naïve cats and reactivation in latently infected cats.

Following infection via the nasal, oral or conjunctival route and after the acute phase of the disease, FHV frequently develops latent chronic infection, similarly to many other herpesviruses. During chronic infection, intermittent reactivation may occur, which gives rise to the re-activation of viral shedding in oronasal and conjunctival secretions. Except in catteries with more densely housed multiple cats, contamination of the environment does not generally play a role in transmission. During latency, virus is not shed, but virus shedding by acutely infected cats, as well as by latently infected cats experiencing reactivation, are the two main sources of infection (Gaskell and Povey, 1982). Transplacental infection has not been described in the field. Latently infected queens can however transmit FHV to their offspring because parturition and lactation are stressful events that can lead to viral reactivation and shedding. Kittens can therefore acquire FHV infection at an early age.

The outcome of infection depends on the presence of maternal-derived antibodies (MDA): when high levels are present, kittens are protected against disease and experience subclinical infection that leads to virus latency, whereas in the absence of sufficient MDA, clinical manifestations of infection can follow (Gaskell and Povey, 1982).

The virus enters the body via the nasal, oral or conjunctival routes. It causes a lytic infection of the nasal epithelium with spread to the conjunctival sac, pharynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles. Lesions are characterised by multifocal necrosis of epithelium, with neutrophil granulocyte infiltration and inflammation. In one study, a transient viraemia associated with blood mononuclear cells was observed after natural infection in young cats (Westermeyer et al., 2009). This has been observed exceptionally also in neonates (Gaskell et al., 2007). Viral shedding or excretion starts as soon as 24 hours after infection and lasts for one to three weeks. Clinical signs usually appear two to six days after experimental infection depending on the infectious dose of virus (Gaskell and Povey, 1979) but the incubation period can be longer. Acute disease usually resolves within 10 to 14 days (Westermeyer et al., 2009) although ocular signs, in cases of keratitis, can persist longer (Nassise et al., 1989). Some animals develop chronic lesions in the upper respiratory tract and in ocular tissues.
