Many studies have demonstrated that sand flies take blood meals from cats (Gonzáles et al., 2017) and they have been found infected by L. infantum after feeding on naturally infected cats (Maroli et al., 2007; da Silva et al., 2010; Mendonça et al., 2020). Experimental xenodiagnoses (in the case of vector-borne infections, xenodiagnoses is a diagnostic method used to document the presence of infectious agents by exposing a host to a vector and then examining the vector for the presence of the infectious agent it may have ingested) by sand flies between a cat naturally infected with L. infantum and a naïve dog was successfully performed (Batista et al., 2020). Additionally, antibodies against sand fly salivary antigens were detected in cats exposed to phlebotomine sand flies in an endemic area and the feline antibody response to Phlebotomus perniciosus saliva was positively associated with Leishmania infection (Pereira et al., 2019a).

Progressive infection and disease development are primarily influenced by immunological factors, which are linked to the complex genetic background of the hosts, as demonstrated by studies in laboratory animals, dogs and humans (Baneth et al., 2008). In people, L. infantum induces two different diseases: cutaneous leishmaniosis is generally a focal papular or ulcerative skin lesion whereas visceral leishmaniosis is a severe disease without cutaneous manifestations. The latter form is the typical presentation in immunocompromised patients (Kaplan et al., 2009). In dogs, leishmaniosis is a multisystemic disease with a wide and dynamic spectrum of severity that reflects the balance between the protective cell-mediated, and the non-protective humoral, immune response. Usually, subclinical infection and self-limiting mild disease forms outnumber non-self-limiting severe disease cases in endemic areas (Baneth et al., 2008; Solano-Gallego et al., 2009). Coinfections with vector-borne pathogens (e.g. Ehrlichia canis, Borrelia burgdorferi) influence parasite burden and the progression of CanL (Baxarias et al., 2018; Pessôa-Pereira et al., 2023).

Coinfections with vector-borne pathogens (e.g. Ehrlichia canis, Borrelia burgdorferi) influence parasite burden and the progression of CanL (Baxarias et al., 2018; Pessôa-Pereira et al., 2023). In all host species, macrophages play a central role in the control of the infection. Cytokines such as IFN-γ, IL-2 and TNF-α, secreted by activated T cells, stimulate macrophages to kill intracellular Leishmania amastigotes. The presence of Leishmania-infected macrophages is usually associated with a granulomatous inflammatory reaction and a variable number of lymphocytes and plasmacells (Baneth et al., 2008). Lymphoid hyperplasia is the most common cytological pattern in both dogs and cats (Solano-Gallego et al., 2009, 2011; Pennisi et al., 2015a). A massive antibody response is associated with more severe disease and is responsible for immune complex deposition in the kidney, with glomerulonephritis and subsequent chronic kidney disease (CKD) (Baneth et al., 2008; SolanoGallego et al., 2009). Many data from experimental infections of dogs are available but experimental infections of cats with L. infantum were performed in only two studies.

Findings from these two studies suggest that cats are more resistant than dogs to experimental infection; however, chronic infection cannot be excluded. This is what has been inferred from a previous longitudinal study on naturally infected cats that remained PCR- and antibody-positive for a long time, with either no clinical manifestations or with a mild disease, and from cats diagnosed with FeL years after rehoming from an endemic area (Pennisi et al., 2015a; Schäfer et al., 2023).

The description of histopathological patterns associated with FeL is available mostly from biopsied lesions from the skin, mucosal lesions and the eye. Feline skin lesions show a diffuse granulomatous dermatitis with Leishmania parasites inside macrophages, or a granulomatous perifolliculitis and lichenoid tissue reaction/interface dermatitis, with a lower parasite load (Navarro et al., 2010; Puleio et al., 2011; Schäfer et al., 2023). Granulomatous inflammation with many amastigotes has also been seen in mucosal nodules, subcutaneous panniculitis, eye, spleen, liver, the intestines and the kidneys (Navarro et al., 2010; Puleio et al., 2011; Verneuil, 2013; Migliazzo et al., 2014; Tabar et al., 2022; Mestrinho et al., 2022; Matralis et al., 2023; Schäfer et al., 2023).

Leishmania immunity is complex. In the dog, a susceptible species, protective immunity against L. infantum is CD4 T cell-mediated, and the release of IFN-γ, IL-2 and TNF-α is associated with anti-Leishmania activation of macrophages. A combination of high antibody levels and a reduced cell-mediated response are found in dogs that develop disease (Baneth et al., 2008; Solano-Gallego et al., 2009). Cats with L. infantum associated clinical disease have high blood parasitaemia, low to very high antibody levels and hyperglobulinaemia. As reported for dogs, Leishmania PCR-positive healthy cats can be negative for anti-Leishmania antibodies (Pennisi et al., 2012, 2015a). As in other host species, both humoral and cell-mediated adaptive immune responses are elicited by L. infantum in exposed cats from endemic areas (Priolo et al., 2019). Specific IFN-γ was in fact detected in 21% of these cats that were all negative on Leishmania PCR performed on EDTA blood samples and negative or border-line antibody-positive (Priolo et al., 2019).

Specific IFN-γ was in fact detected in 21% of these cats that were all negative on Leishmania PCR performed on EDTA blood samples and negative or border-line antibody-positive (Priolo et al., 2019). Similar results were reported in cats where the cell-mediated immune response was tested by intradermal leishmanin test (Montenegro skin test) (Alves et al., 2022). The relationship between the pattern of adaptive immune response and the severity of FeL has not yet been investigated, but cats seem to have lower levels of adaptive immune response compared to dogs (Priolo et al., 2022a). Infection experiments with L. braziliensis have shown that the development of skin lesions usually precedes antibody appearance, and seroconversion occurs when the lesions are healing (Simoes-Mattos et al., 2005).

Many cats that developed clinical signs were suspected to have an impaired immune system because of concurrent FIV infection, dual FIV and FeLV infection, neoplasia (squamous cell carcinoma), diabetes mellitus, immune-mediated diseases (e.g., eosinophilic granuloma, pemphigus foliaceus, feline chronic stomatitis) or had been treated with immunosuppressive drugs such as corticosteroids (Pennisi and Persichetti, 2018; Pennisi et al., 2019; Fernandez-Gallego et al., 2020; Schäfer et al., 2023; Tiozzo Ambrosi et al., 2023). Based on a retrospective case-control study, in cats exposed to L. infantum, antibody positivity to FIV is predictive for L. infantum antibody positivity, which is also marker of infection progression (Priolo et al., 2022b). However, specific IFN-γ production has been detected in both FIV- and FeLV-coinfected cats, including a FeLV-infected cat with concurrent squamous cell carcinoma (Priolo et al., 2019).

Canine leishmaniosis has been extensively investigated by field cross sectional and longitudinal controlled studies. It is usually a chronic and progressive disease, with an incubation period lasting for months or even years. Any tissue or organ can be involved, but skin lesions are most suggestive, and renal disease is most important prognostically for reduced survival time (Solano-Gallego et al., 2009; Clinical cases of FeL have been documented - mainly in the last 25 years and in Southern Europe - and case reports and case series at present provide the only published information about the disease. Feline leishmaniosis is probably underreported and more frequent than it is currently considered, and the less severe clinical presentations are probably missed, as occurred previously with CanL. Additionally, coinfections and comorbidities are commonly seen in cats with FeL and these can contribute to a misrepresentation of disease (Pennisi et al., 2015a). The age range of cats at diagnosis is wide (2-21 years) but FeL is more common in mature animals (median age seven years). Very few cases are diagnosed in 2-3 year old cats.

The most frequent skin lesion is focal and multifocal ulcerative and crusty-ulcerative dermatitis (Pennisi et al., 2015b; Basso et al., 2016; Fernandez-Gallego et al., 2020; Schäfer et al., 2023; Tiozzo Ambrosi et al., 2023) (Fig. 4). However, anti-Leishmania therapy cured non-seasonal pruritus of head and neck non-responsive to previous treatments in a cat (Tiozzo Ambrosi et al., 2023). Mild to severe lymph node enlargement is seen in about half of cases and a multicentric pattern is most common (Pennisi et al., 2015a; Tabar et al., 2022; Tiozzo Ambrosi et al., 2023). Among the common clinical signs, non-specific manifestations such as lethargy, anorexia and weight loss predominate (Pennisi et al., 2015a; Pennisi et al., 2019; Fernandez-Gallego et al., 2020; Schäfer et al., 2023). About one third of cats show ocular involvement with eyelid, conjunctival, corneal, uveal, and retinal lesions.

A severe obstructive syndrome was seen in three cats which was associated with nodular or infiltrative masses formed by granulomatous leishmanial inflammation in the nasal cavity and the rhinopharynx (Leal et al., 2018; Franchi et al., 2019; Altuzarra et al., 2020). Dehydration, pale mucous membranes, vomiting, hepatomegaly, fever, jaundice, polyuria/polydipsia, spleen enlargement, chronic diarrhoea, abortion and mastitis form a miscellaneous list of rare findings and a causative role for L. infantum has not always been demonstrated (Pennisi et al., 2015a; Pereira et al., 2019b; Napoli et al., 2022; Tabar et al., 2022).

In three cats with severe obstructive syndrome in the upper respiratory tract caused by L. infantum, computed tomography (CT) of the head (Franchi et al., 2019; Altuzarra et al., 2020) and rhinoscopy (Leal et al., 2018; Altuzarra et al., 2020) were used to evaluate anatomical abnormalities and to take guided biopsies of nodular or infiltrative lesions. In one very severe case the osteolytic damage involved even the ethmoidal cribriform plate and the nasal mass extended into the rostral cranial cavity affecting the olfactory bulbs (Altuzarra et al., 2020). Neoplastic diseases and fungal rhinitis are the main conditions that can show similar imaging patterns. Ultrasound examination of abdomen was reported in two cases and splenomegaly was seen with a honeycomb appearance in one of them (Tabar et al., 2022; Tiozzo Ambrosi et al., 2023). In the case described by Tabar et al (2022), the cat suffered from chronic diarrhoea and a slight increase in the thickness of the duodenum was also found (Tabar et al., 2022).

Gastrointestinal endoscopy, with biopsies, was performed to exclude any concurrent disease causing the diarrhoea, and a diagnosis of diffuse granulomatous gastroenteritis caused by Leishmania infection was made, with more severe lesions in the duodenum (Tabar et al., 2022).

Diagnosis is often easily confirmed by direct detection of the parasite by cytological evaluation of skin, mucosal and mucocutaneous lesions and enlarged lymph nodes and spleen (Fig. 6). Fig. 6. Lymph node smear from a cat: Leishmania amastigotes in a macrophage (MG-G stain; x64 objective). Photomicrograph courtesy Maria Grazia Pennisi) When cytological evaluation is not diagnostic, histology (with IHC for increasing sensitivity compared to histopathology alone) is performed in biopsied lesional samples. Histological evaluation of lesions evidenced by rhinoscopy and gastrointestinal tract endoscopy is performed also to exclude comorbidities (Leal et al., 2018; Franchi et al., 2019; Altuzarra et al., 2020; Tabar et al., 2022). In some cases ocular disease caused by L. infantum was diagnosed and studied by histology after enucleation of the eyes affected by panophthalmitis (Leiva et al., 2005; Schäfer et al., 2023). The detection of parasite DNA by PCR in lesional samples, target tissues (lymphoid organs, bone marrow), blood, mucosal swabs, etc.

by panophthalmitis (Leiva et al., 2005; Schäfer et al., 2023). The detection of parasite DNA by PCR in lesional samples, target tissues (lymphoid organs, bone marrow), blood, mucosal swabs, etc. confirm the infection but the diagnosis of clinical leishmaniosis is obtained when the lesional cytological/histological patterns, clinical signs and other laboratory changes are compatible with leishmaniosis. One study estimated the prevalence of FeL in 2,632 feline skin and ocular biopsies examined over a four-year period to be 0.57% (Navarro et al., 2010). Upon post-mortem examination, the parasite was identified also in histopathological samples of the spleen, liver, kidney, pancreas, and gastrointestinal tract (Pennisi et al., 2015a). Nodular or diffuse granulomatous leishmanial inflammation was observed in affected tissues (Navarro et al., 2010; Puleio et al., 2011).

Anti-Leishmania antibody detection can be performed using Western Blot and quantitative methods (IFA, ELISA, direct agglutination). Antibody tests for specifically detecting feline anti-Leishmania antibodies are not commercially available, and veterinary laboratories have to validate their quantitative method for feline sera. Studies that validated IFA tests for usage on feline samples set a 1:80 dilution as the cut off level (Pennisi et al., 2012; Persichetti et al., 2017; Iatta et al., 2020). When the diagnostic performance of IFA, ELISA and WB was compared, all three techniques were similarly reliable, but WB was the most accurate (Persichetti et al., 2017). Rapid tests on the market for the qualitative detection of canine anti-L. infantum antibodies are not validated for use with cat serum. One of these commercial rapid tests was compared to an IFA validated assay, and low levels of sensitivity, negative predictive values, specificity, and positive predictive values were obtained (Pennisi et al., 2017).

High levels of antibodies detected by quantitative serology confirm a diagnosis of leishmaniosis in cats at risk of exposure to Leishmania and with suggestive clinical signs and/or clinicopathological alterations. In endemic areas it is advised to screen for L. infantum infection in cats with FIV infection, those requiring chronic immunosuppressive therapies and clinically healthy cats being screened for blood donation and those being relocated to non-endemic areas. Cats travelling to, or imported from, endemic areas should be tested, but one must remember that seroconversion occurs from few weeks to many months after exposure.

The available information about efficacy and safety of treatments used is based on single case reports or case series of FeL caused by L. infantum, not always with an appropriate follow-up (EBM grade IV) (Pennisi et al., 2015a). This means that the current level of evidence for statements and recommendations about FeL management is lower compared to CanL. Treatment of cats with clinical leishmaniosis is still empirically based and off label, using the most common drugs administered to dogs. Therefore, cats under therapy should be carefully monitored for possible adverse effects (table 1). In table 2 the dosage and duration of treatments used in FeL, as well as the total numbers of cats treated and those clinically improved, are reported. Long-term administration of allopurinol (5-50 mg/kg SID or BID PO) is the most used drug regimen and usually clinically effective, even in FIV-infected cats (Pennisi et al., 2015a; Maia et al., 2015; Pennisi et al., 2019; Altuzarra et al., 2020; Fernandez- Gallego et al., 2020; Mestrinho et al., 2022; Napoli et al., 2022; Schäfer et al., 2023).

In dogs, L. infantum infection is primarily prevented by reducing, as much as possible, exposure to sand fly bites via the use of topical pyrethroids. In recent years, vaccination has also been available, and it is an optional measure aimed to prevent the development of clinical disease in dogs (Miró et al., 2017). Almost all pyrethroids are toxic to cats, but flumethrin is licenced for cats as a collar application and in a controlled field study it decreased the incidence of L. infantum infection in cats, as had been previously seen in dogs (Brianti et al., 2014, 2017). According to current knowledge, testing of blood donors by antibody detection and Leishmania PCR performed on EDTA blood is the only reasonable measure for preventing non-vectorial transmission to cats (Pennisi et al., 2015b).

The Leishmania species reported in cats are of zoonotic concern, but no information is available on the risk for owners of infected cats. Vectorial transmission is considered the main way of transmission for L. infantum in humans, and dogs are considered the primary peridomestic reservoir. However, it is currently recognised that L. infantum has multiple mammalian hosts and non-canine hosts can play a primary epidemiological role in particular ecological situations (Bourdeau et al., 2020; Cardoso et al., 2021). One study performed in Iran found that owners of infected dogs had a higher risk for leishmaniosis caused by L. infantum (Gavgani et al., 2002). Currently, ownership of an infected dog is not considered a risk for the family members. However, mass preventative measures applied to dogs have a positive impact on the incidence of the human disease and on vector abundance (Silva et al., 2018; Courtenay et al., 2019).

- Virus Characteristics: FeLV is a gammaretrovirus affecting domestic and some wild felids. It is fragile outside the host and easily inactivated by disinfectants, soap, heat, and drying. However, moist environments can preserve infectivity for up to 48 hours and therefore susceptible animals could be infected by sharing food bowls contaminated by saliva. - Prevalence & Trends: FeLV infections occur worldwide. While prevalence has decreased in many European countries due to testing, segregation, and vaccination, rates remain high in some regions (up to 8.8%), particularly in southern Europe. A stagnation in prevalence decline highlights the need for continued awareness and prevention efforts. - Transmission & Risk Factors: - Main source: Progressively infected cats, shedding high amounts of virus in saliva, as well as lower amounts in nasal secretions, milk, and faeces. - Routes of infection: - Friendly interactions (grooming) - Aggressive encounters (biting) - Sharing food and water bowls. FeLV is a gammaretrovirus affecting domestic and some wild cats. It was first identified in 1964 and primarily spreads through saliva and close contact. FeLV is an RNA virus that integrates into the host's genome in its DNA form (provirus), allowing lifelong persistence. The virus is fragile in the environment due to its lipid envelope. FeLV can infect a wide range of tissues, including bone marrow, salivary glands, gastrointestinal tract, and respiratory epithelium. The cat undergoes progressive infection if the immune system fails to control the virus. If the cat can raise a strong immune response, it will undergo regressive infection, or even - the best case - abortive infection. Diagnostic tests detect mainly p27 capsid antigen (ELISA, POC tests), provirus (PCR), or less frequently viral RNA (reverse-transcriptase [RT]-PCR).

Endogenous feline leukaemia viruses (enFeLV) are remnants of ancient retroviral infections in all domestic cats, originating from murine leukaemia viruses (MuLV). While enFeLV cannot replicate or cause disease alone, they can recombine with FeLV-A, potentially creating more pathogenic variants. Interestingly, higher enFeLV loads correlate with better FeLV infection outcomes, possibly by interfering with replication. From a clinical standpoint, endogenous retroviruses do not typically require direct intervention but could also potentially influence FeLV diagnostics, and vaccine development. Monitoring FeLV variants and ensuring safe vaccine production remain important considerations. RD-114, an endogenous retrovirus from primates, is present in cats but not linked to disease. However, its detection in feline cell lines used for vaccines raises concerns about potential effects on non-domestic felids. Newly identified ERV-DC endogenous retroviruses, including ERV-DC10 and ERV-DC18, show mobility in the cat's genome and can produce infectious viruses.

Their role in feline health is unclear, but they contribute to FeLV recombination and genetic diversity, generating some FeLV variants found in cats with lymphoma or leukaemia.

FeLV is classified into several subgroups (Table 1) based on viral interference testing, neutralisation assays, and host cell receptor usage. The various subgroups use distinct cellular receptors, which affects their pathogenicity and transmission. FeLV-A is usually necessary for replication of FeLV-B, FeLV-C, and FeSV. As only FeLV-A is naturally transmitted, effective immunity against FeLV-A protects against all subgroups. The other subgroups arise within FeLV-A-infected cats through recombination and mutations, contributing to the emergence of new FeLV variants and impacting disease progression and severity (Table 1). From a diagnostic and preventative perspective, FeLV-A testing remains the primary screening tool. Vaccines targeting FeLV-A can help prevent the development of recombinant subgroups. Cats infected with FeLV should undergo regular veterinary monitoring for conditions such as anaemia, lymphoma, and immunosuppression, as these are common complications associated with different FeLV subgroups.

FeLV structure & key proteins FeLV is an RNA retrovirus with three major genes: gag (encodes structural proteins, including p27 used for FeLV diagnostic tests). - pol (encodes enzymes essential for viral replication and integration into host DNA). - env (encodes envelope proteins, including gp70, which defines virus subgroups and is a key target for immunity and vaccination). In clinical practice, diagnostic testing for FeLV focuses on detecting the p27 capsid protein antigen. The p27 antigen is present in high amounts in the cells and blood of infected cats. Vaccine strategies should aim to target gp70 due to its critical role in immunity. While understanding FeLV genotypes can assist in epidemiological tracking, they currently do not influence clinical decision-making.

FeLV primarily affects domestic cats, but there is increasing evidence that closely related wild felids can also be susceptible to infection. While FeLV was once thought to infect only domestic cats, studies have shown that certain isolates can infect non-feline cells, including those from rabbits, pigs, mink, and humans. Despite the ability of FeLV to replicate in non-feline cells in vitro, there is no evidence of natural transmission to non-felids. In humans, FeLV originating from infected cats would be readily recognised and destroyed and not pose a risk to human health. FeLV has been documented in several wild felid species, and there is growing concern about its impact on those populations, such as the European wildcat, and endangered species like the Florida panther and Iberian lynx. Domestic cats have been identified as a primary source of FeLV transmission to these wild felids. For example, in European wildcats, FeLV is highly prevalent, though they show no significant signs of disease apart from poorer body condition in some infected individuals.

to these wild felids. For example, in European wildcats, FeLV is highly prevalent, though they show no significant signs of disease apart from poorer body condition in some infected individuals. A severe FeLV outbreak occurred in Florida panthers between 2002 and 2005, likely originating from domestic cats, and led to the introduction of a vaccination programme. Similarly, wild pumas and jaguarundis in the Americas have been found to carry FeLV, with some suffering from diseases linked to the infection. Captive cheetahs have been found to be FeLV-infected and some of them have developed severe FeLV-associated disease. However, surveys of free-ranging cheetahs in Namibia have shown no evidence of infection, whereas wildcats of the ocelot lineage were found to be infected. However, servals and Panthera species (lions, tigers, jaguars), showed no evidence of FeLV infection, suggesting that certain wild felids, particularly those less closely related to domestic cats, are less susceptible.

Overall, the spread of FeLV in wild felid populations, especially in regions with high domestic cat density, raises concerns for wildlife conservation, prompting the need for surveillance, vaccination programmes, and controlling domestic cat populations to reduce the risk of transmission.

FeLV has a global presence, with its prevalence varying depending on cat population density and geographic location. Reported rates range from 0% to 28.4%, with higher rates observed in some regions, such as South America and Asia. Regional differences are evident, e.g., in Europe, with studies showing low prevalence (<1%) in northern and western Europe, while higher rates are found in southern Europe (up to 8.8%; Fig. 1). Fig. 1. Origin and FeLV viraemia status of cats visiting veterinarians in 30 European countries. Black: all cats; red: FeLV-positive cats (Studer et al., 2019). High prevalence has also been documented in Thailand (25%), parts of China (>11%), and Brazil (10% in healthy and 28% in sick cats). Different testing methods also play a role in the interpretation of prevalence findings, as different diagnostic approaches, such as antigen tests and PCR for viral RNA or provirus, can yield varying results. Over the past decades, FeLV prevalence has decreased thanks to test-and-removal programs and vaccination; however, recent data suggest that this decline has stagnated.

can yield varying results. Over the past decades, FeLV prevalence has decreased thanks to test-and-removal programs and vaccination; however, recent data suggest that this decline has stagnated. Continued awareness and prevention efforts remain crucial to controlling the spread of the virus. Higher FeLV prevalence is linked to several risk factors, including living in a geographic area with a high FeLV prevalence, such as southern Europe. Cats with outdoor access or those with a free-roaming lifestyle are at increased risk, as are those living in large groups of five or more cats with unknown FeLV status. Male intact cats, cats aged 1 to 6 years, and non-pedigree cats also face a higher risk of infection. In terms of clinical relevance, testing and preventative strategies, such as screening, vaccination, and control of introductions in multi-cat environments, are essential to limit the spread of FeLV.

- Gender & Behaviour: Male cats, especially intact ones, are at higher risk, likely due to aggressive behaviours, such as fighting and biting. - Age: While young cats are more susceptible to FeLV (and more commonly develop progressive infection), studies show that adult cats are more commonly found to be infected (if infected as an adult less commonly progressively infected), possibly due to increased awareness of the need for testing, earlier testing, and better veterinary care of FeLV-infected cats leading to longer life spans. - Breed: FeLV is less common in purebred cats, likely due to more common indoor housing and proactive testing by breeders. - Health Status: In cats showing certain clinical signs or presentations, e.g. bite wounds, abscesses, secondary infections, lymphoma, anaemia, neuropathies, reproductive disorders, fading kitten syndrome, FeLV infection is more common. - Vaccination Status: Cats unvaccinated for FeLV are at higher risk.

- Outdoor Access: Cats with outdoor access are at higher risk due to increased exposure to infected cats. - Shelters & Hoarding Situations: FeLV prevalence varies among shelters depending on testing and hygiene policies. Cats in overcrowded, unsanitary conditions-such as animal hoarding cases-are at elevated risk. - Stray Cats & Regional Differences: In some southern European regions, free-roaming cats face higher FeLV prevalence due to unregulated breeding and limited veterinary care. However, trap-neuter-return (TNR) programmes were effective in reducing FeLV prevalence over time. - Economic Factors: Cats from areas of a low purchasing power parity per capita and income are at higher risk.

FeLV primarily spreads through close contact between infected and susceptible cats. The main route of transmission is via saliva, with progressively infected cats shedding large amounts of the virus continuously. Social behaviours, such as grooming, sharing food/water dishes, and using common litter trays, as well as aggressive interactions like biting, contribute significantly to viral spread. While FeLV is present in multiple body fluids, transmission through urine and faeces is considered minor under natural conditions. However, shedding in faeces has been documented, and exposure to contaminated litter trays could contribute to infection risk. Fleas have also been implicated as potential vectors, but their role in natural transmission is likely minimal. Iatrogenic transmission can occur through contaminated needles, surgical instruments, fomites, or blood transfusions, reinforcing the importance of strict hygiene and testing blood donors for FeLV (by proviral PCR to identify regressive infection). The virus is fragile outside the host and is easily inactivated by disinfectants, soaps, heat, and drying.

and testing blood donors for FeLV (by proviral PCR to identify regressive infection). The virus is fragile outside the host and is easily inactivated by disinfectants, soaps, heat, and drying. While indirect transmission (e.g., via contaminated human hands or surfaces) is unlikely, FeLV can persist under moist conditions for up to 48 hours. Despite this, close and prolonged contact between cats is generally required for infection. Thorough cleaning is advised when introducing a new cat into an environment previously occupied by an infected cat, though a waiting period is unnecessary. Vertical transmission is common in FeLV-positive queens. Infection can occur in utero, during birth, via licking and nursing, or through milk, even in some queens who test FeLV antigen-negative. In utero infections often result in foetal resorption, abortion, or neonatal death, but some kittens survive and become progressively infected. Testing kittens individually is crucial, as not all siblings might be infected.

If any kitten in the litter is FeLV-positive, the entire group should be managed as infected and isolated from uninfected cats (but preferably not the mother) until further testing confirms the FeLV status of all kittens.

The outcome of FeLV infection is determined by a dynamic interaction between the virus and the cat's immune system. This balance is particularly critical during the early stages of infection, typically within the first twelve weeks after exposure. The immune system's response to the virus is crucial, and the eventual outcome will depend on whether the cat's immune system can control the infection or if the virus prevails. This "battle" can shift over time, especially if the cat's immune system is compromised by factors such as immunosuppression or co-infections.

The virus initially infects the mucosa of the oropharynx and replicates in nearby lymphatic tissues such as the tonsils and local lymph nodes. From there, FeLV spreads through the body, primarily via infected lymphocytes and monocytes, leading to primary viraemia. As the infection progresses, the virus can reach the bone marrow, infecting rapidly dividing precursor cells and initiating secondary viraemia. This secondary phase spreads the infection further, such as to the salivary glands and intestinal lining, resulting in the virus being shed in saliva and faeces. This shedding occurs when viraemia is present, which can happen months after the initial exposure, especially in cats continuously exposed to FeLV-shedding individuals.

The outcome of FeLV infection is highly variable and depends on several factors, including the cat's immune status, age, the Printed from the ABCD website abcdcatsvets.org pathogenicity of the virus, and the infection pressure. Genetic differences in both the virus and the host population also play a significant role. Certain mutations in FeLV strains can accelerate disease onset and influence clinical presentation, with specific genes being linked to pathogenesis, more progression, and oncogenesis. The classification of FeLV infection includes four main courses: - Abortive infection: The cat has an immune response that prevents provirus integration and viraemia. 1. - Regressive infection: This can (but does not always) include a transient viraemia. FeLV is integrated into the host's cell 2. as provirus and can be reactivated if the cat undergoes stress. - Progressive infection: Cats show persistent viraemia and shedding and subsequently FeLV-associated disease. 3. - Focal infection: Rare cases where FeLV is sequestered to certain tissues. Also called atypical infection. 4. Diagnostic advances, particularly PCR, have reshaped the understanding of FeLV.

3. - Focal infection: Rare cases where FeLV is sequestered to certain tissues. Also called atypical infection. 4. Diagnostic advances, particularly PCR, have reshaped the understanding of FeLV. Cats previously thought not to be FeLV-infected still carry proviral DNA, which persists (regressively infected cats). These cats can later reactivate the virus, acting as sources of infection. Host-virus balance is critical throughout the infection, and while the majority of cats will eventually follow one of the four courses, the initial phase of infection is marked by fluctuating test results and ongoing changes in immune responses. The outcome of FeLV infection can shift even after a certain time, with some cats transitioning from progressive to regressive infections or vice versa. Therefore, the outcome of FeLV infection is not fixed and remains subject to both viral and host factors throughout the cat's life. Diagnosis of FeLV infection should rely on repeated testing over time, as some cases might not be clear at first due to recent infection, fluctuating antigen levels or varying immune responses.

The outcome of FeLV infection is influenced by several key factors: - Infection Pressure: The extent of exposure to FeLV plays a significant role in the disease outcome. Cats with limited, 1. one-time exposure to FeLV-shedding cats have a lower risk (around 3%) of developing a progressive infection. In contrast, prolonged exposure in environments with multiple shedding cats increases the risk of developing persistent viraemia (around 30%). For example, in an experiment, cats exposed only to faeces from FeLV antigen-positive cats developed only abortive infections, showing that low levels of viral exposure can result in a low-grade infection with an immune response but without detectable virus. - FeLV Subgroups (Table 1): FeLV strains are divided into different subgroups, each influencing disease progression. 2. FeLV-A is the only subgroup that is contagious, while FeLV-B and FeLV-C arise through mutations and recombinations in FeLV-A.

FeLV-B is linked to malignancies such as mediastinal lymphoma, while FeLV-C is associated with aplastic anaemia due to its impact on erythropoiesis. Infections with FeLV-B are associated with higher viral loads and more severe disease. New subgroups, such as FeLV-D and FeLV-T, have been identified, although their clinical significance remains unclear. - Mutations in the FeLV Genome: Mutations within the FeLV genome, especially in the receptor binding proteins, can 3. increase disease progression by enhancing the virus's ability to infect cells. Oncogene capture (where the virus incorporates cellular genes) is also a mechanism that can generate more aggressive FeLV variants, leading to faster disease onset. - Age of the Cat: The age of the cat at the time of infection is a major factor determining the course of the disease. 4.

Kittens are more susceptible to developing progressive infection, often showing rapid disease progression, while adult cats tend to have abortive or regressive infections and exhibit milder clinical signs. Age-related resistance is not absolute, but older cats are less likely to develop progressive infection, particularly after short-term exposure to FeLV. - Genetic Host Factors: Genetic predisposition can influence susceptibility to FeLV. Studies on single-nucleotide 5. polymorphisms (SNPs) in certain genes, such as APOBEC3H, suggest that genetic variability is able to affect a cat's immune response to FeLV and its ability to control the infection. Cats with an early FeLV-specific cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) response before neutralising antibodies are present tend to recover, while those with persistent viraemia have suppressed humoral and cellular immune responses.

In this outcome, the cat's immune system effectively contains the virus before it can integrate into the host's genome, preventing any systemic spread. These cats remain asymptomatic, test negative for FeLV-specific antigens, and only show past exposure through the presence of antibodies. This is considered the best possible outcome for the cat, as these cats have strong immunity to FeLV. Detection of past exposure via detection of antibodies is currently possible only in a few specialised laboratories. A point-of-care test that detects not only FeLV antigen but also antibodies is available but does not have sufficient sensitivity yet to reliably detect abortive infection.

Regressive infection occurs when the immune system partially controls the virus, preventing persistent viraemia. Some cats in this group experience transient viraemia but eventually clear it, although the provirus remains in the bone marrow and other tissues, detectable by PCR tests in blood. Reactivation can occur under immunosuppressive conditions, such as stress, pregnancy, or coinfections. Regressively infected cats generally have a good prognosis and are not infectious, unless reactivation occurs (believed to be uncommon).

The most serious form of FeLV infection is characterised by persistent viraemia due to an insufficient immune response. Cats with this course of infection continuously shed high amounts of FeLV, posing a risk to other cats. These cats typically have a poor prognosis (although with good veterinary care and no exposure to other infectious agents can also live many years), often developing severe FeLV-associated diseases, such as lymphoma, anaemia, or myelosuppression. The primary risk factors for developing progressive infection include age and immune status, with younger or immunocompromised cats being more likely to develop progressive infection. Diagnosis is confirmed through persistent positive FeLV antigen test results and is distinguished from regressive infections by repeated testing.

This rare form of FeLV infection course is marked by the replication of virus being confined to specific tissues, such as the spleen or mammary glands. As a result, antigen test results on blood can be intermittent or discordant. This is why this course is also called "atypical infection". While these infections are often not a major concern from an epidemiological perspective, they can be confusing in diagnostic tests.

Research shows that susceptible kittens can be protected from FeLV infection through passive immunisation with high-titre antisera; serum from aviraemic FeLV-infected queens with neutralising antibodies can protect their kittens against high doses of FeLV. However, this protection observed in the kittens in that study was short-lived, with antibodies becoming undetectable by 16 weeks of age, leaving the kittens vulnerable. Passive immunisation is also ineffective once progressive infection is established.

Cats that successfully overcome FeLV viraemia typically have high titres of virus-neutralising antibodies, generally higher than progressively infected cats. However, the effective immune response is not solely antibody dependent. The cellular immune response plays an important role, with CTLs specific to FeLV appearing before antibodies. FeLV-specific CTLs can reduce the viral load in persistently infected cats. Furthermore, vaccination with a recombinant FeLV canarypox vaccine, which does not induce antibodies but provides protection against progressive infection, supports the important role of CTLs in immunity.

FeLV infection can lead to various clinical signs, primarily in cases of progressive infection where active viral replication is responsible for disease development. These cats can remain clinically healthy for extended periods, although their life expectancy is generally reduced. Progressive FeLV infection is associated with a significant increase in mortality, especially in multicat households with other endemic infections, such as feline coronavirus, feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV), and upper respiratory viruses. However, cats in indoor single-cat households with appropriate veterinary care exhibit higher survival rates. FeLV infection can cause a range of clinical manifestations, including bone marrow disorders (primarily anaemia), tumours (especially lymphoma), immunosuppression, and secondary infections. It can also result in immune-mediated diseases, neurological conditions, and reproductive issues. In some cases, it is difficult to determine whether other concurrent problems are directly related to FeLV or are independent of the infection.

neurological conditions, and reproductive issues. In some cases, it is difficult to determine whether other concurrent problems are directly related to FeLV or are independent of the infection. Clinical signs that have commonly been described in FeLV-infected cats include weight loss, fever, dehydration, rhinitis, diarrhoea, conjunctivitis, and lymphadenopathy. Anaemia and lymphoma are frequently found in progressively FeLV-infected cats. Reactivating regressive FeLV infections can lead to similar risks as progressive infections, including the development of lymphoma or bone marrow suppression. However, regressive infection typically does not affect life expectancy unless it reactivates and cats become viraemic. Regressive FeLV infections can sometimes cause myelosuppression or lymphoma in rare cases, even without detectable FeLV antigen.

FeLV is a significant cause of tumours in cats, with lymphoma and leukaemia being the most common. Other haematopoietic tumours can also arise, though less frequently. Additionally, FeLV infection has been associated with more unusual tumour types, including feline neurolymphomatosis, osteochondromas, olfactory neuroblastoma, uterine adenocarcinoma, and cutaneous horns. A key antigen, feline oncornavirus cell membrane antigen (FOCMA), was first identified in 1973. FOCMA is found on the surface of transformed cells and has been linked with FeLV infection, though its clinical relevance remains uncertain. FOCMA has been detected on lymphoma cells, as well as on fibrosarcoma cells induced by FeSV. It is not present on normal feline lymphocytes. Initially, FOCMA was believed to be a cellular antigen expressed after FeLV infection or tumour transformation, but later studies revealed it to be similar to the FeLV-C-gp70 protein, though not identical. Some researchers suggested that high antibody levels against FOCMA could help prevent tumour development by facilitating the destruction of tumour cells.

However, there are conflicting data and thus, the role of FOCMA in tumour prevention is still debated. It is widely accepted that FOCMA represents a group of viral antigens that can be present on FeLV-infected cells, although not always. The presence of FOCMA antibodies indicates exposure to FeLV but does not necessarily correlate with immunity against tumour development. However, in some cases, these antibodies could offer a degree of protection from tumour formation. Lymphoma. Lymphoma is one of the most common malignancies in cats, accounting for a significant portion of feline cancers, particularly in FeLV-infected cats. Approximately 25% of cats with progressive FeLV infection will develop lymphoma, with FeLV-infected cats being about 60 times more likely to develop lymphoma compared to non-infected cats. Mediastinal lymphoma, also known as thymic lymphoma, is the most commonly observed form of FeLV-associated lymphoma, followed by multicentric lymphoma.

Less frequently, other forms of lymphoma, including renal, ocular, and spinal lymphoma, are seen in FeLV-infected cats. FeLV has been linked to lymphoma development through both experimental and natural infections, with a history of 80% of feline lymphoma and leukaemia cases being associated with FeLV before the virus' prevalence decreased. However, the incidence of FeLV-associated lymphoma has decreased significantly with the reduced prevalence of FeLV in recent decades, with studies also demonstrating a decline in progressive FeLV infections among cats diagnosed with lymphoma. FeLV contributes to tumour development primarily through insertional mutagenesis, where the virus integrates into the host genome near oncogenes, often leading to their activation and uncontrolled cellular proliferation. Studies have identified specific loci, such as cmyc and flit-1, as key areas where proviral insertion occurs, facilitating lymphoma development.

Notably, FeLV-associated lymphoma can also result from the recombination of FeLV with cellular oncogenes, generating oncogenic viral strains like FeLV-B. Although the role of regressive FeLV infection in lymphoma is still debated, it has been suggested that even in the absence of detectable FeLV antigens, proviral DNA found in lymphoma cells could play a significant role in tumour development. The risk of lymphoma in cats with regressive FeLV infection is higher, particularly in those from FeLV cluster households. However, recent studies have found minimal involvement of regressive FeLV infection in lymphoma cases, as proviral DNA was detected in only a small percentage of FeLV antigen-negative lymphomas. The mechanism for lymphoma development in regressive FeLV infection could be related to the virus' ability to integrate into different sites of the host genome, causing disruption of regulatory genes or enhancing oncogenic pathways.

The presentation of lymphoma in FeLV-infected cats varies. While alimentary and extranodal lymphomas only rarely seem to be associated with FeLV infection, cats with progressive FeLV infection tend to develop mediastinal lymphoma more frequently. Despite this, the role of FeLV in the pathogenesis of lymphoma has diminished in recent years, especially in regions with low FeLV prevalence. This shift suggests that other environmental and genetic factors are now contributing more to lymphoma development in cats. Prognosis for cats with FeLV-associated lymphoma tends to be poor due to the immunosuppressive effects of the virus and the increased risk of secondary infections during chemotherapy. Additionally, FeLV-associated lymphomas are often more aggressive, with higher mitotic activity observed in tumour cells, which negatively impacts treatment outcomes.

The prognosis for FeLV antigen-positive cats with lymphoma is generally worse, with shorter remission and survival times observed following treatment. However, even cats with progressive FeLV infection and lymphoma can respond favourably to chemotherapy and this option should be offered to owners. Leukaemia. Leukaemia in cats can affect lymphoid cells as well as other haematopoietic cell lines, including myeloid, granulocytic, erythroid, and megakaryocytic cells. The most common form is lymphoid leukaemia, but non-lymphoid leukaemias are also seen, with more than half of these cases being linked to progressive FeLV infection. FeLV can induce myeloproliferative diseases or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), with poor prognoses. In acute leukaemia or MDS, bone marrow is infiltrated with blast cells, and normal haematopoiesis is suppressed. Diagnosis involves a complete blood count (CBC) and bone marrow examination, with characteristic cytological abnormalities.

Cats with acute leukaemia can present with a high number of circulating blast cells, which can be diagnostic in some cases. However, identifying the predominant cell type can be difficult due to a lack of specific markers or speciesspecific antibodies. Transformation in non-lymphoid leukaemias usually occurs at the stem-cell level, often affecting multiple cell lines. FeLV infection has been documented in some cases of acute leukaemia, particularly rare forms such as myelomonocytic and monoblastic leukaemia. A study of acute myelocytic leukaemia (AML) found that certain FeLV variants, particularly those with URE repeats in their LTR, are strongly associated with the development of MDS and AML in cats. Cats infected with FeLV clone33 showed development of MDS, with peripheral blood cytopenias and dysplastic changes in the bone marrow. In these cases, apoptosis-related genes were highly expressed, and bone marrow cultures produced fewer erythroid and myeloid colonies.

Chronic leukaemias are less common but can also be linked to FeLV. These include chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, chronic myelogenous leukaemia, polycythaemia vera, and essential thrombocythaemia. Erythraemic myelosis, often associated with FeLV-C, leads to a low haematocrit and non-regenerative anaemia, with abnormal erythrocyte stages found in both the bone marrow and peripheral blood. Additionally, MDS can develop as a preleukaemic state before progressing to acute myeloid leukaemia. Eosinophilic leukaemia, which can be a subtype of chronic myelogenous leukaemia, has been described in association with FeLV, although distinguishing it from hypereosinophilic syndrome is challenging. Finally, polycythaemia vera and essential thrombocythaemia, both of which involve abnormal haematopoiesis, have also been linked to FeLV infection in some cases. Fibrosarcoma. Fibrosarcomas can be caused by FeSV, a recombinant virus that arises from the recombination of the FeLV-A genome with cellular oncogenes.

This process leads to FeSV acquiring oncogenes, such as fes, fms, or fgr, making it an acutely transforming virus that causes polyclonal malignancies. These fibrosarcomas typically present as multifocal tumours that appear simultaneously after a short incubation period, primarily in young cats. However, with the decline in FeLV prevalence, FeSV-induced fibrosarcomas have become rare. FeSV requires FeLV-A as a helper virus to replicate. FeSV-induced fibrosarcomas tend to be multicentric and are characterised by rapid growth, often with multiple cutaneous or subcutaneous nodules that are locally invasive and can metastasise to the lungs and other sites. These tumours can spontaneously regress, even when large, and those that regress typically have high titres of FOCMA antibodies. Differentiating FeSV-induced fibrosarcomas from solitary fibrosarcomas in older cats (that are not caused by FeSV) is important.

The latter, known as feline injection site-associated sarcomas (FISS), are slower-growing, locally invasive, and metastasise less quickly. FISS can sometimes be cured through excision combined with radiation or gene therapy. It is important to note that FeSV and FeLV do not contribute to the development of FISS, which typically results from a granulomatous inflammatory response at the injection site. In addition to fibrosarcomas, FeSV has been experimentally shown to cause melanomas by transforming both ectodermal and mesodermal cells. FeSV-induced melanomas have been produced in kittens through intradermal or intraocular inoculation, resulting in melanomas in the skin or anterior eye chamber. However, FeSV has not been linked to naturally occurring melanomas in cats. Other tumours. Several other tumours have been observed in FeLV-infected cats, although the association with FeLV is not always clear.

Iris melanomas, previously thought to be linked to FeLV, were not found to contain FeLV or FeSV in more recent studies, suggesting no clear connection. Uterine adenocarcinoma, though rare, has been described in a young FeLV-infected cat, but the role of FeLV in tumour development remains uncertain. Osteochondromas, benign tumours of cartilage on flat bones, have also been seen in FeLV-infected cats. While typically benign, these tumours can cause significant morbidity if they affect areas like the spine. Their pathogenesis remains unclear. Spontaneous feline olfactory neuroblastomas, aggressive tumours of the nose and pharynx, have been found in some FeLV antigenpositive cats. These tumours metastasise quickly, and while FeLV DNA was detected in the tumours, the exact role of FeLV in their development is uncertain. Other rare skin disorders, including cutaneous horns and FeLV-induced giant-cell dermatosis, have also been documented, though the link to FeLV is not fully understood.

In some cases, FeLV co-infection with FIV has been noted, as seen in a cat with plasma cell pododermatitis.

In terms of haematological disorders, FeLV infection is associated with a range of conditions, including anaemia (both regenerative and non-regenerative), neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and aplastic anaemia. One study found that FeLV RNA was present in the blood, bone marrow, and spleen of cats with cytopenias, with the spleen showing the highest viral copy numbers. While active FeLV replication is generally required for bone marrow suppression, regressive FeLV infections in antigen-negative cats have also been linked to myelosuppression. In these cases, viral provirus might interfere with cellular genes or alter bone marrow cell functions, potentially leading to immune-mediated destruction of bone marrow cells. Anaemia. Anaemia is a significant non-neoplastic complication seen in many symptomatic FeLV-infected cats. While in the past, it was thought that over two-thirds of non-regenerative anaemias in cats were due to FeLV, this figure is likely overestimated in regions where FeLV prevalence has decreased.

FeLV-associated anaemia can have various causes, with approximately 10% being regenerative, characterised by high reticulocyte counts and macrocytosis, typically responding well to treatment. However, most FeLV-associated anaemias are non-regenerative and result from the bone marrow suppression caused by the virus. FeLV infection of haematopoietic stem cells and stromal cells disrupts normal blood cell production. Haemolytic anaemia, often secondary to infections, can also occur in FeLV-infected cats, typically due to haemotropic Mycoplasma spp. In some cases, FeLV infection can trigger immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia (IMHA), and the presence of FeLV in cases of IMHA has been reported, but its direct role remains uncertain. Additionally, anaemia due to blood loss can occur in FeLV-infected cats with concurrent thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction.

Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA), a severe form of non-regenerative anaemia, is another potential complication in FeLV-infected cats, particularly associated with FeLV-C. This condition is characterised by a lack of erythroid precursors in the bone marrow and macrocytic anaemia. PRCA can often be treated with immunosuppressive drugs, but relapses are common after treatment discontinuation. In rare cases, PRCA can present atypically, as seen in a kitten with FeLV infection that also exhibited central nervous system abnormalities. Anaemia of chronic disease, often associated with secondary conditions, like chronic infections or tumours, is another non-regenerative form of anaemia observed in FeLV-infected cats. This typically results in mild anaemia, which improves if the underlying disease is treated. Anaemia caused by "crowding out" in the bone marrow can also occur, particularly when infectious agents or neoplastic cells infiltrate and replace erythroid precursors.

Haematopoietic tumours, such as lymphoma, leukaemia, or secondary infections, can lead to severe anaemia. MDS and myelofibrosis, conditions related to abnormal bone marrow activity, can also result in bone marrow suppression and anaemia. MDS, a pre-stage of acute myeloid leukaemia, has been linked to FeLV infection, particularly with certain viral genetic features. Aplastic anaemia or pancytopenia, where all cell lines are affected, can also be seen in FeLV-infected cats, with bone marrow typically appearing hypocellular or necrotic. The virus likely impacts precursor cells near the stem cell level, disrupting normal haematopoiesis. In some cases, treatment with glucocorticoids might lead to improvement, but usually, long-term treatment is required. Platelet abnormalities. FeLV infection can lead to a variety of platelet abnormalities, including thrombocytopenia and platelet function deficits.

Thrombocytopenia can result from decreased platelet production due to FeLV-induced bone marrow suppression or haematopoietic tumours. Platelets in FeLV-infected cats can also harbour FeLV proteins, and megakaryocytes, the precursors of platelets, are frequently targeted by the virus. Immune-mediated thrombocytopenia, although rare as an isolated condition, often occurs in conjunction with IMHA in FeLV-infected cats, potentially leading to bleeding tendencies. A retrospective study in the UK found that thrombocytopenia was present in 6% of cats, with 11% of these being progressively FeLV-infected, which is lower than previously reported. FeLV can also cause thrombocytopathy, which involves changes in platelet size, shape, and function, with some cats exhibiting giant platelets and thrombocytosis. Additionally, the life span of platelets is shortened in some infected cats. White Blood Cell Abnormalities.

In terms of white blood cell abnormalities, FeLV can result in reduced white blood cell counts or impaired function. Lymphopenia is commonly seen in cats with progressive FeLV infection, often due to thymic atrophy and depletion of lymph node paracortical zones. The loss of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells can lead to immune system dysfunction, and a decreased CD4/CD8 ratio can be observed in some cases. Neutropenia is also frequently seen in FeLV-infected cats and is often associated with other cytopenias. In some cases, myeloid hypoplasia of neutrophil precursors is observed, suggesting direct infection by FeLV. Neutropenia can also manifest as cyclic neutropenia, which typically responds to glucocorticoid treatment, indicating a possible immune-mediated cause. These cats are prone to recurrent infections, including persistent gingivitis and bacterial infections, due to the reduced number and function of neutrophils.

Myeloblastopenia, a severe form of leukopenia with enteritis, is another complication in FeLV-infected cats, previously linked to feline panleukopenia virus (FPV). This condition, also known as FeLV-associated enteritis (FAE), causes gastrointestinal signs such as haemorrhagic diarrhoea, vomiting, anorexia, and weight loss. It has been suggested that this syndrome might not be directly caused by FeLV but by co-infection with FPV, though some studies have indicated that FeLV itself might contribute, particularly in cases with FeLVFAIDS variants. This condition leads to significant immunodeficiency and opportunistic infections, highlighting the complexity of FeLV's impact on the immune system.

Immunosuppression is a significant consequence of FeLV infection and is a major factor contributing to morbidity and mortality in affected cats. FeLV-induced immunosuppression is more severe than that caused by FIV, with infected cats becoming susceptible to a range of secondary infections. The immunosuppression seen in these cats can result in an increased risk of bacterial, viral, parasitic, and fungal infections, as well as tumour development. The mechanisms behind FeLV's suppression of the immune system are not fully understood, and the degree of immunosuppression varies among individuals. FeLV-T, a viral variant, has been shown to target T lymphocytes, leading to thymic atrophy and depletion of lymph node areas critical for immune function. Lymphopenia and neutropenia are common in FeLV-infected cats, contributing to the impaired immune response. Additionally, neutrophils in viraemic cats have decreased chemotactic and phagocytic functions, further impairing the immune system. CD4+ helper T cells are preferentially lost, and this can lead to an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio, although this is more typically seen in FIV-infected cats.

Immune function tests often show abnormalities, such as poor T-cell responses, depressed neutrophil function, and decreased immunoglobulin production. FeLV-infected cats can have reduced responses to vaccinations, as shown for rabies, and their primary and secondary humoral antibody responses are delayed or decreased. This can necessitate more frequent vaccination, as protection after vaccination is not as robust as in healthy cats. Immunosuppression increases susceptibility to a variety of secondary diseases, including respiratory infections, feline infectious peritonitis (FIP), and coccidiosis. However, studies have not consistently shown that FeLV-infected cats are more prone to infections or have a less favourable response to therapy than non-infected cats. Secondary infections, such as Bartonella henselae or haemotropic Mycoplasma spp. infections have been observed in FeLV-infected cats, with the latter coinfection sometimes aggravating clinical signs.

Secondary infections, such as Bartonella henselae or haemotropic Mycoplasma spp. infections have been observed in FeLV-infected cats, with the latter coinfection sometimes aggravating clinical signs. FeLV infection can also affect the course of sporotrichosis, altering the severity of the clinical presentation, though it does not appear to influence treatment outcomes. Cutaneous and mucosal infections are more common in FeLV-infected cats, with a greater diversity of microflora noted on the skin and mucous membranes. Dermatological infections can develop from injuries or parasites and can be complicated by secondary bacterial infections. Additionally, chronic gingivostomatitis has been linked to FeLV, with some studies detecting FeLV antigens in oral mucosal biopsies from affected cats, suggesting a potential role in the development of this disease.

Immune-mediated diseases in FeLV-infected cats are rare but can result from an aberrant immune response to the virus. Unlike FIV, FeLV infection primarily leads to immune suppression rather than hyperactivation, although non-specific increases in IgG and IgM have been observed. Immune dysregulation is associated with the loss of T-cell activity and the formation of antigen-antibody complexes, involving viral proteins such as gp70, p27, and p15E. Documented immune-mediated conditions in FeLV-infected cats include IMHA, glomerulonephritis, uveitis due to immune complex deposition, and polyarthritis. Chronic progressive polyarthritis has been linked to FeLV infection, but the causal relationship is unclear. Glomerulonephritis, though uncommon in cats (compared to interstitial chronic kidney disease), has been linked to FeLV through immune complex deposition. Studies suggest that cats with retrovirus infections and proteinuria typically exhibit immune complex glomerulonephritis (ICGN), though FIV appears to have a stronger association than FeLV. Experimental studies have indicated mild renal dysfunction in long-term FeLV infection, possibly due to circulating immune complexes.

though FIV appears to have a stronger association than FeLV. Experimental studies have indicated mild renal dysfunction in long-term FeLV infection, possibly due to circulating immune complexes. However, unlike FIV, FeLV does not commonly cause hypergammaglobulinaemia, a key feature of immune complex-mediated disease. Instead, renal disease in FeLV-infected cats is more often linked to virus-induced lymphoma rather than primary immune-mediated mechanisms. While earlier studies have reported ICGN in FeLV-infected cats, many of these cases were associated with lymphoma, suggesting that FeLV contributes to glomerulopathy primarily as a tumour-promoting factor rather than as a direct cause of immune-mediated kidney disease.

Haematology. Many cats with progressive FeLV infection do not exhibit abnormalities on a complete blood count (CBC), though regenerative or non-regenerative anaemia, neutropenia, lymphopenia, monocytopenia, and thrombocytopenia can occur. Studies have shown that progressively FeLV-infected cats are significantly more likely to develop anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and lymphocytosis compared to uninfected cats. While experimental studies have reported no significant changes in total white blood cell counts, a reduction in CD4+ and, to a lesser extent, CD8+ T lymphocytes has been noted, even in cats with regressive infection, potentially impacting immune function. IMHA can present with agglutination, while moderate to marked leucocytosis due to neutrophilia and increased band neutrophils can be observed. Circulating blasts, megakaryocytes, or dysplastic cells, such as erythrocytes with giant Howell-Jolly bodies, can be seen in cases of leukaemia or MDS. Macrocytic anaemia and increased mean corpuscular volume and haemoglobin have also been documented, particularly in symptomatic progressively infected cats with high viral and proviral loads. Serum biochemistry.

and increased mean corpuscular volume and haemoglobin have also been documented, particularly in symptomatic progressively infected cats with high viral and proviral loads. Serum biochemistry. Serum biochemistry findings are non-specific and usually reflect secondary disease processes. Hyperbilirubinaemia and bilirubinuria can be present in cats with IMHA or secondary haemotropic Mycoplasma spp. infection. Urinalysis. Urinalysis findings are also non-specific, though proteinuria can be seen in FeLV-associated glomerulonephritis, and bacterial urinary tract infections can occur due to immunosuppression. In suspected urinary infections, urine culture and susceptibility testing via cystocentesis are recommended for diagnosis and to inform treatment. Bone marrow cytology and histology. Bone marrow cytology and histology are indicated in cases of pancytopenia or nonregenerative anaemia, with both aspirate and core biopsy samples recommended, particularly if aspirates are non-diagnostic.

marrow cytology and histology are indicated in cases of pancytopenia or nonregenerative anaemia, with both aspirate and core biopsy samples recommended, particularly if aspirates are non-diagnostic. Bone marrow findings in FeLV-infected cats can include neoplastic lymphoid, erythroid, or myeloid cells, as seen in leukaemia, as well as myelodysplasia, hypoplasia or aplasia of erythroid, myeloid, or megakaryocyte cell lines, and hyperplasia of these cell lines despite peripheral cytopenias. Megakaryocyte hypoplasia might also be observed. In some cases of acute undifferentiated leukaemia, definitive cell lineage identification might require cytochemical staining, immunocytochemistry, or flow cytometry targeting cell surface cluster of differentiation (CD) molecules.

Diagnostic imaging findings in FeLV-infected cats are highly variable and usually reflect secondary disease processes. Thoracic radiography can reveal a mediastinal mass in cases of FeLV-associated thymic lymphoma, often accompanied by pleural effusion. Renal lymphoma can present as unilateral or bilateral renal enlargement. Ultrasonography. Abdominal ultrasonography in cats with multicentric lymphoma can demonstrate hypoechoic and enlarged abdominal lymph nodes, as well as splenic, hepatic, or renal enlargement with hypoechogenicity or mottling. Increased hepatic echogenicity can be observed in cases of hepatic lymphoma. Intestinal lymphoma can manifest as masses with loss of normal bowel wall layering, while splenomegaly can occur in cats with immune-mediated cytopenias.

At necropsy, the most common findings in progressively FeLV-infected cats are lymphoma, leukaemia, or myelodysplasia, although secondary infections are also frequently detected. Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia is a typical feature. Bone marrow histology can reveal lymphoma, leukaemia, or myelodysplasia, while FeLV-associated enteritis is characterised by crypt cell necrosis and regeneration, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, and villous blunting and fusion. Central nervous system lesions can include axonal loss and dilated myelin sheaths within the spinal cord. Immunohistochemical staining of tissues, such as bone marrow or tumour samples, can be used to confirm the presence of FeLV antigen.

secao: Approach to the diagnosis of FeLV infection
texto: Diagnosis of FeLV infection is crucial for both individual patient management and prevention of disease transmission. Testing all cats to determine their FeLV status helps to identify infected individuals and prevent exposure of healthy cats to the virus. Progressive infection can have serious health consequences, and early identification allows for appropriate medical care and lifestyle adjustments. Misdiagnosis can lead to unnecessary lifestyle changes or even euthanasia in uninfected cats, highlighting the importance of accurate testing. Initial testing should be followed up six weeks later, particularly when introducing a new cat into a household, to account for the possibility of early-stage infection at the time of the first test. Screening can be performed at any age, as the tests detect an antigen and not antibodies, meaning that maternal or vaccine-induced antibodies do not interfere.

Diagnosing FeLV infection is complex due to variations in disease progression, immune response, and test interpretation over time. As test results guide critical clinical decisions, a structured diagnostic approach is essential. The ABCD has developed a diagnostic tree to assist veterinarians in assessing risk, interpreting test results, and confirming infection status through repeat testing when necessary (Table 2 and Fig. 2, see also the ABCD FeLV diagnostic tool). Direct virus detection is preferred, with commonly used point-of-care (POC) tests detecting free FeLV p27 antigen via ELISA or other immunochromatography (rapid or lateral flow) tests. Other methods include the immunofluorescence assay (IFA) testing for cell-bound antigens, PCR for proviral DNA, RT-PCR for plasma viral RNA, and virus isolation. Antibody detection (indirect detection of the virus) is less widely available, though a new POC test has been introduced in Europe, but limitations exist with its use. Virus neutralising antibody testing, conducted in some specialised laboratories, can be used to identify cats that are protected against infection.

in Europe, but limitations exist with its use. Virus neutralising antibody testing, conducted in some specialised laboratories, can be used to identify cats that are protected against infection. Following experimental FeLV infection, virus isolation and RT-PCR for viral RNA are the first tests to become positive, followed by PCR for proviral DNA, test for free antigen (e.g., ELISA), and later test for cell-bound antigens (in an IFA). Cats with progressive infection are typically positive across all these tests. In clinical practice, FeLV diagnosis is typically based on detecting free FeLV p27 antigen using POC tests. However, these tests identify progressively infected cats and those with transient viraemia during early regressive infection or following reactivation. Most cats with regressive or abortive infections remain undetected by antigen testing. PCR, which detects genome-integrated FeLV provirus, identifies a greater number of FeLV-infected cats than antigen-based methods, as it can also detect regressively infected individuals. Fig. 2. secao: Detection of intracellular gag proteins using the immunofluorescence assay
texto: The IFA was the first method developed for detecting FeLV infection in progressively infected cats under field conditions. It identifies intracellular gag proteins, including FeLV p27, within granulocytes, lymphocytes, and platelets, cells that become FeLV-infected after bone marrow infection. IFA becomes positive later than tests detecting free antigen, typically around three weeks after infection, and is usually associated with progressive infection. However, its diagnostic sensitivity is lower than tests detecting free antigen, and leukopenia or a low percentage of infected leukocytes can lead to false-negative results. Additionally, eosinophil binding, thick smears, background fluorescence, or improper handling can cause false positives. IFA requires specialised processing, fluorescent microscopy, and experienced personnel, with variations in quality control between laboratories necessitating careful selection of a reference testing facility. IFA is not recommended for screening, as it does not detect cats in the early stages of viraemia who are already infectious.

Despite its limitations, IFA remains in use in some countries, such as the USA, primarily for prognostic purposes or to confirm positive or inconclusive POC test results.

secao: Detection of free FeLV p27 antigen using ELISA or similar immunochromatography
texto: Testing for free FeLV p27 antigen is recommended in various clinical scenarios, including for cats with unknown FeLV status, suspected FeLV infection, illness, or before vaccination. It is also useful for identifying FeLV shedders in multi-cat environments or before introducing new cats. ELISA remains the primary test for detecting free FeLV p27 antigen, offering high sensitivity and specificity. While early ELISA versions had issues with false positives, later monoclonal antibody-based assays improved specificity. Plate-based ELISA allows antigen quantification, which can aid in distinguishing progressive from regressive infections. ELISA are also available as POC tests. However, false positive ELISA results can still occur, particularly with haemolysed whole blood samples, certain reagents, and technical errors. Immunomigration tests, another point-of-care (POC) method, show comparable sensitivity and specificity to ELISA and are unaffected by sample type. Testing of saliva or tears is not recommended due to intermittent antigen shedding. False-positive FeLV p27 antigen results are more likely in populations with low FeLV prevalence, necessitating confirmatory testing.

texto: or tears is not recommended due to intermittent antigen shedding. False-positive FeLV p27 antigen results are more likely in populations with low FeLV prevalence, necessitating confirmatory testing. If PCR is unavailable, a second POC test using a different brand can improve diagnostic confidence. Immediate repeat testing is advised for unexpected positive results in low-risk cats or when euthanasia is a consideration, and for negative results in high-risk cats. A negative FeLV p27 antigen test suggests no exposure, regressive infection, abortive infection, or very early infection. A confirmed positive result indicates active antigenaemia; however, differentiating between regressive and progressive infection requires repeated testing after six weeks or more, with further testing after six weeks potentially needed if the result remains indecisive. Persistently positive cats are likely progressively infected. Immediate IFA testing alongside ELISA can provide additional prognostic value, as IFApositive cats have a high likelihood of being progressively infected. Discordant ELISA and IFA results can indicate focal or atypical infections.

secao: Detection of FeLV genome using molecular assays (PCR, RT-PCR)
texto: PCR and RT-PCR are highly sensitive molecular techniques used to detect FeLV nucleic acid, with PCR identifying proviral DNA integrated into the feline genome and RT-PCR detecting free viral RNA from replicating virus. These tests can be performed on various sample types, including blood, saliva, and bone marrow but blood is used most frequently. Their high sensitivity stems from the amplification of FeLV gene sequences, making them particularly useful for resolving cases with discordant antigen test results. PCR and RT-PCR assays target conserved genomic regions to minimise the risk of false-negative results. However, differences in assay design might affect analytical sensitivity and specificity, and distinguishing endogenous FeLV-like sequences from exogenous infection remains a critical consideration. Despite these challenges, PCR has significantly improved the detection of FeLV in various sample types, including fixed tissues. Quantitative (real-time) PCR, and RT-PCR, further allow the measurement of proviral and viral RNA loads, respectively.

Quantitative (real-time) PCR, and RT-PCR, further allow the measurement of proviral and viral RNA loads, respectively. Studies have shown that regressively infected cats, which mount an effective immune response, exhibit significantly lower proviral loads compared to progressively infected cats, highlighting the clinical utility of these techniques in assessing disease progression. Proviral PCR: PCR is particularly useful for confirming FeLV antigen results, early infection detection, identifying regressive infections, screening in multi-cat environments, investigating clinical cases with suspected FeLV involvement, and ensuring blood donor safety. Interpreting PCR results correctly is essential for FeLV diagnosis. A positive proviral PCR result confirms FeLV exposure and indicates either progressive or regressive infection. It can support the interpretation of positive or questionable FeLV p27 antigen test results. Some laboratories also quantify proviral load, with progressively infected cats generally exhibiting higher levels than regressively infected cats after the initial weeks of infection.

Some laboratories also quantify proviral load, with progressively infected cats generally exhibiting higher levels than regressively infected cats after the initial weeks of infection. However, as the timing of natural infection is often unknown, proviral load alone cannot reliably differentiate infection outcomes, especially at one time point. FeLV p27 antigen testing is required to identify antigenaemic cats, and repeated testing is necessary to distinguish between regressive and progressive infections. A negative proviral PCR result confirms the absence of integrated provirus and is consistent with no FeLV exposure, abortive infection, or an early-stage infection within the first one to two weeks post-exposure. False-positive results can arise from laboratory contamination, while false-negative results can occur due to suboptimal assay design, inappropriate test materials, or laboratory errors. Therefore, testing should be conducted by experienced reference laboratories with validated PCR assays and stringent quality controls to ensure reliable results.
