texto: Early experiments revealed that cats are susceptible to some IAVs isolated from humans, birds and seals, usually inducing only subclinical infections or mild fever (Paniker and Nair, 1970; Romváry et al., 1975; Hinshaw et al., 1981). Additionally, canine IAV can occasionally be transmitted to cats. The first outbreak of severe influenza in dogs occurred in 2002 in English foxhounds and was caused by equine H3N8 IAV (Daly et al., 2008). Serological studies revealed that this agent, adapted to dogs and known as canine IAV, was circulating among racing greyhounds in the USA from the early 2000s (Anderson et al., 2012). After an outbreak in Florida, this virus spread to other breeds and regions of the USA, particularly to shelters (Crawford et al., 2005; Payungporn et al., 2008; Rivailler et al., 2010). Another cross-species transmission of the H3N8 IAV to dogs was documented during an epidemic of equine influenza in Australia 2007 (Crawford et al., 2011). Natural equine H3N8 IAV infection has not been found in cats so far, but after experimental inoculation, cats do develop disease, shed virus, and transmit the infection to other cats via contact (Su et al., 2014; Deng et al., 2025).

In South Korea and China, around 2004-2005, a H3N2 IAV emerged in dogs, which was most probably of avian origin and became enzootic there (Song et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2015). Since 2015, this agent has been repeatedly introduced to the USA and Canada by dogs rescued from Asian meat production farms, resulting in several outbreaks (Voorhees et al., 2017; Wasik et al., 2021). Crossspecies transmission of this virus is possible as, after experimental inoculations, ferrets, guinea pigs and cats have been infected (Kim et al., 2013; Deng et al., 2025). Furthermore, natural feline outbreaks with fever, tachypnea, sneezing, coughing, dyspnoea and lethargy were noted in two shelters (Song et al., 2011; Jeoung et al., 2013). In one of these shelters, the morbidity rate was 100% and the mortality rate was 40%. Although cats can be infected via direct dog-to-cat or cat-to-cat transfer, natural feline outbreaks appear to be very rare.

secao: Highly pathogenic avian influenza virus H5N1
texto: In Asia, a highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) virus strain H5N1 emerged in 1996, causing a substantial epidemic of "avian flu" with a high mortality rate. Hundreds of millions of poultry were destroyed (Webster et al., 2005) but, due to migrations of wild birds, this epidemic has been further expanding. Since 2003, this virus has caused countless outbreaks of HPAI, initially devastating poultry farming in Southeast Asia, then spreading to Europe, Africa, and eventually to the Americas (Wille and Barr, 2022). Mammals were sporadically affected, including 939 humans (from 01.01.2003 to 27.09.2024), with a fatality rate of almost 50% (World Health Organization, 2024). Severe cases in domestic cats were also noted (Kuiken et al., 2004; Thiry et al., 2007), as well as in tigers and leopards kept at a zoo in Thailand and fed fresh chicken carcasses (Keawcharoen et al., 2004). In one outbreak, tiger-to-tiger transmission was suspected (Thanawongnuwech et al., 2005).

It was believed that, even in areas in which birds are infected with H5N1 virus, cats only rarely test positive by serology for antibodies or reverse transcriptase (RT)-PCR for viral RNA (Marschall et al., 2008; Zhao FR et al., 2015; Golke et al., 2025). In contrast, among owned cats that are fed and often kept indoors, antibodies against H5 were found in less than 0.5% (4/871) of cats.

In summary, the data presented above clearly show that domestic cats are susceptible to natural IAV infections from other species. Infection results most likely from close contact with infected humans or animals, especially birds. Serological surveys suggest low to moderate rates of antibody seroconversion in response to low pathogenic seasonal human or animal strains, and sporadic seroconversions to highly pathogenic avian strains.

However, IAVs appear to spread inefficiently among feline populations, probably reflecting cats' social organisation, which limits the direct cat-to-cat contact that is required for viral transmission (Deng et al., 2025). So far, feline influenza epidemics have not been recorded, with only rare outbreaks in dense populations, such as shelters. Therefore, cats are not considered as a reservoir of influenza. In contrast to humans, horses, pigs, bats, dogs and some other species, adaptation of IAVs to feline hosts has not yet been reported. On the other hand, the ongoing pandemic of HPAI caused by the H5N1 virus creates a constant risk for cats having access to raw poultry meat, unpasteurized milk, as well as birds or their droppings. The resulting feline disease seems to be rare, but is usually very severe with fatality rates of 70% of cats (Coleman et al., 2025).

texto: In cats showing signs of acute upper respiratory tract inflammation, influenza should be considered if other aetiological agents, such as feline herpesvirus and calicivirus, have been excluded. Risk factors include being in a shelter and close contact with humans or animals suffering from influenza. This applies especially when quickly progressing severe respiratory disease and/or neurologic signs are seen in a cat that had outdoor access during an outbreak of HPAI in poultry and/or aquatic wild birds in the region or could have access to raw poultry products as well as milk (Thiry et al., 2007; Kang et al., 2024). texto: IAVs can be isolated in tissue culture or embryonated eggs from nasal or oropharyngeal swabs, or during a post-mortem examination from pulmonary tissue (and, in the case of highly pathogenic strains, from rectal swabs or faecal samples, affected organs, intestinal content and pleural fluid). Viral RNA can be detected in nasal swabs by RT-PCR during the first 4 days of infection. For dogs and some other animal species, commercial point-of-care tests are offered for the quick detection of IAV antigens in nasal swabs. These assays have not been validated for cats so far.

texto: The upper respiratory tract disease that occurs as a result of infection is usually mild and self-limiting. In rare, complicated cases, symptomatic medication, combined with the control of secondary bacterial infections, should be implemented alongside other procedures used in cats suffering from other acute viral upper respiratory diseases. In humans, oseltamivir is commonly used for the treatment or prevention of IAV infections. This antiviral drug has been given to healthy tigers at risk of highly pathogenic H5N1 IAV infection, but there was no evidence of protection (Thanawongnuwech et al., 2005). In another study 2 domestic cats recovered from H5N1 HPAI after early treatment with 15 mg oseltamivir PO q12h for 10 days in addition to subcutaneous fluid therapy and NSAIDs (Gomez et al., 2025). One of these cats was treated due to lethargy, anorexia, fever, dehydration and hypopyon, whereas the other one presented with lethargy, anorexia, fever, nasal discharge and unkempt hair. Both survivors regained full health and high titers of neutralizing antibodies against H5N1 were detected in their sera at least 3-4 months post recovery.

texto: Though it has been shown that a heterologous avian H5N6 IAV vaccine can protect cats against lethal challenge with the highly pathogenic H5N1 IAV (Vahlenkamp et al., 2008), no commercial vaccines for cats are available at present. It was shown that a commercial inactivated H3N2 canine IAV vaccine was well tolerated and induced seroconversion in cats (Velineni et al., 2020). Even if this vaccine was to be licensed for cats, its usage in Europe is not recommended as this virus has been never detected in Europe and, in regions with canine influenza outbreaks, infections in cats are very rare.

arquivo: ABCD_MD/Terrestrial Manual/Felidae/Influenza virus infections in cats.md
texto: In the case of an influenza outbreak in a cattery, routine isolation and quarantine procedures should be followed to prevent the spread, as cat-to-cat transmission can occur. Importantly, infection prevention and control measures and a risk assessment-based protocol should be considered in veterinary settings for resident clinic or personal pets (Maddock, 2025). Any contact of cats with poultry or wild birds infected by H5N1 or other highly pathogenic IAVs should be prevented. The European Commission has therefore recommended to keep cats indoors in areas in which outbreaks of H5N1 IAV infections are recorded in poultry or wild birds (Council of the European Union, 2006), and cats living in such areas should not be fed raw poultry products.

texto: Cats are not considered a reservoir of IAVs. Only two cases of cat-to-human transmission of a low pathogenic avian H7N2 IAV have been documented so far (Belser et al., 2017; Borland et al., 2020). These cases occurred in a shelter after the prolonged and unprotected exposure of a veterinarian and a worker to sick cats and their respiratory secretions, which indicates that the risk of cat-to-human transmission is low (Lee et al., 2017). In contrast, infected humans can be the source of feline infections with seasonal IAVs. Although cats are sensitive to the highly pathogenic avian H5N1 IAV that caused at least 939 human cases worldwide, not one human case was acquired from cats. In USA, RT-PCR to H5 sequences was negative in all 139 persons exposed to H5N1 IAV-infected cats that became moribund after consumption of raw milk, meat, or pet food. Later, 25 of these persons were tested serologically, and H5N1specific antibodies were found only in one serum. It was derived from a veterinary professional, who did not use respiratory or eye protection during the exposure, but remained asymptomatic (Vaughan et al., 2026).

arquivo: ABCD_MD/Terrestrial Manual/Felidae/Leptospira spp. infection in cats.md
texto: - Leptospira species (spp.) infection can cause leptospirosis, a bacterial disease affecting a variety of domestic and wild animals and humans worldwide that has been reported in over 150 mammalian species. - Leptospirosis is considered an emerging infectious disease in humans and in dogs, and also in cats. - Subclinically infected wild and domestic animals serve as reservoir hosts and are a potential source of infection for incidental hosts, including humans. - Leptospira infection in cats is common, and cats usually acquire the infection from hunting rodents. - The disease leptospirosis, however, is considered rare in cats, but the number of reports in field cats with clinical signs caused byLeptospira infection is increasing, and the disease is now seen more commonly. - In addition, the fact that cats can shedLeptospira with their urine, and thus, serve as a potential source of infection, has gained increasing attention. - Antibodies againstLeptospira are commonly present in the feline population, and Leptospira spp. shedding in cats with outdoor exposure has been demonstrated in many different regions worldwide.

texto: Leptospires (Leptospira spp.) are mobile, thin, filamentous bacteria, 6.0-25.0 mm long and 0.1-0.2 mm wide, that appear as fine spirals often with hook-shaped ends (Fig. 1) (Bharti et al., 2003; Adler and de la Pena Moctezuma, 2010). They actively move by rotating around their axes, with clockwise rotation resulting in hook-shaped ends and counterclockwise rotation resulting in spiral-shaped ends (Wolgemuth et al., 2006). Leptospires can remain infectious for several months under optimal environmental conditions, such as at temperatures around 25 °C, in moisture, and in a neutral soil pH (Sykes et al., 2011; Schuller et al., 2015). Fig. 1. Dark field photomicrograph (a) and shadowed electron micrograph (b) of Leptospira spp. (courtesy of Ben Adler, Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence in Structural and Functional Microbial Genomics, Monash University, Clayton, Australia). The genus Leptospira belongs to the order Spirochaetales. There are over 250 pathogenic serovars of leptospires, based on differences in the carbohydrate component of the bacterial lipopolysaccharide. Serovars are grouped into antigenically related serogroups.

texto: are over 250 pathogenic serovars of leptospires, based on differences in the carbohydrate component of the bacterial lipopolysaccharide. Serovars are grouped into antigenically related serogroups. Immunity to leptospires is serogroup-specific. Different serovars are adapted to different wild or domestic animal reservoir hosts. Leptospirosis in dogs and humans is caused primarily by pathogenic serovars of the species Leptospira interrogans sensu lato. Several of those serovars also have been reported to cause infections in cats (Sykes et al., 2011; Weis et al., 2017; Sprißler et al., 2019; Dorsch et al., 2020). In dogs, serovars Icterohaemorrhagiae and Canicola were responsible for most cases of canine leptospirosis prior to 1960. Since the widespread use of bivalent serovar-specific vaccines against Canicola and Icterohaemorrhagiae, there had been an apparent shift to other serovars that are now more commonly identified in dogs suffering from leptospirosis. This had subsequently led to an increase in canine cases associated with other serovars (Sykes et al., 2011; Schuller et al., 2015).

This had subsequently led to an increase in canine cases associated with other serovars (Sykes et al., 2011; Schuller et al., 2015). In recent years, new vaccines for dogs have reached the market in USA and several European countries, which contain not only Canicola and Icterohaemorrhagiae, but also Grippotyphosa and Bratislava (or Australis, which is in the same serogroup) or Pomona, and this has once again decreased the incidence of leptospirosis in dogs in countries where these new vaccines are used (Francey et al., 2018).

texto: Leptospires can cause infections in many animal species and have been identified in more than 150 mammalian species as well as in avian, fish, amphibian, and reptile species (Everard et al., 1985; Pappas et al., 2008). Subclinically, and often chronically infected, wild and domestic animals serve as reservoir hosts and shed leptospires mainly through urine, and thus, are a potential source for contamination of the environment (Adler and de la Pena Moctezuma, 2010; Sykes et al., 2011; Schuller et al., 2015). Mainly rodents serve as reservoir hosts, but companion and production animals, such as dogs, cats, pigs, and cattle, can also act as reservoir hosts (Everard et al., 1985; Pappas et al., 2008; Adler and de la Pena Moctezuma, 2010; Sykes et al., 2011; Mayer-Scholl et al., 2014; Schuller et al., 2015; Llewellyn et al., 2016; Weis and Hartmann, 2017; Dorsch et al., 2020; Muhd et al., 2025).

In a study screening urine samples for Leptospira spp. DNA by PCR in clinically healthy cats during neutering programs in 7 provinces across Thailand, 22/264 (8.3%) cats tested positive (Thongdee et al., 2026). According to a meta-analysis including many studies worldwide, the frequency of Leptospira spp. urinary shedding in cats overall was estimated to be approximately 8%, with Leptospira interrogans identified in most samples (Miotto et al., 2024). In a study in Taiwan, an extremely high prevalence of Leptospira spp. urinary shedding of 67.8% was detected (Chan et al., 2014); however in this study sampling hadoccurred following a natural disaster that had caused an unusual epidemic of leptospirosis in humans (Su et al., 2011). texto: Leptospires can be transmitted by direct contact or indirectly. Direct transmission between hosts occurs through urine, venereal routes, placental transfer, bites, or ingestion of infected animals or tissues. Spirochaetales have also been demonstrated to survive in insects and other invertebrates, but their role as vectors of Leptospira spp. is unknown. In dogs and humans, indirect transmission is more frequent than direct transmission and occurs through exposure to contaminated environments, e.g., water, soil, food, bedding. Water contact is most important in dogs and humans, and habitats with stagnant or slow-moving warm water favour the survival of the organism. Leptospires in contaminated water invade the host through skin wounds but also through intact mucous membranes (Sykes et al., 2011; Schuller et al., 2015). In cats, indirect transmission through water contact is less likely (Hartmann et al., 2013; Weis et al., 2017) due to the aversion of cats to swimming in water, but they might become infected by drinking out of natural water sources. Cats are thought to become infected most commonly through direct rodent contact.

It has been shown experimentally that feeding on rodents harbouring leptospires can lead to infection in cats (Shophet and Marshall, 1980). Rodents are the natural reservoir for many serovars, and prey-to-predator transmission between cats and rodents seems to occur commonly (Shophet, 1979). In Germany, in almost 10% of rodents, leptospiral DNA was detected (Mayer-Scholl et al., 2014). On the Reunion Island, DNA of Leptospira spp. was found in the kidney samples of more than 50% of rodents (Desvars et al., 2013), although the antibody prevalence in 172 feral cats was low (0.6%) (Gomard et al., 2019). texto: The pathogenesis of feline leptospirosis is not well known but is likely similar to that in dogs and humans. Infection occurs through direct contact with a host or its urine, or indirectly through contaminated soil or water (e.g., drinking or bathing). After penetration through mucous membranes, abraded or scratched skin, leptospires multiply rapidly upon entering the blood vascular space as early as one day after infection and can circulate up to seven days in the blood. They invade the kidneys, liver, spleen, central nervous system (CNS), eyes, and genital tract amongst others, and can damage these organs by replicating and causing inflammation (Adler and de la Pena Moctezuma, 2010). Initial replication mainly causes damage to kidneys and liver. The extent of damage is variable and depends on the virulence of the organism and host susceptibility. The immune response can clear the leptospires from most organs except from the kidneys, where the agent can persist (Levett, 2001; Schuller et al., 2015). In dogs, shedding can continue for weeks to months (Adler and de la Pena Moctezuma, 2010; Sykes et al., 2011) and this might be the case in cats as well (Weis et al., 2017).

arquivo: ABCD_MD/Terrestrial Manual/Felidae/Leptospira spp. infection in cats.md
texto: Immunity after infection with Leptospira spp. is considered to be short-lived. In dogs, the duration of immunity after natural infection is unclear, and it is unknown whether or not life-long immunity develops after natural infection. So far, there are no reports of reinfection of dogs with Leptospira spp. after successful treatment. Immunity to leptospires is serogroup-specific, with little cross-protection between different serogroups (Schuller et al., 2015).

arquivo: ABCD_MD/Terrestrial Manual/Felidae/Leptospira spp. infection in cats.md
texto: Little is known about passively acquired (maternally derived) antibodies against Leptospira spp. in cats or dogs. However, two studies found that in pigs, vaccinated mothers transferred antibodies to their piglets (Millar et al., 1987; Martins Soto et al., 2008). In one study, the mean neutralizing antibodies titers were low, and passive immunity was of short duration (Martins Soto et al., 2008). In another study, antibody titres varied greatly between piglets. Titres declined between 4 and 10 weeks of age, with a half-life of 15.5 days. Colostrum-derived antibodies protected half of the piglets from intravenous challenge at eight weeks of age (Millar et al., 1987).

arquivo: ABCD_MD/Terrestrial Manual/Felidae/Leptospira spp. infection in cats.md
texto: Recovery from infection depends upon the production of specific antibodies. Antibodies are usually detectable three to ten days after the first clinical signs appear (Merien et al., 1995; Levett, 2001; Sykes et al., 2011). In an experimental study, cats developed antibodies detectable in MAT three weeks after infection (Shropshire et al., 2016). As antibody titres increase, leptospires are cleared from most tissues, except from the kidneys. Renal colonization occurs in most infected animals and the organism usually persists in the tubular epithelial cells, causing shedding for months to years after clinical recovery (Sykes et al., 2011; Greene et al., 2012; Schuller et al., 2015).

texto: Although Leptospira spp. infection and shedding in cats seem to be as common as in dogs, clinical disease is less frequently observed. However, some cases of clinical manifestation in cats have been described. During an outbreak of leptospirosis in dogs in UK, several cats with clinical signs of leptospirosis were identified (Murphy, 2015). It has been suggested that presence of immunosuppressive comorbidities might favour development of Leptospira spp. infection-associated clinical signs (Mazzotta et al., 2023). In few experimental studies in which cats were infected with pathogenic Leptospira spp., disease was usually mild, or infection remained subclinical (Dickeson and Love, 1993; Agunloye and Nash, 1996; André-Fontaine, 2006). Some cats showed mild clinical signs, including polyuria and polydipsia, mild diarrhoea, and a slight increase in body temperature (Semmel, 1954; Fessler and Morter, 1964; Larsson et al., 1985). Laboratory diagnostics revealed a mild leukocytosis (Semmel, 1954). Six of seven experimentally infected cats displayed liver enlargement at necropsy, and histopathological degenerative changes of the liver were noted.

The most common clinical manifestation after natural infection was interstitial nephritis (Hemsley, 1956; Rees, 1964; Fessler and Morter, 1964; Arbour et al., 2012), and affected cats were presented with acute polyuria and polydipsia, anorexia, and lethargy (Arbour et al., 2012). In an older case description, a cat with ascites, enlarged liver, and impaired hepatic function, but without icterus, had antibodies against serovar Hardjo (Agunloye and Nash, 1996).

texto: Usually, cats infected with Leptospira spp. do not show laboratory changes (Weis and Hartmann, 2017; Weis et al., 2017). One study, however, suggested that acute phase proteins, such as serum amyloid A (SAA), might be increased in infected cats (Murillo et al., 2023). In a study investigating 112 cats in Southern Italy, the presence of anaemia, monocytosis, neutrophilia, eosinopenia, increased alanine aminotransferase activity, hypoalbuminaemia and hyperglobulinaemia were significantly associated with testing positive for Leptospira spp. (either for antibodies in blood or DNA in urine) (Donato et al., 2022). If clinical signs occur, laboratory changes are likely to be similar to those commonly seen in dogs with leptospirosis. The majority of dogs presents with leukocytosis, with white blood cell (WBC) counts reaching 40,000/µl or even up to 80,000/µl. Differential cell counts often reveal neutrophilia, sometimes with a left shift, lymphopenia, and monocytosis. Mild to severe thrombocytopenia is common. Approximately half of dogs with leptospirosis are presented with anaemia, which is mostly mild to moderate (Schuller et al., 2015).

Blood urea and creatinine are increased in the majority of dogs. Hepatic injury, as evidenced by increases in the activity of serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and hyperbilirubinaemia, almost exclusively occur in conjunction with azotaemia (Goldstein et al., 2006; Geisen et al., 2007). Electrolyte abnormalities, such as hypoand hyperkalaemia, hyper- and hypophosphataemia, hyponatraemia, and hypochloraemia, are also common in canine leptospirosis and usually parallel the degree of renal and gastrointestinal dysfunction. Increases of creatine kinase (and AST) activity and troponin I were reported in about 50% of dogs, and suggest skeletal and myocardial injury (Mastrorilli et al., 2007). Various abnormalities of haemostatic parameters can be present indicating that both hyper- and hypocoagulable states can occur (Mastrorilli et al., 2007).

texto: Most cats with Leptospira spp. infection will not show diagnostic imaging abnormalities, but those with clinical disease are likely to show changes that are similar to those described in dogs. In dogs, radiographic as well as computerised tomography (CT), pulmonary changes can reflect leptospiral pulmonary haemorrhage syndrome (LPHS), although changes can be present in the absence of respiratory signs (Baumann and Fluckiger, 2001). Thoracic radiography might underestimate lesion type and severity as compared to thoracic CT (Gendron et al., 2014). The most common abdominal ultrasonographic examination findings in dogs relate to the kidneys and include cortical hyperechogenicity, renomegaly, mild pyelectasia, a medullary band of hyperechogenicity, and mild perirenal fluid accumulation. Other findings include hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, evidence of ascites, enlargement and hypoechogenicity of the pancreas, thickening of the gastric and (rarely) intestinal wall, and mild lymphadenomegaly (Birnbaum et al., 1998; Adin and Cowgill, 2000; Mastrorilli et al., 2007).

texto: Direct detection of Leptospira spp. (especially in urine samples) in cats is particularly important to assess a potential zoonotic risk (Weis et al., 2017). However, indirect detection of antibodies using MAT (which has been validated for cats) is the most commonly used diagnostic method to assess infection status.

arquivo: ABCD_MD/Terrestrial Manual/Felidae/Leptospira spp. infection in cats.md
texto: Direct identification of the organisms can be achieved by several techniques, including visualisation in fresh urine by dark-field microscopy or in tissue sections or on air-dried smears by light microscopy, culturing of the organism, or detection of DNA by PCR. All direct methods, however, are only reliable if a positive result is obtained, and a negative result never excludes the presence of the infectious agent because leptospires are only shed intermittently and sometimes in low numbers (Levett, 2001). The sensitivity of direct detection methods can be increased when an immunomagnetic separation-coupled technique is used (Dorsch et al., 2020), but this is not for routine use and is restricted to research purposes. Direct identification of viable leptospires by dark field microscopy is not reliable and thus not recommended (Levett, 2001; Hartmann et al., 2013). A more reliable method is antibody staining (by immunofluorescence or immunoperoxidase), which can be used to identify leptospiral agents in body fluids and cytological samples of organs, such as liver or kidneys (Fig. 2), if appropriate samples are available (Adler and de la Pena Moctezuma, 2010). Thus, in most cases, culture is not a useful option.

texto: Antibodies can be detected using MAT or an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). MAT is the most common diagnostic method to detect antibodies in dogs and humans. It is also the antibody test of choice in cats and has been validated for cats (Larsson et al., 1984; Batza and Weiss, 1987; Dickeson and Love, 1993; Agunloye and Nash, 1996; Mylonakis et al., 2005; Markovich et al., 2012; Rodriguez et al., 2012; Shropshire et al., 2016; Weis et al., 2017; Sprißler et al., 2019). However, as shown in dogs, MAT has marked limitations with regards to sensitivity, specificity, and repeatability, especially if single titres are interpreted (Miller et al., 2011; Fraune et al., 2013). MAT is not serovar-specific (Sykes et al., 2011; Schuller et al., 2015), and cross-reactions make identification of the infecting serovar difficult. Infected animals can test antibody-negative in the acute phase of the disease, reflecting the normal delay in appearance of serum antibodies. In addition, a defined panel of serogroup antigens is included in the assay, and false-negative results will occur when the infecting serogroup is not included.

In dogs, the widespread use of vaccines also limits the usefulness of the MAT. Non-infected dogs vaccinated with whole cell anti-leptospiral vaccines, especially with the newer vaccines that contain four serovars, can develop very high post-vaccinal titres to both vaccinal and non-vaccinal serovars (Barr et al., 2005; Midence et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2014; Schmitt et al., 2025a), and vaccine-induced titres can persist for a year or more in some dogs (Martin et al., 2014; Schmitt et al., 2025a). The reactivity of anti-leptospiral antibodies with multiple serogroups often prevents the determination of the infecting serogroup. Moreover, the serogroup with the highest MAT titre can vary over time, indicating that the MAT does not reliably predict the infecting serogroup in infected animals (Miller et al., 2011).

arquivo: ABCD_MD/Terrestrial Manual/Felidae/Leptospira spp. infection in cats.md
texto: Antimicrobial therapy usually consists of two stages. The first stage is aimed at immediately inhibiting the multiplication of the organism and rapidly reducing the fatal complications of infection, such as hepatic and renal failure. Penicillin and its derivatives are the antibiotics of choice for terminating Leptospira spp. replication. Initially, ampicillin (20 mg/kg q 8 h IV) or amoxicillin, if available for IV use (20 mg/kg q 12 h IV), should be given parenterally to vomiting, uraemic, or hepatically compromised animals. These drugs prevent shedding and transmission of the organism within 24 hours of initiation of therapy. They are, however, neither able to clear the infection from the kidneys nor to prevent a carrier state with chronic shedding. Thus, in the second stage, other drugs should be administered to treat the carrier state. Doxycycline (5 mg/kg q 12 h PO for three weeks) is the drug of choice, and treatment should start as soon as the clinical condition allows its oral application (Sykes et al., 2011; Schuller et al., 2015).

Intravenous administration of doxycycline (e.g., of human preparations that are available in some countries) is not recommended in cats because it can cause shock, and subcutaneous injection can lead to the development of abscesses in cats. Doxycycline can also cause liver toxicity. Thus, it should only be started orally after the animal has stopped vomiting, and liver enzyme activities have decreased. In cats, the use of doxycycline suspension, if available, is preferred over tablets or capsules to lower the risk of oesophagitis and secondary oesophageal strictures, especially with those containing doxycycline salts (hyclate) (German et al., 2005; Trumble, 2005). Administration of doxycycline should always be followed by food or water to avoid incomplete swallowing. In animals with no or mild clinical signs, doxycycline can be used for both initial and elimination therapy (Sykes et al., 2011; Schuller et al., 2015).

If healthy cats are identified as shedding leptospires, treatment with doxycycline (5 mg/kg q 12 h PO for three weeks) should be initiated to control the carrier state (Weis and Hartmann, 2017). This minimizes the risk of infection for other animals and humans. However, in hunting cats, reinfection with leptospires is possible. Testing for Leptospira spp. shedding in healthy cats might be indicated if the owner is immunosuppressed or if an animal or human being in the household is diagnosed with leptospirosis.

arquivo: ABCD_MD/Terrestrial Manual/Felidae/Leptospira spp. infection in cats.md
texto: Symptomatic and supportive treatment depends on the severity of clinical signs and the presence of renal or hepatic dysfunction and other complicating factors. Treatment of acute kidney injury is the most critical aspect in dogs and the same is likely true for cats. Medical management comprises of assessing volume status and correcting fluid deficits, evaluating for signs of volume overload throughout, and addressing any hyperkalaemia or uraemic acidosis. Severe acute kidney injury with anuria often requires renal replacement therapy with haemodialysis that is life saving for many animals with severe anuric leptospirosis. Early referral to facilities with haemodialysis should be considered, although haemodialysis is currently used only in specialised referral centres and might not be available for small cats. Haemodialysis is indicated in animals with inadequate urine output that are developing volume overload, hyperkalaemia, or signs of uraemia that are not responsive to medical management.

Haemodialysis is indicated in animals with inadequate urine output that are developing volume overload, hyperkalaemia, or signs of uraemia that are not responsive to medical management. After stabilisation, ongoing medical treatment comprises carefully matching the input volumes of fluid therapy with the cat's requirements for maintenance and its ongoing losses (including urine), so-called measuring fluid 'ins and outs'. The extent of renal damage after treatment determines the overall prognosis (Sykes et al., 2011; Schuller et al., 2015).

arquivo: ABCD_MD/Terrestrial Manual/Felidae/Leptospira spp. infection in cats.md
texto: In order to minimize the risk for people handling leptospires-shedding cats, e.g., in a veterinary clinic, the same precautions should be taken as if handling an infected dog, such as wearing gloves and goggles and taking specific measures when handling urinecontaminated areas and objects, such as litter boxes.

arquivo: ABCD_MD/Terrestrial Manual/Felidae/Leptospira spp. infection in cats.md
texto: Veterinarians should advise owners of cats with suspected Leptospira spp. infection to seek medical advice if they become ill and to advise their own medical doctor of their cat's illness. Owners should be instructed to wash their hands after handling their cat and to wear gloves when cleaning up urine spills. Routine household disinfectants should be used to clean urine-contaminated areas.

arquivo: ABCD_MD/Terrestrial Manual/Felidae/Leptospira spp. infection in cats.md
texto: In dogs, the prognosis of leptospirosis generally depends on the severity of the kidney injury, and the same is likely true for cats. In more severe cases, the prognosis largely depends on the availability of renal replacement therapy and on the patient's suitability for this intervention, which is often necessary for animals with severe acute kidney injury to survive long enough to recover from renal failure. In dogs, approximately 50% of those surviving the acute phase of the disease display impairment of their renal function for more than one year after hospital discharge.

arquivo: ABCD_MD/Terrestrial Manual/Felidae/Leptospira spp. infection in cats.md
texto: Although several vaccines are available commercially for dogs, no vaccine is available for cats. However, one study evaluated the potential efficacy of a canine four-serovar vaccine in two specific pathogen-free cats; both cats developed antibodies against several vaccine serovars (Shropshirer et al., 2016) indicating that cats might be protected after vaccination.

arquivo: ABCD_MD/Terrestrial Manual/Felidae/Leptospira spp. infection in cats.md
texto: The number of people suffering from leptospirosis worldwide is estimated at over one million per year, and the number that die from the disease to be around 60,000 per year (Costa et al., 2015). Still, the role of domestic cats in the transmission of Leptospira spp. is controversial, being considered either as a protective factor or a potential source of infection for humans. Systematic reviews and metaanalyses, mainly from South America (Ricardo et al., 2023; Miotto et al., 2024; Ricardo et al., 2024b) analyzing the literature have been published. Results suggest that feline leptospirosis should receive particular attention in veterinary care, as exposure to leptospires can occur in approximately one in every ten cats, and more frequently in outdoor cats (Ricardo et al., 2023). A study in Brazil investigating the role of cats as a reservoir of infection detected DNA from Leptospira spp. in 22.1% (67/303) of feline kidney samples at necropsy (Ulsenheimer et al., 2025). Thus, domestic cats should be considered as potential Leptospira spp. carriers when designing public health strategies for the control and prevention of leptospirosis (Ricardo et al., 2023).

Thus, domestic cats should be considered as potential Leptospira spp. carriers when designing public health strategies for the control and prevention of leptospirosis (Ricardo et al., 2023). The exact role of cats in the transmission of leptospires to humans is unclear. Since cats can shed viable leptospires in their urine, they are considered to pose a zoonotic risk, and appropriate precautions should be taken when handling potentially infected cats, such as disinfection of hands after contact with urine or prey, and antibiotic treatment of cats shedding leptospires (Weis and Hartmann, 2017). Close contact with a high number of dogs (or cats) has been discussed as a risk factor for human leptospirosis, but a study investigating households of individuals with hoarding disorders that could favour environmental contamination and the spread of zoonotic pathogens did not demonstrate an increased risk of Leptospira spp. exposure in humans or dogs (Cunha et al., 2022). Interestingly, in one study, dogs living with more than one cat at home were more likely to display antibodies against Leptospira spp. (Azócar-Aedo and Monti, 2022).

Pathogenic leptospires were detected by PCR in kidney samples of 42.4% of investigated cats (Dybing et al., 2017). The risk of infection is especially high if potentially infected outdoor cats use an indoor litter box, and their owners should generally be advised to wear gloves during litter box cleaning. Accordingly, in a study in Vietnam including 504 human participants (252 cases and 252 controls), being a cat owner was, among other factors (such as being a pig owner), significantly associated with human leptospirosis (Dung et al., 2022). On the other hand, cats might reduce their owners' risk of infection by eliminating reservoir hosts (e.g., rodents) and thus, minimizing the continuous environmental spread of leptospires (Childs et al., 1992).

Infection of the lower respiratory tract can be caused by a number of parasitic nematodes and trematodes. Certain metastrongyloid worms are commonly defined as lungworms because the adult stage is located in the lungs of their hosts, but actually some trichuroids and flukes also live in the respiratory system (Bowman, 2000; Conboy, 2009; Traversa et al., 2010; Traversa and Di Cesare, 2013; Morelli et al., 2021). Lungworms are the most prevalent parasites (10.6 %) detected in European cats after ascarids (16.5 %) and Aelurostrongylus (A.) abstrusus (Strongylida, Angiostrongylidae) is the most well-known and the most common (Giannelli et al., 2017). It is small in length (5-10 mm) and very thin (less than 100 μm width) and therefore capable of colonising the respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts of domestic cats and other felids worldwide (Traversa et al., 2010; Morelli et al., 2021). Apart from A. abstrusus, other respiratory mollusc-borne metastrongylids are commonly reported at necropsy in wild felids but they are considered rare in domestic cats. Troglostrongylus spp.

Aelurostrongylus abstrusus, O. rostratus and T. brevior all have indirect life cycles involving terrestrial molluscs. Eggs laid by female worms hatch in the respiratory tract and L1 larvae are coughed up, swallowed and eliminated in the environment with the faeces. They can actively enter slugs and snails where they moult into the infectious L3 stage (Lòpez et al., 2005; Di Cesare et al., 2013; Jezewski et al., 2013; Giannelli et al., 2014b; Valente et al., 2017). The biological cycle in the intermediate host is influenced by environmental temperature: a higher rate of larval development is observed at warmer temperatures (Di Cesare et al., 2013). However, in an experimental setting, higher T. brevior L3 burdens were detected in hibernated infected snails compared to the non-hibernated specimens (Morelli et al., 2020). Slugs and snails are not usually predated or ingested by cats, but in experimental settings infective larvae of A. abstrusus and T. brevior were shed in the mucus of snails and they were found in water where infected gastropods drowned (Giannelli et al., 2015; Napoli et al., 2023).

In case this occurs under natural conditions, drinking water from outdoor water bowls could be a source for cat and paratenic host infections. The L3 larvae of A. abstrusus are also found in a wide range of paratenic hosts (rat, mouse, lizard, frog, birds, and cockroaches) commonly predated by cats (Bowman, 2000; Conboy, 2009; Jezewski et al., 2013; Colella et al., 2019). Cockroaches (Periplaneta americana) were proposed as further paratenic hosts (Falsone et al., 2017). The role of paratenic hosts in the epidemiology of O. rostratus and T. brevior has been less investigated. Rats and gecko lizards were found to be infected by L3 of T. brevior (BezerraSantos et al., 2020). The ingestion of L3 by the cat is the most recognized means of transmission of lungworms but vertical transmission via the placenta or milk cannot be excluded, as adult egg-laying worms have been found in kittens as young as eight weeks of age (Tamponi et al., 2014; Crisi et al., 2017).

vertical transmission occurs in case of maternal infection in advanced phase of pregnancy and/or in infected queens that become pregnant (Traversa et al., 2021). Troglostrongylus brevior and A. abstrusus larvae may develop simultaneously in the same terrestrial slug (Cornu aspersum, formerly named Helix aspersa) and overwinter for at least 120 days (Giannelli et al., 2014b). An experimental study showed that Cornu aspersum is an intermediate host for A. chabaudi too (Colella et al., 2017). Eucoleus aerophilus has a direct cycle and eggs laid by female worms in the respiratory tract are swallowed and reach the environment in the faeces. After 30-45 days, embryonated eggs become infective when ingested by cats. Earthworms are facultative paratenic hosts (Traversa et al., 2009a). When cats ingest infective eggs or earthworms carrying larvae, the larvae migrate to the lung and develop into the adult stage in 3-6 weeks (Anderson, 2000). The life cycle of Paragonimus spp. is associated with freshwater environments and is complex as it involves two intermediate hosts.

Motile miracidia are freed from eggs when swallowed and then passed in faeces from infected cats and penetrate aquatic snails; cercarial stages develop in snails and then move from them, actively entering the second intermediate host (crab or crayfish). Cats are infected after eating the second intermediate host where metacercariae finally develop. Young flukes develop from metacercariae in the cat intestine, cross the intestinal wall and the diaphragm to the pleural cavity where they penetrate the lung parenchyma and become reproducing adults in about 6 weeks (Conboy, 2009; Dubey, 2023).

The severity of lesions depends on the worm species and burden. Kittens also seem to develop more severe disease caused by A. abstrusus and T. brevior (Barrs et al., 1999; Grandi et al., 2005; Risitano et al., 2008; Dirven et al., 2012; Bezerra-Santos et al., 2020). This may be explained by their smaller lung volume and the small diameter of their trachea and bronchi, which are more easily blocked by worms, in particular by T. brevior. Their immature immune system also seems to facilitate infection: experimental re-infection of kittens with A. abstrusus L3 larvae about one year after the initial symptomatic infection failed to induce respiratory signs or lung lesions (Hamilton, 1968a). In cats with natural aelurostrongylosis, the more severe radiologic abnormalities and the higher larval burdens were found in younger animals (Genchi et al., 2014) (Fig. 1). Young age also seems to predispose cats to pulmonary hypertension that may be reversable (Dirven et al., 2012) or so severe as to cause fatal right-sided heart failure (Vezzosi et al., 2020).

A. abstrusus larvae (<100 L3) does not induce clinical signs (Hamilton, 1967) but very high doses (800-3200) severely affect the lung and may even be fatal (Hamilton, 1967; Dennler et al., 2013). Despite a low infectious dose (100 L3), which may not be followed by patency nor respiratory signs, mild pulmonary and bronchial lesions, as well as lymphadenomegaly, are evidenced by computed tomography (CT) and histopathology (Dennler et al., 2013; Schnyder et al., 2014; Raue et al., 2021). Individual variations in immune response are observed and play a role in the lungworm life cycle and severity of inflammatory lesions (Schnyder et al., 2014; Raue et al., 2021). Cats repeatedly infected with a low number of larvae do not develop clinical disease when challenged with a high dose (Hamilton, 1969). The role of immunity is also confirmed by the fact that passive immunity protects experimentally infected kittens (Hamilton, 1968b). Fig. 1. Data regarding antibody production in infected cats are available from an experimental setting with A. abstrusus where six adult cats (aged between 13 and 105 months) received 300 L3 larvae (Raue et al., 2021). Results could not confirm the role of antibodies in completion of the parasite life cycle in hosts with patency. Antibodies were measured by a validated ELISA measuring major anti-sperm protein (MSP) of a bovine lungworm and results were influenced by the number of adult male worms and their copulation activity. Seroconversion occurred in 5/6 cats between three and 16 weeks pi (Raue et al., 2021). Larval excretion was observed both before and after seropositivity (Raue et al., 2021). An individual unique cat that did not seroconvert was the one with the lowest maximum number of L1 excreted. Moreover, the cat with the earliest onset and the shortest duration of seropositivity (from 3 to 4 weeks pi only) did not shed L1 in the faeces despite the development of pulmonary alterations in diagnostic imaging that resolved after anthelmintic treatment (Raue et al., 2021).

Cats infected by A. abstrusus, T. brevior, O. rostratus and E. aerophilus may be apparently healthy, but they frequently develop respiratory signs and coughing is the most common sign. Most publications describe in cats disease associated with A. abstrusus infections, but it has been suggested that in the past infection or co-infections caused by other metastrongyloids may have been erroneously reported as A. abstrusus infections because of difficulties with the morphometric differentiation of L1 larvae (Jefferies et al., 2010; Traversa and Di Cesare, 2013; Brianti et al., 2014a). Genetic characterization of larvae now offers new insights and allows more accurate diagnoses (Morelli et al., 2021). Aelurostrongylosis may be asymptomatic, or cause mild to severe respiratory signs due to bronchopneumonia, sometimes complicated by pleural effusion or pneumothorax (Barrs et al., 1999; Grandi et al., 2005; Mooney et al., 2012; Crisi et al., 2017; Napoli et al., 2023). A productive cough is therefore the more frequent clinical sign, together with mucopurulent nasal discharge, tachypnoea and dyspnoea with laboured, abdominal breathing.

Increased vesicular breath sounds, wheezing and end-inspiratory crackles can be heard on auscultation. Pyrexia is rare and, in more severe cases, there is lethargy and anorexia, and respiratory failure causes cyanosis and respiratory acidosis (Risitano et al., 2008; Traversa et al., 2008a; Jefferies et al., 2010; Yldiz et al., 2011; Dirven et al., 2012; Crisi et al., 2017; Martinavičienė et al., 2025). Acute onset of respiratory distress may follow premedication for elective surgery in apparently healthy cats (Swanstein et al., 2026). Hypertension may be reversable in treated cats and, after clinical cure of bronchopneumonia, the murmur disappears (Driven et al., 2012).

Paragonimosis causes coughing, sometimes with haemoptysis, but some cats are asymptomatic despite infection patency and radiologically evident cysts (Dubey, 2023; Huang et al., 2025). Acute tachypnoea and respiratory distress manifest the onset of pneumothorax due to bulla rupture (Huang et al., 2025).

In a case series (26 cats) where only individuals without comorbidities and retroviral coinfections were selected for evaluating clinical findings of cats with respiratory nematodes, mild normocytic, normochromic anaemia was the most common clinicopathological finding (7/26 cats), probably caused by chronic inflammation (Crisi et al., 2017). Interestingly, most anaemic cats (6/7) had aelurostrongylosis, no cats with A. abstrusus and T. brevior coinfections (6/26), and only 1/10 cats with T. brevior infection, were anaemic (Crisi et al., 2017). Possibly, duration of the disease may influence occurrence of anaemia in these cases. In natural disease, eosinophilia is not frequently found in cell blood counts (Reinhardt et al., 2004; Grandi et al., 2005; Risitano et al., 2008; Crisi et al., 2017; Morelli et al., 2021) or in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cytology (Foster et al., 2004). From experimental data, it seems that eosinophilia depends on the duration of infection and it is seen in the first weeks or months pi (Schnyder et al., 2014). Prolonged aPTT was detected in 6/15 studied cats and was positively correlated with faecal LPG counts; five of these cats showed also prolonged PT (Napoli et al., 2023). Thoracic radiograph is routinely performed in any stabilized patient and includes ventro-dorsal (V-D), dorso-ventral (D-V) and lateral projections. Subclinically infected cats may have radiographic mild-to-moderate abnormalities (particularly in the caudal lobes) only seen in V-D or D-V projections (Febo et al., 2019). Experimental studies with A. abstrusus showed that the severity of radiographic signs depends on the infective dose and duration of infection (Dennler et al., 2013) and in a case series of natural aelurostrongylosis (15 cats), radiographic lung alterations (interstitial nodular patterns) were correlated with the number of LPG in the faeces (Napoli et al., 2023). In contrast, Raue et al. (2021), did not find any clear correlation among imaging severity scores, antibody level, and faecal excretion of larvae in six experimentally infected cats. The authors hypothesized that in antibody-negative cats with low larval excretion and marked imaging changes, a non-antibody mediated immune response is responsible for both imaging alterations and impaired maturation of worms and egg production (Raue et al., 2021).

During the patent phase of aelurostrongylosis interstitial (reticular or nodular), bronchial or mixed patterns are seen, with individual variability, more frequently than alveolar or vascular changes (Crisi et al., 2017; Febo et al., 2019; Martinavičienė et al., 2025). A diffuse alveolar pattern is seen when the exudate surrounds eggs and larvae and it is a marker of acute severe lung damage (Fig. 2) (Crisi et al., 2017; Vezzosi et al., 2020). The poorly defined nodular pattern is multifocal and differential diagnosis includes mycotic and neoplastic disease. Bronchial abnormalities may persist after clearing infection and should be differentiated from other chronic bronchial diseases such as asthma (Losonsky et al., 1983; Payo-Puente et al., 2008). Experimental studies showed that imaging changes may be evident even before patency and may precede clinical signs (Dennler et al., 2013; Schnyder et al., 2014).

In both experimental and spontaneous infections, CT thoracic examination was able to evidence mild-to-moderate abnormalities (particularly in the caudal lobes) not evidenced by radiographic evaluation (Febo et al., 2019; Raue et al., 2021). In experimental infections with A. abstrusus, dose-dependent CT changes in the thorax consisted of pulmonary nodules, bronchointerstitial pattern and lymphadenomegaly, which were consistent with the pathological findings (Dennler et al., 2013). Interestingly, abnormal CT images were found even in cats that did not develop clinical signs or with low or negative larval excretion (Dennler et al., 2013; Raue et al., 2021). No abnormalities were seen in angiographic CTs of heart, outflow tracts, and pulmonary vessels (Dennler et al., 2013).

Point of care ultrasound examination (POCUS) of lungs can be used for cat-friendly ultrasound examination of pleural surfaces and spaces, and superficial lung parenchyma; it can be performed in cats with respiratory distress (Swanstein et al., 2024). It has been used in few cases of confirmed or suspected feline lungworm disease (Swanstein et al., 2026; Jańczak et al., 2026). Several lung ultrasound (LUS) abnormalities (increased and coalescent B-lines, subpleural nodules, focal lung consolidation) consistent with thoracic radiography patterns were seen in a 4-month-old kitten with acute onset of severe respiratory distress caused by A. abstrusus (Swanstein et al., 2026). Fluctuation of the respiratory function during hospitalization and after therapy were easily followed up by LUS (Swanstein et al., 2026; Jańczak et al., 2026). In particular, hospitalization in an oxygen cage of a kitten with aelurostrongylosis rapidly reduced the number of B-lines suggesting the non-cardiogenic origin of pulmonary oedema and provided a cage-side real-time functional monitoring of treatment response (Swanstein et al., 2026).

Echocardiography Echocardiographic evaluation is required when a heart murmur or signs of right-sided heart failure are found on clinical examination. In two kittens with severe bronchopneumonia caused by A. abstrusus, right-sided cardiomegaly with eccentric hypertrophy and tricuspidal regurgitation, has been described (Dirven et al., 2012). In one kitten, pulmonary hypertension and pulmonary regurgitation were also found. One of the kittens died within few days, and in the surviving kitten the heart murmur disappeared and echo-doppler examination confirmed resolution of pulmonary hypertension several months after parasitological and clinical cure (Dirven et al., 2012). An additional case of fatal aelurostrongylosis with bronchopneumonia complicated by severe pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure has been reported in a six-month old cat (Vezzosi et al., 2020).

In a case series of aelurostrongylosis (15 cats), ultrasonographic findings of pulmonary hypertension were not found (Napoli et al., 2023), however it is advisable to investigate the presence of lungworm (A. abstrusus and T. brevior) infections in cats with outdoor access and signs of pulmonary hypertension.

In case of evidence of cardiac rhythm disturbances on clinical examination, and suspicion of heart conditions, electrocardiography (ECG) investigation is required. Echocardiographic evaluation simultaneously provides a 1-lead ECG, and no ECG tracing abnormalities were reported in cats with lungworm disease evaluated with echocardiography up to now (Napoli et al., 2023). However, in a cat with respiratory signs and a heart murmur with dual cardiopulmonary parasitic disease caused by A. abstrusus and D. immitis, the six-lead ECG evaluation showed increased P wave amplitude (P-pulmonale) that indicated right atrial enlargement compatible with pulmonary hypertension (Tonev et al., 2021).

Direct detection Microscopical detection The major limitation of microscopical techniques is the inability to obtain a diagnosis during the 1-2 months of pre-patency when radiographic changes are already evident, or when egg shedding has stopped but parasites persist and clinical signs still occur (Losonsky et al., 1983; Payo-Puente et al., 2008; Dennler et al., 2013; Schnyder et al., 2014; Febo et al., 2019). A well-trained observer is required to differentiate the species of the strongylid L1 excreted (i.e between A. abstrusus, T. brevior and O. rostratus) based on their morphometric and morphologic characteristics (Figs. 5 and 6; Brianti et al., 2012; Traversa and Di Cesare, 2013). Larvae of A. chabaudi have not yet been found in domestic cat faeces, and angiostrongylosis has been diagnosed at post mortem examination (Varcasia et al., 2014b; Traversa et al., 2015; Garcia-Livia et al., 2023). Eucoleus aerophilus eggs may be misdiagnosed with eggs of the very rare Trichuris felis or Trichuris muris. The latter species can pass in the cat's faeces from a preyed rodent (pseudoparasitism) (Morelli et al., 2021).

Copromicroscopy is the first line routine method for diagnosing infectious agents of parasitic bronchopneumonia. Due to the possibility of coinfections, overlapping of some risk factors (endemicity, outdoor lifestyle) and of some clinical and imaging signs, both standard faecal flotation and the Baermann method should be performed in suspected cases and at annual health checks of cats with outdoor access. The above methods, respectively, target E. aerophilus eggs, and A. abstrusus, T. brevior and O. rostratus larvae. In apparently healthy cats, parasitological diagnosis provides early diagnosis and a more favourable prognosis in treated cats. Respiratory mollusc-borne metastrongylids L1 larvae are very active in the faeces and are readily detected in fresh faecal samples. Care should be taken to prevent soil contamination, as the presence of free-living nematodes may lead to misdiagnosis by an unskilled observer. L1 can be observed in direct faecal smears or by the floatation technique. In the latter method, the high specific gravity of concentrated salt or sugar solutions may induce osmotic damage to the larvae, making identification difficult (Conboy, 2009).

The Baermann migration method (Figs. 4a and 4b and table 2) is considered the enrichment technique of choice for metastrongyloid lungworms and is based on the positive hydro-thermo tropism observed for live nematode larvae (Willard et al., 1988; Traversa et al., 2008a; Lacorcia et al., 2009). It can provide quantitative information on the number of larvae found in each gram of faeces, which correlates well with severity of disease (Brianti et al., 2008; Genchi et al., 2014). However, dehydration of faeces occurs within a few hours of defaecation, particularly when faeces are shed into cat litter, and this affects L1 survival and the sensitivity of the Baermann test (Abbate et al., 2019). Bogunović et al. (2026) monitored the motility of L1 larvae collected from the Baerman apparatus and maintained in a Petri dish with tap water at 12-22°C. Most L1 died within 12 days, and motile larvae were observed up to 45 days.

Aelurostrongylus abstrusus larvae have been found by cytological evaluation of tracheal swabs or washings and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) or lung fine needle aspiration samples, but with less sensitivity than in faeces; so, there is no benefit in performing these riskier procedures over faecal examination methods for a parasitological diagnosis, particularly in case of severe respiratory disease (Lacorcia et al., 2009; Gambino et al., 2016; Crisi et al., 2019; Fagundes-Moreira et al., 2023; Bogunović et al., 2026). Information obtained from bronchoscopic examination and cytological evaluation of BALs can neither confirm nor rule out the diagnosis of aelurostrongylosis if L1 larvae are not detected (Crisi et al., 2019). No significant differences in bronchoscopic, cytological, and bacteriological findings of BALs were found compared to cats with feline idiopathic bronchial disease. However, in cats with aelurostrongylosis airway hyperaemia, epithelial irregularities and bronchial stenosis were less frequent, and bronchiectasia was seen only in these cats (Crisi et al., 2019).

The Baermann method separates live larvae from a faecal sample as they are attracted by humidity (hydrotropism). It can be performed using an in-house system (Figs. 4a and 4b). - ✜ Fill a large (60 ml) syringe with tap water - ✜ Connect the cone of the syringe to a rubber tube, which is clamped at the end - ✜ Orientate the syringe vertically - ✜ Fill a cheesecloth pouch with approximately 5-10 g of faeces - ✜ Clamp the pouch and dip it in the water-filled syringe (Fig. 4a) - ✜ After 24 h any live larvae will have passed into the water and sedimented at the bottom of the system - ✜ Collect a few millilitres of the water in a tube (Fig. 4b) and centrifuge (400 g x 2 mins). - ✜Discharge the supernatant and put one drop of the sediment fluid on a microscope slide. Significant progress has been made in the diagnosis of lungworm disease using molecular methods. Species-specific PCR assays are available for A. abstrusus, T. brevior, E. aerophilus and A. chabaudi. These assays have been validated on different biological samples (faeces, floatation supernatant, Baermann sediment and pharyngeal swabs) collected from cats with natural infections (Morelli et al., 2021). The PCR test for A. abstrusus provides 100 % specificity and a sensitivity of up to 96.6 %, with the best results obtained using pharyngeal swabs (Traversa et al., 2008b; Morelli et al., 2022). New multiplex PCR assays are also available for the simultaneous detection of two or three different species including A. abstrusus, T. brevior and A. chabaudi (Annoscia et al., 2014; Di Cesare et al., 2014a, 2014b, 2015c) or A. abstrusus and Gurltia paralysans, a metastrongylid of felids in South America, reported in Tenerife (Spain) (Barrios et al., 2021). These methods allow early diagnosis in the pre-patent phase with a potential positive impact on prognosis due to earlier possibility of treatment.

Eucoleus aerophilus molecular techniques are also available as screening tests and for investigating animal and human disease cases (Traversa et al., 2010; Di Cesare et al., 2012). Molecular methods for the diagnosis of paragonomiasis are available for epidemiological purposes in cats and are used for diagnosis of human cases (Intapan et al., 2005; Tantrawatpan et al., 2013).

Antiparasitic treatment is required for both apparently healthy and symptomatic cats with lung worm infections. Apparently healthy cats are treated to prevent, at an individual level, the onset of clinical signs and, at a population level, to control diffusion of lungworms. Fenbendazole (oral paste formulation) is the first drug licensed in some countries for treating aelurostrongylosis. Milbemycin oxime (tablets, available also in combination with praziquantel) and selamectin (spot on, in combination with sarolaner) are the first macrocyclic lactones used for treating aelurostrongylosis in case reports, but their use remains extra-label. Currently various spot-on combinations are licensed as antiparasitic treatments and controlled studies have evaluated their efficacy and safety under experimental or natural conditions of single infections (A. abstrusus, T. brevior, E. aerophilus) and in mixed (A. abstrusus and T. brevior) natural infections (Table 3). Efficacy studies primarily investigate the parasitological cure based on post-treatment stopping of larval excretion evaluated by the Baermann test result and the number of days after treatment when larval excretion stops.

In some studies, necropsy provided direct confirmation of efficacy by searching for adult parasites, eggs and larvae in the respiratory tract (Traversa et al., 2022). Importantly, some studies also aimed to evaluate clinical efficacy measured by changes in clinical and radiographic scores (Crisi et al., 2019; Rauf et al., 2024; Di Cesare et al., 2024a, 2024b). Most licensed products include multiple active ingredients and treat multiple endo- and ectoparasites at the same time. They should be used in case of polyparasitism, which is frequent in outdoor cats at risk not only for lungworm disease but also for ectoparasites and intestinal nematodes and cestodes (Giannelli et al., 2017; Rodich et al., 2018; Györke et al., 2022; Fagundes-Moreira et al., 2023). The appropriate drug choice should take into account compliance towards oral drugs and spot-ons, restrictions due to kitten age and weight, pregnancy or lactation, and concurrent skin lesions advising against spot-on use. In addition to antiparasitic treatments, the administration of antibiotics and corticosteroids at anti-inflammatory doses, as well as intensive care medical procedures specific for respiratory or cardiorespiratory failure, should be considered based on clinical, clinicopathological and imaging findings. Emergency cases of disease complicated by pneumothorax or pleural effusion may occur and require stabilization and thoracocentesis of the cat at first. Cats receiving antiparasitic treatment should be kept indoors and monitored, as the death of parasites induces an inflammatory response and respiratory signs may appear or worsen (Swanstein et al., 2026).

In cases of A. abstrusus or T. brevior infections, a delay in the diagnosis and treatment may lead to a worsening of clinical signs and risk for fatal cardio-pulmonary lesions, while early diagnosis and treatment greatly improve the prognosis. This may explain why in some cases affected cats die despite being treated with drugs said to be effective against the causative lungworm species (Brianti et al., 2012; Dirven et al., 2012; Crisi et al., 2017). The lungworm species and the level of larval burden measured by the Baermann test are usually related to the severity of the disease, but prognosis should be mainly based on physical examination (severity of dyspnoea and occurrence of cyanosis) and severity of diagnostic imaging findings (thoracic radiography, LUS, and echocardiography). Some fatal cases may, however, have only mild thoracic radiographic abnormalities at diagnosis and death can be the consequence of post-treatment death of parasites. Moreover, kittens affected by troglostrongylosis have a more severe prognosis (Crisi et al., 2018).

Stray and free-roaming cats have a higher risk of becoming infected with lungworms in endemic areas and, particularly in young cats included in spay-neutering programs, anaesthesia can be lethal (Iorio and Traversa, 2008; Gerdin et al., 2011). Avoiding predation is useful for preventing infections caused by metastrongyloid or trematode pulmonary worms with indirect life cycles and it is the only preventative measure for the latter. Some spot-on formulations are licensed for preventing A. abstrusus and T. brevior infections (table 3).

In endemic areas regular treatment for preventing lungworm infections is recommended in outdoor and hunting cats, particularly in kittens and pregnant cats. In pregnant cats, preventative treatment is useful to protect newborns from vertical transmission of T. brevior and potentially lethal troglostrongylosis (see table 3 for drugs that cannot be used in pregnant and/or lactating queens).

Eucoleus aerophilus has zoonotic potential and sporadic cases of human capillariosis have been described worldwide. The disease manifests in humans as bronchitis with a productive cough, but the presence of haemoptysis and nodular infiltrative lesions in the lung requires differential diagnoses regarding lung neoplasia (Lalosević et al., 2008). Paragonimiasis is a food-borne zoonosis acquired by people eating raw crustaceans in endemic areas. It is considered an emerging parasitic human disease in the US (Dubey, 2023). Infected cats are not dangerous for people (Macpherson, 2005; Liu et al., 2008).

- Mycobacteria are intracellular, acid-fast bacilliform Gram-positive bacteria. - Cats can become infected by a range of mycobacterial species: - Members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), notably Mycobacterium bovis and Mycobacterium microti but cats seem to be inherently resistant to Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. - Members of the non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) such as those of the Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) and other slow-growing and rapid-growing mycobacterial species, and the fastidious-growing group (e.g. Mycobacterium lepraemurium). - Geographical variation exists with respect to which mycobacterial species are most commonly seen in cats, e.g. bovis has been eradicated from much of central Europe but is prevalent in the UK. - Mycobacteria can be transmitted by inoculation via the skin (e.g. through hunting of infected host species such as voles), by inhalation, by ingestion (e.g. prey, contaminated raw food) and by direct contact of open wounds or with contaminated environments or discharges. - Clinical signs are often cutaneous in nature (e.g.

inhalation, by ingestion (e.g. prey, contaminated raw food) and by direct contact of open wounds or with contaminated environments or discharges. - Clinical signs are often cutaneous in nature (e.g. skin nodules with or without ulceration, draining wounds), regional or more generalised lymphadenopathy (e.g. lymphadenomegaly) and/or respiratory signs (coughing, tachypnoea, dyspnoea). Occasionally bone or joint (swelling, lameness, pain), neurological or ocular (e.g. uveitis) signs occur and/or involvement of other organs (e.g. intestines, kidney) via granulomatous changes in those organs. - Consider mycobacteriosis as a possible aetiology (or as a possible source of infection), especially in cats with skin lesions, non-healing wounds, lymphadenopathy, respiratory abnormalities (coughing, tachypnoea, dyspnoea, thoracic imaging changes) whilst being aware of the mycobacterial species in your geographical area. - Definitive diagnosis is reliant on mycobacterial culture, but this is limited as not all mycobacterial species can be cultured.

Further supportive diagnostic testing includes the demonstration of the presence of pyogranulomatous inflammation on cytology or typical histopathological changes with acid-fast bacilli (AFB) organisms, positive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays on lesion samples and positive blood interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) results. - Treatment usually requires a long period (several months), using multiple antibiotics such as rifampicin, a macrolide and a fluoroquinolone. - Cats infected with bovis pose a zoonotic risk. Although the risk is very low, care should be taken in the handling of infected cats, especially by any immunocompromised people in the household. However, globally, most tuberculosis cases in people are due to M. tuberculosis infection, not M. bovis infection. - In some countries, bovis infection is notifiable to the government and M. bovis-infected cats may need to be euthanised.

Mycobacteria (genus Mycobacterium, family Mycobacteriaceae, order Actinomycetales) are acid-fast bacilli (AFB), which are non-motile, 2-4 µm long Gram-positive aerobic (or microaerophilic) bacteria that are highly resistant to environmental conditions within organic material (e.g. in faeces, carcasses) and to routine disinfection (O'Brien et al., 2023). Their resistance is in part due to their thick hydrophobic cell wall. Mycobacterial taxonomy is complex, and many Mycobacteria species can infect cats and cause different clinical presentations. Different classifications have been suggested in the past based on the features of the mycobacteria and their ability to grow in culture, as well as their biochemical properties (O'Brien et al., 2023). They also vary in pathogenicity from obligate pathogens to opportunistic environmental species. However, the use of molecular techniques has led to taxonomic changes, and some species have been classified into different groups.

from obligate pathogens to opportunistic environmental species. However, the use of molecular techniques has led to taxonomic changes, and some species have been classified into different groups. For practical purposes, mycobacteria will be classified in this guideline on the basis of their biological behaviour, including aspects of clinical presentation, diagnosis and culture, their response to treatment and zoonotic aspects (see Table 1).

The MTBC group contains host-adapted species i.e. species with reservoir hosts, although spillover from these hosts to other mammals is frequent (O'Brien et al., 2023). The MTBC bacteria are obligate intracellular pathogens and can be grown only in specific culture media. They include: - Mycobacterium tuberculosis- mainly infecting humans as the reservoir, but can infect dogs (Martinho et al., 2013; Mentula et al., 2020; Haydock et al., 2022; Dutra et al., 2025) (when infection is usually acquired from an infected human) and only very rarely cats (Haligur et al., 2007) and other species. Note that the majority of human tuberculosis (TB) globally is due to infection with tuberculosis, not M. bovis. - Mycobacterium bovis- infecting cattle, badgers and rodents as reservoir hosts but can also infect cats, dogs and rarely humans - Mycobacterium microti- infecting small rodents like field voles (Peterhans et al., 2020) and shrews as reservoir hosts, but can also infect cats (O'Brien et al., 2023). Other MTBC species exist, such as Mycobacterium caprae (infects ruminants), Mycobacterium africanum (a rare cause of human TB that occurs mainly in Africa) and Mycobacterium orygis.

This group includes a large number (over 180 species worldwide) of species that have pathogenic potential but are generally saprophytic (especially in the soil or water) in nature; thus, they are opportunistic pathogens. NTM can be further divided into: - Slow-growing species, e.g. those of the Mycobacterium avium-intracellularecomplex (MAC), which typically take longer than 7 days to grow in culture in the laboratory, and can take up to 10 weeks to grow (Bergen et al., 2025). - Rapid-growing species, which typically grow within 7 days of culturing in the laboratory at appropriate temperatures e.g. Mycobacterium fortuitum, Mycobacterium smegmatis, Mycobacterium chelonae, although in some cases growth is slower than this (e.g. six weeks to grow Mycobacterium porcinum from a cat (Lee et al., 2025)). - Fastidious species; these cannot be cultured by routine laboratory mycobacterial methods. These include some very slow-growing species and those species associated with the 'feline leprosy-like syndromes', which cannot be grown in culture at all.

Feline leprosy was assumed to be due to only Mycobacterium lepraemurium (O'Brien et al., 2017c), a species that infects mice and rats as well as cats (Ghielmetti et al., 2021), but other species are now known to be involved in 'feline leprosy-like syndromes' e.g. Mycobacterium visibile, 'Candidatus Mycobacterium lapraefelis' (O'Brien et al., 2017b) and 'Candidatus Mycobacterium tarwinense' (O'Brien et al., 2017a). Knowledge on the leprae group of species is evolving rapidly, particularly in Australia and New Zealand, where most cases are diagnosed and reported. However, the division into slow-growing, fast-growing and fastidious feline leprosy-like species may be redundant with the advance of molecular techniques, as mentioned earlier, and the overlap in their clinical presentation. For example M. lepraemurium is now known to be a member of MAC based on sequencing (Ghielmetti et al., 2021).

M. bovis can be directly transmitted to cats by several methods such as ingestion of unpasteurised milk from infected cattle or by direct or indirect environmental contact with badgers (or rodents) (Malik et al., 2000; Monies et al., 2000; Dutra et al., 2025). Importantly, several cats have been diagnosed with M. bovisinfection associated via the ingestion of a commercial raw food (O'Halloran et al., 2018a; O'Halloran and Gunn-Moore, 2019; O'Halloran et al., 2019). Thirteen indoor cats in five different households from different areas were diagnosed with mycobacteriosis by culture, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and/or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) (see Diagnosis section). Six of the 13 cats presented with severe clinical disease, five of them dying. Seven cats tested positive by IGRA without showing clinical signs at the time the report was submitted for publication. Following publication, the authors identified up to 30 more infected cats.

Seven cats tested positive by IGRA without showing clinical signs at the time the report was submitted for publication. Following publication, the authors identified up to 30 more infected cats. All the cats had been fed with the same commercial raw food and so, while still not definitively proven (Middlemiss and Clark, 2018), the food was the likely source of M. bovis infection. It was suspected that the wild venison had been supplied to the food manufacturer without any inspection of the meat, thus TB was not checked for. Interestingly, an additional four cats, that had consumed the same raw food diet, presented with clinical signs of M. bovis a long time after they had last eaten the diet (e.g. 18months), showing the importance of asking about diet history in the past, as well as present (Mitchell et al., 2021a) No cat-to-owner transmission was reported with those outbreaks (O'Halloran et al., 2021). Interestingly, the cats described in these studies were young (often < 2 years old) pedigree cats. Infections of M. bovis in cats have also been reported in the Netherlands (Commandeur et al., 2025), a country believed to be 'officially TB free'.
