- Orbiviruses are insect-transmitted viruses that can cause serious disease and death in a range of macropod species in Australia. - Tammar wallaby sudden death syndrome (TSDS) is caused by viruses of the Eubenangee serogroup of the Orbivirus genus, and occurs as outbreaks in tammar wallabies held outside their geographic range. - Kangaroo blindness, also referred to as epidemic blindness, choroid blindness or chorioretinitis of kangaroos, is caused by viruses in the Wallal (and perhaps Warrego) serogroup of the Orbivirus genus. This disease has been associated with intermittent outbreaks of disease and deaths in large numbers of kangaroos in inland areas of Australia. - Other orbiviruses of the Eubenangee, Wongorr and Wallal serogroups have been linked to disease in macropods in the NT, generally in animals held outside their normal geographic or ecological niche. - Orbiviruses are usually spread by blood-feeding insects (often midges of the Culicoides genus and similar species, but also mosquitoes) and outbreaks often occur in in warming weather following periods of very heavy rain, when insects are abundant.

Viruses of the Orbivirus genus (family Reoviridae) are non-enveloped RNA viruses. Orbiviruses from the Eubenangee, Wallal, Wongorr (and perhaps Warrego) serogroups have been associated with disease in macropods in Australia. The viruses associated with blindness in kangaroos are considered to be variants to the reference strains of the Wallal serogroup of Orbivirus [1] , originally described in Qld and the NT [2] . Warrego serogroups may also be involved in kangaroo blindness, but the evidence is less convincing [3] . The viruses associated with TSDS are from the Eubenangee serogroup of orbiviruses which was first described from insect vectors in northern Qld [4] . Other viruses within the Orbivirus genus include bluetongue virus which affects cattle and sheep.

Wildlife and the environment: strains of Orbiviruses cause significant and sometimes fatal disease in a range of macropod species, generally when they are held outside their normal ecosystem or geographic range. Large numbers of macropods have been affected by outbreaks of kangaroo blindness, however population level impacts as a result of disease have not been confirmed. Domestic animals: there is no indication that these viruses cause disease in domestic animal species, although antibodies to Wallal and Wongorr serogroup orbiviruses have been found in cattle in Qld [2] . Humans: these viruses are not considered zoonotic.

Tammar sudden death syndrome has only been reported in the tammar wallaby (Macropus eugenii). Tammar wallabies are small, nocturnal macropods that originally ranged throughout south-western WA, southern SA and their offshore islands. Free-ranging tammar wallabies are now restricted to small areas of WA, a small, reintroduced colony on the Yorke Peninsula in SA and several offshore islands. Tammar wallabies are also held at a number of mainland captive breeding centres, zoos and research centres where they are an important model species for the study of marsupials (Kirkland 2005). The true natural hosts of the viruses that cause TSDS are not confirmed and the susceptibility of other macropod species to these viruses is not known. Kangaroo blindness: has been most commonly reported in western grey kangaroos (Macropus fulginosis), and also in eastern grey kangaroos (M. giganteus), red kangaroos (M. rufus) and euros (M. robustus). Other Orbivirus-related disease has been reported in red kangaroos and black wallaroos (M. bernardus) in the NT, generally in animals held outside their natural range [5] .

Disease related to these viruses has only been reported in macropods in Australia. The viruses are believed to be endemic to the northern parts of Australia [2] but may occur more widely. Virus from the Wallal serogroup was first identified from insect vectors in south-western Qld [2] , and later in NT [6] . Marsupials, possibly the agile wallaby (M. agilis), are thought to be the vertebrate host [6] . The Warrego serogroup was first identified in insect vectors and is believed to have a macropod host, based on high seropositivity on antibody studies of wild wallabies and kangaroos [2] . Eubenangee virus was first described from insect vectors in northern Qld in 1968 [4] and was also detected in insect vectors [6] and in macropods in the Top End of the NT [5] . Tammar sudden death syndrome has been described from Qld, NSW and the ACT and was first reported in October 1998. Over six weeks, 85 of 234 tammar wallabies at a research facility in Sydney died. Sudden deaths were observed in six other research facilities and zoos in NSW between October and December 1998 and in one research facility in Qld in March 1999.

a research facility in Sydney died. Sudden deaths were observed in six other research facilities and zoos in NSW between October and December 1998 and in one research facility in Qld in March 1999. In total 120 deaths were confirmed; as many as 230 tammars may have died, the majority without warning signs. In all cases, animals died in less than 12 hours of being noticed to be ill [7, 8] . A second outbreak of TSDS occurred between November 2010 and March 2011, when 35 of 70 tammar wallabies died at Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve, ACT, with peak mortalities occurring in December and January. During this period two Canberra research and breeding facilities reported deaths in 28/60 and 60/200 tammar wallabies. Around 40 deaths were also reported from a Newcastle research and breeding facility (eWHIS 3473 and 3522). A single death was recorded in April 2011 from a small captive tammar wallaby colony in Qld. Kangaroo blindness: outbreaks occurred in north-western Vic in 1975 and in between April 1994 and July 1996 in western NSW, north-western Vic, south-eastern SA and WA. Smaller outbreaks have occurred in subsequent years. Macropods in the NT have exhibited Orbivirus-related disease.

April 1994 and July 1996 in western NSW, north-western Vic, south-eastern SA and WA. Smaller outbreaks have occurred in subsequent years. Macropods in the NT have exhibited Orbivirus-related disease. Wongorr, Wallal, Warrego and Eubenangee serogroups were associated (as well as flaviviruses). Prior to these reports, there was little evidence of macropod disease associated with Wongorr viruses [5] . During the 1998-99 wet season, 17 red kangaroos held at Territory Wildlife Park (TWP), 50 km south of Darwin, suffered lethargy, oedema, pruritis and alopecia. All recovered fully over several days. Wongorr virus was isolated from one individual [5] . The following wet season 3 black wallaroos at TWP became acutely unwell with depression, facial oedema and conjunctivitis; two died and one recovered after a prolonged period with significant complications. Wallal serogroup virus was isolated from spleen or blood of all three animals. The virus was significantly different both to the Wallal virus associated with kangaroo blindness, and to the Wallal prototype virus [5, 9] . Wongorr virus was isolated from one clinically ill red kangaroo in Alice Springs [5] .

both to the Wallal virus associated with kangaroo blindness, and to the Wallal prototype virus [5, 9] . Wongorr virus was isolated from one clinically ill red kangaroo in Alice Springs [5] . Free-ranging eastern bettongs (Bettongia gaimardi) in the ACT experienced a mass mortality event in 2016 (at least 21 animals died or were euthanased after being found moribund). Post mortem histopathological findings were consistent with a macropod orbivirus infection but no virus was isolated [10] .

Orbiviruses are arthropod borne viruses, usually spread by biting midges (Culicoides spp.), but sometimes by mosquitoes. Outbreaks of TSDS and other Orbivirus-related disease typically begin in early summer following periods of very heavy rain, when insects were abundant. As TSDS has only been reported from Qld, NSW and the ACT it is possible that the vector is not present in other parts of Australia. A mosquito vector has been hypothesized for TSDS [7] . It has been suggested that some disease outbreaks occur as a result of species of macropods being held in geographic locations and ecological niches outside their usual habitat, which may expose them to novel pathogens and vectors, as well as potentially placing them under physiological stress [5, 8] . Kangaroo blindness: the virus is transmitted by midges (Culicoides austropalpalis, C. dycei and C. marksi). Up to 30% of animals in a mob may be clinically affected during an outbreak [11] . Disease occurs mainly in adult animals of either sex.

by midges (Culicoides austropalpalis, C. dycei and C. marksi). Up to 30% of animals in a mob may be clinically affected during an outbreak [11] . Disease occurs mainly in adult animals of either sex. A possible explanation for the outbreaks may be the entry of the viruses, or a pathogenic strain, into southern midge populations, leading to the infection of susceptible groups of macropods, that are not routinely exposed to these viruses and therefore have limited immunity. During outbreaks infection is widespread, but often asymptomatic. Only severely affected animals which become blind are generally detected. Animals are viraemic (thus capable of transmitting infection to biting midges) within several weeks of first infection, weeks to months before clinical signs appear. The damage to the eyes may be immunologically mediated [3] .

Tammar sudden death syndrome: most wallabies die without warning signs, or die within 12 hours showing signs of illness [8] . Animals may exhibit lethargy, depression, increased respiratory rate, an inability to hold the head up, ataxia and collapse in lateral recumbency with muscle fasciculations [7] . Kangaroo blindness: kangaroos are blind, stumbling into objects, especially when disturbed. Otherwise animals are apparently normal, being able to hear, move and feed freely. There are few external signs of eye disease, however there are obvious changes in optic reflectivity when animals are spotlighted [1] . Orbivirus-related disease in NT macropods: affected animals were lethargic, pruritic and had oedema of the lower hindlegs and tail and alopecia [5] .

Tammar sudden death syndrome: diagnosis is by signalment, gross pathology, histopathology and virus isolation. Kangaroo blindness: diagnosis is based on clinical signs, and histopathological changes to the eye. Ophthalmic examination reveals acute retinal inflammation in early stages and retinal atrophy later in the disease [12] . Serology, PCR, immunoperoxidase tests and electron-microscopy have been used to aid diagnosis.

Tammar sudden death syndrome: post mortem findings consist of extensive congestion and haemorrhage in a range of thoracic and abdominal organs, major muscle groups and in subcutaneous tissues [8] . Other gross findings include massive pulmonary congestion, mottled hepatic parenchyma and subcutaneous oedema throughout the hind limbs and inguinal region. Approximately 30% of animals also have extensive haemorrhage within the fascial planes of the hind limb adductor muscles, inguinal region, ventral thorax, dorsal cervical region and peri-renal retroperitoneal area. Many animals are in excellent body condition. Marked and diffuse pulmonary congestion, hepatic congestion, and necrosis of lymphoid germinal centres are consistent microscopic findings. Approximately 30% of animals had gastric ulceration and acute, periacinar hepatocellular necrosis. The tissues of affected animals become autolytic within a short period after death [7] . Kangaroo blindness: the pathology of choroiditis in kangaroos has been reviewed by Ladds 2009 [12]. The main lesions are retinitis or retinal degeneration, and uveitis.

short period after death [7] . Kangaroo blindness: the pathology of choroiditis in kangaroos has been reviewed by Ladds 2009 [12]. The main lesions are retinitis or retinal degeneration, and uveitis. The retinal lesions vary from small segmental lesions to cases in which the whole of the retina is involved. Acute cases show active retinal degeneration. Severe long-standing cases show scant atrophic retinal remnants and few inflammatory cells. Uveitis, characterised by infiltration with mononuclear cells, is most prominent in the choroid overlying affected retina. Wallerian degeneration is seen in optic nerves. Mild multifocal non-suppurative encephalitis occurs in some cases, but may be coincidental. Intranuclear inclusion bodies were present in the renal tubular epithelial cells and focal lesions of the epidermis [9] .

There is no specific treatment for TSDS, kangaroo blindness or other Orbivirus-related disease in macropods. Captive animals may be treated with supportive care, but treatment of free-ranging macropods is not likely to be feasible. In captive situations, management of vectors during and after periods of heavy rain may be helpful for prevention of orbiviral disease. Suggested actions include improved drainage of soils around macropod holding yards, regular treatment of macropods with long-acting pyrethrin insecticides during the summer months and treatment of animal shelters with dichlorvos impregnated strips [7] . Management of vectors is unlikely to be feasible in cases involving free-living macropods.

- ∞ Brucella ceti is an important bacterial pathogen of cetaceans (dolphins & whales) and B. pinnipedialis a less well-documented pathogen of pinnipeds (seals and sea lions). - ∞ Both of these Brucella species are considered zoonotic. - ∞ Marine Brucella species can cause disease of the reproductive organs, nervous system, heart and joints in their marine mammal hosts. - ∞ There have been very few demonstrated cases of brucellosis in marine mammals from Australian waters.

Wildlife and the environment: Brucella most likely poses a risk to individual marine mammals rather than populations. Marine Brucella species are not considered a major risk to terrestrial native wildlife but may pose a risk to species such as dingos, scavenging on marine mammal carcasses. Domestic animals: Marine Brucella species are not considered a direct risk to production animals, although infection of livestock is believed to be possible. They may pose a risk to domestic and feral canids in coastal regions, that may scavenge stranded marine mammals [4, 5] . Humans: Low numbers of infections with marine Brucella have been documented with two severe cases from the southern hemisphere (South America and New Zealand) [6, 7] . People considered particularly at risk include veterinarians, marine biologists, wildlife rescuers and any person handling marine mammal tissues (sample collection, carcass disposal or traditional practises). Some human cases have had no known direct contact with marine mammals, but had handled and consumed raw fish [8] .

Evidence suggest that cetaceans are the natural hosts of B. ceti and pinnipeds are the natural hosts for B. pinnipedialis. While there is clear evidence of disease associated with B. ceti infection in some cetacean species [9-12] , B. pinnipedialis infections in pinnipeds have not been associated with a clear pattern of disease. Most members of the genus Brucella can infect mammalian species other than their natural host. There are no reports of natural spillover infections occurring from marine to terrestrial mammals. Experimental infections of sheep and cattle with marine Brucella showed the ability to infect and cause disease was low, although there was the potential to induce abortion [4, 5] . There are no reports of Brucella in Sirenians (dugongs & manatees).

secao: World distribution and occurrences in Australia
texto: Marine Brucella species have been isolated from numerous Northern Hemisphere marine mammal species [13, 14] . Outside Australia, there is serological evidence of exposure to Brucella in Southern Hemisphere cetaceans and pinnipeds [15-17] , with isolation of Brucella sp. only from a small number of cetaceans. There have been very few demonstrated cases of brucellosis in marine mammals from Australian waters. There is a report of brucellosis in a late-term foetus of an Indo-Pacific bottle-nosed dolphin (Tursiops aduncus) in Qld [18] . There is molecular (PCR) evidence of Brucella infection from one wild short-beaked common dolphin (Delphinus delphis) from Port Campbell, western Vic and a humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) calf in Qld [19] . The common dolphin presented dead from trauma, with Brucella sp. in lung tissue [19] . There is molecular evidence of B. pinnipedii in aborted foetuses from Australian fur seals breeding in Vic [20] . Serological evidence of exposure to the bacteria in Australian marine mammal species is described in Epidemiology.

is likely indicative of active infection and disease. The significance of positive antibodies in pinnipeds is unknown [12] . The routes of transmission of marine Brucella have not been confirmed. Isolation of Brucella from the reproductive tract of cetaceans suggests that (as with terrestrial mammals) infection may be transmitted from mother to offspring [23] . Parasitic worms (nematodes) have been suggested as a means of infection as Brucella has been isolated from lungworms (Pseudalius inflexus, Halocercus spp., Parafilaroides spp.) [8] from cetaceans and pinnipeds [24, 25] . Ingestion of infected prey items may play a role in infection [26] . Direct transmission by between marine mammals through bites from fighting is likely and Brucella has been isolated from subcutaneous abscesses of marine mammals [27] . In addition, congregation of pinnipeds on land may allow respiratory transmission to occur. Neurological brucellosis in cetaceans may occur alongside other pathogens such as Toxoplasma gondii, Listeria monocytogenes and Morbillivirus [28, 29] .

Marine mammals carrying Brucella may not show any clinical signs. When they occur, typical signs are generally associated with the reproductive organs, nervous system, heart and joints [8] . Brucella infection may be associated with stillbirth and abortion [18, 20] . Marine mammals with active Brucella infection may present in poor body condition and, respiratory signs can predominate in pinnipeds, due to Brucella-associated bronchopneumonia [30] .

Detection of Brucella antibodies uses serological tests developed for cattle [31] . Care should be taken in interpretation as tests are not validated for marine mammals and may produce false results [32] . It is recommended to use two or more of these serological tests to determine the presence of Brucella antibodies [16] . Definitive diagnosis of Brucella infection is by isolation of the organism from tissues [33] , which can be difficult in marine mammals [34] . In addition, fresh or frozen tissue samples may be examined for evidence of infection by Brucella-specific PCR [20, 21] . Immunohistochemistry has been used in Brucella investigations in marine mammals [12] , but can be difficult to evaluate and is prone to false results [35] . CT scans of the cranium are recommended in stranded dolphins and other small cetaceans, pre- or post-mortem, due to the common occurrence of neurological brucellosis.

The following samples should be collected from marine mammals suspected of brucellosis: - ∞ serum (frozen): serological testing - ∞ cerebrospinal fluid: Brucella-specific culture - ∞ fresh tissues (brain, lung, lymph node, placenta, abscess material): Brucella-specific culture - ∞ impression smears: cytology & possible immunohistochemistry - ∞ tissues in formalin: histology and immunohistochemistry - ∞ frozen tissues: molecular diagnostics including Bruce-ladder multiplex PCR (offered at ACDP), multilocus sequence typing and whole genome sequencing. Collected tissues should include brain, lung, mediastinal lymph node, placenta, foetal fluids, mammary tissue/milk, testes, mesenteric lymph node, heart and spleen. Ideally, surveillance samples should be collected from all marine mammals irrespective of whether Brucella is a primary differential.

The histopathological lesions produced by Brucella infection are distinct. Brucella infection in cetaceans can cause central nervous system lesions such as meningoencephalitis [10, 36] . Some cetaceans with widespread infections may also display osteoarthritis [23] , especially of the scapula and neck joints [36, 37] , pneumonia and endocarditis [12] . Reproductive tract lesions in cetaceans include inflammation of the placenta [38] , and inflammation of the testicle and epididymis [23, 27] . Pneumonia is a common feature of aborted cetacean foetuses [36] . In pinnipeds, Brucella has been most commonly associated with pneumonia [30] although it has been suggested as a cause of abortion [20, 39] . In both cetaceans and pinnipeds, Brucella has been isolated from subcutaneous abscesses [27] . Brucella ceti was cultured from an Indo-Pacific bottle nose dolphin from the spleen, kidney and liver [18] . It appears that some Brucella have different genetic fingerprints and vary in their association with different lesion types [8, 36] .

Differential diagnoses vary according to organ systems affected and clinical signs. Encephalitis may be caused by morbilliviruses, other bacteria, avian influenza (H5N1) and Toxoplasma gondii [40-42] . Bronchopneumonia from lungworm infection may occur, particularly in juveniles. Infectious and non-infectious causes of abortion in pinnipeds include influenza viruses, toxoplasmosis, coxiellosis, harmful algal blooms, leptospirosis and mycoplasma [20, 43-47] .

Treatment is generally not considered feasible once systemic clinical signs are present. Given the lack of knowledge about brucellosis in marine mammals in Australasia, animals suspected of severe or disseminated brucellosis should be euthanased and thoroughly investigated. It may be reasonable to treat individuals presenting with subcutaneous abscesses caused by Brucella, with drainage and flushing the foundation of treatment. Antimicrobial selection should be based on sensitivity testing, when possible, otherwise should be based on accepted Brucella treatment in domestic animals.

Exposure to infected animals poses a risk to humans and at-risk groups such as veterinarians, marine biologists, wildlife rescuers and any person handling marine mammal tissues (sample collection, carcass disposal or traditional practises) should take precautions. This may include use of personal protective equipment and appropriate hygiene and disinfection of self and equipment. Brucella species are susceptible to most disinfectants. Washing of hands with chlorhexidine gluconate and chemical sterilisation of equipment should be practiced as a minimum standard after interacting with free-ranging marine mammals. Brucella may be a biosecurity risk when introducing new animals to captive marine mammal collections or in animals undergoing rehabilitation. However, the lack of epidemiological understanding means that antibody status may not help to inform infection risk.

There are significant global knowledge gaps in understanding the importance and population effects of Brucella species on marine mammals. Focused surveillance is needed to establish how widely brucellosis is present in Australian cetaceans in particular. Post-mortem investigations of stranded cetaceans in Australasia should include targeted sampling and testing for brucellosis. Ongoing surveillance with comprehensive testing including culture and molecular techniques is required to determine how frequently the presence of antibodies is associated with clinical disease. Serological data would provide information as to species, age, spatial and temporal differences in exposure to Brucella and help understand the epidemiology of Brucella in Australian marine mammals. Serum samples should be collected and tested from all stranded marine mammals irrespective if Brucella is suspected. Whole genome sequencing of positive cases will help to better understand the diversity and pathogenicity of these bacteria.

- Biotoxins are produced by microalgae, and are harmful to all marine mammals. - The most important biotoxins for marine mammals are brevetoxin, domoic acid, saxitoxin, microcystins and okadaic acid. - Marine biotoxins can produce acute and chronic toxicity, mainly with disease of the liver, nervous and gastrointestinal systems. The role of biotoxins in Australian marine mammal morbidity and mortality is largely unknown. - The global incidence of marine biotoxicity is increasing, largely associated with climate change, with greater severity and frequency of algal blooms, and newly affected geographic regions. - Marine mammals are considered ocean sentinels and their exposure to harmful algal blooms (HAB) is a very strong indicator of the potential of biotoxicity in general.

Biotoxins are usually produced by microalgae in the marine environment, although some Cyanobacteria spp. can occur in freshwater [1] . Microalgae are single-celled algae that can replicate extremely rapidly with sufficient light and nutrients. About 200 species of microalgae are known or suspected to have the potential to produce toxins harmful to aquatic organisms. Biotoxins have the potential to be harmful to all marine invertebrates, fish, reptiles, birds and mammals. Harmful algal blooms (HABs; excessive growth of algae) can result in production of a wide range of biotoxins [2, 3] . Toxins can occur on the sea surface, in the overall body of water, strictly on the sea floor or can accumulate in the environment (for example brevetoxin and microcystins). Biotoxins of significance to marine mammal health and the microalgae that are known to produce them, include: - brevetoxins (dinoflagellate; Karenia brevis, K.

example brevetoxin and microcystins). Biotoxins of significance to marine mammal health and the microalgae that are known to produce them, include: - brevetoxins (dinoflagellate; Karenia brevis, K. cristata, other Karenia spp.) - saxitoxins (dinoflagellates; Gymnodinium catenatum, Pyrodinium bahamense, and Alexandrium minutum) - okadaic acid (dinoflagellates; Prorocentrum and Dinophysis spp.) - domoic acid (diatoms of Pseudo-nitzschia spp.) - microcystins (Cyanobacteria spp. - bluegreen algae).

Wildlife and the environment: biotoxins can harm invertebrates, fish, reptiles, birds and mammals. Biotoxins have been associated with mass morbidity and mortality in numerous cetacean and pinniped species [3-6] and are a leading cause of wildlife mass mortalities globally [7] . Marine biotoxins can also have indirect effects on aquatic species due to resulting food scarcity. A massive HAB of Karenia cristata, K. mikimotoi and other Karenia spp. in South Australia (March 2025 to 2026) [8] caused widespread food shortage for wild Australian sea lions (Neophoca cinerea), with possible associated lactation issues and pup mortality. There were possible associations with deaths in other marine mammal species (whales, dolphins and pinnipeds) [see Murray et al. 2026 [8, (Supplementary Table 1)], but no conclusive evidence of harm in these species. Illness and deaths in western grey kangaroos (Macropus fuliginosus), were hypothesized to be linked to the HAB in SA, however post-mortem investigation did not find levels of brevetoxins sufficient to cause death [9] . The SA HAB caused catastrophic mortality in over 400 species of fish and marine invertebrates [10] .

post-mortem investigation did not find levels of brevetoxins sufficient to cause death [9] . The SA HAB caused catastrophic mortality in over 400 species of fish and marine invertebrates [10] . The global increase in HABs demonstrates one of the larger ecosystem consequences of climate change. See https://www.algalbloom.sa.gov.au/learn-about-algal-bloom for additional details of the HAB in SA. Humans and domestic animals: the biggest health risks for humans and pets is the consumption of seafood, including marine mammal organs and meat, containing toxins. Inhalation of aerosolized toxin on beaches, or drinking water containing biotoxins, may also be a health risk [11, 12] . Advice for both people and pets regarding the harmful algal bloom in SA is available at [https://pir.sa.gov.au/sardi/aquatic-sciences/marine-ecosystems/algal-bloom?shorturl\_algal-bloom.](https://pir.sa.gov.au/sardi/aquatic-sciences/marine-ecosystems/algal-bloom?shorturl_algal-bloom)

Biotoxins have the potential to be harmful to all marine invertebrates, fish, reptiles, birds and mammals. Host species susceptibility to biotoxins is expected to be similar between marine mammal species although the tolerable daily toxin intake varies between different toxins [12] . Variation in the incidence of marine mammal toxicity events is believed to relate to exposure, which is influenced by host distribution and foraging patterns [13] . The first recorded marine mammal death from HAB exposure was in humpback whales (Megaptera novaeanliae) from saxitoxin in 1982 [14] .

Microalgae are ubiquitous in the marine environment but the distribution of individual species (including those known to potentially produce biotoxins) is influenced by factors including sea temperature, nutrient availability, salinity, currents and anthropogenic influences. Mass mortality events of aquatic animals due to biotoxins have been recognised worldwide. However, investigations of marine mammal disease and mortality events have only recently included analysis for biotoxins. Most reports of biotoxicity in marine mammals are from the Northern Hemisphere. In Peru, biotoxicity was suspected in a mass mortality of over 800 common dolphins (Delphinus capensis) and evidence of exposure to saxitoxins, okadaic acid and domoic acid was found in Peruvian fur seals (A. australis ssp.) and South American sea lions (Otaria byronia) [15] . Domoic acid toxicity causes acute, subacute and chronic, often fatal, disease in sea otters (Enhydra lutris nereis) on the North American Pacific coast [16] . A mass mortality of bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) and Florida manatees (Trichechus manatus latirostris) was associated with aK. brevis bloom in Florida in 2007-2008 [17] .

There is currently no definitive evidence of direct toxic effects of biotoxins in Australian marine mammals. Okadaic acid, domoic acid and microcystin-producing marine microalgae are known to be present in Australian waters [18-20] . It is thought that domoic acid toxicity may contribute to cetacean mass stranding events in Tas waters [21, 22] , presumed to be due to neurological impacts on the hippocampus region of the brain involved in spatial memory.

There is limited information on whether biotoxins are a cause of morbidity and mortality in Australian marine mammals. Marine mammals may act as sentinel species for biotoxins of human health concern. Fluctuations in the incidence of marine mammals affected by biotoxins can indicate changes in marine ecosystem relationships and can be used as a measure of ecosystem health. Broadwater et al. 2018 [3] provides a comprehensive global review of this topic. Marine biotoxins mainly exert their toxic effects through ingestion but some toxins can have effects through inhalation [11] , as observed with the 2025-6 Karenia bloom in SA. Marine mammals are typically exposed to harmful concentrations of toxic algae when environmental conditions favour `blooming' and the algal species dominate the food web. This appears to be occurring more frequently with climate change. Environmental factors and different foraging strategies influence the risk of exposure of marine mammals to biotoxins [13] . The SA HAB was a prolonged event, sustained by unusually persistent environmental and climatic factors: a prolonged marine heatwave, continuous nutrient influx and ocean upwelling [23] .

[13] . The SA HAB was a prolonged event, sustained by unusually persistent environmental and climatic factors: a prolonged marine heatwave, continuous nutrient influx and ocean upwelling [23] . Prey species may consume or accumulate toxic algae in a variety of ways, and algal toxins may be retained in the prey's internal organs. Some toxins are fat-soluble (such as brevetoxin) and others water-soluble (such as domoic acid) in the host's body. Toxic algal cells may be directly ingested from the water column and algal toxins released into the water may be concentrated by filter feeders such as mussels, oysters, other shellfish and small filter-feeding fish species such as anchovies. Marine mammals may ingest toxic algae from contaminated fish or marine invertebrates, or toxic algae may be ingested along with marine plants, by herbivorous marine mammals. Biotoxins can may be transformed by the prey into compounds of increased toxicity, which are then consumed when they are predated by animals at higher levels in the food chain [2] .

Table 1 shows the most common signs and pathology associated with biotoxins in marine mammals. Sub-lethal effects of HAB exposure in marine mammals may not cause immediately obvious clinical signs [3] . Chronic low-level exposure to biotoxins can influence cognition (domoic acid) and immune function (saxitoxin) [24] . Investigations of stranding events and ill-health in marine mammals should include consideration of biotoxin analysis in all instances as part of routine surveillance. See McClain et al. 2023 [25] for full details | Hippocampal vacuolation, neuronal necrosis, ophthalmitis, myocardial necrosis, placental necrosis, foetal brain oedema Eosinophilia | Silvagni et al. 2005 [26], Ramsdell and Zabka 2008 [27]; Nash et al. 2017 [21], McClain et al.

For most HAB there is insufficient data to reliably diagnose HAB-related illness in marine mammals. Presumptive diagnosis therefore requires a "weight of evidence" approach. This includes demonstration of biotoxins in gastric and intestinal contents and/or tissues at concentrations known to be significant (may be extrapolated from other mammal species), along with evidence of the algal bloom in the water body and food chain. A negative result for toxin in a body fluid sample does not rule out HAB toxicity [25] . However, for some conditions such as domoic acid there are extensive descriptions of clinical signs and diagnostics - see McClain et al. 2023 [25].

- gastric and intestinal contents (frozen) - urine, 1-2ml (frozen) - aqueous humour, 1-2ml (frozen) - foetal fluid, 1-2ml (frozen) - whole blood on FTA paper, air-dried 24-48 hrs and then frozen and/or separated serum (frozen) - tissue samples (liver, brain, lung, kidney, heart, muscle, blubber) >5g frozen and most representative organs in 10% buffered formalin Freezing at -20℃ is suitable for short-term storage of samples but long-term storage requires -80℃ as the toxins degrade easily. Samples can be analysed by mass spectrometry coupled with liquid chromatography, ELISA, radioimmune toxin assays and histopathology.

Differential diagnoses will depend on the presenting signs and number of animals affected. Causes of sudden death in large numbers of marine mammals include acute viral (morbilliviruses, influenza viruses) and bacterial (Campylobacter spp.) infections. Individual cases can easily be confused with a variety of other diseases including Toxoplasma gondii [30] .

Investigations into marine mammal mortality events, including cetacean strandings, should include the collection of samples suitable for biotoxin detection and sampling should be standardized across states and jurisdictions. The indirect and chronic effects of lesser known biotoxins and emerging biotoxins such as K. mikimotoi should also be studied.

Carcasses from fisheries bycatch, strandings, shark control programs and other sources of mortalities should be routinely sampled to establish baseline surveillance data due to the difficulty and limitations of detecting toxin in live animals. - Marine mammals are prone to accumulating environmental pollutants due to their longevity and diet, making them excellent sentinels of ocean health. - A wide range of diseases and clinical signs can result from exposure to environmental pollutants in marine mammals. - Most pollutants of concern are persistent organic compounds or heavy metals, originating from human activities. - Pollutants can act synergistically with other pathologies such as infectious organisms to cause disease.

Globally, a very large number of substances capable of polluting the oceans are produced by humans. These can be divided into chemical compounds, often referred to as persistent organic pollutants (POP), and heavy metals. The term "contaminants of emerging concern" (CEC) is often more appropriate and includes pharmaceutical drugs, agricultural residues, nanomaterials (microscopic materials with one external dimension <100nm in size, often bound with a metal or a carbon), personal health care products and plastics including plastic additives [1] . While plastics and microplastics are of great concern in ocean pollution, they are outside the scope of this Fact Sheet. Only a few classes of chemical compounds have been studied in marine mammals, usually those associated with serious health effects in humans or other terrestrial species. The organohalogens (OH - organic compounds bound to either chlorine, bromine, fluorine, or iodine) include organochlorine (OC) compounds, which are of particular importance due to their toxicity and persistence. Organochlorines include dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) and its metabolites and the polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).

which are of particular importance due to their toxicity and persistence. Organochlorines include dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) and its metabolites and the polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs). Some of these compounds, such as the polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDE), are included as flame retardants in many manufacturing processes. Many chemical pollutants that have recently been identified as problematic, such as poly-andperfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), causing outright toxicity, endocrine disruption, and immunosuppression. Some of these are still poorly understood. Metal pollutants are either non-essential for the normal functioning of the body or essential but ingested in excessive amounts, with mercury, lead and cadmium the most important [2, 3] .

Wildlife and the environment: marine mammals are key sentinels of ocean pollution because most contaminants are obtained via the diet and many marine mammal species are apex predators and bio-accumulators of contaminants [4] . Scavengers consuming dead marine mammals might be exposed to high levels of toxins, particularly if consuming liver, kidney, and blubber. There is significant risk for aquatic organisms that feed on dead marine mammals at sea, especially large whales that form entire ecosystems around their demise as lifelong bioaccumulation of toxins is rapidly and readily available at these feeding hotspots [5] . A range of diseases have been described in marine mammals as a result of exposure to pollutants and evidence indicates environmental pollutants/toxicants may have population level impacts in Australian marine mammals [6-8] . Domestic animals: at present there is no evidence for risk to domestic animals following pollutant exposure in marine mammals. However domestic animals themselves may be exposed to harmful pollutants via environmental exposure as contaminants move across different environmental compartments [4] .

exposure in marine mammals. However domestic animals themselves may be exposed to harmful pollutants via environmental exposure as contaminants move across different environmental compartments [4] . Humans: the major risk for humans (other than exposure from environmental contamination) is through consumption of marine mammal products. The risk is lower when consuming herbivorous species such as dugongs (Dugong dugong), which are commonly harvested for consumption by Indigenous people in the far north of Australia [9] .

Marine mammals are key sentinels of ocean health due to their trophic level (the position of the animal in the food chain), their longevity, use of multiple habitats across a wide region of the oceans, the propensity of fatty tissues to accumulate harmful pollutants and the cumulative effects these pollutants have on them [4, 22] . Marine mammals are exposed simultaneously to multiple stressors of both natural and anthropogenic origin. The cumulative stress can combine with the toxic effects of pollutants to produce disease [1, 2] . These same factors together with large body surfaces that can increase exposure and occasionally low metabolic rates (e.g. dugongs and bowhead whales) predispose marine mammals to the effects of environmental pollutant [23] . POP, heavy metals and other non-essential metals bio-accumulate in the food web, with increasing concentrations at higher trophic levels (this includes many of the marine mammal species) [2] . The pollutant risk is dependent on the feeding strategy and the distribution of the host species. Dietary intake of pollutants will also vary with fluctuations in prey species, animal age, sex and physiological status (i.e.

on the feeding strategy and the distribution of the host species. Dietary intake of pollutants will also vary with fluctuations in prey species, animal age, sex and physiological status (i.e. lactating vs non-lactating), as these all influence feeding behaviour [2] . Herbivorous dugongs, despite their size, longevity and large amounts of body fat have much lower POP concentrations [20] compared to apex predators such as dolphins [7] . Strictly inshore species, especially those exposed to terrestrial run-off, often demonstrate higher levels of POP, as shown in Australian humpback and snubfin dolphins [10] and inshore dolphin species [18] . The distribution of pollutants within the body varies with both pollutant and tissue type. Organohalogens accumulate in the highest concentrations in the body's fat stores. Distribution of metal pollutants in tissues varies but they tend to accumulate in the liver and kidney (and for some compounds also bone) [2, 3] . There are large geographic, species and temporal gaps in our knowledge of Australian marine mammal environmental toxicology.

in the liver and kidney (and for some compounds also bone) [2, 3] . There are large geographic, species and temporal gaps in our knowledge of Australian marine mammal environmental toxicology. Most samples are opportunistically obtained from strandings and bycatch with a lack of targeted live animal surveillance [24] . The sub-lethal effects are mostly unstudied and it is often difficult to prove the link between exposure and effects. For those Australian species that have been subject to toxicological assessments, sampling has largely occurred over a limited part of their distribution and only as opportunistic cross-sectional studies. There is limited data for OHs in Australian marine mammals [10] . Historically, concentrations of some pollutants were lower in Southern Hemisphere marine mammals compared to those in the Northern Hemisphere, with considerable variations between species and geographical areas [25] . More recent information suggests that POP levels in dolphins in SA are increasing over time [26] . Metals are introduced into the environment by both natural (e.g. weathering of volcanic soils) and anthropogenic means, such as run-off from industry.

dolphins in SA are increasing over time [26] . Metals are introduced into the environment by both natural (e.g. weathering of volcanic soils) and anthropogenic means, such as run-off from industry. Trophic transfer varies between species. Australian marine mammals have levels of mercury reflecting ingestion from both natural and anthropogenic sources and levels may be influenced by an individual's proximity to urbanised and industrial run-off [27] . Most animals are exposed through ingestion via their food source. In rare instances pollutants are absorbed through the skin and mucosal membranes (e.g. byproducts of oil spills) [3] .

A wide range of clinical effects including alopecia [28] , immunosuppression [29, 30] , reproductive failure [31] , endocrine disruption [3] and neoplasia [2] have been associated with environmental pollutant accumulation and exposure in marine mammals. The immunosuppressive effects of OCs may make individuals more susceptible to opportunistic infections [29, 32-34] . Endocrine disruption, reproductive failure and bone lesions associated with OCs have been reported in marine mammals [6, 15, 30, 35, 36] . Thyroid hypoplasia in aborted Australian fur seal (Arctocephalus pusillus doriferus) foetuses was suspected to originate from endocrine disrupting toxicants [37] . Australian fur seal pups have high PFAS levels that could possibly cause immunosuppression and endocrine disruption [38] . A symmetrical alopecic syndrome in Australian fur seals may be associated with higher levels of heavy metals and POP [28] , as well as with lower overall body condition scores [39] . The effect of excessive mercury tissue concentrations is the most commonly reported metal toxicity in marine mammals. Studies suggest mercury can cause immunosuppression by impairing lymphocyte function [40] .

The types of pathology caused by environmental toxicants is extremely varied. It is beyond the scope of this document to cover all the various possible pathologies but they can cause liver disease, kidney disease, immunosuppression, reproductive disorders, neurological disease and disrupt the endocrine system [3] . As an example, bottlenose dolphins from SA waters had renal damage and bone malformations associated with chronic exposure to metal pollutants [41] .

The overall health of the host should be evaluated as toxicants often cause co-morbidities or predispose to other pathological conditions [2] . Physiological status should be taken into account when interpreting toxin accumulation in tissues, because some lesions may be toxin-induced or naturally acquired. For example, pulmonary and renal fibrosis occurs naturally in geriatric bowhead whales (Balaena mysticetus) but can be clinically significant in younger animals exposed to cadmium toxicity [42, 43] . In cases of suspect metal toxicity it is important to examine selenium status as this element has a protective effect against heavy metals such as mercury [3] .

- Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS): OHs - Atomic absorption spectrophotometer: metals - Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS): metals - Histopathology - Biomarkers: determine exposure through gene activation, stress markers, genetic erosion. Whenever possible, always record the mass and the length of the animal. More detailed sampling guidance is available in https://www.dcceew.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/cetaceanprotocols.pdf.

For adequate baseline information on the pollutant challenge faced by Australian marine mammals, surveillance activities need to be greatly expanded and repeated more frequently. Sampling and testing for known pollutants and CECs should be performed on all marine mammal deaths [2] . The longevity of most marine mammals allows for significant deductions to be made from the negative effects seen in marine mammals to potential effects in humans and domestic animals. Due to the omnipresent ecological nature of pollutants, understanding their effects in one of the largest groups of marine apex predators will allow us to understand pollutant effects in entire ecosystems.

Wildlife Health Australia administers Australia's general wildlife health surveillance system, in partnership with government and non-government agencies. Wildlife health data is collected into a national database, the electronic Wildlife Health Information System (eWHIS). Information is reported by a variety of sources including government agencies, zoo-based wildlife hospitals, sentinel veterinary clinics, universities, wildlife rehabilitators, and a range of other organisations and individuals. Targeted surveillance data is also collected by WHA. See the WHA website for more information https://wildlifehealthaustralia.com.au/Our-Work/Surveillance and https://wildlifehealthaustralia.com.au/Our-Work/Surveillance/eWHIS-Wildlife-Health-InformationSystem. We are interested in hearing from anyone with information on these conditions in Australia, including laboratory reports, historical datasets or survey results that could be added to the National Wildlife Health Information System. If you can help, please contact us at admin@wildlifehealthaustralia.com.au.

- Morbilliviruses have caused worldwide unusual mortality events (UME) in both cetaceans (whales and dolphins) and phocids (true seals) since first being documented in the 1980's. - They have caused deaths of cetaceans in Australian waters, in Queensland, South Australia and Western Australia. - The typical clinical signs are respiratory and neurological. - Morbillivirus should be a differential diagnosis in any UME or mass stranding of cetaceans in Australian waters. - Morbilliviruses do not seem to cause obvious clinical disease in fur seals and sea lions (otariids).

Three morbilliviruses have been identified as causing disease in marine mammals - cetacean morbillivirus (CeMV), phocine distemper virus (PDV) and canine distemper virus (CDV), all belonging to the genus Morbillivirus in the Paramyxoviridae family [1] . CeMV has six known strains. Four of these have been identified in the northern hemisphere and are all grouped together as CeMV-1. This includes porpoise morbillivirus (PMV), dolphin morbillivirus (DMV), pilot whale morbillivirus (PWMV), and beaked whale morbillivirus (BWMV). Those in the southern hemisphere are grouped as CeMV-2 [2-5] . Recent molecular work has indicated that CeMV is more closely related to ruminant morbillivirus (i.e. rinderpest) and human measles than to CDV and PDV [5] . It is currently thought that PDV had its origins in CDV due to close structural genetic similarities, with a hypothesized original spillover from dogs [6] .

Wildlife and the environment: species of cetaceans in Australian waters are considered susceptible to morbilliviruses. The population level impacts of these viruses on Australian cetaceans are not known [5, 7] . The susceptibility of Australian otariids is unknown, but disease has been reported only once in a captive otariid, a California sea lion (Zalopthus californianus) and not in wild populations of otariids [8] . Domestic animals: there is no evidence of domestic animals acquiring morbillivirus infection from marine mammals but it has been shown that CeMV has the ability to cross species barriers and is closely related to morbilliviruses of ruminants [9] . Humans: there is no evidence that marine mammal morbilliviruses pose a zoonotic risk [1] .

Both CeMV and PDV exposure has been reported globally in many marine mammal species. Species that are thought to be less susceptible, that may act as reservoir hosts include pilot whales (Globicpehala spp.), Fraser's dolphins (Lagenodelphis hosei), melon-headed whales (Peponocephala electra), dusky dolphins (Lagenorhynchus obscurus), gray seals (Halichoerus grypus), hooded seals (Cistophora cristata), and harp seals (Pagophilus groenlandicus) [1, 5, 7, 10] . Pilot whales are thought to be particularly important as potential reservoirs of CeMV. They are a highly gregarious species with presumed low susceptibility to disease, which migrate between north America and the Mediterranean. They are often seen in the proximity of other cetaceans and in instances where immunity might be waning there is the potential that they may serve a vector for the transmission to other more susceptible species [5, 11] .

the proximity of other cetaceans and in instances where immunity might be waning there is the potential that they may serve a vector for the transmission to other more susceptible species [5, 11] . Cetaceans and phocids (true or earless seals) show varying susceptibility to morbilliviruses, depending on the host species, with harbor porpoises (Phocoena phocoena), striped dolphins (Stenella coeruleoalba), Caspian seals, and North Atlantic harbor seals (Phoca vitulina vitulina) having experienced epidemics with associated unusual mortalities [5, 7, 10] . It is believed that CDV (both from domestic canids and other terrestrial carnivores) has a considerable spillover risk to naïve phocid species and may result in UME such as that seen in Caspian seals [6, 10] . Evidence suggests that otariids are not susceptible to disease, although some may develop antibodies to infection [1] .

Most data for CeMV, PDV and CDV in marine mammals originate from the northern hemisphere where most UME in both cetaceans and phocids have been reported [5, 7] . UME caused by CeMV have been recorded in multiple regions of the world including Europe, North America, Australia, and Brazil [3, 5] . There is serological evidence that since the first documented cases of UME in both phocids and cetaceans in the 1980's, morbilliviruses are now present in both polar regions [5, 6, 10] . Two southern hemisphere species of otariids, New Zealand sea lions (Phocarctos hookeri) and New Zealand fur seal (Arctocephalus forsteri) have shown serological evidence of exposure to morbilliviruses [12] .

Marine morbilliviruses have been reported from clinical cases in cetaceans in Australian waters but not from pinnipeds. CeMV has been determined as the cause of death in Australian inshore bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncates - Qld & SA) [13, 14] , in stranded coastal Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins (T. aduncus - WA & SA) [4, 14] and short-beaked common dolphin (Delphinus delphis - SA) [14] . Serological evidence for the presence of CeMV is more widespread with positive titers detected in wild melon-headed whale (Peponocephala electra - Qld & NSW), inshore bottle-nose dolphin (Qld), coastal Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin (Qld & NSW), Fraser's dolphin (Lagenodelphis hosei - Qld), humpback whale (Megaptera novaengliae - NSW & WA), pygmy killer whale (Feresa attentuata - NSW), Bryde's whale (Balaenoptera edeni - NSW). It has also been detected in captive inshore and coastal Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins [11, 14] . A large survey of Australian fur seals (Arctocephalus pusillus doriferus), the most abundant and widespread otariid in Australian waters, did not detect any serological evidence for exposure to morbilliviruses [15] .

It is assumed that the main route of transmission is horizontal through aerosolized virus, facilitated by the gregarious nature of certain cetaceans with synchronized surface breathing and the tightly packed terrestrial habits of phocids at haul-out sites during breeding and molting. Occasionally, vertical transmission is possible (through the fetal-placental unit and lactation) [1, 5] . The duration of active viral shedding is unknown in most species, but bottlenose dolphins can be infectious for up to 24 days [17] . This study was based on statistical modelling. One of the main conclusions was that spread might be contact-dependent rather than density-dependent, with juvenile animals (in which maternal immunity is often waning) having proportionately more contacts. Morbilliviruses are highly contagious and naïve populations often experience UME. Mortalities in phocids are well documented with mortality rates of 60% and more than 95% of the population becoming infected [18] . In some more resistant species and in populations with waning immunity, lowgrade and chronic infections may create conditions that allow for endemic circulation of virus (e.g.

infected [18] . In some more resistant species and in populations with waning immunity, lowgrade and chronic infections may create conditions that allow for endemic circulation of virus (e.g. pilot whales and gray seals) [1, 10, 19] . Morbilliviruses often cause severe immunosuppression in infected hosts [5, 7] . UME are often multifactorial and are often associated with multiple contributing factors such as elevated water temperature, diatom bloom, coinfections with other pathogens and significant fish dieoff [14, 20] .

It is more common to see clinical signs in phocids than in cetaceans due to their ability to haul-out into terrestrial habitats, whereas cetaceans are often presented stranded dead or moribund. Non-specific clinical signs in phocids include respiratory signs such as diving deficits (due to pneumonia or emphysema), coughing and difficulty breathing. Additionally, phocids may present with serous to mucopurulent ocular and nasal discharges, depression, lethargy, fever and hyperkeratotic dermatitis [7] . Neurological signs in phocids are similar to canids with CDV and include tremors, convulsions and seizures [21] . Neurological signs such as tremors have been observed in dolphins when seen alive [5] . Cetaceans often present in a compromised nutritional state with poor fat reserves [1] . Secondary infection with a wide range of pathogens (i.e. Toxoplasma gondii, poxvirus, herpesvirus, fungi and various bacteria) as a result of morbillivirus-induced immunosuppression is common in both cetaceans and phocids, often associated with high ectoparasite burdens and excessive epibionts such as barnacle Xenobalanus globicipitis [1, 4, 21, 22] .

immunosuppression is common in both cetaceans and phocids, often associated with high ectoparasite burdens and excessive epibionts such as barnacle Xenobalanus globicipitis [1, 4, 21, 22] . Mucosal ulcers have been reported in both cetaceans and phocids [11, 21] . Abortion has been recorded in morbillivirus-infected female cetaceans and phocids [1] .

It is generally assumed that a confirmatory diagnosis should be made by more than one diagnostic modality including histopathology, immunohistochemistry and molecular detection of the virus in at least two tissue types [23] . A presumptive diagnosis of morbillivirus infection can be made on a combination of gross and histopathological lesions. Confirmation of diagnosis is through immunohistochemistry or molecular techniques such as reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). A definitive diagnosis requires virus isolation and sequencing of the respective viral agent [1, 5, 7] . Serology is not suitable for diagnosing clinical cases but can be extremely helpful for studying the epidemiology of marine morbilliviruses. Serology allows for the detection of potential naïve hosts and potential chronically infected reservoir hosts [5, 7] . The most common serological test is the serum neutralization test (SNT), with cross reactivity between antibodies, especially to PDV and CDV [24] . Some cross-reactivity is translatable in CeMV, allowing the use of domestic animal morbillivirus serology as a diagnostic tool in cetaceans [1, 5, 10] .

Histology: tissue samples of lung, brain, kidney, lymph node, liver, spleen and any suspicious lesions are stored in 10% buffered formalin. Molecular: ideal samples would include lung, brain, liver, kidney, spleen and lymph nodes that can be analyzed with RT-PCR [23] . Ideally these samples should be stored in an RNA-specific preservative such RNAlater™ (Invitrogen) or RNAshield™ (Zymo). Alternatively, they can be frozen immediately after collection. Virus isolation: ideally fresh, uncontaminated samples collected individually from each of the following organs: brain, lung, liver, kidney, spleen, lymph node stored immediately on ice [1] . This can be very challenging in stranded carcasses undergoing decomposition [5] . Serology: aspirate 10 - 20ml of blood either from the heart or from a large blood vessel and store this in plain (serum) tubes. Can be frozen for extended storage. [More information on sampling can be found in www.environment.gov.au/resource/standardisedprotocols-collection-biological-samples-stranded-cetacean.](http://www.environment.gov.au/resource/standardised-protocols-collection-biological-samples-stranded-cetacean)

Typical lesions in both cetaceans and phocids include interstitial bronchopneumonia, encephalitis, lymphoid depletion, syncytia and secondary infections [5, 7, 25] . Changes include non-suppurative meningoencephalitis, intranuclear inclusion bodies and mononuclear perivascular cuffing [23] . Secondary infections are more common in sub-acute and chronic cases with predominantly bacterial and mycotic organisms. Pneumonia in phocids often produces severe tracking emphysema of the thorax and neck, from an extension of interstitial pneumonia, which may significantly impair their ability to dive [1] .

There is no effective treatment for either cetaceans and pinnipeds, with only supportive treatment being recommended [1] . Overseas, vaccination has been used to protect critically endangered Hawaiian monk seals (Neomonachus schauinslandi) and highly susceptible Harbor seals (Phoca vitulina) [24, 26] . Inactivated or canarypox vectored modified CDV are required to be given as a primary and booster vaccination [24] . These vaccines are not available in Australia, with only an inactivated three in one vaccine containing CDV available in Australia. In small populations of pinnipeds, quarantining of affected animals in combination with prophylactic vaccination programs has been recommended [26] . There are few vaccination trial data in cetaceans but there are promising results in captive Atlantic bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncates) [27] . In captive populations or wild animals in rehabilitation, strict biosecurity practices need to be applied.

Research is required into the epidemiology of marine morbilliviruses both in Australia and other regions of the world. Data from the southern hemisphere are sparse. Identifying potential reservoir species and understanding which populations are naïve are essential to modelling potential future UME. Additional vaccination studies are required under captive controlled conditions, which could then be extrapolated to at risk populations in the wild, especially with inactivated vaccines currently available in Australia. Disease risk assessments are recommended for marine mammals in Australian waters, as there is currently a void in modelling and predicting future risks in the region. CDV is uncommon in domestic Australian dogs and pet ferrets [28] , but surveillance in foxes and dingos is needed. Sero-surveillance of both otariids and cetaceans is required, both locally and in the sub-Antarctic.

There are over 30 events involving cetaceans in which detection of morbillivirus is reported in the National Wildlife Health Information System database (eWHIS).
